#6422. Einstein’s Equations Reveal an Unusual New Way Space-Time Can Transfer Energy

Einstein’s equations suggest that gravity may be capable of a process resembling the one behind powerful solar explosions. In a new theoretical study, physicists show how gravitational field structures can change their connections and transfer energy into matter. They call this process “gravitational reconnection.”

Luca Comisso of Columbia University and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile describe the discovery in Physical Review D. Their work reveals a mathematical connection between gravity and the behavior of plasmas, electrically charged gases found in stars and throughout space.

In plasmas, magnetic field lines can become stretched and twisted until they rearrange through a process called “magnetic reconnection.” This releases stored magnetic energy and drives powerful events such as solar flares.

“Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration,” Comisso said. “When they break and reconnect, they release energy.” He added, “It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events.”

Gravity operates differently because Einstein’s theory describes space-time as a four-dimensional structure rather than three-dimensional space.

“Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field ‘sheets’ rather than field lines,” explained Comisso. “Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a ‘sheet.’”

These sheets are mathematical structures, not physical surfaces. The researchers found that when the conditions preserving their connections break down, the sheets can reconnect, allowing energy to transfer from the gravitational field into matter.

The researchers uncovered this behavior by expressing Einstein’s equations using different mathematical variables, revealing similarities with equations that describe plasmas. Their study builds on earlier research with Maricarmen A. Winkler that identified previously unrecognized constraints on how space-time can evolve.

“Einstein’s equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent,” said Asenjo. “By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves.”

“Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them,” Comisso said. “You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior.”

One potential application involves merging black holes, where extreme gravity severely distorts space-time. Scientists rely on powerful computer simulations to predict the gravitational waves produced by these collisions, which detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) are designed to measure.

The newly identified constraints could help researchers determine how gravitational fields must behave without calculating every detail of their evolution.

“It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time,” Comisso said. “Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints.”

Gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical discovery. Researchers must now investigate whether it occurs in astrophysical environments, how much energy it could transfer, and whether it might produce detectable signatures in gravitational waves.

Reference: “Reconnection of gravitational fields” by Luca Comisso and Felipe A. Asenjo, 28 October 2026, Physical Review D. DOI: 10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

The research was supported by the National Science Foundation and NASA.

#6421. The 5 Best Gas Snowblowers Can Move Mountains (of Snow)

Too much snow to shovel? A snowblower offers the most power and the longest runtime.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter will be here before you know it, which means the best time to prepare for cold weather and potential snowstorms is now. While snowfall isn't as regular in many parts of the country as it used to be, storm systems can still dump big piles of snow at once. When it comes time to dig out, there are few tools as effective as a gas-powered snowblower.

Although electric snowblowers are certainly attractive—they are relatively lightweight, easy to use, and require little maintenance—they lack the raw power and long runtime you’ll need if a storm drops 18 inches of snow or more on your home, especially if you have a large driveway.

The best gas snowblowers can carve a path as wide as two feet—giving you plenty of room to walk through as much as 21 inches of snow on a single pass. And if you keep a spare tank handy, you should have more than enough runtime to clear your walks and driveway multiple times. If you’re in the market for a heavy-duty snow removal machine, we’ve researched and tested plenty. These are our top picks, plus a breakdown of everything you need to know to pick out the best gas snowblower for your home.

If you have a large driveway and get a lot of snow, this is the machine you want. This big Ariens has a 30-inch-wide clearing path and an ideal clearing depth of 18 inches. Its four-stroke gas engine means no fussing with mixed fuel, and the push-button electric start means you don't have to exhaust yourself with a recoil starter.

This is a stout machine that is made for working. Test Editor Brad Ford runs a similar machine on his property, which is extra demanding because he has a gravel driveway. Thankfully, this machine can handle gravel surfaces thanks to its adjustable skid shoes, which allow extra clearance between the base of the auger and the driveway.

This machine is not for everybody; smaller properties will be well-served by the smaller picks below. But for those with the capacity for this kind of snowblower, this Ariens is a solid choice.

This model from Champion Power Equipment lists at $899, which is a good price point considering many two-stage snowblowers are more than $1,000. But it’s not short on features. This model gives you push-button electric start, a self-propelled drive system, remote chute control, and an LED headlight for clearing snow at night. After all, the snow doesn’t always stop falling during work hours.

It also handles fairly deep snowfall with a 24-inch width and a 20.5-inch height. To help keep the blades safe on uneven terrain, you can adjust the height to handle that, or clear areas like gravel paths. Another feature we really like is the ability to turn the wheels 180 degrees to help make tighter turns. Features like that can’t always be found at this price point, which is why it’s our pick for a snowblower that packs a lot of value.

A medium-sized property that only gets a moderate amount of guaranteed snowfall each year doesn’t need a two-stage snowblower. A single-stage model is fully capable of clearing your driveway and sidewalks. This model from Toro has plenty of power to get that job done, with a 212-cc engine that should cut through even wet snow and throw it up to 40 feet away. This model is also self-propelled to help you do the pushing.

Some of the features we like on it are a trigger and slide that can change the direction of the discharge chute from the handle and a push-button electric start—both make operating it a little bit easier.

Like most single-stage snowblowers, its intake is lower than a two-stage, so you can only expect to clear snowfall up to 9 inches. If you commonly get much higher than that, you’ll want a more robust snowblower, but if you only have a few moderate snow events each winter, this Toro will get the job done.

The Toro Snowmaster 824 QXE stands apart from other single-stage gas snowblowers because of its intuitive controls and powerful engine. With a 252-cc engine, it chews rapidly through snow, carving a 24-inch path through banks up to 18 inches high.

With a lighter, more compact frame and automatic steering, the 824 QXE is easier to maneuver than its dual-stage counterparts. And, unlike most single-stage snowblowers, the auger is slightly elevated, so you can use it on gravel surfaces without having to worry about sucking rocks into it.

This machine also brings lots of special features to make the clearing process easier. Not only is it self-propelled, but it features a “personal pace system” that automatically adjusts the snowblower’s speed to match your walking pace, so you don’t have to fumble with speed controls. If you're familiar with Toro's self-propelled lawn mowers, this system should be familiar.

The snowblower also has a push-button starter and joystick-operated chute control, which makes it easy to adjust your snow output on the fly. If you’re looking for a snowblower to clear up to 18 inches of snow from a small to medium-sized driveway, the SnowMaster 824 QXE is a worthy choice.

This snowblower from Murray is another great example of a two-stage snowblower from a respected company that doesn’t cost more than $1,000. It doesn’t have some of the extra features like our best value pick—namely, a headlight and a 180-degree wheel rotation—but it otherwise matches it in size and power.

It also has all the primary features you would want, including an adjustable chute that lets you aim the snow where you want, push-button electric start, an auger that can propel snow up to 40 feet away, and a self-propel drive with six forward speeds and two reverse speeds.

Something unique to the model, however, is a set of 15-inch snow-terrain tires that handle icy and rocky conditions better than others. Wheels are something other brands can skimp on, but Murray hasn’t done that here. If you have gravel paths or older sidewalks that present a challenge, this model is likely up to the task.

Gas snowblowers are the best tools for heavy-duty snow removal jobs at home. They’re effective against snowbanks piled up to two feet high, and can clear out larger areas, including wide driveways and walking paths. If you live somewhere that gets hit by many large snowstorms each season, and you’ve got a considerable-sized area to clear, then this is what you need.

Not everyone needs a gas snowblower, though. For homes with smaller needs, they may feel like more trouble than they’re worth. Gas-powered machines require more maintenance. Plus, they’re usually quite heavy, which makes them hard to use on tiered walkways with steps. If heavy snow is a rare occurrence, we’d recommend going with an electric snowblower instead, which will be more nimble and won’t produce any fumes.

Most gas snowblowers feature either a single-stage or two-stage mechanism, depending on how the snowblower collects, processes, and expels snow.

Also known as “snow throwers,” they use an auger to pull in snow, break it up, and throw the snow out through the chute in a single action.

These also use an auger to pull in snow, but then mash it up with a spinning impeller before spitting it out through the chute. Separating the snow-pulling and snow-crushing/throwing mechanisms allows the two-stage snowblowers to move snow more quickly and throw it a longer distance, which can be helpful when clearing larger driveways. These robust machines also work better on gravel, since their augers are slightly elevated and won’t draw rocks into the tines.

With an extra component that requires a more powerful engine to operate properly, two-stage snowblowers are generally larger, making them more difficult to maneuver around tight spaces. If you have a small walkway or gardens with uneven ground to avoid, operating one may feel unwieldy. As you might expect, they also cost more than their single-stage counterparts.

As with deciding between electric and gas snowblowers, consider the size of the area you normally clear before picking a single- or two-stage model. Single-stage snowblowers work well for clearing walking paths and the average-sized two- to four-car paved driveway. Dual-stage models are ideal for clearing deep snow from long paved or gravel driveways.

A snowblower’s clearing width and intake height determine how much snow it can move with each pass. The larger the snowblower’s intake, the more quickly you can get the job done.

Most single-stage gas-powered snowblowers have intakes that range from 22 to 24 inches wide, while two-stage snowblowers can have intakes that are up to 32 inches wide. The height of the snowblower’s intake, which is sometimes referred to as “clearing depth,” indicates the maximum snow depth it can handle. The intake height for a gas snowblower ranges from 18 to 21 inches.

Purchasing the snowblower with the widest, tallest intake may seem like a no-brainer, but keep in mind that there’s a correlation between intake dimensions and the overall size of the snowblower. The largest gas snowblowers will have a harder time maneuvering through tight turns. Ultimately, you should choose the smallest option that can effectively clear the paths you need and the amount of snow you expect to see.

A snowblower's job is to take snow in front of you and move it somewhere out of the way. With a more powerful snowblower, you can send the snow farther away. That’s crucial when you’re clearing out a large space, and you need to pile it up dozens of feet from you. Single-stage gas snowblowers can launch snow up to 40 feet, while two-stage snowblowers have a snow-throwing range of 50 feet or more.

Some gas snowblowers come equipped with a throttle on the dashboard that allows you to adjust the throwing distance by changing the speed of the impeller, allowing you to target a specific snow-piling plot.

Beyond the basics, many gas snowblowers have additional features that make them easier to use. Since they weigh hundreds of pounds, many are self-propelled, so you don’t have to push them forward. Most also have electric starters that eliminate the need to pull a starter cord. Some even have built-in power steering that automatically slows one wheel for easy turning.

Other quality-of-life features abound: You may find dashboard controls that allow you to change the chute direction and snowblower speed with one hand, LED headlights for late-night (or early morning) jobs, and handlebars that heat up to keep your hands nice and toasty as you work.

We selected the best gas snowblowers based on recommendations from the Popular Mechanics test team, as well as research and personal testing experience. Some of our picks were recommended by PM test editor Brad Ford, who has logged hours and hours testing snowblowers over the years. The final lineup includes a mix of single-stage gas-powered models for small to moderate driveways that can house four to six cars, and larger two-stage models that can clear snow from the longer and larger driveways you usually find on rural properties.

There are a few things you need to do to make sure your gas snowblower runs smoothly through the season:

First, check the oil level between each use and top off as needed. You should change the oil once a year, even if you didn’t use your snowblower all winter.

Change the spark plug at the beginning of each season to ensure it starts smoothly. A dirty spark plug can make it difficult to get your snowblower going, especially in extreme cold.

Lastly, small gas engines require plenty of airflow to run smoothly, so check the air filter once a season and replace it if it's dirty.

Snowblowers use unleaded gasoline—the same thing you put in your car—which begins to degrade after about 60 days. Running a snowblower with old fuel can clog the carburetor and make the engine hard to start, so you should never store your snowblower with fuel left in the tank.

Before putting your snowblower to bed for the season, either run the fuel tank dry or add fuel stabilizer, which keeps gasoline fresh for up to 24 months, to the tank. If you use fuel stabilizer, run the snowblower for a minute or two after adding it to the tank to circulate it through the engine.

A snowblower should be able to handle the lion’s share of your snow removal duties, but you should definitely keep a snow shovel around to clean up whatever the snowblower leaves behind. You may also want to save the gas and dig out with a shovel after a light, soft snowfall.

#6420. This Unusual Spider’s Genome Is Roughly 50% Larger Than a Human’s

Scientists have sequenced the unusually large genome of a trapdoor spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert, uncovering surprising features of its DNA.

A spider no bigger than a quarter has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome. Known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, this elusive trapdoor spider lives beneath California’s coastal dunes and carries 4.6 billion DNA base pairs. Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have now sequenced its genome, uncovering features that could help explain how spider DNA has evolved.

“At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it’s not the largest genome among the spiders, but it’s significant,” said Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology. The research, published in the Journal of Heredity, marks the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a species in this spider family.

The spider’s enormous genome is not packed with an unusually large number of genes. Instead, approximately 77% consists of repetitive DNA sequences, stretches of genetic material copied many times throughout the genome. Its DNA is organized into 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human body cells.

Another feature involves telomeres, protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional telomere repeat sequences found in many other animals, a difference that may help explain why their chromosomes evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

“It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life,” Bond said.

A. stephencolberti lives in coastal sand dunes between the San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey, often sharing beaches with people who never realize the spiders are there. Females spend their entire lives inside underground burrows lined with silk and concealed beneath hinged, camouflaged doors. They detect vibrations from approaching prey and rapidly emerge to capture unsuspecting insects and other small animals.

Although these spiders use venom to subdue their prey, they are not dangerous to humans. According to Bond, among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

The genome sequencing is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative developing genetic resources to support wildlife conservation. Because trapdoor spiders rarely travel far from their burrows, populations can become genetically isolated when their habitats are separated. Examining their DNA could help scientists identify distinct populations that may need protection.

“We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us,” Bond said. “We’re hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.”

The spider’s limited coastal range makes it particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels threaten the dunes where it lives, while invasive species place additional pressure on its habitat. “They’re going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they’re also very sensitive to invasive species,” Bond said.

The species has an unusual connection to comedian Stephen Colbert. In 2008, after learning that Bond had named another trapdoor spider after musician Neil Young, Colbert demanded similar recognition. He made his case during the “Who’s Not Honoring Me Now?” segment of his former Comedy Central program, “The Colbert Report.”

Bond granted the request, naming the species Aptostichus stephencolberti (the “t” in Colbert is silent). The spider’s oversized genome now provides an unexpected scientific distinction for an animal named after a comedian known for playing an exaggerated, self-important television pundit.

Beyond conservation and evolutionary research, spider genomes may help scientists investigate venom compounds with potential medical or agricultural applications. Some molecules found in spider venoms are being studied for their possible use in pain relief, while others could offer new approaches to controlling agricultural pests.

The full range of these substances remains largely unexplored, and the newly sequenced genome could provide a foundation for further investigations.

“We don’t really know what’s out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms,” Bond said.

Reference: “Reference genome of the Californian trapdoor spider Aptostichus stephencolberti Bond 2008 (Araneae: Mygalomorphae: Euctenizidae)” by Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe, Oanh Nguyen, Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann, Merly Escalona, Robert D Cooper, H Bradley Shaffer, Erin Toffelmier and Jason E Bond, 8 September 2026, Journal of Heredity. DOI: 10.1093/jhered/esag069

This research was supported by the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California by the state of California, State Budget Act of 2019 and by the National Science Foundation.

#6417. Scientists Create a Tiny Electronic Device That Can Learn Like the Human Brain

A breakthrough in brain-inspired electronics could lead to devices that process information and learn without relying on conventional computing architectures.

A single nanoscale electronic component can perform three different jobs, switching electrical current, storing information through resistance, and remembering past electrical activity through changes in capacitance. Researchers in Germany have demonstrated this versatility using unusual oxide materials, opening a possible path toward computer hardware that processes information and adapts more like the human brain.

Today’s artificial intelligence systems can consume enormous amounts of electricity, particularly during the training of large models. One reason researchers are exploring alternative hardware is that conventional computers typically separate memory from computation, requiring information to move between them. The brain operates differently. Its neurons communicate through synapses, connections that can change in response to repeated or intense signals. This ability to adapt, known as neuroplasticity, helps the brain learn from experience.

A research team at the University of Würzburg, working within the Würzburg and Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, has developed electronic components that reproduce several important behaviors of neurons and synapses. Their approach uses complex oxides, materials whose electrical properties can be adjusted to support different functions within the same system.

The devices rely on two materials: lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO₃, or LAO for short) and strontium titanate (SrTiO₃, or STO for short). Both are electrical insulators individually, but when brought together, they form an extremely thin conductive layer at their interface. This layer, called a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas, allows electrons to move through a region confined to the boundary between the materials.

By carefully patterning the interface, researchers can create microscopic conductive pathways, sometimes described as “electron highways.” Electrical current can displace oxygen atoms within the structure, altering its resistance. These changes allow the device to be “trained” through electrical stimulation, providing a physical mechanism for storing information about previous activity.

Using this material platform, the Würzburg researchers created components that can act as a transistor, a memristor, or a memcapacitor. A transistor controls current flow, while a memristor stores information through changes in electrical resistance. A memcapacitor behaves differently: its ability to store electrical charge depends on its previous electrical state.

The researchers demonstrated that a single nanoscale component can provide any of these three functions depending on how it is connected electrically. This versatility could simplify the design of artificial neural networks built directly into electronic hardware.

“What makes our platform so exciting is that we can realize very different functions using the same material system. This brings us closer to hardware that not only computes but can also learn directly within the component and temporarily store information,” says Soumen Pradhan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Technical Physics in Würzburg.

“Brain-inspired computing” seeks to reproduce some of the brain’s information processing and learning mechanisms in electronic circuits. Rather than continually transferring data between separate processing and memory units, these systems aim to combine computation, information storage, and adaptation within individual components.

“Complex oxides are an especially exciting field for us because they combine many electronic properties in a single material platform. That is precisely what makes them so interesting for a new generation of energy-efficient and adaptable computer hardware,” says Ralph Claessen, spokesperson at JMU Würzburg for the Würzburg–Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat and a co-author of the study.

One potential application is health monitoring. Wearable devices incorporating this type of adaptive electronics might eventually analyze physiological signals directly, without requiring separate computing hardware for every processing task.

Such “self-learning” sensors could potentially track heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen saturation, or blood glucose while adapting their responses to incoming data. Processing signals locally could also reduce the energy required to transfer information to external systems.

For now, these possibilities remain long-term goals. The research demonstrates the underlying electronic functions rather than a complete artificial intelligence system or medical sensor. Further development will be needed to establish whether the technology can deliver practical improvements in energy consumption, reliability, and performance.

#6416. Scientists Finally Identify Mysterious Creature Nearly 90 Years After It Was First Found

A millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago in South Australia has finally been identified as a new species, challenging assumptions about where its moisture-loving relatives can survive. Named Colobothrix deckeri, the species belongs to the family Dalodesmidae, which typically inhabits damp environments. Yet its original collection site receives just 400 to 500 millimeters (15.7 to 19.7 inches) of annual rainfall, making it the first member of its family recorded from such a dry region of Australia.

The new species also possesses an unusual microscopic feature. Mature males in Dalodesmidae and certain other millipede families have tiny, ball-shaped structures on their legs called sphaerotrichomes, normally topped by a long, pointed bristle known as a seta. In C. deckeri, that bristle is reduced to a short, blunt rod. This distinctive anatomy inspired the new genus name Colobothrix, meaning “stunted hair.”

The discovery began with a specimen collected in 1936 on South Australia’s lower Yorke Peninsula. It remained unidentified in the South Australian Museum (SAMA) until 2015, when German researcher Peter Decker encountered it while examining borrowed museum specimens for his doctoral research on a different millipede family, Paradoxosomatidae.

Recognizing that the animal belonged to Dalodesmidae, Decker sent photographs of its microscopic features to Australian millipede specialist Robert Mesibov. The specimen provided the first evidence that this family occurred in dry South Australia. Mesibov searched the original collection area in 2016 and 2017, but neither expedition located another specimen. He later named the species in Decker’s honor, publishing the description in the peer-reviewed, open-access journal ZooKeys.

Unknown to the researchers at the time, additional specimens had already been collected about 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the original location. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were surveying spiders and leaf-litter invertebrates on Kangaroo Island when they discovered a remarkable new assassin spider species in the island’s relatively wet northwestern region. Their collections also included several unidentified millipedes, which were deposited in the Western Australian Museum (WAM).

The island’s devastating 2020 bushfires later destroyed the original collection site, raising fears that the rare assassin spider might be approaching extinction. During a follow-up survey in 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh found the spider at additional locations several kilometers (a few miles) away. Her collections of other invertebrates also contained specimens of the unidentified millipede.

In early 2026, Mesibov discovered the Western Australian Museum’s millipede record online and contacted curator Mark Harvey. Close-up photographs supplied by Harvey confirmed that the Kangaroo Island specimens belonged to the same species collected on the Yorke Peninsula in 1936.

Mesibov subsequently visited Kangaroo Island and successfully located living specimens near the earlier collection sites. “Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”

He collected several specimens for the formal species description and future genetic research. The specimens collected in 1936, 2021, and 2026 are now housed at the South Australian Museum.

Although C. deckeri has been confirmed on Kangaroo Island, researchers still do not know whether it survives at its original Yorke Peninsula location. That mainland site receives considerably less rainfall than the species’ known habitats in northwestern Kangaroo Island.

Mesibov suspects that the peninsula’s underlying limestone could provide a possible explanation for how the millipede survives in such a dry environment.

“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface. I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past. That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”

Reference: “Two new millipede genera and species from Kangaroo Island, South Australia (Polydesmida, Dalodesmidae, Spirostreptida, Cambalidae)” by Robert Mesibov, 23 October 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1295.214938

Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

An aerial view of the tomb where archaeologists found the shrine maiden statuette.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.

The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6413. Scientists Discover That a Giant Bird Thought Extinct for Thousands of Years Never Actually Disappeared

Ancient DNA analysis has challenged a 150-year-old belief about a giant bird thought to have disappeared after the last Ice Age.

For more than 150 years, scientists believed that enormous crane bones found in European caves belonged to a giant bird species that disappeared after the last Ice Age. Now, ancient DNA has overturned that identification, revealing that the supposedly extinct bird was actually a larger version of a species still living in Europe today.

Researchers at Bournemouth University (BU) found that the fossils attributed to Grus primigenia belonged to the common crane. Their findings also raise questions about whether other prehistoric birds classified as extinct species were simply larger forms of birds that survive today.

The mystery began in the 19th century when French biologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards examined unusually large crane bones discovered in caves in southern France. Believing they represented a distinct species, he named the bird Grus primigenia. The remains dated to the end of the last Ice Age and were long considered evidence of an extinct giant crane.

To investigate the bird’s identity, a team led by Dr. John Stewart, Professor of Evolutionary Paleoecology at BU, analyzed ancient DNA from 18 crane bones recovered across England, Wales, France, Germany, and the Balearic Islands. Working with the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden, the researchers used genetic evidence to determine which species the bones belonged to.

“Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart explained.

The genetic findings indicate that the oversized fossils belonged to common cranes rather than a separate extinct species. Stewart believes differences in body size between male and female cranes may have contributed to the original misidentification.

“We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes. We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females, and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species: the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species,” Stewart said.

Although the DNA evidence clarifies the birds’ identity, it leaves another question unanswered: Why were some prehistoric common cranes considerably larger than those living today?

“The challenge going forward is to investigate the reason for the cranes decrease in size. Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that,” Stewart said.

The researchers plan to investigate whether changes in wetland habitats and human land use contributed to the reduction in crane body size. These remain possible explanations rather than established causes.

The findings suggest that some prehistoric bird species identified primarily through fossil measurements may need to be reconsidered. Differences in bone size do not necessarily indicate separate species, and ancient DNA could help determine whether other supposedly extinct birds were actually larger or smaller populations of surviving species.

“While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past,” Stewart said.

“Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he concluded.

Reference: “Ancient DNA study resolves the taxonomic status of the extinct large Palaearctic crane Grus primigenia Milne-Edwards, 1871 (Aves: Gruiformes: Gruidae)” by John R. Stewart, Rebecca Rickard, Sheila Hamilton-Dyer, Keith Dobney, Veronique Laroulandie, Josep Antoni Alcover, Joan Femenias-Gual, Nadja Pöllath, Erik Ersmark, Bodil Cronholm, Per G. P. Ericson and Love Dalén, 1 October 2026, Royal Society Open Science. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260699

#6411. Human Bodies Are Producing Two Billion Tons of CO2 a Year

A new study reveals that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased dramatically over three decades.

The carbon dioxide produced by human bodies as they convert food into energy increased by 74% over three decades, according to a University of Bath-led study. By 2015, the global total had reached an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) annually, highlighting a substantial component of the Earth’s carbon cycle that scientists had not previously quantified on this scale.

Unlike emissions from burning fossil fuels, the CO2 humans exhale largely comes from carbon recently absorbed from the atmosphere by plants and transferred through food. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years, adding it to the active carbon cycle.

Published in The Lancet Planetary Health, the study found that annual CO2 production from human metabolism rose from 1.18 billion metric tons (1.30 billion U.S. tons) in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) in 2015. More than 60% of that increase was attributable to population growth rather than a substantial rise in the amount produced by each individual.

To estimate global emissions from metabolism, the researchers analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people ranging from infants to older adults. They combined these findings with worldwide population and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic activity changed over time.

Professor Javier Gonzalez, who led the research at the University of Bath’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, explained:

“We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven’t had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

“What we’ve found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.”

Human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment, particularly in densely populated cities. Accounting for that activity could help researchers develop more accurate carbon budgets and better assess the effects of strategies designed to reduce emissions.

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest people should exercise less, change their diets, or attempt to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out. The purpose is to improve scientific measurements of carbon movement, not identify respiration as a contributor to fossil fuel emissions.

Gonzalez stressed the distinction: “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

“What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs.”

Reference: “Accounting for global carbon dioxide production from human metabolism between 1985 and 2015: a modelling study” by Javier T Gonzalez, Lorenzo Lolli, Bruno Spellanzon, Greg Atkinson, Ed Maunder, Alfonso Moreno-Cabañas, Jariya Buniam, Dylan Thompson, James Betts, Philip N Ainslie, Heliodoro Alemán-Mateo, Linda Bandini, Ellen E Blaak, Carlijn V C Bouten, Pascal Bovet, Soren Brage, Regina Casper, Prasangi Dabare, Barry W Fudge, Melanie Gillingham, Annalies H Goris, Michael Gurven, Hinke Haisma, Marije B Hoos, Noorjehan Joonas, Peter Katzmarzyk, Misaka Kimura, Sai Krupa Das, Pulani Lanerolle, Christel L Larsson, Marie Löf, Aviva Must, Marian Neuhouser, Theresa A Nicklas, Robert M Ojiambo, Kirsi H Pietilainen, Susan B Racette, Eric Ravussin, Leanne M Redman, John J Reilly, Susan Roberts, Luis B Sardinha, Analiza M Silva, Srishti Sinha, Anders M Sjödin, Eric Stice, Samuel S Urlacher, Edgar A Van Mil, Jeanine A Verbunt, Jonathan C K Wells, Tsukasa Yoshida, Xueying Zhang, Alexia Murphy-Alford, Cornelia U Loechl, Amy Luke, Michele Novaes Ravelli, Herman Pontzer, Jennifer Rood, Hiroyuki Sagayama, Dale A Schoeller, Klaas R Westerterp, William W Wong, Yosuke Yamada and John Speakman, 26 October 2026, The Lancet Planetary Health. How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

A chart showing the evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today. The first stars started to appear from the hydrogen fog a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.

These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.

The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.

Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts. Nature Astronomy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02999-z

#6409. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

#6405. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”
