#6404. The 9 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

Our editor-tested and researched portable and whole-home options keep appliances and other essentials running during an emergency—no matter what.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

The generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Offering 22 kilowatts of power, this model from Generac is designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment. If your home is much larger than 2,500 square feet and you need more power, we also recommend Generac’s 26-kilowatt home standby generator as an alternative.

The other benefit to this bundle is that it comes with a transfer switch, which is a required piece of equipment if you’re planning on installing this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

While we have not reviewed this specific model, Generac is one of the leading companies in standby generators and offers a five-year warranty and 24/7 customer service.

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, they also make a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of their power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate start-up, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s important to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review

Battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12 kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Pulsar is a relatively new brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.)

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, plan on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

When you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

My generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6403. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

#6395. Humans ate insects for thousands of years, so why did we stop?

Ancient evidence reveals that humans have eaten insects for thousands of years, challenging Western attitudes about what belongs on the dinner plate.

For many people in Western countries, a cricket or beetle is about the last thing they’d want on their plate.

Ancient human feces preserved in dry caves contain the remains of crickets and beetles, revealing that people were eating insects back in the Stone Age.

A new review suggests that history and culture help explain this disgust. It isn’t a feeling everyone shares, argues Lisa-Marie Shillito, a professor of geoarchaeology and heritage science in Durham University’s Department of Archaeology.

Shillito didn’t report a new dig. She went through decades of research on ancient feces, pottery residues, and written records to ask why insects get so little attention in accounts of what people ate.

“We often hear about edible insects as a food of the future, but for many people they are already part of a long culinary heritage,” Shillito said.

Archaeologists call preserved human feces coprolites, and there’s plenty to learn from what they contain. A meal can leave behind bits of bone, plants, and insect shells.

In Oregon’s Paisley Caves, that record goes back about 12,800 to 10,850 years.

People there ate Jerusalem crickets and June beetles, along with rodents, other small animals, and plants, choosing different foods as the seasons changed.

Nevada’s Bonneville Estates Rockshelter has yielded more than 200 coprolites, several with evidence of a parasitic worm. Swallowing a cockroach or beetle carrying the worm can pass it to a person.

Later evidence comes from Antelope House in Arizona. There, people ate grasshoppers with squash and corn between about 1075 and 1140 AD.

One large tally gives a sense of how widespread insect eating was.

Presented at a 2024 meeting of the Society for American Archaeology, it brought together more than 9,000 human coprolites from 52 sites across the Americas.

The samples span the end of the last Ice Age through the period before European contact. About a third of the collections showed signs that people had eaten insects on purpose.

The patterns also differed by region. Those differences suggest that people gathered insects during predictable seasons.

At Crypt Cave in Nevada, archaeologists found around 1,000 Rocky Mountain locusts dating back about 14,000 years.

They interpreted the spot as a storage pit, suggesting someone had kept the insects for later.

A grinding stone from Cloggs Cave in Australia tells another part of the story. Tiny remains on its surface show that people cooked and ground Bogong moths about 2,000 years ago.

Shillito thinks people probably used wooden tools to gather insects, although archaeology’s focus on stone tools can make that equipment easy to miss. Chimpanzees using sticks to fish for termites offer a possible comparison.

Honey gathering left traces as well: chemicals in West African pottery put it at about 3,500 years ago.

Beeswax survives in Neolithic pots at least 8,000 years old, and, as Shillito points out, eating honey may sometimes have gone hand in hand with eating bee larvae.

Long after an insect has decayed, a stone tool, piece of pottery, or mammal bone may still be there. Those durable finds dominate archaeology, and researchers seldom test for insect remains.

That uneven record has helped put hunting ahead of gathering in accounts of early meals. An insect may turn up only to be classified as a clue to the environment, or a pest that got into someone’s stored food.

Consider Lakeside Cave in the Great Basin: researchers examined bones and plants from its sediments, but treated many grasshopper parts as contamination.

To Shillito, that decision may say something about the researchers’ own cultures and the foods they consider worth eating.

“I wanted to show how archaeology can challenge our assumptions about what counts as food – including our own assumptions as archaeologists,” Shillito said.

“If we don’t think of insects as food, we can overlook evidence that people ate them.”

There may be a missing insect meal in the Neanderthal story, too.

Researchers usually interpret the unusually high amounts of a heavy form of nitrogen in some Neanderthal remains as evidence of a diet rich in meat from large plant-eating animals.

But in 2025, a team studying fly larvae found that eating rotting meat can give the larvae very high amounts of that same nitrogen.

Eating those larvae often, the authors proposed, could explain the amounts found in Neanderthals.

Europeans haven’t always turned down insects. The ancient writer Athenaeus described cicadas served at banquets to stimulate the appetite.

Other writers left examples from Roman life: Pliny the Elder described a grub fattened on flour, while the satirist Martial mentioned locusts and ants eaten by poorer Romans. Clearly, insects weren’t reserved for rich diners.

What changed is less certain, though one idea traces the shift to medieval Europe, when insects became associated with disease and the range of acceptable foods shrank.

Later came Victorian campaigns for hygiene and colonial attitudes that cast insect eating as uncivilized.

European colonists arriving in North America in the 17th and 18th centuries already came from cultures where few people ate insects.

They wrote with disgust about Native foods, helping to spread racist views of Native people as savages.

For plenty of people in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, there’s nothing unusual about eating insects.

In Mexico, the tradition goes back to before European contact, with foods such as chapulines, a kind of grasshopper, and ahuahutle, made from the eggs of water insects.

Uganda has nsenene, the long-horned grasshoppers people eat there, while shoppers in Thailand can buy fried bamboo worms at street markets and supermarkets.

Even in Thailand, though, there are concerns about the habit fading as Western diets spread.

These foods can supply iron, zinc, and vitamin B12 as well as protein. In several species approved for food, protein makes up about 50% to 70% of their dry weight.

Raising insects can also take less land and release fewer greenhouse gases for the same amount of protein than many kinds of livestock farming. How much it saves comes down to the species, what farmers feed it, and how they raise it.

Vincent M. Holt raised a fair question back in 1885, in a book called Why Not Eat Insects? People ate eels, octopus, cuttlefish, and oysters, he pointed out, so why did insects provoke such disgust?

Businesses trying to sell insect foods in Western countries still have to deal with that reaction. Often, they make the insects less visible by mixing them into protein powders or other processed foods.

Shillito’s review looks instead at how food habits vary across cultures and change over time.

Take casu marzu, the Sardinian cheese associated with cheese fly larvae: it has a place in local food traditions, however strange it may seem to someone from elsewhere.

“Recognizing that history can help us think differently about what we might eat in the future,” Shillito said.

This review makes its case using other researchers’ work, rather than new measurements. The review’s biggest tally, more than 9,000 coprolites, comes from a conference talk rather than a published journal paper.

Then there’s the problem of what survives for anyone to find: insect remains last mainly in dry caves, waterlogged ground, preserved feces, and residues on pots and tools.

Their absence at a site doesn’t prove that the people there never ate insects.

Shillito expects more evidence to turn up as archaeologists look for it.

Chemical markers used in forensic science and soil science can identify insects, and researchers have already found insect-related compounds in coprolites at Paisley Caves.

Other teams have recovered ancient DNA from grain weevils in Roman and medieval deposits. Tiny insect pieces have also turned up in hardened plaque on ancient teeth.

Shillito argues that researchers need to collect and study plaque and coprolite samples in a consistent way. That would let them compare what they find at different sites.

The evidence suggests that insects have long been a familiar part of human diets. What changed was how certain cultures learned to see them.

The study is published in the journal World Archaeology.

#6391. Ancient sea monsters reveal a new pattern in Earth’s evolution

Ancient marine reptiles found in Colombia reveal a possible new pattern in Earth's evolution, where declining species coexisted with emerging groups.

About 120 million years ago, an ancient sea covering part of Colombia was home to enormous marine reptiles, some belonging to evolutionary lineages nearing extinction and others representing groups just beginning to thrive.

Now, scientists believe this remarkable collection of fossils may reveal a previously unrecognized pattern in Earth’s evolutionary history.

Rather than following a catastrophic mass extinction, the transition appears to have unfolded as older animal groups lived alongside emerging ones, potentially reshaping how scientists understand biodiversity change.

Dirley Cortés, of the Polish Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Paleobiology in Warsaw, reviewed decades of research with McGill University biology professor Hans Larsson.

The team’s review brings together studies of fossils, rocks and ancient climate from Colombia’s Paja Formation.

The researchers call this proposed pattern a “biotic inflection,” a period when declining evolutionary lineages coexist with emerging groups that later become more widespread.

The idea still needs testing, and Cortés developed the review during her PhD through a joint program at McGill and the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute.

The Paja Formation lies around Villa de Leyva, with its richest fossil beds dating back about 120 million years. At the time, Earth had no ice at either pole.

During the Cretaceous, global temperatures were more than 18°F (10°C) higher than today, and atmospheric carbon dioxide was about three times today’s level.

Sea level peaked about 820 feet (250 meters) above its present height.

As Pangaea broke apart, seawater flooded northwestern South America, placing the Colombian site near the middle of a passage between the eastern Pacific and the ancient Tethys Ocean, which stretched toward present-day Europe.

Models of continental movement suggest this passage became a broad, open channel in the Early Cretaceous, around the time the Paja animals lived.

Heavy erosion on land would have carried nutrients into coastal waters. Larsson described the combination as “a ‘perfect storm’ of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity.”

Some Paja animals belonged to groups that had largely vanished elsewhere. One was a teleosauroid, an armored relative of crocodiles that lived in the sea.

Scientists once thought these animals died out at the end of the Jurassic, and most known fossils come from Europe.

But the Colombian specimen comes from a well-dated layer about 120 million years old, making it the group’s first and only clear Cretaceous record.

At an estimated 31 feet (9.6 meters) long, it may also be the largest teleosauroid known. Cortés and Larsson suggest warm tropical seas offered a refuge after the animals disappeared farther north.

Pliosaurs, marine reptiles with short necks, tell a similar story. Most large Jurassic pliosaurs that hunted big prey died out, but one branch, the brachaucheniines, survived.

These survivors reached their largest sizes during the Cretaceous, with some exceeding 33 feet (10 meters).

The Paja rocks contain most known brachaucheniine species, including Sachicasaurus vitae, Stenorhynchosaurus munozi, and at least two new species.

Together, they represent a final burst of new species before the lineage disappeared.

Alongside them lived early elasmosaurs, long-necked plesiosaurs whose group began branching into more species soon after the Jurassic ended.

Paja contains two early elasmosaur species, although they look so similar that researchers disagree about whether they are separate species.

Either way, these early members of a growing group lived alongside the last brachaucheniine pliosaurs.

Sea turtles were getting started too. Desmatochelys padillai is the oldest known member of the extinct protostegid family, and its age led researchers to suggest that marine turtles first evolved in the American tropics.

Another turtle, Leyvachelys cipadi, is the oldest and most complete fossil from its family. Its body structure suggests it fed on hard-shelled animals near shore.

Researchers once gave some small turtle fossils a different name, but later identified them as hatchlings. Their presence suggests young turtles grew up in the shallows.

The formation also holds two of the earliest and most complete true crab species known from the Early Cretaceous. The oldest known frog crabs come from these rocks too.

A food chain starts with organisms such as plants and algae. Scientists call each feeding step above that base a trophic level.

In an earlier reconstruction of Paja’s food web, Cortés and Larsson placed giant pliosaurs such as Sachicasaurus above the levels occupied by modern orcas and sharks.

Their reconstruction suggests the ancient ecosystem supported an additional feeding level beyond those typically found in modern oceans, with giant pliosaurs occupying positions above today’s top marine predators.

Fish-shaped marine reptiles called ichthyosaurs also ate in different ways.

Kyhytysuka sachicarum had large, cone-shaped front teeth for catching prey and flattened, serrated teeth farther back for processing it, a combination unknown in any other Cretaceous ichthyosaur.

The smaller Muiscasaurus catheti may have eaten smaller or softer prey, while several new species still under study appear suited to catching fish.

The authors describe this as the first evidence anywhere that Cretaceous ichthyosaurs divided up food resources this way.

Farther down the food web, researchers have identified more than 100 ammonite species, shelled relatives of squid.

Most other invertebrates and fish from the formation remain poorly studied.

Life in this sea also faced disruptions. Rocks near Curití record at least one episode of severe oxygen loss, among several that affected oceans worldwide during the Cretaceous.

The authors suggest that recovery after these events could have created opportunities for new species.

Near Villa de Leyva, however, researchers still need chemical tests to confirm the low-oxygen conditions suggested by the rocks.

Cortés and Larsson considered whether Paja qualified as an ancient biodiversity hotspot.

Conservation scientists use that term for places with exceptional species diversity, many species found nowhere else, and threats from human activity.

Human damage does not apply to a sea from 120 million years ago, so the authors assessed the other features.

Paja scored strongly for species numbers and food-web complexity, and moderately for species found only there.

It scored weakly on whether the region supplied species to other places, something fossils rarely reveal clearly. The authors concluded that the evidence does not yet justify calling Paja an ancient hotspot.

The hotspot label also misses something the researchers see as central to Paja: change over millions of years. These rocks preserve old groups near their end alongside new groups near their beginning.

The authors point to a possible comparison during the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, a period of extreme warmth when early mammal groups gave way to modern ones.

If scientists knew that change only from one well-preserved site in the American West, they argue, it might look much like Paja.

“I think we’ve discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we’ll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth’s history and how we can quantify its impacts,” Larsson said.

The fossils of Colombia’s Paja Formation offer a rare glimpse of an ancient ocean undergoing extraordinary evolutionary change.

But scientists still need more precise fossil dates and comparisons with other ancient marine ecosystems to determine whether this transition was unique or part of a much larger pattern.

If the proposed biotic inflection holds up, it could reveal an overlooked way that life on Earth transforms, even without the catastrophic extinctions that have traditionally dominated its evolutionary history.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.

#6389. Scientists trace mysterious solar wind structures back to their origins

Solar Orbiter flew through a switchback in the solar wind, and the oxygen and carbon inside still carried the heat of their source.

The solar wind pours off the Sun in every direction, dragging the Sun’s magnetic field out with it. Now and then that field bends back on itself in a sharp, S-shaped kink called a switchback.

When a spacecraft flew straight through a big one, the particles inside still carried a chemical record of where they originated.

The chemical record points to hot magnetic loops, low in the Sun’s atmosphere.

It supports one of two competing ideas about where switchbacks come from, and it shows they can keep a signature of their source across tens of millions of miles.

The team’s evidence comes from one switchback that crossed the path of the European Space Agency‘s Solar Orbiter spacecraft in 2022.

Jesse Coburn of the Laboratoire de Physique des Plasmas in France, and the Mullard Space Science Laboratory at University College London, led the analysis.

Switchbacks show up often in the solar wind close to the Sun, and NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has found them more common the nearer it gets. How they form is still a matter of debate.

Solar Orbiter had already photographed one from a distance in 2022 and confirmed its S shape, which scientists had predicted but hadn’t seen directly.

On March 2, Solar Orbiter was about 51 million miles (82 million kilometers) from the Sun, a little over halfway out to Earth’s orbit.

Over six hours, its instruments recorded five stretches when the magnetic field flipped back toward the Sun.

One of them lasted about 90 minutes, long by the standards of earlier studies.

“Solar Orbiter flew through a very large switchback,” said Coburn. “Because of this, we were able to sample rarely observed particles there that have tell-tale fingerprints of their origin.”

The fingerprints are atoms of oxygen and carbon that have lost different numbers of electrons. Hotter gas strips off more of them.

Once the particles leave the dense, hot region near the Sun, that count freezes in place and travels with them.

Solar Orbiter’s Solar Wind Analyser, a set of sensors that samples the gas streaming past, picked it up.

Inside the big switchback, the share of the most heavily stripped oxygen and carbon rose. Helium dropped relative to hydrogen.

Both changes match gas that had been trapped in hot, closed magnetic loops before it escaped.

The team then modeled the Sun’s atmosphere using temperature and density readings from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory.

The results pointed to the edge of a coronal hole, a region of the Sun’s atmosphere with a relatively weak glow, or to small magnetic loops within it.

“There are two main competing theories for how a switchback, and by extension the solar wind, forms,” Coburn said.

“The specific mix of particles detected by Solar Orbiter is the smoking gun for a formation process known as interchange reconnection.”

In that process, a closed magnetic loop meets a field line that stretches out into space. The two break and reconnect, and gas that was trapped in the loop escapes.

The other theory says waves and turbulence in the solar wind create switchbacks along the way. The team saw signs of that too.

Inside the switchback, the hydrogen sped up by about 30 miles (50 kilometers) per second, close to the speed at which magnetic waves travel through the wind.

Outside the switchback, the heavier atoms moved a bit faster than the hydrogen, and inside it they moved a bit slower.

The authors interpret that as a sign that the atoms ride along with the switchback as it heads outward.

“Overall, it seems that both processes – interchange reconnection and waves and turbulence – are involved in how switchbacks form and move through space,” said co-author Stephanie Yardley of Northumbria University.

“Our finding reconciles the two, showing that they simply operate at different stages in a switchback’s lifetime.”

The solar wind links Earth to the Sun, and its gusts feed the space weather that can disrupt satellites. Daniel Müller, ESA’s project scientist for Solar Orbiter, tied the work to that.

“The more we know, the better we can prepare for solar storms to protect our space-based infrastructure and technology,” Müller said.

The authors are careful about what a single case can show. The study provides evidence for how switchbacks form but doesn’t establish that all switchbacks originate the same way.

Shorter switchbacks in the same stretch showed similar signs, but those changes were about the size of the instruments’ noise.

Tracing the gas back also depended on a simplified model of the Sun’s magnetic field. The team tested how much its choices mattered and found the source location barely moved.

The authors say larger statistical studies are needed, along with future missions carrying better instruments for measuring heavy atoms.

Those would show whether this switchback was typical or just a lucky catch.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#6388. Breastfeeding may have been England’s greatest investment in its future

In the 1500s, breastfeeding's value may have topped England's spending on schooling, and nursing time shrank as the country grew richer.

Breastfeeding is work, hours of it every week, but its value has long been left out of the official tally of a nation’s economy. Two historians have now put a price on it anyway, across five centuries of English history.

At its peak in the 1500s, the unpaid labor of nursing mothers may have been worth more than everything the country spent on schooling and apprenticeships.

That would make breastfeeding possibly the largest investment early modern England made in the health and skills of its future workers, the authors wrote.

Louis Henderson and Jane Humphries are economic historians in the Department of Economic History at the London School of Economics.

Humphries is also affiliated with All Souls College at the University of Oxford, and her earlier work put a value on other unpaid care, such as cooking and cleaning.

Their new figures run from 1540 to 2000, and they’re estimates built from scattered records, so each one comes as a range.

Mothers weren’t paid to nurse their own babies. Some families did pay other women, called wet nurses, to breastfeed for them, and those wages give a rough price for the work.

Records from Christ’s Hospital show live-in wet nurses receiving about 3.61 pence a day, board included, in the 1550s.

Married women hired by the day to do other work earned 2 pence. A century later the figures were 7.95 pence and 4.32 pence respectively.

So a wet nurse earned roughly twice what a comparable unskilled woman did.

For the high end of their range, the authors valued breastfeeding at roughly twice a married woman’s daily wage.

For the low end, they used the price of cow’s milk. They assumed a hand-fed baby needed one gallon (3.8 liters) a week, a generous amount that allows for milk spoiling without refrigeration.

They compared both values with gross domestic product, or GDP, the total value of everything the economy produced each year.

The other half of the calculation is how long babies nursed before weaning, the switch from milk to solid food.

The diarist John Evelyn, born in 1620, wrote, “It appears, by a note of my father’s, that I sucked till 17th of January, 1622.” He was about 14 and a half months old.

The team added medical advice books, welfare records and 30 health surveys.

They also used medical reports on 25 nursing mothers who were sentenced to be shipped to Australia between 1825 and 1852, held by The National Archives.

Bones offer another way to tell how long a baby nursed. A heavier form of nitrogen shows up at higher levels in the ribs of babies who were still drinking breast milk.

The team used infant remains from two burial grounds, one at Spitalfields in London and a Catholic cemetery on Lukin Street.

Each kind of source has its own bias. Diarists, for example, reported weaning almost six months later than the health surveys did, so the team corrected each source against the others.

In 1540, babies nursed for about 17.5 months on average. By 1600, that was down to 12.7 months, and in 1770 it hit a low of 5.32 months.

In other words, as England grew richer over the 1600s and 1700s, its babies were weaned sooner.

Breastfeeding’s share of the economy fell with it. In 1540, it was worth between 0.55 and 6.58 percent of GDP, the highest share the team found.

By 1800, the range was 0.09 to 0.49 percent, partly because prices and the wider economy grew faster than breastfeeding’s value did.

Then the trend flipped. Average nursing rose again in the late 1800s, reaching 7.54 months by 1890, before falling to around four months by 2000 as formula spread and breastfeeding rates at birth dropped.

Church records support the early decline. The gaps between a mother’s births grew shorter from 1550 into the 1810s, which fits with shorter nursing, since breastfeeding delays a woman’s return to fertility.

In 1841, all of England’s public administration and defense made up roughly 1 percent of GDP. Pottery, glassmaking and brickmaking together made up about 0.8 percent.

The authors wrote that breastfeeding’s value rivaled those industries and even the public sector.

Spending on children’s skills was small by comparison. Total spending on education in 1833 didn’t exceed 1 percent of GDP, and it was probably much less in earlier centuries.

Apprenticeship fees came to a fraction of a percent, far below the 6.58 percent high-end estimate for breastfeeding in 1540.

The low end of the estimate is far smaller. Even that, in the authors’ view, still mattered to the economy.

Breast milk helps babies survive in dirty surroundings. In Brighton in 1905, 1.8 percent of breastfed babies up to three months old died. Among babies that age who got no breast milk at all, 65.4 percent died.

That matters for an idea from Thomas Malthus, an 18th-century economist. He argued that before modern times, poorer years meant more deaths from hunger and disease.

Breastfeeding points the other way. Until about 1800, as income per person rose, mothers weaned their babies sooner. Since early weaning was closely tied to infant deaths, richer years may not have been safer ones for babies.

During the 19th century, that link between income and nursing reversed.

The findings complicate Malthus’s theory by suggesting that rising incomes did not always translate into better survival prospects for infants.

The scarcity of data is the study’s main limitation, the authors wrote.

Only 22 wet nurse wages are known from 1500 to 1800, and those wages often covered chores beyond feeding.

Most of the records also come from towns and cities. Rural mothers may have nursed for longer, which would mean the estimates before the 1800s run low.

Where they had to guess, the authors chose assumptions that would understate breastfeeding’s value.

Studies of chemical traces in children’s teeth could show whether country babies nursed longer than city babies. That work is still rare, mostly because it’s expensive.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6387. Butterfly wings create a stunning illusion that fools predators

Butterflies may use their wing patterns to distort motion, causing predators to misjudge their speed and direction during an attack.

Bold stripes make a butterfly easy for a bird to spot. Once the wings start flapping, though, those stripes create a motion illusion that can make an attacker aim behind the butterfly or off to one side.

That could help explain why relatively few predators specialize in catching butterflies in flight, even though they’re among the most visible insects around.

A wide range of birds hunt night-flying moths in the air, and those moths tend to have duller patterns and faster wingbeats.

Butterflies, by contrast, generally have brighter wings and slower wingbeats.

George Hancock, a researcher in the Centre for Ecology and Conservation at the University of Exeter, led the work.

The team included Anna Hughes of the Department of Psychology at the University of Essex.

No birds took part in the study. Instead, the researchers analyzed butterfly footage using a computer model of bird vision, then asked human volunteers to play the role of predators in a touch-screen game.

The illusion works much like a barber pole. The striped pole only spins in place, but the stripes seem to climb.

“Butterfly wings deform as they fly – clapping together on the upstroke and peeling apart on the downstroke – so their stripes shift angle and point in different directions as they flap,” said Jolyon Troscianko, a co-author at Exeter.

Inside an eye, simple motion detectors compare one moment to the next and report which way things are moving.

Hancock’s team measured two kinds of false signal those detectors could pick up, which the researchers call motion confusion.

Backward motion is likely to make a predator misjudge how fast the butterfly is going, so it strikes behind it. Sideways motion is likely to throw off its aim to the left or right.

The first clue looked like a software bug.

“The first slow-motion video of a butterfly I put through our bird-vision computer model was glowing with downwards motion even though the butterfly was moving up,” Troscianko said.

“First I checked this wasn’t a coding error, that I’d swapped up and down somehow, but then it dawned on me that this would be a perfect way to confuse attacking predators.”

The team filmed real butterflies, including the red admiral and two swallowtails, taking off in front of a green screen at 1,057 frames per second.

Most predator attacks start on a butterfly that’s sitting still, so the first fraction of a second of flight is the moment that counts.

The researchers converted each clip to match how a small songbird’s eye sees brightness, then blurred it to match how quickly the bird’s vision can update.

The researchers then swapped each butterfly’s pattern for plain gray, black, or white. The patterned wings produced more of both kinds of confusion than any of the plain versions.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hancock was asked what a person would see watching the illusion in slow motion.

“When viewed in slow motion and when the eye has enough time to track the butterfly’s position there is no obvious illusion, though some butterflies are certainly hypnotic to watch,” Hancock said.

The patterns interfere with motion detection at the earliest stage of vision, Hancock explained. That makes a butterfly harder to catch during take-off, when it moves too fast for a bird to follow it by turning its head.

“To understand how animal patterns act as a defense requires looking at them through the lens of their predators, not just for the colors that they might see but also for the speed that they can see,” Hancock said.

Next, the team checked how common the effect is. They scanned the illustrations in a field guide covering 397 European butterfly species.

That came to 757 wing forms once males, females, and subspecies were counted separately. Each form was then animated in a three-dimensional flight simulation.

Several features of butterfly wing patterns stood out. For the backward illusion, high contrast on the front wings mattered most, followed by vertical stripes on the back wings, a single bold band, and the tails some species carry.

Swallowtails, all of them striped, scored consistently high on both kinds of confusion. Brush-footed butterflies, the family that includes the red admiral, ranged from the highest scores to almost none.

The main surprise, Hancock said, was how widely the strategy was spread across European butterflies.

“It might seem strange that a butterfly would evolve to be so visible, especially as very few European species are toxic or unpalatable,” Hancock said.

“But our study reveals the wide variety of different patterns butterflies can use to create illusions that confuse predators.”

Genes and growth constrain how butterfly wings develop, so a pattern that appears to create motion confusion could still arise by coincidence. To test that, the team had a computer program evolve its own wings.

The program started with populations of 24 random butterflies on three different wing shapes.

In each generation, the eight that produced the most motion confusion survived. The survivors produced mixed and mutated offspring that replaced the other 16.

Over 20 generations per run, the program produced 57,600 patterns in all.

Wings bred for the backward illusion came to resemble real European butterflies more closely than the random starting wings did, or wings that survived by chance alone.

Selecting for strong forward motion produced plain white butterflies, much like the ones commonly called whites. In the authors’ view, that look would lead a predator to overestimate a butterfly’s speed and strike too far ahead.

Much of the past work on butterfly wings has focused on warning colors, mimicry, and camouflage. The authors wrote that motion confusion may work alongside those jobs rather than replace them.

To see whether the measurements predicted missed attempts, the team built a fast touch-screen game.

One hundred volunteers at Exeter’s Penryn Campus in Cornwall played it. Together they made 3,000 attempts.

Animated versions of five butterfly species flew across the screen along wavy paths, and players tapped to catch them.

People see motion more slowly than birds do. So the butterflies flew at about 16 inches (40 centimeters) per second, but carried the wing blur of one moving twice as fast.

The species with the strongest backward illusion drew taps that landed farther behind them and spread out more along their path.

Between the most and least confusing species, the center of the taps shifted by about 38% of the average butterfly’s body length.

Birds and butterflies both live at a much faster pace than people, Hancock said, and butterfly defenses like these illusions are tailored to that speed.

“By using these illusions, butterflies can redirect attacks from birds by interfering with their ability to track motion at high speeds,” Hancock told Earth.com.

Hancock said the strategy is likely most common in butterflies because their wings are larger and flap more slowly than those of other insects.

Day-flying moths such as the Jersey tiger moth might use it too, though that still needs testing.

Lengthwise stripes on lizards, snakes, fish, and bird wings could work the same way, Hancock said. “Within all these groups there is a correlation between moving a lot and being stripier!”

Broadclub cuttlefish already pass dark stripes down their bodies while stalking crabs, and the motion model used here was first tested on them. Shiny, reflective animals confuse predators with a different kind of optical illusion.

No real birds were tested, so whether they miss striped butterflies more often in the wild is still an open question. The simulations also used only the upper sides of the wings, one style of flapping, and plain backgrounds.

The authors call for future simulations that add the undersides of the wings, a wider range of flight, other viewing angles and distances, and more kinds of background.

For butterflies, bright wings may do more than attract attention. Once those wings begin moving, their patterns could help keep predators from landing a successful strike.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6385. A new pathway to treat depression? Psilocybin may rewire the brain without psychedelic effects

Scientists discovered that psilocybin can rewire the brain through pathways separate from its psychedelic effects, opening doors to new depression treatments.

Psychedelic drugs such as psilocybin can help brain cells form lasting new connections, raising hopes for new depression treatments.

But scientists have struggled to determine whether those changes depend on the mind-altering effects of the drugs.

Now, a study in mice suggests that the brain’s rewiring and its response to psychedelics can occur through separate cellular pathways.

Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz gave mice one dose of psilocybin, the compound in magic mushrooms.

Then they watched individual connection points on living brain cells for three weeks. They also took the receptor psilocybin acts on out of one group of cells, and put it back in another group.

The rewiring and the drug’s signature behavior came apart.

Everything here happened in mice, and the behavior in question is a head twitch, not a hallucination.

Jacob Baker and Emily Kogan share first authorship, with senior author Yi Zuo, in the Department of Molecular, Cell and Developmental Biology at UC Santa Cruz.

Brain cells pass signals across junctions called synapses, and each one sits on a small bump on a branch of the receiving cell.

The team used a microscope that sees those bumps through the skull of a living mouse, so the same branch can be checked again days later.

Within 24 hours of a dose, new bumps appeared faster than in mice given saline. Of the three doses tried, the middle and high ones worked about equally.

The new connections were also sturdier. In untreated mice, most new bumps start out as short stubs that rarely last, and 40.6% survived a week. After psilocybin, 61.3% did.

The gap widened with time: three weeks out, 48.0% of the new bumps in treated mice were still there, compared with 29.3% in controls. More of what psilocybin built stayed built.

Shape tracked that durability. Only 2.2% of new bumps in control mice grew the broad mushroom head that marks a mature, strong synapse, compared with 28.4% after psilocybin.

“These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin’s effects on the brain,” said Baker, a doctoral student in Zuo’s lab.

A rewiring drug that only added connections would leave the brain denser every time, and that is not what happened.

The burst of new bumps was brief, and over three weeks the drug also sped up the loss of older connections.

Pre-existing bumps in treated mice were less likely to survive than the same bumps in control mice, and the net density drifted back toward where it started.

So in a healthy mouse brain, psilocybin did not inflate the wiring. It swapped some of it out.

The team then put mice through 21 days of unpredictable mild stress, a standard way to produce something like a depressive state in a rodent. The dose came the day after the stress stopped.

Stress had been stripping connections away, and that loss kept running after the stress ended in mice given saline.

In mice given psilocybin, the rate of connection loss returned to the level seen in unstressed animals, while new connections formed in greater numbers. The result was a bigger net gain.

In psilocybin-treated mice, 7.8% of connections lost during stress reappeared, compared with 4.8% in saline-treated controls.

That looks like a side effect of building more everywhere, because new bumps were no likelier to appear where old ones had been lost.

“These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain’s underlying condition,” Zuo said.

Psilocybin acts on a serotonin receptor called 5-HT2A, thickest in one class of output cells in the cortex. The team built two kinds of mice to ask what those cells do.

In the first, the receptor was missing everywhere except those cortical output cells. Psilocybin still drove new connections and still made them stick.

The mice did not show the head-twitch response.

In the second, the receptor was deleted from those cells and left everywhere else. Psilocybin did nothing to the wiring. The head twitching came through intact.

That pattern points to the receptor on those cells being both necessary and sufficient for the structural changes, and neither necessary nor sufficient for the twitch.

The authors found one limit on it. In both engineered strains, psilocybin stopped accelerating the loss of old connections, so clearing out the old wiring appears to need other cell types too.

The head-twitch response is a rapid shake of the head, counted by an observer, and it is the field’s standard stand-in for whether a serotonin psychedelic is hallucinogenic in people.

The authors are blunt that it measures a movement rather than an experience, and write that their results should not be read as directly addressing what causes hallucinations in humans.

The caveat matters, because the result is being framed as a route to drugs without the trip.

Chemists have already built non-hallucinogenic relatives of several psychedelics that promote the same kind of connection growth in animals, and the paper names four of them.

“By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs,” Zuo said.

The imaging covered the somatosensory cortex, the part that handles touch.

An earlier study of the frontal cortex reported that psilocybin’s new connections were not preferentially stabilized, and this paper reports the opposite. The authors put the disagreement down to the region.

None of it has been shown in a human brain, and nothing here tested whether the mice behaved less like animals under stress.

Depression is diagnosed by how a person feels and functions, and a count of connection points on a mouse neuron is a long way from that.

The findings identify a specific receptor and class of brain cells responsible for some of psilocybin’s lasting structural effects.

Whether scientists can use that knowledge to develop treatments for depression or PTSD without psychedelic experiences remains uncertain.

For now, the study offers a clearer picture of how psilocybin changes the brain, and a possible path toward drugs that preserve those changes without producing the same mind-altering effects.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.
