#6384. Exploding stars carved a giant bubble in a neighboring galaxy

Hubble reveals a vast cosmic bubble where massive stars cleared away gas, only for the compressed material around it to begin forming thousands of new stars.

Today’s Image of the Day from the European Space Agency reveals an enormous stellar nursery where generations of stars have reshaped the surrounding landscape.

Bright young stars, dark clouds of dust, and glowing gas fill the scene. Near the middle lies an enormous empty-looking cavity.

Far from being quiet, this hollow region records some of the most violent events in the lives of massive stars.

The view from the Hubble Space Telescope features LHA 120-N44, also known as N44.

The nebula sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small neighboring galaxy about 160,000 light-years from Earth.

The Large Magellanic Cloud is the largest of the small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way.

Its relative closeness gives astronomers an unusually detailed view of places where stars are being born.

N44 lies within the constellation Dorado and contains a mix of young stars, thick gas, and dust.

Its most striking feature is a vast central cavity measuring roughly 210 by 140 light-years. Astronomers call this kind of structure a superbubble.

The stars inside the cavity helped create it. Massive young stars throw material into space through powerful stellar winds.

Some eventually explode as supernovae, releasing enormous amounts of energy and pushing surrounding gas outward.

Over time, those forces cleared much of the material from the central region of N44.

Instead of simply disappearing, the displaced gas accumulated around the edges. It formed the dense, dusty shell visible around the superbubble today.

The shell also contains young stars, suggesting that material compressed along the bubble’s edges may be helping new generations form.

Gas compressed along the bubble’s boundary can become dense enough to collapse under its own gravity, forming new stars.

N44 therefore gives astronomers a chance to study several stages of star formation within the same complex.

Researchers want to measure how long the process takes, beginning when cold clouds of gas collapse into dense knots and ending when nuclear fusion starts inside a newborn star.

Researchers used Hubble to conduct a remarkably large census of N44.

The telescope catalogued nearly half a million stars, including stars belonging to the complex and unrelated objects lying along the same line of sight.

Nearly 30,000 of the objects are pre-main-sequence stars. These are young stars that have not yet reached the long, relatively stable stage of life in which hydrogen fusion powers their cores.

Finding so many of them gives researchers a large population for studying the earliest phases of stellar development.

Young, low-mass stars can be difficult to detect, especially when they sit among brighter objects and glowing clouds of gas.

Hubble’s sensitivity and sharp spatial resolution allow astronomers to separate many of these faint points of light even in densely packed stellar neighborhoods.

The observations also help scientists investigate the masses of newborn stars.

That matters because the amount of mass a star acquires during formation largely determines what happens during the rest of its life, from how brightly it shines to how long it survives.

Ultraviolet radiation pouring from massive stars energizes the gas surrounding N44’s superbubble.

That radiation helps produce the nebula’s bright glow and reveals smaller structures scattered throughout the larger complex.

Astronomer Karl Henize catalogued these individual features during the 1950s. One of them, N44F, appears near the upper-right portion of the Hubble view.

Unlike the enormous central superbubble, N44F was shaped largely by the fierce wind of a single hot, massive star.

Radiation and stellar winds from that star have pushed against nearby material, producing a smaller interstellar bubble.

Hubble observations have also revealed pillars of dusty gas shaped by the intense activity.

Such structures show how strongly stars can alter the clouds that produced them.

A young massive star does not remain a passive resident of its birthplace. Its radiation and outflowing material immediately begin reshaping the surrounding environment.

The Hubble observations came from observing program 14689, led by Dimitrios Gouliermis. The project focused on stars in N44 that have not yet begun sustained hydrogen fusion.

N44 is especially useful because the Large Magellanic Cloud contains fewer elements heavier than helium than the environment around the Sun.

Astronomers call these heavier elements metals, even though many would not normally be considered metals on Earth.

Studying low-mass stars in this setting can help researchers understand how stars form when fewer heavy elements are available.

Similar chemical conditions were more common in galaxies much earlier in cosmic history.

N44 therefore offers more than a striking photograph.

Its hollow center, compressed shell, and thousands of unfinished stars preserve different chapters of the same process, giving astronomers a nearby laboratory for tracing how new suns take shape.

Image Credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, D. Gouliermis

#6383. Floating scarecrows could save thousands of seabirds from deadly fishing nets

A floating buoy with fake eyes and a bird-of-prey kite cut seabird bycatch in Cornish gillnets, with the biggest gains in winter.

A scarecrow usually stands in a field. During a trial off the coast of southwest England, fishers floated two kinds on the sea instead, and both made their nets much less likely to catch diving seabirds.

One was a buoy topped with a spinning head of large, fake eyes. The other was a kite shaped like a bird of prey. With kites over a net, the odds of it catching any guillemots or razorbills fell by 71%, and with the buoys they fell by 59%.

Until now, evidence that anything keeps diving seabirds out of fishing nets has been limited.

Tom Horton of the University of Exeter led the analysis.

The trial itself was run by Fishtek Marine, a Devon company that makes the buoy, with Cornish fishers who had cameras fitted to their boats.

It covered one stretch of coast and one kind of fishing, so it can’t yet say how the devices would do anywhere else.

A gillnet is a wall of fine mesh set in the water to catch fish. Seabirds that chase fish underwater, such as guillemots and razorbills, can swim into the same mesh and drown. Fishers call any animal caught by accident bycatch.

Researchers estimated in 2024 that about 31,000 common guillemots die this way each year in European waters alone. Fishers and scientists have tried fixes, from lighting up nets to changing the gear itself.

Even so, the authors describe the tools for protecting seabirds in gillnets as poorly developed.

The buoy came out of eight years of work by Fishtek Marine and the RSPB, Britain’s bird conservation charity.

In Estonia it cut the number of sea ducks nearby, but its record since then has been mixed. A 2023 trial found it didn’t reduce seabird bycatch in Iceland’s lumpfish fishery.

The Cornish trial ran from October 2023 to March 2025. Ten fishers took part, all working close to shore, and each one set nets in matched groups.

In each group, one net had kites and another had buoys. A third had nothing. All three went into the same fishing grounds, so they could be compared fairly.

Over that stretch the boats set 1,057 nets, about 80 miles (129 kilometers) of net in all.

A camera system on every boat recorded each haul, and reviewers logged every animal that came up. The fishers were paid for taking part.

Three of the paper’s co-authors work for Fishtek Marine, which manufactures the buoy, and the paper declares that link. The kite is an off-the-shelf product.

The nets brought up 191 animals that nobody was trying to catch, and most of them were birds.

Guillemots and razorbills alone made up 138. Almost every animal was dead by the time it reached the boat.

The remaining animals included seals and cetaceans, such as dolphins and porpoises.

Both devices lowered the odds that a net would catch any guillemots or razorbills at all, compared with plain nets. On that measure, the kite and the buoy did about equally well.

When birds were caught, nets with buoys held 68% fewer of them for the same amount of fishing. Kite nets held fewer as well, but that gap was too uncertain to rule out chance.

In an interview with Earth.com, Horton said the size of the effect was what stood out. “The clearest surprise was just how strong and consistent the results were,” he said.

GPS on each boat logged where along the net every animal turned up, so the team could measure how far each one was from the nearest device. Close in, the kites did better.

Only five birds were caught within about 80 feet (24 meters) of a kite.

Near the buoys, five birds had been caught within about 23 feet (7 meters). The buoys offered moderate protection over a wider area instead.

Where fishers put the devices may be just as important as which one they choose.

Birds can still be caught in the gaps between them, and the authors suggest kites placed every 200 to 260 feet (60 to 80 meters) could suit coastal gillnet fisheries.

Fishers caught the most birds for their effort in January and February.

Fishers targeting sea bass and mackerel caught birds at the highest rates, and so did those using mesh about 4 inches (100 to 110 millimeters) wide.

The authors wrote that deterrents aimed at those winter nets could protect many birds in a way fishers are likely to accept.

The fishers generally found the buoys easy to handle and store. The kites performed worse in very light winds and were harder to manage in strong ones.

Setting extra devices along longer nets was the hardest part of the job, and several of the fishers’ suggestions have already gone into new prototypes.

Horton said one of the most encouraging parts of the study was how willing the fishers were to work together on testing new ideas.

“These are simple, low-cost tools that can help address the important issue of seabird bycatch in gillnet fisheries,” he told Earth.com.

Micky Bacon, a fisherman from Mousehole who took part, saw the trial as a chance to show what his industry wants.

“Fishermen don’t just want to go and catch fish, we also want to be part and parcel of improving the environment,” he said.

Seals are one open question. Fifteen seals turned up in nets with buoys, against six in plain ones. Kite nets held four.

Horton and his colleagues read that as a hint that the buoys might attract seals, and said more testing would be needed to confirm it.

They also noted that the trial spaced its devices to suit the buoy, which probably left gaps for the kites and may have affected the results.

Nor did the team measure water depth or wind, or whether birds stop reacting to the devices over time. Nearly a third of the nets stayed out overnight, and deterrents that birds have to see probably work best in daylight.

Horton said the next step is other waters. “We are keen to explore how these approaches perform in other fisheries and environmental settings, and whether they can be adapted to reduce bycatch more broadly,” he added.

The buoy deterred ducks in Estonia and then made no difference in Iceland, so one good result settles little.

Further trials will show whether these simple devices can protect seabirds across different fisheries, potentially preventing thousands of accidental deaths.

The full study was published in the journal Conservation Letters.

#6382. Scientists give AI chatbots a new way to read, with surprising results

Scientists have found a way to teach AI chatbots to read individual letters instead of word chunks, improving spelling skills without sacrificing overall performance.

An AI chatbot can write a whole essay about a word and still struggle to spell that word backward. That’s because most AI language models never see individual letters.

Before reading anything, they break text into chunks of whole words or pieces of words.

Researchers have now converted several existing models to read text in bytes, the small units computers use to represent text. Unlike word-based chunks, bytes allow models to process text at a much finer level.

The conversion took less than 1% of the training such a model normally needs. Until now, a model that read text this way had to be built from scratch, and those models lagged behind.

Benjamin Minixhofer of the Allen Institute for AI and the University of Cambridge led the work.

Valentin Hofmann of the Allen Institute and LMU Munich was the senior author, with co-authors at the University of Washington and Imperial College London.

The team tested openly available models with up to about 8 billion parameters, the adjustable values a model learns in training.

Before a language model reads a sentence, a separate program splits it into tokens. A common word usually becomes one token, and a rarer word gets broken into a few pieces.

The model learns from those pieces and never directly sees the letters inside them.

Chunking makes models efficient, but it has costs.

Models built this way have trouble with tasks that depend on single characters, which matters for computer code and for DNA and other biological sequences.

A fixed vocabulary of chunks also tends to favor English.

Models that read raw bytes avoid those problems. But byte-level models trained from scratch have trailed the chunk-based kind, and every leading chatbot model still reads in chunks.

Minixhofer’s team didn’t start over. They kept the core of each finished model and added new, smaller parts that read bytes and group them into chunks the core can work with. They call the process byteification.

In the first stage, only the new parts were trained, with the goal of making the converted model behave exactly like the original. In the second stage, the whole model learned to use the letter-level detail.

The whole process used about 49 billion tokens of text, less than 1% of the training data typically used to build a comparable model from scratch.

The team converted three openly available models this way: Qwen3, Llama 3 and Olmo 3. The converted versions got new names, Bwen, Blama and Bolmo.

On a set of tests covering science, math, coding, reading and general knowledge, the converted models landed close to the models they came from.

Bolmo averaged 62.5, against 62.3 for the original Olmo 3. Bwen averaged 69.8, against 70.3 for Qwen3.

In other words, the converted models retained nearly all of their general abilities.

The converted models also beat every earlier byte-reading model of similar size.

On science, technology, engineering and math questions, Bolmo scored 16.5 points higher than one such model trained from scratch.

The team could also give a converted model new skills without more training.

Copying over the changes that had taught Olmo 3 to follow instructions raised Bolmo’s instruction-following score by 36 percentage points, roughly matching the instruction-trained Olmo 3.

In speed, the converted models came close to the originals. They can also be trained to read bigger chunks at once, which makes them faster at some cost in accuracy.

The biggest gains came on letter-level tasks, such as spelling out a word, reversing it, or swapping and deleting characters.

On those tests, Bolmo scored 78.1 against 54.3 for the original Olmo 3, and Blama scored 81.0 against 57.2 for Llama 3.

Hofmann, a junior professor at LMU Munich who studies language processing with AI, described the gap directly.

“Traditional LLMs struggle with tasks that require character-level capabilities, such as spelling a word backwards,” Hofmann said. “Our byteified models are substantively better at this.”

Part of that gain came from practice rather than from reading bytes. The team added about 75 million tokens of training text built around letter tasks, roughly 0.04% of the training data.

An unconverted copy of Olmo 3 trained on the same mix reached 70.7, so the byte-reading design added the rest.

Not every score went up. The converted models were less likely than the originals to write working computer code on the first try. Given many tries, though, they more often produced at least one answer that worked.

A split result like that could mean the converted models write more varied code, but differences in the settings used to generate answers could also explain it.

The letter-practice text was all in English, and the models tested stopped at about 8 billion parameters.

Whether the conversion works as well on much larger models hasn’t been tested. Neither has the idea that reading bytes would help with languages other than English, which the team lists as a potential benefit.

The team has released its models, code and training data, so other groups can run those checks themselves.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6380. Saving water in the West could come with a hidden wildfire risk

Retiring farmland in the western U.S. saves water but may increase wildfire risk by removing natural firebreaks that help stop advancing flames.

Letting a thirsty field go dry in a drought looks like a clean trade: less water pumped, more left in the river. The field doesn’t stay empty, though.

Across most of the West where farmland has gone out of production, grass and brush grew back in its place, and both burn more readily than a crop does.

Farmland, meanwhile, often acts as a barrier to advancing wildfires.

Retiring farmland therefore involves another trade-off: water saved at the potential cost of a natural firebreak.

Until now, nobody had measured the second half of that bargain across the region.

Austen Lorenz of Aythya Analytics and Beatrice Gordon of the Desert Research Institute in Reno co-led the work, alongside a fire manager from the National Interagency Fire Center.

They mapped 9,948 wildfires across 11 western states between 1985 and 2024, each one at least 247 acres (100 hectares).

Then they compared the land just inside each fire’s final edge with the land just outside.

Each fire perimeter came from Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity, a federal satellite record of large fires. The team drew a ring about 300 feet (90 meters) wide on either side of each edge.

Everything inside the ring was sorted into forest, grass, scrub, wetland, bare ground, developed land, or cropland.

Cropland was about 2.8 times as likely to lie in the outer ring as in the inner one. Grass was the only cover found more often inside a fire than outside it.

Of the 2,452 fires with cropland within 300 feet of the edge, 2,242 had more of it outside than inside, which is 91.4%. Only bare ground did as well at that distance.

When the team widened the rings to about 3,300 feet (1,000 meters), cropland outperformed bare ground as well.

Cropland stayed outside fires in every year of the record. It still did when the team looked only at valley bottoms, where most farms sit, so the low ground alone doesn’t explain it.

Crops hold more water in their tissue than wild grass does. Irrigation keeps them wet through the fire season in California’s Central Valley, Washington’s Columbia Basin, and Idaho’s Snake River Plain.

A harvested or tilled field is also low and even, with no tall fuel to carry flames upward.

Firefighters add a third reason. They use irrigated fields as safety zones and as anchor points for control lines. A field’s edge is often where a crew built its control line.

Gordon is a hydrologist, and she said her field has asked how much water crops use far more often than what the land becomes afterward.

“After working with wildfire managers, it became clear that drought adaptation strategies that alter cropland can influence how wildfire moves through the landscape,” Gordon said.

“It’s a reminder that out here in the West, we don’t have the luxury of thinking of just one hazard anymore.”

The reasons to retire a field are real. Irrigated farms are the region’s largest water user, and the snowpack and groundwater they draw on are both shrinking.

In the Central Valley, taking an acre out of production saves between half an acre-foot of water a year for grain or hay and 2.3 acre-feet for almonds.

A typical American household uses about 0.45 acre-feet a year. One fallowed almond acre, then, frees up roughly what five households use.

In the 477 watersheds where farms and fires have met since 1985, about 10.6 million acres (4.29 million hectares) of cropland have become something else.

In 77% of those watersheds, most of that land went to grass or scrub. That shift runs across the Pacific Northwest, the Inland Northwest, the Intermountain West, and the Great Basin.

Grass was about one-fifth as likely as cropland to lie outside a fire line, and scrub about half as likely. Much of that land is old farmland left fallow on purpose, which the authors call a practical and widely used way to cut farm water use.

The water savings are real. But losing farmland can also mean losing a valuable firebreak.

In the other 19% of watersheds, 91 in all, the biggest change was cropland turning into housing.

Those watersheds cluster around growing metro areas in California, the Pacific Northwest, Utah’s Wasatch Front, and Colorado’s Front Range. They account for about 1.9 million acres (774,000 hectares) of lost cropland.

The loss works out to roughly 130 acres a day for 39 years, close to a hundred football fields every day. Developed land was about half as likely as cropland to lie outside a fire’s edge.

Building on a field removes the buffer and adds the things that start fires and make them harder to fight.

Houses bring ignition sources, structures to protect, and people to evacuate while the fire is still growing.

A fire’s final edge is set by weather, terrain, fuel, and how hard crews fought it, and this study can’t pull those apart. It shows that cropland lies where fires stop, not how much of that is the crop itself.

The authors argue the distinction matters less for planning than it sounds, though. Wet plants, open ground, or a place for crews to work all leave with the cropland, whichever one matters most.

The authors also did not estimate how much wildfire risk any one field’s retirement adds, or how that compares with the water it saves.

The team wants to build that calculation next, so a water district weighing a fallowing program can set the water saved against the fire risk added.

They also point to the USDA’s Conservation Reserve Program, which already pays landowners to idle sensitive land and could add fire buffering to its criteria.

“We want to stress that there’s no binary answer here – the complexity can’t be reduced to simply ‘fire is bad’ or ‘cropland is water intensive.’ Hopefully, this can help us evaluate where the trade-offs are steepest when we’re looking at compounding hazards,” Gordon said.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research Letters.

#6379. A scorching planet that should have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago still has one

NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has found evidence of a thick atmosphere and reflective mineral clouds on a scorching lava planet.

A rocky planet orbiting extremely close to its star might be expected to be bare, scorched stone, its atmosphere stripped away long ago by intense radiation.

Yet new observations from the James Webb Space Telescope suggest that a lava planet called TOI-561 b still has a thick atmosphere.

Something in that atmosphere reflects most of the starlight that hits it.

If that reading holds up, a small rocky planet can keep its gas in a place where astronomers expected only bare rock. The planet is about 280 light-years away, and its atmosphere is not livable.

Anjali Piette, an assistant professor of astronomy at the University of Birmingham in the U.K., is part of the international team behind the work.

“Our discovery challenges current theories,” Piette said. “We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.”

The study was led by Samuel Boucher of the Université de Montréal, with Lisa Dang of the University of Waterloo in Canada as project lead.

TOI-561 b is a little more than twice Earth’s mass and about 1.4 times as wide. It circles its star in about 10.7 hours, so a full year there passes in less than half an Earth day.

At that distance, one side of the planet always faces the star and the other always faces away.

The day side is likely covered by an ocean of molten rock, which is why astronomers call it one of the lava planets.

TOI-561 b is also lighter for its size than most planets in such tight orbits, which tend to match Earth-like rock. Its star is unusual too: at least 10 billion years old, more than twice the age of the sun, and poorer in heavy elements.

The first hint of air came from a 2025 study led by Johanna Teske. Her team measured heat from the planet’s day side each time it passed behind its star.

It was too cool for bare rock, and too cool even for an atmosphere made only of rock vapor.

The heat measurements came from a single 37-hour stretch in one Webb observing program.

During that time, the planet passed behind its star four times. Boucher’s team analyzed the whole stretch, night side included.

The long watch also let the team separate the planet’s signal from slow flickering on the star’s surface, where hot gas rises and sinks.

The researchers calculated how hot the day side would get if the planet were dark, bare rock with no air to carry heat around. The answer was about 5,300°F (3,200 K). Webb measured about 3,200°F (2,050 K) instead.

The missing heat could have gone one of two ways. Air could have carried it around to the night side, or the planet could have reflected it away before absorbing it.

The night side came in at about 1,500°F (1,100 K). That’s warm for a side that never sees its star, so some heat is reaching it. It isn’t warm enough to explain the gap, though.

Reflection has to cover the rest. The team estimates the planet reflects about 74% of the starlight that hits it, close to the share reflected by Venus, the brightest planet in our night sky.

Lab tests show that molten-rock surfaces reflect very little light, so something above the surface has to be doing the reflecting.

To find out what that could be, the team compared Webb’s readings with computer simulations of the planet’s climate.

Heat moving around the planet couldn’t explain the readings alone. The best matches came from a thick atmosphere, with surface air pressure between one and 10 times Earth’s, holding something that reflected a lot of light.

The leading candidates are mineral clouds, made from rock that evaporates off the molten surface.

In the simulations, clouds of silicon dioxide, the mineral in quartz and most sand, and magnesium silicate could form on the day side.

They would gather near the edge where day turns to night, where the air cools enough for those minerals to condense.

Clouds like that would work as a sunscreen, sending starlight back out before it can heat the planet.

The gas that makes up most of the atmosphere is still unknown. It could be a thick layer of carbon dioxide, like a much hotter version of Venus.

Or it could be rich in sulfur dioxide, a gas released by the volcanoes on Io, one of Jupiter’s moons.

Another lava planet, 55 Cancri e, is also thought to have a substantial atmosphere, probably carrying carbon dioxide or carbon monoxide.

Earlier work by Dang, Piette and their colleagues pointed to gases from TOI-561 b’s interior refilling its air.

How the atmosphere is still there at all is the bigger puzzle.

“This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere,” Piette said.

The temperatures are best estimates. Webb watched the planet in a narrow band of infrared light, and that band misses the wavelengths where the planet gives off the most heat.

The two detectors inside Webb’s instrument also didn’t agree perfectly once their data were compared with the climate simulations.

The difference could come from the instrument, from the star, or from clouds or gases that look different at different wavelengths, and the team can’t yet say which.

Webb also recorded the planet passing in front of its star during the same observation.

Those data will get a paper of their own, which should help show how thick the atmosphere is and whether clouds are really there.

“The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b’s atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io,” Dang said.

“Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years.”

Carbon dioxide absorbs light at one of those longer wavelengths. A full orbit watched there with Webb’s mid-infrared instrument could show whether the sky over TOI-561 b looks more like Venus.

The full study was published in the journal The Astronomical Journal.

#6378. Ozone pollution reached dangerous levels for billions of people in 2026

A new global report reveals that billions of people faced unhealthy ground-level ozone pollution in 2026, with Asia experiencing the worst exposure.

The ozone most people have heard of sits miles overhead and blocks the sun’s ultraviolet light.

The same gas also forms near the ground when pollutants from vehicles, factories and other sources react in sunlight.

Down there it irritates lungs instead of protecting them.

A new analysis from Europe’s atmosphere monitoring service estimates that only 5 percent of the world’s people breathed ozone at a level the World Health Organization calls good this year.

Almost 40 percent were exposed to the highest category the service tracks, and Asia was hit hardest. The figures come from a global model fed with satellite and ground readings, not from a monitor outside every home.

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, or CAMS, is run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for the European Commission.

Its new report, Atmosphere Watch, covers ozone, wildfire smoke and desert dust from January 1 to September 15.

Laurence Rouil directs CAMS. In written answers sent to Earth.com through the Copernicus press office, Rouil said the year’s surprise was how many big pollution events piled up at once.

“When we brought together the huge amount of data produced every day by CAMS, the most striking finding was that more than half of the world’s population was still exposed to unhealthy levels of air pollution,” Rouil said.

Nothing emits ground-level ozone directly. Nitrogen oxides from burning fuel react in sunlight with organic vapors from traffic, industry, household solvents, plants and wildfires.

Hot, still summer weather speeds the reactions and lets the gas build up.

Ozone lasts a few days near the ground and a few weeks higher up. That is long enough to drift across borders and oceans.

During the heatwave of July 28, CAMS calculated that ozone arriving in Bergamo, Italy, from elsewhere in the Northern Hemisphere mattered as much as every human source in Europe combined.

The report measures exposure the way the World Health Organization does. It takes each day’s highest eight-hour ozone reading and averages it over the six worst months of the year.

The WHO guideline is 60 micrograms per cubic meter. Above 110, CAMS calls the air extremely poor, and that is the band almost 40 percent of people fell into.

CAMS estimates that six in ten people in Asia experienced extremely poor ozone levels, while nine in ten experienced air rated poor or worse.

Delhi, Cairo, Milan, Mexico City and Rio de Janeiro had some of the highest exposure on their continents.

Europe has cut every pollutant its air quality law regulates except ozone, the service’s annual assessments show. This summer’s repeated heatwaves pushed half of Europeans into poor air or worse.

European ozone standards limit how often concentrations can exceed 120 micrograms per cubic meter, and much of the continent struggled with elevated levels.

In North America, more than two thirds of people breathed poor ozone or worse, mostly on the two U.S. coasts and in big cities.

Decades of emission cuts have left ozone there largely unchanged, the report says, partly because wildfires supply the ingredients.

Oceania, South America and much of Africa did far better. Everyone in Oceania, 81 percent of South Americans and 56 percent of Africans had good or fair ozone levels.

On July 22, fires in France’s Gironde and Landes regions burned close to 124,000 acres (50,000 hectares) and forced 40,000 people from their homes.

Their smoke fouled the air hundreds of miles away. Fires near Ávila and Madrid in Spain burned a similar area and sent 56,000 people fleeing.

Belgium’s High Fens fire in August was the country’s largest in a century, and its smoke crossed Germany into Poland.

In July, wildfire smoke from Canada’s Northwest Territories and Ontario spread over the northern United States.

Cities from Chicago to Philadelphia issued air advisories days before the World Cup final in New Jersey, and storms washed the air clean just before the match.

In Indonesia, peat fires on Borneo, fed by a building El Niño, pushed fine particle levels to several hundred micrograms per cubic meter.

Saharan dust crossed the Atlantic toward the Caribbean, and the Canary Islands topped Europe’s list of cities with dust alerts.

Asked by Earth.com what someone in a high-ozone region should do on the worst days, Rouil pointed to the WHO.

Ozone forecasts are now widely available and increasingly reliable, Rouil said, so people can act before an episode peaks.

“WHO advises reducing prolonged or intense outdoor physical activity, especially in the afternoon,” Rouil said.

Further guidelines recommend that children, older adults, and people with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions take extra precautions, he told Earth.com.

The director also said that the fixes are known. Decades of European rules have brought down sulfur dioxide, fine particles and nitrogen dioxide, Rouil said, and the job now is to keep that momentum.

The exposure figures are model estimates rather than direct measurements at every location.

CAMS combines satellite and ground observations with a model that tracks more than 50 chemicals, then matches the results to population maps.

A model fills the gaps where no monitor stands, but it isn’t the same as a sensor on the street outside.

The report stops at September 15 and doesn’t count deaths from this year’s ozone. For scale, the WHO estimates that outdoor air pollution causes more than 4 million early deaths a year.

The Health Effects Institute’s State of Global Air report finds ozone exposure in Asia has risen in recent years.

How much of Europe’s summer ozone came from its own wildfires is still an open question, and CAMS says it is actively researching it.

With a strong El Niño building and fires already burning in Indonesia, the service expects more fires to make headlines in the months ahead.

Atmosphere Watch 2026 is a monitoring report published by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service on September 30.

#6377. Ancient sled dogs had a surprising physical advantage that helped them pull heavy loads

Scientists discovered that Arctic sled dogs have unusually short lower leg bones, a trait that may have helped them pull heavy loads for thousands of years.

Pull a heavy sled and the load tries to tip you over backward. A dog that carries its weight closer to the ground resists that pull better, and Arctic sled dogs appear to have been built that way.

For their size, their lower leg bones run about 6 percent shorter than the same bones in wolves, village dogs and spitz breeds.

The same short legs turn up in dogs from Chukotka, in far eastern Russia, that lived as much as 2,000 years ago.

That matters because sled gear rarely survives in the ground. For most of the history of dog sledding, the dogs are all that remains.

Mitya Kletzerman, an archaeologist at the University of Haifa in Israel, led the study.

His co-authors are affiliated with the Severtsov Institute of Ecology and Evolution in Moscow, Tel Aviv University and the University of Algarve in Portugal.

A dog standing still rests about 60 percent of its weight on its front legs and 40 percent on its back legs.

Once it leans into the sled lines, the backward drag of the sled and the forward push of its paws together try to rotate the dog nose-up. The back legs end up bearing more of its weight.

Kletzerman’s team worked out which body shape handles that best.

The team’s calculations suggest that halving the height of a dog’s center of mass could double the pulling force it can generate before tipping backward.

Shifting that center of mass forward by a tenth of the body’s length does the same.

In a short, all-out pull, when the back legs do all the work, a lower center of mass still doubles the force, but the forward shift adds only about 17 percent. So a heavy hauler should carry its weight low.

The team then measured five long bones in the legs of 80 modern animals.

There were 22 working sled dogs from Greenland, Chukotka and Kamchatka, plus 32 village and stray dogs, 13 spitz-type dogs and 13 wolves.

Sled dogs were the tallest dogs in the sample, standing an estimated 22.6 inches (57.3 cm) at the shoulder, and only the wolves were larger.

So the team scaled every measurement to each animal’s overall size before comparing.

After that adjustment, three bones stood out. The radius and ulna in the forearm, and the tibia in the lower hind leg, were about 6 percent shorter in sled dogs than in the other three groups.

Sex made no difference, and the cold climates the sled dogs came from didn’t explain the pattern either.

Arctic dogs appear to have formed a distinct lineage by about 9,500 years ago.

The oldest evidence of sledding, sled parts beside dog remains on Zhokhov Island in the Russian Arctic, is about 9,000 years old.

The 82 ancient bones came from three sites on the Chukchi Peninsula, across the Bering Strait from Alaska: Paipelghak, Kaniskak and Ekven.

The sites span the first centuries BC to the 16th century AD and are associated with ancient Arctic communities ancestral to modern Indigenous populations of the region.

The team scored each ancient bone on how likely it was to have come from a sled dog.

All 15 upper arm bones scored as sled dog, along with 20 of the 25 forearm bones and 38 of the 42 shin bones. Altogether, 89 percent of the ancient bones matched the sled dog pattern.

Three dogs that had been buried on purpose scored as sled dogs too.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kletzerman described one of them, found at Paipelghak in 2009, beneath the wooden floor of a passage leading out of a house.

Permafrost had kept its dense brown fur. It was an old male, around ten years of age, and a walrus penis bone and a cut piece of reindeer antler had been placed near its tail.

“We identified possible traces of a harness in the fur of this dog,” he said.

Dog teams let people hunt together and trade ideas between communities, Kletzerman said, and the technology also changed the dogs it depended on.

Nothing in the bones shows how the trait arose. Kletzerman told Earth.com that his team has no good evidence that prehistoric Arctic communities deliberately bred dogs for particular traits.

A less deliberate process may be the better explanation.

People didn’t need to select for cold tolerance, he said. Dogs lived and slept in the snow, and those without the right coats were less likely to survive and breed.

“Once people began relying on dogs for traction, animals physically better suited to this work were more likely to endure it and leave descendants,” he said.

He added that this process of selection was probably not consciously directed by humans, but driven by the working conditions they had created for the dogs.

Kletzerman also emphasized that the ways people managed working dogs likely differed between communities.

“Such practices probably varied between communities and over time, combining accumulated practical experience with culturally specific understandings of animals and the world,” he told Earth.com.

Other routes are possible. Arctic sled dogs share ancestry, so the proportions could have been inherited and then kept because they worked.

Sled dogs also start work before their skeletons finish growing, and hard loading at that age can slow the lengthening of bones. So can a diet rich in vitamin A, which Arctic dogs may have been fed.

Short legs alone don’t make a sled dog. The authors wrote that similar proportions can arise in dog lineages shaped by something other than hauling.

This test thus only works where sledding is already a plausible explanation.

Most of the ancient bones were loose rather than part of a skeleton, so each score is a probability rather than a verdict. And none of the three sites has yet produced clear evidence of sleds alongside the dogs.

How far back the short-legged build goes, and how far across the Arctic it reaches, are open questions.

Kletzerman’s team has an early impression that it was more pronounced in some ancient dogs than in modern sled dogs.

Their next study looks inside the bones, at how shortening may have changed their strength.

If that fuller profile holds up, a single leg bone could tell archaeologists whether a dog pulled sleds, at sites where the sleds themselves rotted away long ago.

The full study was published in the journal iScience.

#6376. A six-year-old flipped over a rock in a Nebraska park and found a kind of fossil not recorded in the state for more than 55 years

A six-year-old boy discovered a rare ancient marine fossil in Nebraska's Schramm Park, the first known conulariid found in the state in over 55 years.

During a late-summer Rafting and Rocks event at Schramm Park State Recreation Area near Gretna, Nebraska, six-year-old Leo Youngdahl turned over a rock at an outcrop of exposed bedrock. The boy from Eagle hoped to find one of his favorite fossils on its underside.

He was looking for a crinoid. Instead, the rock held a 2.75-inch (7-centimeter) conulariid, an ancient marine animal that rarely survives as a fossil.

The only other known Nebraska specimens turned up more than 55 years ago, in the towns of Louisville and Weeping Water.

Kelly Ekue, an outdoor education specialist at the Schramm Education Center, leads fossil programs at the park for the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission.

“I’ve been leading programs at the outcrop for over seven years, and there are six main types of fossils we find,” Ekue said.

“This fossil didn’t look anything like any of the species we see,” she added.

“It was larger and seemed fish-like,” she explained. That stood out because the outcrop’s rock layers contain only invertebrate fossils.

Ekue emailed a photo to a geologist she knew, who passed it along. It reached Shane Tucker, a paleontologist with the University of Nebraska State Museum, and Bob Diffendal, a geologist who curates the museum’s invertebrate fossils.

The two experts identified the animal from a herringbone-style imprint on the limestone. That imprint is the only part of the conulariid that fossilized.

Conulariids were ancient cnidarians, members of the animal group that includes jellyfish. Park staff describe them as jellyfish-like creatures shaped like an upside-down pyramid.

A 2022 study of a Brazilian conulariid classifies them as an extinct order of marine cnidarians. Their outer shell, or periderm, was steeply pyramidal or conical, and their bodies showed four-part radial symmetry.

Their closest living relatives may be crown jellyfish of the order Coronata, the authors suggest.

The oldest conulariids known before that work date to the late Cambrian. The Brazilian fossil comes from the final stage of the earlier Ediacaran Period, and the team calls it the oldest documented conulariid.

Unlike later conulariids, the Brazilian specimen shows no calcium phosphate in its shell.

The last conulariids lived in the Norian Stage, near the end of the Triassic Period. For most of that history, between 200 million and 500 million years ago, conulariids lived in eastern Nebraska and around the globe, the commission said.

Nebraska has few conulariids preserved as fossils. Their soft bodies and thin skeletons usually broke apart and disintegrated too quickly to fossilize.

Those skeletons were made of carbonate-rich apatite, a phosphate mineral, according to a 2023 micro-CT study of conulariids.

That work scanned unusually well-preserved specimens from Pennsylvanian rocks in Texas and Oklahoma, in the North American Midcontinent. Conulariids have been studied for more than two centuries, the authors note.

The X-ray images showed structures the team identified as longitudinal muscle bundles, along with a possible gastric cavity. The bundles often joined in V-shaped pairs and ran toward the animal’s opening.

Preservation varied from one fossil to the next. Some showed both features, while others kept only the muscle bundles.

Such internal structures had never before been shown with micro-CT. Leo’s specimen preserves far less, only the patterned surface pressed into stone.

Fossils from the outcrop date from a time when Nebraska was covered by a saltwater sea, the commission noted.

A geologic display at the park’s east entrance highlights limestone and shale from the Pennsylvanian Period. Visitors may also spot Paleozoic marine fossils such as brachiopods or corals, the park’s official page notes.

The Rafting and Rocks program pairs round-raft floats on a pond with an outcrop visit. There, participants explore limestone layers and look for fossils.

Schramm Park, midway between Lincoln and Omaha, is home to Nebraska’s oldest state fish hatchery. In 1937, the hatchery became the state recreation area.

The park takes its name from geology professor E.F. Schramm, who gave land so it could be used for teaching.

“It is really amazing that among all those rocks in the Schramm outcrop, Leo not only picked up this one, but recognized it as a fossil and thought to ask about it,” Ekue said.

Leo said he had been told the conulariid was rarer to find than a mammoth bone. He plans to show his finds to naturalist Heidi Swanson at Platte River State Park, near Louisville.

He doesn’t mind leaving the fossil behind. Park staff will use it in educational programs, continuing the tradition E.F. Schramm started.

“Delight in all discoveries, not just the big ones like a rare fossil, but the little ones, too,” Ekue advised.

State collecting laws bar visitors from taking fossils, feathers or nests, so Ekue suggests photographing finds instead. Picks and shovels are not allowed at the outcrop, and visitors should stay out from under overhanging rocks.

The information was obtained from the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission.

#6375. A switch made of folded DNA doesn’t flip by itself, even though heat keeps shaking it

A switch folded from DNA holds its position while heat shakes it, flips on command, and in the best cases kept working through more than 200,000 electric pulses.

A light switch stays wherever you leave it, but if you shrink it to the size of a molecule, that no longer holds because heat shakes every part of it.

A team in Germany has folded DNA into a switch that holds its position anyway and flips on command, and it kept working through more than 200,000 electric pulses.

DNA origami folds DNA strands into a precise shape. Researchers at the Technical University of Munich tested the switch in the lab, with copies stuck to a glass slide, not inside a cell or body.

“With our design, we were able to show that a DNA-based switch can not only be controlled quickly and precisely, but is also exceptionally long-lived,” said Friedrich Simmel, a physics professor at the TUM School of Natural Sciences and a co-author of the study.

DNA origami takes its name from paper folding, a craft that also shapes some plant-inspired robots. At the University of Sydney Nano Institute, researchers built more than 50 nanoscale objects from DNA blocks, including a tiny dinosaur. They said the approach could lead to nanorobots that deliver drugs.

But a shape can’t do a job. A machine needs parts that move on command, and at this size, heat makes that hard. Other labs build tiny machines from human cells or plant-based gels instead.

Earlier DNA switches all had a flaw. Some needed a constant push to stay in place. Others flipped slowly or wore out fast. Many used DNA “latches” that came apart when heat jostled them.

The Munich researchers borrowed an idea from large-scale engineering, the snap-through mechanism, which rests in either of two positions and moves only when pushed hard enough. Their switch has two stiff DNA arms joined by a hinge.

The arms sit on a square base plate about two millionths of an inch across (55 nanometers), roughly a thousand times narrower than a human hair.

The arms have two resting positions. Moving from one to the other means passing each other, and where they overlap, a barrier that heat alone rarely gets past forms. In one test, the researchers watched 70 switches under a microscope for an hour. Not one flipped by itself.

The same barrier that keeps the switch still means it takes a real push to move it.

DNA carries a negative charge, so an electric field pushes on it. To use that, the researchers attached a lever to one arm; the DNA rod is more than seven times longer than the base plate is wide. When a pulse hits, the lever swings and pushes the arms past the barrier.

A flip takes milliseconds. Afterward, the switch stays put with no power at all.

One caveat first. The switches lay on the glass at random angles, and the field flips them best at one angle. So the researchers tracked only switches that flipped in a first test, and the numbers below describe switches that lined up well with the field.

In one run, a single switch got 500 pulses of 10 milliseconds each over 50 seconds and flipped on 447 of them. An hour later, it got 500 more and flipped 434 of them.

A second test used a switch as a gate. It hid and exposed a spot where other DNA strands attach, and flipping it changed how fast those strands attached. So an electric field could regulate how fast that reaction ran.

Fluorescent dyes were the first way to track each switch, with a cluster on the lever tip. Dyes fade under light, so that works for minutes, not days, but gold doesn’t fade. The researchers attached a gold rod, about as long as the base plate is wide, to the lever.

Under a microscope with a filter that favors light of one orientation, the rod looks bright when it lines up with the filter and nearly dark when it turns sideways. Each flip changed its brightness, letting the researchers track one switch for days.

Switches didn’t wear out evenly. One dropped out after 6,500 pulses. The best took 206,800 pulses over more than five and a half hours and flipped on 195,000 of them, about 94%, before its success rate began to fall.

That’s more than 30 times as many pulses as the early dropout. Some devices still flipped after several days of repeated use.

The researchers tested single switches on a glass slide. The authors envision arrays, with many switches working together, but they remain untested. The data behind the paper sit in a public Zenodo archive.

The authors also suggested the switch could serve as nanoscale memory, since it rests in one of two positions.

Simmel, first author Florian Rothfischer and co-author Enzo Kopperger have filed a patent application on the technology.

Why one switch outlasts another is still unsettled, though the setup gives the group a way to study how switches wear out and fail.

More development is needed before any of this works outside a laboratory. The authors want to build arrays of switches that work together.

The full study was published in the journal Science Robotics.

#6374. A fabricated documentary scene is responsible for the enduring urban legend that lemmings willingly throw themselves off steep cliffs

Lemmings do not commit mass suicide. Discover how a staged 1958 Disney documentary spread the myth and what these Arctic rodents really do.

For decades, lemmings have stood for blind group behavior, rushing together toward a cliff edge and the water below. The small Arctic rodents do nothing of the kind.

Much of that picture comes from White Wilderness, a 1958 Disney nature film. Its famous lemming sequence was shot in Alberta, a landlocked Canadian province, with animals brought in from elsewhere.

State wildlife biologists in Alaska tell a far less dramatic story. Populations of these Arctic animals rise and crash in cycles, and crowded lemmings spread out in search of food, sometimes crossing rivers and lakes on the way.

White Wilderness belonged to the studio’s “True-Life Adventures” series of nature films. It went on to win the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature at the 1959 ceremony.

In one segment, narrator Winston Hibler follows a column of lemmings on what he calls “a march that will take them to a strange destiny.”

Hibler sets the story in the lemmings’ “weird world of frozen chaos.”

He calls the animals “victims of an obsession,” driven onward until they reach the edge above the water.

“Yet over they go, casting themselves out bodily into space,” Hibler says as the lemmings tumble from the ledge.

The film’s lemming footage was not shot on the Arctic tundra where lemmings live. The filmmakers bought lemmings from Inuit children in Manitoba, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game reported in a 2003 article.

A few dozen of the animals were then filmed running on a snow-covered turntable.

For the climax, crew members threw the lemmings off a cliff, the agency’s article says. The “sea” below was actually a river, shot with tight framing.

An investigation by Canadian television producer Brian Vallee exposed the staging in the early 1980s, the state agency noted.

Disney historian Jim Korkis addressed the scene in a 2012 post for the Walt Disney Family Museum. He wrote that the crew reportedly acted without the knowledge or approval of Walt Disney and the studio.

“…jumping off cliffs into the sea is an urban myth that only becomes reality when a nature cameraman steps in to make it a reality,” Korkis wrote.

Another lemming legend has a longer history. From the eastern Canadian Arctic to western Alaska, a common story held that lemmings fell from the sky.

That legend may come from the way lemmings suddenly appear in spring during peak years, according to an Alaska wildlife notebook on lemmings.

Thomas McDonough was a state wildlife biologist with the department when he discussed the suicide story in 2003.

“It’s a complete urban legend,” McDonough said. “I think it blew out of proportion based on a Disney documentary in the ’50s, and that brought it to the mainstream,” he added.

“Disney had to have gotten that idea from somewhere,” McDonough noted.

He suggested that Disney likely confused dispersal with migration and embellished a kernel of truth.

Alaska has one true lemming, the brown lemming. Several close relatives, including the collared lemming and the northern bog lemming, are also commonly called lemmings.

True lemmings measure 4 to 5.5 inches (100 to 135 millimeters) long. In some areas, their numbers peak every three to five years.

When lemmings exhaust the local food supply, they disperse, as moose, beaver and many other animals do. “Actual migrations do not occur,” the state’s notebook states.

Lemmings can swim and will cross bodies of water in search of new ground. Sometimes they drown.

At a lake or river, dispersing lemmings may stop and build up along the shore before swimming across. One account from Barrow, Alaska, tells of lemmings drowning and piling up on the shore.

Mass dispersal has been observed most dramatically in the Scandinavian mountains, home of the Norwegian lemming.

A 15-year study in northeast Greenland followed collared lemmings and four of their predators from 1988 to 2002. The predators were the stoat, a type of weasel, plus the Arctic fox, snowy owl and long-tailed skua.

The team worked across about 29 square miles (75 square kilometers) of the Karup Valley. Its model reproduced the four-year lemming cycle seen there.

The 2003 analysis in Science traced it to a one-year lag in the stoat’s response to lemming numbers.

A 2008 study of Norwegian alpine rodents, mostly lemmings, linked their swings from 1970 to 1997 to winter weather and snow conditions.

Shifts in temperature and humidity change conditions under the snow, the authors suggest, and less regular peaks may spread as the climate changes.

Their model also matched the observed absence of rodent peak years in that habitat after 1994.

The information was obtained from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.

#6373. A common substance in everyday foods is linked to better memory

Older adults in the study who ate more lecithin, found in eggs and soybeans, tended to score better on thinking tests.

Eggs for breakfast, beans with lunch, meat at dinner: each can provide lecithin, a mixture of fatty substances found in many foods.

Lecithin has a reputation as a memory aid, although the evidence is thin.

In a Chinese study, older adults with more lecithin in their diets had slightly better memory and thinking scores.

They also had lower odds of mild cognitive impairment: thinking problems that are worse than normal aging, but haven’t reached dementia.

The researchers assessed everyone just once. That gave them a snapshot of diet and memory, but no way to tell whether lecithin caused the difference.

Two hospital researchers in Beijing, Xiaoying Li and Chengyan Qi, are the first authors. Both hospitals are affiliated with Capital Medical University, where coauthor Yuandi Xi, a public health professor, studies nutrition, memory and muscle loss in older adults.

Cells use lecithin in the thin membranes that surround them. When we digest lecithin, we also get choline, which the body uses to make a chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells.

So there is a reason to look at lecithin and memory together.

A Finnish study involving 2,497 middle-aged men linked higher dietary phosphatidylcholine intake with a lower risk of dementia.

But lecithin has a less promising record as a treatment for dementia. A review of randomized trials, published in 2003, found that the evidence didn’t support using it that way.

Li and Qi’s team wanted to know about the years before dementia. Was getting more lecithin through ordinary meals linked with better memory and thinking?

The work involved 1,917 people in three Chinese cities: Beijing, Jincheng and Linyi.

The team recruited them between 2020 and 2023 from census or village records; every participant was 60 or older and had lived locally for at least a year.

In face-to-face interviews, they talked about their health and the foods they ate. A questionnaire recorded how often they ate different foods.

Using those answers and China’s food composition database, the researchers estimated each person’s daily lecithin intake.

About 88 milligrams marked the midpoint, so the main comparison was between people who ate more and those who ate less.

The team used a 30-point test called the Montreal Cognitive Assessment to screen for memory and thinking problems. A low score meant different things depending on a person’s education.

A score of 13 or below flagged possible trouble for someone who could not read. For people with seven or more years of schooling, the cutoff was 24 or below.

Neurologists examined everyone flagged by the screening. They used criteria from the U.S. National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer’s Association to decide who had mild cognitive impairment.

They diagnosed 1,023 of the 1,917 participants, just over half the group.

The two intake groups were separated by about half a point, with the advantage going to those above 88 milligrams a day.

That calculation took account of age, sex, schooling, calories, blood fats, body composition and seven chronic diseases, including diabetes and stroke.

Half a point was a modest difference on this test. The typical score was 23 for people without mild cognitive impairment and 19 for those with it.

The higher-lecithin group had about 20% lower odds of a diagnosis. Dividing participants into thirds by intake gave a similar result: the top third had about 27% lower odds than the bottom third.

The team described the work as epidemiological evidence, meaning it revealed a health pattern across a group of people.

“This study provides important epidemiological evidence that ensuring adequate lecithin intake through a balanced diet could be a feasible approach to support cognitive health in the elderly,” the research team wrote.

The authors pointed to China’s daily reference intake for choline: 450 milligrams for men and 380 for women. These are choline targets, so they should not be confused with the lecithin amounts measured here.

According to the authors, a balanced diet with eggs, legumes and lean meats can readily meet those choline targets.

Earlier studies, they noted, have also linked eating patterns such as the Mediterranean diet with better thinking later in life.

The clearest link appeared among people with the least education. Of those taking part, 1,025 had gone no further than primary school, including 387 who could not read.

Within this group, people eating more lecithin scored nearly a point higher. For the other 892, who had reached junior high school or beyond, there was barely any gap.

The pattern didn’t vary reliably with age, sex or the chronic diseases the team checked. Education was different, and the authors think cognitive reserve could help explain why.

Schooling and mental effort may give the brain more ways to cope with damage.

Someone with less of that reserve might be more sensitive to dietary differences, although the study cannot establish whether changing their meals would help.

Red blood cell membranes offered another way to compare the groups, since they can reflect fats eaten over time.

For this part, the team randomly chose 15 people with mild cognitive impairment and 15 without it, then examined blood samples.

There was less lecithin in the cell membranes of people with impairment. And what was there contained a different mix: less of it carried polyunsaturated fatty acids, while more carried saturated fatty acids.

One member of the polyunsaturated family is DHA, a fat found in high amounts in nerve cells.

A form of lecithin carrying linoleic acid, another polyunsaturated fat, was one of six membrane fats that best distinguished the groups.

This was a small comparison, with only 30 people in all. The analysis also could not single out lecithin carrying DHA.

One thing this study cannot settle is the direction of the link. Diet and thinking were measured together, so it’s possible that memory problems had already changed people’s eating habits.

The team had no information on household income or household size, which can influence both diet and brain health. Participants also had to remember what they ate, leaving room for errors.

All participants came from three cities in China, and doctors made diagnoses without a full set of memory tests.

Studies elsewhere might find a different pattern.

The authors suggested that asking about lecithin intake could eventually become an inexpensive first step in community memory screening.

A model that combined intake with age, sex, schooling, calories and several health measures told the two groups apart reasonably well.

For now, the study cannot tell us whether eating more lecithin slows memory decline. To find out, the authors called for research that follows older adults for years, tracking their meals and their thinking.

The study is published in the journal Chinese Medical Journal.

#6372. Ancient Indigenous practice may help clams survive ocean acidification

Scientists found that adding crushed shells to clam beds may help young clams cope with ocean acidification, supporting a traditional Indigenous practice.

For a young clam, growing a shell takes energy. As the ocean absorbs more carbon dioxide and becomes more acidic, that job gets harder.

A new lab experiment suggests that mixing crushed shells into the sand can ease some of that strain. The practice has long been part of how some Indigenous communities care for clam beds.

Young clams in acidified seawater showed substantial changes in gene activity.

When researchers added crushed shells to their sand, those changes largely disappeared, and their gene activity looked much like that of clams in regular seawater.

Hannah Kempf led the study as a doctoral student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at the University of California, Davis. Her team raised the clams in buckets at Bodega Marine Laboratory for 90 days.

The ocean’s surface has become about 30% more acidic since the industrial era began.

As seawater absorbs carbon dioxide released by people, it loses some of the chemical building blocks that animals need to make shells.

That means clams, oysters and mussels must spend more energy building their shells. Acidic water can also dissolve them.

In the early 2000s, coastal acidification contributed to widespread losses at Pacific Northwest oyster hatcheries.

Scientists and hatchery workers tested ways to help, including adding soda ash to tanks holding oyster larvae.

Burrowing clams face the problem beneath the sand.

Pacific littleneck clams live about two to six inches (five to 15 centimeters) below the surface, where water between the sand grains, called pore water, is usually more acidic than the seawater above.

Along North America’s Northwest coast, some Indigenous communities have long cared for beaches as clam gardens.

That care can include mixing crushed shells, known as shell hash, into the sediment.

These gardens reflect traditional ecological knowledge built through generations of tending coastal habitats.

Near Bodega Bay, about 60 miles (97 kilometers) north of San Francisco, archaeological sites show that Coast Miwok communities managed clam beds.

Coast Miwok clam gardening ended in the 1930s under a federal policy based on the belief that harvesting would reduce clam numbers.

The restrictions instead led to smaller clam populations across the region, with clams nearly disappearing from some places.

The experiment began with 19 adult Pacific littleneck clams from Bodega Harbor.

They spawned overnight in the lab, and their offspring grew for 200 days before the test began.

Researchers divided the young clams between regular seawater and water made more acidic by adding carbon dioxide.

Within each water treatment, some clams lived in plain sand and others lived in sand mixed with crushed shells.

The team broke the shells with a mortar and pestle. Shell pieces made up 10% of the sand mixture by weight.

The acidified seawater averaged a pH of 7.3, compared with 7.8 in regular seawater. A lower pH means more acidic water.

Each week, researchers collected pore water from about three inches (eight centimeters) below the sand’s surface. In plain sand beneath regular seawater, this water became more acidic as the experiment continued.

Adding crushed shells helped keep the pore water’s acidity steadier. It also left that water less acidic than pore water in plain sand under the same seawater conditions.

The team also calculated how favorable the water was for forming aragonite, a mineral that clams use to build their shells.

Under acidified seawater, this measure stayed below 0.5 for most of the experiment in plain sand, while crushed shells kept it close to one.

Before the experiment, the clams spent a day in a dye that marked their shell edges and glowed under a special microscope.

At the end, researchers measured how much shell had grown beyond that line in 130 clams.

In acidified seawater, clams in plain sand added new shell equal to 4.7% of their length. Those living with crushed shells added 6.4%.

Under regular seawater, the two groups grew by similar amounts: 7.7% in plain sand and 7.9% with crushed shells.

Clams generally grew less in acidified water. Although those living with crushed shells showed greater growth, the difference was not statistically significant.

The genetic results revealed a clearer pattern than the growth measurements.

The team examined tissue from 24 clams and found 284 genes whose activity was at least four times higher or lower in one group than in another.

Clams raised in acidified water over plain sand had gene activity that stood apart from every other group.

Among the other three groups, no more than 11 of those 284 genes differed between any two of them.

So the clams living in acidified water over crushed shells had gene activity much like that of clams in regular seawater.

Researchers couldn’t match most of the 284 genes to a known job.

One that they could match resembles a gene for a protein that helps some mollusks control shell formation, and earlier research found that oysters need that protein to grow proper shells in acidified seawater.

The experiment used only two buckets for each condition, making differences harder to detect. The clams also began at different sizes, which the analysis did not account for.

The buckets contained clean quartz sand. Real beaches have microbes, mixed sediments and changing tides, and field studies have produced mixed results.

On a mudflat in the northeastern United States, an earlier study found that a shell-mineral reading around 0.4 killed many young hard clams. Adding crushed shells tripled their survival over 30 days.

But on a mudflat in New Brunswick, Canada, crushed shells raised the pH only slightly, and the effect disappeared after two months. The authors suggested that the approach may work best in small, local patches of habitat.

Study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz, described how this research could support communities.

“If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices,” said Schneider.

The team did not test the thin surface layer of sand where baby clams first settle.

The authors called for field studies of clam bed tending, designed for individual sites in partnership with Indigenous communities.

The study is published in the journal Biogeosciences.

#6371. Nearly one million hospital stays reveal a surprising pattern in patient survival

Patients treated by female doctors had lower death rates in a study of nearly one million hospital stays, with the greatest difference among female patients.

When you need hospital care, you usually don’t get to choose your doctor. Who looks after you often depends on the hospital’s rotating schedule.

A study of nearly a million hospital stays in Ontario found that patients were less likely to die within 30 days of admission when a woman led their care.

That finding shows a link, but it doesn’t prove that the doctor’s sex caused the difference.

Angela Jerath, a scientist at ICES, an independent health research institute in Ontario, led the study. She is also an associate professor of anesthesiology at the University of Toronto’s Temerty Faculty of Medicine.

“Past research has largely focused on surgical patients and the admitting physician only,” Jerath said.

“Our findings add to the growing body of research examining the relationship between physician sex and patient outcomes, broadening the evidence beyond surgical care to a wider range of medical conditions and other physicians.”

The researchers studied health records for 958,150 adults admitted to Ontario hospitals between 2008 and 2022. Each patient had one of seven common conditions.

These included heart attacks, heart failure, strokes, and pneumonia.

The team also included patients with bleeding in the digestive tract, a long-term lung disease that makes breathing difficult, or an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation.

When patients or referring doctors choose a physician, that doctor’s patients may differ in ways medical records don’t capture.

Researchers call this referral bias, and Jerath said assigning hospital doctors through rotating schedules helps limit it.

Those schedules also mean that several doctors may care for one patient. A typical hospital stay for a medical illness lasts about five days, so a patient might see a male doctor one day and a female doctor the next.

The researchers accounted for these changes by measuring care in two ways. First, they identified each patient’s main doctor, meaning the physician responsible for the most days of their stay.

They also calculated how much of the hospital stay female doctors managed. This let them look beyond the doctor who first admitted the patient.

Of the 15,165 doctors in the study, about 36% were women. A woman served as the main doctor for 259,759 patients, a little more than a quarter of the total.

Before comparing deaths, the team adjusted for patients’ age, income, frailty, and other illnesses. They also accounted for doctors’ age, experience, and workload.

After those adjustments, an estimated 12.3% of patients whose main doctor was female died within 30 days. Among patients whose main doctor was male, the figure was 13.7%.

Each additional 10% of a hospital stay managed by female doctors was associated with about 7% lower odds of dying within 30 days.

Both measures pointed to the same result, which the authors listed as a strength of the study.

The lower death rate appeared in six of the seven illnesses, in teaching and community hospitals, and among patients of both family doctors and specialists. Patients of female doctors were also slightly less likely to return to the hospital within 30 days.

Earlier US research involving older Medicare patients found a similar pattern. That included a 2017 study of patients treated by hospital internists, doctors who specialize in medical care for adults.

The difference was larger among female patients. Their 30-day death rate was about 1.3 percentage points lower when a woman was their main doctor, compared with about 0.75 percentage points among male patients.

Female patients treated by female doctors had the lowest 30-day death rate of any patient-doctor pairing in the study.

A 2024 US study of Medicare patients also found a larger benefit for women treated by female doctors. The Ontario researchers said their finding raises a question for future research, rather than explaining why this happens.

Patients with female main doctors continued to have lower odds of dying over longer periods, but the gap narrowed. Their odds of death were about 12% lower at 30 days, 8% lower at 90 days, and 4% lower at one year.

The pattern for hospital readmissions changed too. By 90 days, patients of male and female main doctors had returned to the hospital at similar rates.

By one year, patients of female doctors were slightly more likely to have been readmitted. Their initial hospital stays also lasted about 5% longer.

Atrial fibrillation was the exception to the early survival finding. For patients with that condition, neither measure showed a link between the doctor’s sex and deaths within 30 days.

The study couldn’t tell the researchers why patients of female doctors had better survival rates. Medical records don’t reveal how much time a doctor spent at the bedside or what the doctor and patient discussed.

Earlier research cited by the authors offers some possible explanations. Female doctors may spend more time with patients, involve them more in decisions, and show more empathy.

They may also order appropriate tests and prescribe treatments that follow clinical guidelines more often.

Some studies suggest that female doctors take a more cautious approach to treatment and seek advice from colleagues more frequently.

“The goal is not to favor one group of physicians over another but to identify practices and behaviors that may help improve care across the health system,” Jerath said.

The researchers used the sex doctors reported when registering to practice, which doesn’t capture gender.

They had no information about ethnicity or disability, or about how trainees and other team members contributed to care.

The female doctors were generally younger, had less experience, and treated fewer patients each year than the male doctors. Their patients were slightly older and frailer.

The team adjusted for those differences, but medical records can only tell part of the story. Factors the researchers couldn’t measure might still explain some of the gap.

They also couldn’t account for handoffs between doctors, differences in how doctors practiced, or expectations about workload and pay.

The study covered people admitted to hospitals, so its findings don’t apply to patients treated in clinics.

The researchers called for closer examination of how doctors deliver care, including their decisions about tests, treatments, and communication with patients.

They also recommended studying hospitals in other countries to see whether the same pattern holds.

Understanding what drives these differences could help improve hospital care for everyone.

The study is published in the journal JAMA Network Open.
