#6370. Satellites reveal hidden flooding along the North Carolina coast

Scientists combined satellite data to create detailed daily flood maps of North Carolina wetlands, revealing hidden flooding that could influence methane emissions.

Flooding along the North Carolina coast doesn’t always look dramatic. There may be no raging rivers or streets swallowed by water.

Sometimes, the difference between dry land and a flooded landscape is just a few inches.

The Albemarle-Pamlico Peninsula just sits there, nearly flat, less than a meter above sea level across almost half its surface, buffered from the Atlantic by a thin chain of barrier islands.

The soils are organic muck. The forests are part hardwood swamp, part moss.

More than 70 percent of the land spends some portion of the year underwater – and has done so long before anyone started worrying about sea-level rise.

It is also, for exactly these reasons, one of the harder places on earth to watch from space. A team at North Carolina State University spent five years trying.

They used a method that fuses radar and optical satellite data into daily flood probability maps at six-meter resolution. That’s fine-grained enough to catch the small, short-lived inundation events that standard products miss entirely.

Wetlands are the planet’s largest natural methane source.

How much methane a wetland releases depends partly on how long and how deeply it floods.

Waterlogged soils contain less oxygen, creating conditions that allow methane-producing microbes to thrive. Brief and small floods matter too.

And yet current global estimates of inundated area carry enough uncertainty to account for roughly a third of what we don’t understand about atmospheric methane.

Most of that uncertainty comes from wetlands smaller than 1,000 square meters. These wetlands are flooding and draining faster than satellites with 30-meter pixels and 16-day revisit cycles can follow.

The study compared three sensors before combining them. Sentinel-2, the European Space Agency’s optical satellite, achieved 93.9 percent accuracy classifying dry land, inundated vegetation, and open water.

PlanetScope, the commercial CubeSat constellation operated by Planet Labs, reached 88.4 percent and resolved fine-scale open-water features particularly well.

Sentinel-1, which uses radar to observe Earth’s surface, achieved 84.6 percent accuracy. Unlike optical satellites, it can collect observations through clouds.

These limitations make it difficult to monitor flooding consistently throughout the year. Persistent cloud cover can block optical satellite observations for weeks at a time.

PlanetScope lacks the shortwave infrared band that most reliably separates water from waterlogged vegetation. Stack those limitations and a single-sensor flood record has systematic gaps.

The team chose to classify each sensor independently and then combine the results, rather than training a joint model from scratch.

The logic was practical: with limited training data, a combined model risks learning the quirks of the training set rather than the actual landscape.

Keeping the sensors separate preserves what each does best – Sentinel-2’s infrared sensitivity, Sentinel-1’s backscatter ratios, and PlanetScope’s spatial density. Using them together handles the disagreements.

To combine the observations, the researchers used a statistical technique called fixed-rank kriging. The method analyzes how flooding changes across both space and time.

Instead of simply averaging the satellite measurements, it accounts for differences in their reliability. This allows scientists to estimate where flooding is likely to occur, even when direct observations are missing.

The result is a five-year record of daily flood probability maps at six-meter resolution, complete with estimates of uncertainty.

The maps were validated against water-table measurements from two AmeriFlux flux towers, a USGS stream gauge, and lake-elevation records. They caught short flood pulses that no individual sensor detected.

The peninsula includes the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge and one of the East Coast’s largest pocosin complexes.

It’s threaded with drainage ditches and canals dug over centuries for agriculture and forestry, now interacting in unpredictable ways with rising groundwater and Atlantic storm surge.

The microtopography alone makes inundation complex. Tree bases sit on hummocks above the waterline while the surrounding ground stays permanently saturated. No single satellite pass, on any given day, can fully capture that.

That complexity is increasingly normal for low-lying coastal wetlands globally. The framework here is modular and sensor-agnostic.

New data streams can be added as they become available. They might include the forthcoming L-band radar satellites.

These should be able to detect flooding beneath the tree canopy that current instruments can’t reliably penetrate.

The immediate use is methane and carbon modeling.

Inundation probability can be fed directly into biogeochemical models rather than handing them a single deterministic map and pretending the uncertainty doesn’t exist.

The longer ambition is a continuous, high-resolution record of the brief floods that rarely make headlines but matter enormously. They drive greenhouse-gas exchange, support migratory wildlife, and recharge aquifers.

They also signal early-stage hydrological change – the kind that sea-level rise is forcing across the coastal zone faster than most monitoring systems can follow.

The study is published in the Journal of Remote Sensing.

#6369. NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

#6368. Keurig and Caraway Take Aim At Coffee Waste With New Plastic-Free Machines

Two new coffee makers are making a case for better coffee and less waste at home.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I was a barista for six years in my late teens and early twenties, and during that time I learned the ins and outs of an espresso machine, how to make latte art, what different bean grinds mean for flavor, and which drinks need more milk foam than others. I love having this kind of knowledge; however, most people who drink coffee daily aren’t familiar with these details. For most coffee drinkers, the morning starts with a simple drip coffee, a flavored cup made with a single-serve K-cup, or a stop at the Starbucks or Dunkin’ drive-thru.

Although single-serve coffee makers are wonderfully convenient for coffee novices, popular models like Keurigs and Nespresso machines create a big problem that environmental advocates have discussed for years: large amounts of plastic and aluminum waste. Every time you make a cup of coffee in one of these machines, you’re discarding a filtered pod. In time, the waste adds up.

If you’re becoming more eco-conscious about your coffee consumption this holiday season, two new products are worth considering: the Keurig Alta and the Caraway Non-Toxic 10-Cup Drip Coffee Maker. Both are fully plastic-free, at-home coffee makers designed to improve your daily coffee routine while reducing waste and exposure to chemicals in plastics.

Keurig is taking its first swing at the espresso market with the Alta, a single-serve machine designed to bring coffeehouse-style drinks to people who don’t want to play barista before their first cup. The big change is the AltaRound, a compact puck of finely ground coffee with a plant-based coating that replaces the traditional K-Cup for espresso brewing. Drop one in, select your drink, and the machine does the rest—no grinder, no tamping, no guesswork. Even the milk steaming is automated, and the machine is programmed to froth different types of milk perfectly, from regular dairy milk to oat milk.

The Alta can brew espresso at up to 10 bars of pressure, and its recipe-reading technology automatically adjusts brewing parameters for different drinks. An integrated milk frother rounds out the setup, making lattes, cappuccinos, and other café staples a few button presses away. It also accepts standard K-Cup pods, so existing Keurig owners don’t have to abandon their old favorites.

The most interesting part may be the new pod format. AltaRounds ditch the rigid plastic capsule in favor of pressed coffee and a plant-based coating, though the individual rounds still come in plastic freshness wrappers. It’s a fresh approach to the single-serve formula, and one that puts Keurig in a more premium corner of the coffee market.

In testing, I was very impressed with the drink quality and the improved taste compared to a regular K-Cup. The AltaRounds preserve freshness very well and do produce a more robust-tasting coffee. I am admittedly not the biggest fan of the taste of classic K-Cups and prefer fresher, stronger coffee, and the AltaRounds delivered for me.

I will also say, at $500, this machine is not cheap, but it is much more affordable than other espresso machines on the market, especially fully automated models. So if you drink coffee every day and want an upgrade, this machine is worth a look.

For drip-coffee folks, Caraway is bringing its signature design-forward approach to the coffee counter with its first-ever coffee maker, a 10-cup drip machine built around one big idea: keeping plastic out of your brew. Its Clean Brew System uses a glass water reservoir and carafe, along with stainless steel tubing, a shower head, and a brew basket, so water and coffee never touch plastic along the way.

The machine is simple to use, too: A single dial handles brewing and cleaning, while a controlled bloom cycle and precise temperature management produce a balanced, evenly extracted cup. A reusable stainless steel filter comes standard, and a warming plate keeps coffee hot for up to 90 minutes. There’s no touchscreen or laundry list of settings to fiddle with — just a straightforward pot of coffee.

Of course, Caraway’s knack for making kitchen essentials look good is part of the appeal. The metal-bodied machine comes in muted shades including Cream, Stone, Clay, and Midnight, and looks more like a considered countertop accessory than a utilitarian appliance. At $495, it's still quite the serious splurge for a drip coffee maker.

Both machines make high-quality coffee conveniently and plastic-free. Personally, I prefer the Keurig. For the price, you get so much more. I love a good cortado or cold foam iced latte, and this machine makes that easier than ever.

For me and my tastes, I’m definitely pro Keurig Alta; I’m even recommending it to friends and family who have reached out asking for espresso machine recommendations. If you don’t know the ins and outs of coffeehouse-style beverages but want an easy latte at home, the Alta is a game-changer.

Meanwhile, our Deputy Editor, Eunice Lucero-Lee, loves how the Caraway 10-Cup Coffee Maker fits perfectly into her new plastic-avoidant lifestyle. Its stainless steel and glass brew path ensures a “clean” drip each time, and a quick, easy one at that. The handy reusable filter also cuts down on waste. As a newbie to the whole home coffee experience (she’s been staunchly #TeamEarlGrey for most of her life), the beginner-friendly single-dial mechanism is super intuitive — and a fantastic, elevated starting point.

#6366. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:

#6364. The Sky Today on Friday, October 30: Mars approaches Leo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Magnitude 0.8 Mars, currently tracking eastward through the sky, now stands at the border of Cancer and Leo. It is still within the bounds of the Crab this morning, roughly 60° high in the southeast and just over 6° to the upper right of brighter Jupiter in Leo, about 90 minutes before sunrise.

To Jupiter’s east (lower left) is magnitude 1.4 Regulus, the brightest star in the Lion, which also serves as the great cat’s heart. Together with Jupiter and Mars, the three form a line slashing upward in the predawn sky.

Far to the planetary pair’s upper right is Procyon, the bright nose of Canis Minor, the Little Dog. And to that star’s far lower right is even brighter Sirius, the nose of Canis Major, the Big Dog — the brightest star in the sky. However, Jupiter (at magnitude –2.0) currently outshines Sirius’ magnitude –1.4 glow.

Mars will continue to move east, joining Jupiter in Leo by tomorrow morning.

#6363. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

#6361. Rubin spots possible dwarf planet

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory may have found its first dwarf planet. Orbiting beyond Pluto, the object may also be one of the brightest and biggest in that stretch of the solar system.

Matthew Holman, a Rubin operations team member and senior astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, discovered the dwarf planet candidate, now designated 2026 ED138, on the night of Oct. 13. Holman was running Rubin data from earlier this year through a computer program that hunts for moving objects in the solar system. When Holman saw ED138, he immediately noticed how bright and far away it was, and wondered if it was a fluke.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief. Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong,” he said in a statement.

The Rubin team investigated whether any other data could confirm what Holman had uncovered. Mario Jurić, Rubin’s solar system lead scientist at the University of Washington, combed through more Rubin data and found 20 more sightings dating back to March 4, 2026. In all, Rubin caught sight of the object 30 times over 20 nights. Researchers also found ED138 in archival images going back to 2016. Those images came from the Dark Energy Camera on the U.S. National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile. With this plethora of observations, the team was able to trace the candidate dwarf planet’s orbit over the last 10 years.

The team presented its findings Oct. 27 at the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences meeting in Spokane, Washington. The International Astronomical Union’s (IAU) Minor Planet Center announced the discovery the same day.

If confirmed, ED138 will become the sixth dwarf planet recognized in our solar system. It would join Ceres, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, and most notably Pluto, which was demoted to dwarf planet status in 2006.

Pluto’s demotion traces back to Eris’ 2005 discovery, which revealed an icy world roughly Pluto’s size and forced astronomers to decide whether both or neither were planets. In 2006, the IAU formally defined the term planet for the first time. A planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to pull itself into a sphere, and have cleared its orbital path of other debris. A dwarf planet meets the first two criteria but not the third.

It wasn’t the first time a discovery had redrawn the map. Ceres was hailed as a planet when it was found in 1801, and is the largest body in the main belt between Mars and Juptier. As similar objects kept turning up over the following decades, Ceres and its neighbors were reclassified as asteroids — although Ceres is now considered a dwarf planet by the IAU, following the 2006 decision.

ED138 also falls under the classification of trans-Neptunian object (TNO), which are bodies that circle the Sun beyond the orbit of Neptune. Aside from Ceres, the solar system’s other four known dwarf planets are also classified as TNOs

RELATED: Could we find Planet Nine using JWST?

Based on the data collected so far, researchers know that ED138 orbits roughly 46 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun, or 46 times Earth’s distance from the Sun. That puts it farther out than Pluto, which averages roughly 40 AU. Its brightness and albedo (surface reflectivity) suggest a diameter between 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 kilometers). Further infrared observations will allow scientists to pin down the object’s size more accurately. For now, it appears to be among the largest and brightest dwarf planet candidates found beyond Neptune.

Located on Cerro Pachón in Chile, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory is funded by the NSF and the Department of Energy’s Office of Science. It is operated jointly by NSF NOIRLab and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The observatory officially began its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) at the end of June. The survey uses the world’s largest digital camera, the 3,200-megapixel LSST Camera, to sweep the entire southern sky every few nights. It is designed to help scientists tackle four big questions: the nature of dark matter and dark energy, the makeup of the solar system, how the sky changes over time, and the structure of the Milky Way.

“Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach,” said Holman.

#6360. The Sky Today on Saturday, October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Let’s send off spooky season on a high note this Halloween with M74, also known as the Phantom Galaxy.

The best time to catch this ghostly galaxy is after darkness falls but before moonrise. Located in eastern Pisces, M74 reaches an altitude of 45° in the east by 9 P.M. local daylight time. You can find it just over 1° northeast of 4th-magnitude Eta (η) Piscium, or by skimming 6.6° southwest of  brighter 3rd-magnitude Beta (β) Arietis, also called Sheratan.

Ninth-magnitude M74 spans roughly 11’ in diameter — that’s quite big, because this galaxy is so nearby, just 24 million light-years away. Because it is so large, its light is spread out over a significant area, lowering its overall surface brightness and making this galaxy harder to spot than its magnitude would imply — hence its “phantom” moniker.

Once you do find it, you’ll see that M74 is a lovely face-on spiral with a bright core wrapped in fainter arms, the latter of which are best seen in 8-inch and larger scopes. The arms are mottled with bright regions of star formation, and a nebula filter can help improve the view. You may also notice the arms are not quite symmetric: the western arm is much longer than the stubby eastern one.

Sunrise: 7:28 A.M.Sunset: 5:59 P.M.Moonrise: 11:08 P.M.Moonset: 1:33 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (58%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time on November 1, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early on the 1st, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6357. November 2026: What’s in the Southern Hemisphere sky this month?

Although Venus has dominated the evening sky since last summer, its long apparition came to an end at inferior conjunction in late October. That leaves Saturn as the only naked-eye planet visible as the sky darkens this month. The ringed planet glows at magnitude 0.5 as it edges westward relative to the background stars of northwestern Cetus the Whale.

Saturn reached opposition and peak visibility in early October, but the distant world’s appearance changes so slowly that you’ll find it nearly as impressive through a telescope as it was last month. In mid-November, the planet measures 19″ across its equator while the ring system spans 43″ and tilts 6° to our line of sight. Any telescope reveals Saturn’s brightest moon, 8th-magnitude Titan, and a 10-centimeter instrument brings in Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, which all glow at 10th magnitude.

November’s morning sky offers a bevy of treats. A few hours after midnight, you’ll see two planets forming an attractive trio with 1st-magnitude Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo the Lion.

During the month’s first half, Mars rises first with Jupiter following close behind. The Red Planet moves eastward against the backdrop of western Leo, passing both Jupiter and Regulus during November. The ruddy world slides 1.2° north of Jupiter on the 15th and 1.8° north of Regulus on the 24th. Mars glows at magnitude 0.7 at midmonth, slightly but noticeably brighter than Regulus. Compare the orange-red color of the planet with the star’s blue-white hue.

Mars’ appearance through a telescope grows a bit more interesting during November. The planet spans 7″ at midmonth, large enough to show some subtle surface detail during moments of good seeing.

Jupiter steals the show in this part of the sky, however. Shining at magnitude –2.1 and with a disk measuring 37″ across, it easily bests its planetary companion in both brightness and telescopic splendor. The gas giant features a series of alternating atmospheric bands, with bright zones and darker belts running parallel to one another. Even under mediocre seeing conditions, the central Equatorial Zone and its neighboring belts stand out.

The approach of dawn brings the final two naked-eye planets into view. Venus appears first. It rises less than an hour before sunrise in early November but more than two hours before the Sun at month’s end. You won’t mistake the brilliant planet for any other object. It brightens from magnitude –4.2 on the 1st to magnitude –4.9 at month’s end.

A telescope reveals impressive changes to Venus during November, though its large crescent remains a treat all month. On the 1st, you’ll see a disk that measures a whopping 1′ across but is only 3 percent lit. By the 30th, the planet spans 40″ while the Sun illuminates 27 percent of its Earth-facing hemisphere.

Mercury passes between the Sun and Earth on Nov. 4 and slowly climbs into view after midmonth. The shallow angle of the ecliptic — the apparent path of the Sun and planets across the sky — to the eastern horizon before dawn at this time of year means the planet never gains a lot of altitude. On the 30th, it stands 5° high 30 minutes before sunrise.

Still, the innermost planet shines brightly at magnitude –0.7 and should be visible in the twilight. Point you telescope at Mercury that morning and you’ll see a disk 6″ in diameter and 83 percent lit.

A waning gibbous Moon occults Regulus on Nov. 30 Universal Time. Residents in New Zealand can watch the event in the early morning hours of Dec. 1 local time. From Auckland, the star disappears behind the Moon’s bright limb at 13h24m UT and reappears from behind the dark limb at 14h23m UT.

Look high in the south on any November evening and the relatively dim constellation Tucana the Toucan comes into view. Tucana’s brightest star, Alpha (α) Tucanae, glows at 3rd magnitude. The easiest way to find the constellation is to look just southwest of magnitude 0.5 Achernar, the brightest star in Eridanus the River. Tucana does possess two deep-sky treasures, however: the Small Magellanic Cloud and the stunning globular star cluster 47 Tucanae.

The origin of the constellation’s name remains a source of confusion. Sixteenth-century Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman devised the constellation in the late 16th century. Flemish astronomer Petrus Plancius first placed Tucana on a celestial globe in 1598.

Yet Keyser and de Houtman observed the sky from what we now know as the East Indies after visiting Madagascar, and the toucan is not native to that part of the world. The brightly colored bird resides in Central and South America, which lies about 180° in longitude from the East Indies.

In 1603, De Houtman published Malay and Madagascan Vocabulary, which included a star catalog. He headed his entry for the constellation Tucana “The Indian Magpie, named by the Indians Lang.” On the line below, he included the subhead “Tucana.”

This is where Keyser comes back into the story. He once visited South America and likely had observed toucans. It seems plausible that the confusion arose because the toucan bears some similarity to the oriental pied hornbill of the East Indies.

The map below portrays the sky as seen near 30° south latitude. Located inside the border are the cardinal directions and their intermediate points. To find stars, hold the map overhead and orient it so one of the labels matches the direction you’re facing. The stars above the map’s horizon now match what’s in the sky.

The all-sky map shows how the sky looks at:

11 p.m. November 110 p.m. November 159 p.m. November 30

Dr. Martin George is an astronomy speaker and writer who currently serves as Chair of International Development and Elections at the International Planetarium Society.

#6356. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

J.M. Young et al. Permafrost detachment slides: a distinct high‐magnitude permafrost mass wasting process. Geophysical Research Letters. 2026. doi: 10.1029/2026GL124103

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

#6355. I Can ‘Smell’ Thoughts. You Can Too—and It’s Secretly Shaping Your Life.

You may be able to sniff out everything from emotions to political beliefs.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Staring into the crowded refrigerator, I pushed containers of cold leftovers to and fro, willing a more appetizing late-night snack to appear. Over the low electric hum, I heard footsteps approaching from the other side of the open door. Before I saw my father’s somber face, a smell, or something like it, caught my attention. Instantly, I recognized it—not from the actual odor, as I couldn’t put my finger on any one recognizable scent, but more so from a memory.

This was the same way my dad smelled when he sat me and my sister down to tell us his own father had died. The same way he smelled when he picked me up early from high school to break the news about my maternal grandmother. The sadness in my dad’s voice came as no shock to me. Someone was dead. I knew with complete certainty that it was true. What I didn’t understand was how my nose knew it first.

Olfaction—or your sense of smell—is an integral part of human perception. It alerts us to potentially dangerous environmental factors such as smoke or gas, supports other senses such as taste, and a good sense of smell is even linked to lower rates of cognitive decline. Thinking back to that day in the kitchen, I began to wonder whether my sense of smell had tuned me into a silent conversation everyone else was missing. As it turns out, a growing volume of research suggests that scent is quietly shaping how we perceive one another and, more broadly, our reality. For some, it even appears to be a superpower—allowing them to detect, just through their sense of smell, illnesses and undiagnosed diseases in others.

One of these super smellers is a woman named Joy Milne, whose sense of smell is so acute that she’s able to detect when someone has tuberculosis, cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer’s disease, or Parkinson’s disease. Researchers put Milne’s nose to the test in a 2019 study published in ACS Central Science. The team asked two groups—one afflicted with Parkinson’s disease and the other healthy—to wear identical T-shirts overnight. When Milne smelled the shirts the next day, she was able to correctly sort all but one using just the power of her sniffer.

Months later, the participant whose smell Milne had mistakenly slotted into the Parkinson’s category reported that he had been diagnosed with the disease. Milne’s nose had picked up on something long before doctors had diagnosed it.

Pamela Dalton, PhD, MPH, studies the link between human olfaction and our cognitive and emotional processes at the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, a scientific institute researching taste and smell. She says that, while not everyone has a nose attuned to medical maladies, the human olfactory system is constantly working overtime to decode and process the world in much more subtle ways.

In fact, when I confessed the story about my father announcing that my great-uncle had died, Dalton wasn’t fazed.

Dalton says humans communicate their feelings to each other through chemical molecules released in sweat, tears, or breath. These are called emotional chemical signals or emotional chemosignals. When the signals you give off reach another person, their olfactory system detects and interprets the chemicals. However, these aren’t processed the same way as regular smells.

Most of the time, we connect our smells to other senses stored in our memories—how a food tastes, or how salty ocean air may feel calming. If you’re sitting in front of a slice of pizza, for example, those molecules bond with the sensory receptors in your nose, generating an electric current that ends up in two areas of your brain that are associated with your sense of smell—the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex. As the current continues traveling through your brain, regions associated with memory and emotional regulation complete higher processing to link that signal with your previously stored understanding of the smell of pizza.

With chemosignaling, on the other hand, a final association is never made. This is likely why the scent on my dad was familiar but not recognizable. In fact, to most people, chemosignals have no recognizable fragrance at all—so you won’t find a Yankee Candle that smells like sadness or an air freshener that reeks of stress.

Instead, chemosignaling acts as an invisible guiding force. It’s something most of us do all the time. We unconsciously filter our perception of people and the world around us through these involuntary olfactory noticings. These signals cause us to constantly make little judgments about others, everything from what someone’s feeling to whether they’d be a good romantic partner.

You May Be Able to Smell Political Beliefs

Opposite-party partnerships are uncommon, according to an ever-growing body of research. Researchers put that partisan divide to the test in a 2014 study published in the American Journal of Political Science where they tried to determine whether our sniffers play a role. The team found that participants were more attracted to the smell of people whose political beliefs aligned closely with their own. Crucially, the study subjects didn’t see the people whose scents they were analyzing, meaning visual attraction played no role in the end results.

Dalton says the process of sending and receiving chemosignals usually bypasses conscious thought, meaning that we do it involuntarily and without noticing it. “It’s not like we’re [observing these chemical signals] and going, ‘Oh… she’s sad, I’m smelling her sad odor,’” Dalton says.

However, that doesn’t mean that these signals go completely unnoticed. When your olfactory system senses someone else’s chemosignals, it can trigger changes in your perception, mood, or physical reaction, Dalton adds. In everyday terms, this may look like feeling inexplicably on edge around a friend who’s secretly stressed about a presentation they have at work the next day.

Nicholas A. Christakis, MD, PhD, MPH, is a social scientist at Yale University and the director of the school’s Human Nature Lab, a project dedicated to understanding human interaction. Christakis affirms Dalton’s ideas about chemosignals, pointing to something much deeper in our species’ history. He explains that humans evolved in a “very logical way,” since we emit volatile chemicals into the air during our most vulnerable, fear-filled moments. These chemicals then change the behavior of those around us in ways that, theoretically, would enhance survival, he says.

Christakis poses a few scenarios in which our ancestors might have felt danger, such as seeing a lion or a fire. “It’s not hard to imagine why, as a social animal, it would be useful to us to communicate to our brethren, ‘I'm afraid,’” he says. In terms of his analogy, if Christakis sees the lion and subconsciously emits these stress chemicals, you may realize he’s in trouble. “By signaling that I’m afraid, I might elicit from you some help,” he adds.

In a more modern example, Christakis points to the intoxicating aroma of a newborn baby. He says that a key part of this smell is an organic compound called hexadecanal. Hexadecanal is completely odorless, meaning that, if you smelled a sample on its own, your brain wouldn’t immediately conjure images of babies.

Despite this, a study published in Science Advances showed that participants unconsciously changed their behavior when asked to smell samples of hexadecanal. Specifically, men showed decreased aggression levels while women displayed the opposite. The theory, Christakis says, is that smelling a baby unconsciously causes people to become more nurturing and protective.

Unlike the participants in the study, I was more conscious of the odor that clung to my dad all those years ago. Still, Dalton explains that what I “smelled” most likely wasn’t the scent of death itself. My olfactory system responded with amplified alertness because it registered the release of chemical signals, perhaps those associated with stress, sadness, or anxiety. Simply put, I didn’t smell the future—I recognized an olfactory pattern I had previously encountered.

Dalton says it’s actually not that uncommon to become attuned to the chemical signals of people you spend a lot of time with. For instance, in a 2010 study published in Social Neuroscience, participants were able to detect heightened emotions in their romantic partners just by smelling their body odors. Additionally, people were more accurate when smelling their partner’s samples compared to those of strangers.

In fact, Dalton herself has even developed a keen nose after years of working with thousands of fear and anxiety sweat samples—a skill that she showed off on an episode of MythBusters. She notes that stress sweat has “a very different quality” than exercise sweat, though she avoids describing the scent to keep herself open to variations, since not everyone’s signals smell the same.

While Dalton acknowledges that there is still much to be learned in this field, she believes that these signals play a major role in shaping human interaction and perception. In short: It seems like sometimes you really should follow your nose.

#6354. Blue whales have gone missing off the Galápagos. Scientists think El Niño could be why.

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

She also participated in the Sharon Dunwoody Mentoring Program 2023 offered by The Open Notebook and has bylines in Science, Scientific American, and Discover Magazine, among other outlets.
