#6353. November 2026: What’s in the sky this month?

Saturn is already visible as darkness falls; some challenging transits of its moons occur this month. Neptune is a binocular object close to Saturn, while Uranus is an easy target in Taurus. A Full Moon courses in front of the Pleiades in late November. Mars and Jupiter dominate the early-morning sky, and in the hour before dawn, look also for Venus and Mercury.

Neptune and Saturn are well placed for observation after sunset. They’re about 7° apart all month, with Neptune in southern Pisces and Saturn just across the border in Cetus. Only Saturn is visible to the naked eye, shining at magnitude 0.5. Neptune, at magnitude 7.7, requires binoculars to spot.

Swing 7×50 binoculars one field of view west of Saturn and look for a parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars: 27, 29, 30, and 33 Piscium. Neptune is within 3° northeast of 29 Psc all month. A waning gibbous Moon hangs 5° northwest of Neptune’s location on the 19th. The following night, Saturn is 6° south of the Moon.

As the month opens, Saturn is 24° high in the east an hour after sunset, reaching 50° by 9 p.m. local time following its opposition last month. It’s observable overnight and by the end of November sets by 2 a.m. local time. The rings are angled 6° to our line of sight and reveal their southern side. The planet spans 19″ through a telescope and the disk exhibits a pale yellowish hue. Atmospheric details are tricky to spot unless you have very good conditions.

Titan, Saturn’s brightest moon (magnitude 8.3), sits closest to the planet Nov. 8 and 24 (north), and Nov. 16 (south). Tenth-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea orbit closer in. Dione and Tethys transit Saturn’s disk this month. These transits and shadow transits are extremely challenging. They’re good targets for advanced observers with video imaging experience. Visit Astronomy.com for more details on the timing of their transits if you’d like to try for them.

Iapetus reaches greatest eastern elongation Nov. 10, when it stands 9.4′ east of Saturn. The moon’s darker face is turned earthward, dimming it to magnitude 11.9. It’s hard to find but as the month progresses, Iapetus brightens nearly a magnitude by the time it reaches inferior conjunction early on the 30th, 1.7′ due north of Saturn.

Uranus remains midway between Aldebaran and the Pleiades (M45). This position makes the planet easier to find than in previous years. It reaches opposition Nov. 25, visible from dusk to dawn. From 1.71 billion miles away, its disk spans 4″. Uranus shines at magnitude 5.6, within easy range of binoculars and potentially visible to the unaided eye from the darkest skies.

To find Uranus, look between Aldebaran and M45 for two stars: 37 and 39 Tauri (4.5° southeast of M45). Brighter 37 Tau glows at magnitude 4.4. On Nov. 1, Uranus is 1.6° southeast of 37 Tau, and by the end of November stands 1.5° due south of this star. Another star, some 2.7° southeast of 37 Tau, shines at magnitude 5.5. This is 43 Tau; in mid-November, Uranus is halfway between the two stars.

The Full Moon crosses the Pleiades early on Nov. 24, setting up a series of occultations of the northern part of the cluster just before dawn across the western half of the U.S. You’ll need a telescope — plan for higher magnification so you can place the brilliant Moon largely out of your field of view. Fifth-magnitude Celaeno is the first of the cluster’s brighter stars to be occulted, around 6 a.m. CST. Both visibility and timing heavily depend on your location, so set up at least 30 minutes before the event starts. You can download timings for the brightest occultations from 40 major North American cities from the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Mars and Jupiter rise close together in Leo. They meet in a conjunction midmonth not far from Leo’s brightest star, Regulus. Mars rises first, soon after midnight on the 1st, followed by Jupiter about 30 minutes later. Jupiter shines at magnitude –2.0 and Mars at 0.8. They’re hard to miss.

On Nov. 1, Jupiter stands midway between Mars and Regulus, each just over 5° from its neighbor. A waning gibbous Moon sits in Cancer only a few degrees west of M44, the Beehive star cluster. On the 2nd, Mars and the Moon are 1.5° apart, and by the 3rd the Moon lies less than 2° from Regulus as they rise in the Midwest. Mars and Jupiter close in on each other, and by the 15th Mars is 1.2° due north of Jupiter.

Mars continues eastward, reaching a point 1.7° due north of Regulus on the 25th. By the 30th, Mars is just over 2° northeast of Regulus and is rejoined by the waning gibbous Moon, just southwest of Regulus. Through a telescope at the end of November, Mars has reached 8″ in diameter and its magnitude has increased to 0.4.

Home to the most visibly dynamic atmosphere in the solar system, Jupiter has a lot to offer through a telescope. The planet shows off a 36″-wide disk on the 1st, which grows to 39″ by the 30th. The hour before dawn can hold remarkable views if there is steady seeing. Look for the occasional appearance of the Great Red Spot.

Jupiter’s moons and their shadows often transit the planet or are eclipsed by it. Nov. 8 finds Io and Callisto transiting Jupiter’s disk along with Io’s shadow. Soon after, Europa exits from an occultation. East Coast observers will see the whole event; the Pacific Coast, only the latter half. It begins as Io’s shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb at 1:29 a.m. EST, followed 24 minutes later by the reappearance of Europa from behind Jupiter. Callisto’s transit begins at 2:07 a.m. EST. Io approaches the eastern limb, passing due north of Europa at 2:23 a.m. EST and beginning its transit 19 minutes later. Because of Io’s faster orbital speed compared with Callisto, it overtakes the larger moon within half an hour. Io’s shadow exits the disk at 3:45 a.m. EST, and Io itself ends its transit 74 minutes later. Callisto’s transit ends at 5:51 a.m. CST, as the sky is growing light in the Midwest.

Ganymede’s huge shadow crosses Jupiter’s face Nov. 11. The start of the transit at 12:27 a.m. EST is visible from the Eastern time zone; it ends at 4:03 a.m. EST, visible across the U.S. Ganymede begins to transit at 5:29 a.m. EST.

Ganymede, Europa, and Io orbit in resonance, so similar events recur, although they are not always observable. On Nov. 15, Io’s shadow begins a transit at 3:22 a.m. EST. Europa reappears at 4:27 a.m. EST, with Io close to the limb. They pass north-south just seven minutes later. Io’s transit begins at 4:36 a.m. EST. Its shadow leaves at 5:38 a.m. EST, and Io departs at 5:52 a.m. CST (in daylight for EST). Ganymede’s shadow transits again three days later, Nov. 18, from 4:25 a.m. EST to 6:01 a.m. MST (note the time zone change).

On Nov. 22, Io and its shadow are already transiting by the time Europa reappears. Io’s shadow transit starts at 5:15 a.m. EST; Io follows at 5:29 a.m. CST, with the sky very bright along the East Coast. Europa reappears at Jupiter’s eastern limb at 6:00 a.m. CST, as twilight begins in the Midwest and visible in darkness farther west.

To cap off the month, watch Ganymede reappear from behind Jupiter Nov. 29 at 5:53 a.m. CST (minutes before sunrise in EST), followed by Io’s shadow transit starting a few minutes later, at 6:08 a.m. CST. Io is due north of Ganymede at 6:49 a.m. CST, seen in twilight in the Midwest.

Mercury is at inferior conjunction Nov. 4, then moves into the morning sky. Northern Hemisphere observers gain good views in the second half of the month. Look for it Nov. 13, when it’s magnitude 0.5. An hour before sunrise, it is 4° high in the eastern sky, nearly 13° to the lower left of Venus. Swing binoculars toward Mercury to spot 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis 0.9° north of the planet.

Mercury reaches its greatest western elongation 20° from the Sun late on Nov. 20. The next morning, it shines at magnitude –0.5 and stands 7° high an hour before sunrise, easy to spot with a clear eastern horizon. Mercury displays a 62%-lit globe when viewed with a telescope, though it spans only 7″, so you’ll need steady air to see the phase. That phase grows to 84% by Nov. 30.

On Nov. 4, look for Venus 2° south of 1st-magnitude Spica, Virgo’s brightest star. A 25-day-old crescent Moon stands high above the pair. Three days later, on Nov. 7, Venus, Spica, and the Moon lie close together in the morning sky. Venus is 1.3° from Spica, with the waning crescent Moon about 2° below Venus, a stunning view in the brightening twilight. Venus rises about 100 minutes before the Sun and the trio is 11° high at 6 a.m. local time.

Venus reaches a stationary point Nov. 11. From the 10th to the 12th, Venus appears not to move in right ascension relative to Spica, as the planet slides due north to stand 1.2° due west of Spica on the 10th.

Check out Venus with a telescope. The bright planet becomes easier on the eyes as twilight grows, reducing the contrast. It’s already dazzling at magnitude –4.2 on the 1st, when its disk is 3% lit. By Nov. 15 it is 14% lit and magnitude –4.8, and reaches its greatest illuminated extent Nov. 29 at magnitude –4.9 and 27% lit. If you’re under Bortle 1 or 2 skies, can you see your shadow? Venus rises more than three hours before the Sun, so you’ll have a dark sky for an hour or so to check.

Much of the Moon’s history is encapsulated in one feature: the crater Schickard, way down in the lunar southwest. Protective measures are necessary to comfortably carry out this observation. Screw in a dark filter, mask off part of your scope’s aperture, or pump up the magnification to reduce the glare of an almost full lunar disk.

Start on the evening of the 21st, when the rays of sunlight strike the flooded crater at a glancing angle, highlighting the differences in height of the smaller features. This is an old crater, its rounded rim pounded down across the ages. The splatter of smaller craters across the smooth floor sport the classic sharp edges of relative youth. The western wall, steep at the instant of formation, slumped abruptly down into terraces that remain visible to this day. Shadows disappear over the next two evenings as the climbing Sun almost erases these features.

During the following nights, Schickard transforms into a two-faced striped crater, an unusual swath of lighter gray painted across the middle of this time-worn feature. The 130-mile-wide depression was carved out some 4 billion years ago as bombardment was ending. Lava soon welled up and covered its central peaks. Then the giant Orientale impact event to the west sprayed the whole region with lighter-hued material. A final surge of lava managed to cover the northern and southern portions, but did not rise enough to erase the lighter stripe.

This year’s annual Leonid meteor shower is active from Nov. 6 to 30 and peaks Nov. 17/18. A nine-day-old gibbous Moon sets right around midnight on this night, favoring the best time for meteor observing, which is after midnight. That’s when we’re on the leading hemisphere as Earth plows into the meteoroid stream.

Leo is also rising around local midnight and the radiant, located in the Sickle asterism, climbs to more than 60° in altitude by dawn. But don’t look at the radiant — meteors come head-on from that direction. Longer trails occur 40° to 60° away from Leo.

Rates are predicted to be 15 meteors per hour if the radiant were overhead. If you get more than a half-dozen per hour, you’re doing well. If you want a change, spend some time with Jupiter (also in Leo) through a telescope — Ganymede’s shadow is transiting the morning of the 18th.

The Leonids are known to be swift and some leave glowing, persistent trains, which are fascinating to experience. The shower is associated with Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which last reached perihelion in 1998.

Comet 10P/Tempel is floating halfway between Fomalhaut and Beta (β) Ceti. It’s about 10th magnitude, but historically has had post-perihelion outbursts, which could help it shine through the thicker air near the ground.

Meanwhile, Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS is higher and in a more interesting sky as darkness settles.

The Moon-free window closes after the 14th but reopens on the 27th. To see this 10th-magnitude fuzzy, a site well away from city lights is needed. Despite Earth’s increasing distance, the comet is sunward bound for perihelion Nov. 27, so its magnitude is fairly constant.

The short, broad fan should sport a circular green coma that looks great on images as it floats across the rich Milky Way north of Altair. At month’s end, Hartley-IRAS lies within 3° of the Coathanger asterism. Visually, a 4-inch scope can pull it in, but a larger one will show more detail, especially the sharp south flank where the solar wind pushes away the expelled dust in a bow shock.

Discovered in 1983, the comet returns every 21.5 years. Next month will be our last chance for a good look until two revolutions down the road, in 2069.

With five minutes of dark adapting, it’s easy to follow a main-belt asteroid along a retrograde curve. Saturn leads the way to 4 Vesta in the midevening sky — just drop down 9°, two binocular fields, to 25 Ceti, a magnitude 5.4 candle compared to the other nearby 8th- to 9th-magnitude stellar points. None of those will get confused with the brighter asteroid.

Use 25 Ceti and the more northerly 20 Ceti (closer to Saturn) to anchor a sketch or your memory. Watch a simple hockey stick pattern morph every three nights or so into a golf club, and then become a vertical line.

Spanning about 320 miles, Vesta is the second-largest body in the main belt. It was initially thought to be a chunk of the “missing” world astronomers expected between Mars and Jupiter. We now know it is an unfinished building block left over from the formation of the solar system, a rocky mantle surrounding an iron core.

The map below portrays the sky as seen near 35° north latitude. Located inside the border are the cardinal directions and their intermediate points. To find stars, hold the map overhead and orient it so one of the labels matches the direction you’re facing. The stars above the map’s horizon now match what’s in the sky.

The all-sky map shows how the sky looks at:

9 p.m. November 18 p.m. November 157 p.m. November 30

Martin Ratcliffe is a planetarium professional with Evans & Sutherland and enjoys observing from Salt Lake City. Alister Ling, who lives in Edmonton, Alberta, is a longtime watcher of the skies.

#6352. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 1: The Moon in Cancer

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time this morning, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early this morning, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

The Moon will reach Last Quarter phase this afternoon at 3:28 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:29 A.M.Sunset: 4:57 P.M.Moonrise: 11:23 P.M.Moonset: 1:11 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (47%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

By 5 A.M. local time on November 2, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter. The gas giant is by far the brightest light here, shining at magnitude –2.0. This morning it lies halfway between the Moon and Regulus to its lower left (east), Leo’s alpha star and the base of the Sickle asterism.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time. Make sure to check out the view tomorrow for comparison.

#6351. A Mysterious Statue Emerged on Easter Island. More Could Be Hiding Right Beneath It.

Three years after the discovery, archaeologists still can’t say how old it is—or whether there are more.

In February 2023, a moai was found lying face-up among reeds in a dried lakebed on Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island. The roughly five-foot statue was small by the island’s standards, but its location surprised archaeologists. It was the first moai reported in the lakebed inside Rano Raraku, the volcanic crater where islanders carved many of their statues.

“The statue was a completed one meant for an ahu platform,” Terry Hunt, an archaeologist and professor of anthropology at the University of Arizona, tells Popular Mechanics. An ahu is a ceremonial platform where moai are displayed. Hunt says this one was carved from the bedrock on the nearby crater walls, then brought to the place where it was discovered.

As reported in our earlier coverage, Hunt described the surprise to Good Morning America. “There have been no moai found in the dry bed or in what was previously a lake, so this is a first.”

The location wasn’t the only surprise. The statue’s small size led Hunt to suggest, in a 2023 University of Arizona account, that it was probably carved early in the period between Polynesian settlement around 1200 and European arrival in 1722—small moai could have been made later, he allowed, but the largest ones likely came after those first years. That possibility is what gives the find its weight: if other early, small statues lie beneath the lakebed, archaeologists could compare them with later moai and trace how the island’s carvers progressed from modest figures to giants. Yet more than three years after the discovery, no one knows how old this moai is or whether it has company. Hunt says there’s been no further investigation.

The small statue could tell a bigger story

In 2023, Hunt was considering ground-penetrating radar to look for buried moai or architecture, particularly in the lakebed. Today, he’s more confident about finding statues buried in quarry rubble than beneath the lakebed. “There are almost certainly statues buried in the rubble and back dirt from quarrying activities in Rano Raraku,” he says. “Perhaps there are others buried in the lakebed sediments.”

A group of statues beneath the lakebed would give researchers more than another addition to the inventory. If they turned out to be early, their appearance and locations could offer clues to how the islanders carved moai and what they were doing around the lake. “Buried statues could be associated with new radiocarbon dates and give us a better idea of the early quarrying activities,” Hunt says. He adds that the statues could reveal stylistic differences that developed over time.

The dates have changed the argument before

Hunt and his colleagues have already shown how much a date can change the story of Rapa Nui. Their research challenged the claim that islanders stopped building monuments after their society collapsed, before Europeans ever arrived.

A 2020 study in the Journal of Archaeological Science examined the chronology of ahu construction at eleven sites. The researchers pieced together radiocarbon dates and evidence from the platforms themselves, alongside accounts from European visitors. They found that islanders kept building and using the monuments for at least 150 years after 1600, when their society was supposedly already in collapse.

The 2020 research changed the account of how long monument-building continued. Early lakebed statues could help fill in the other end of that history, showing what people were carving as the tradition developed.

Finding those statues and studying them are two different problems. “However, excavations in the quarry would be highly unlikely given conservation issues and the islanders’ sentiments about the site,” Hunt says. A geophysical survey could map buried moai without disturbing the ground, but it can’t date them or reveal the carving details that would show how the tradition developed. For that, archaeologists would need to see the stone itself. Conservation pressures cut the other way, too: the Easter Island Statue Project’s discovery report called for stabilizing the newfound moai and protecting its fragile surface, and Hunt notes the soft volcanic tuff continues to erode. The result is a strange bind. A survey could show exactly where Rapa Nui's early history lies, while the most revealing evidence stays underground.

#6349. Four Decades Ago, Scientists Dropped Gophers Onto a Volcano. They Might Try It Again.

Scientists’ experiment on Mount St. Helens suggests rodents can deliver fungi that plants need, but the repair crew has an appetite.

In 1982, scientists brought a pocket gopher to Washington’s Mount St. Helens and put it inside a small enclosure around a plant growing on the Pumice Plain. Two years after the volcano’s infamous eruption, the plant had taken root among volcanic deposits. The gopher stayed for 24 hours before the researchers returned it home.

Michael Allen and his colleagues were testing whether gophers could carry fungi themselves, rather than simply uncovering fungi in buried soil. Allen describes experiments around two plants in different volcanic deposits. When the researchers returned the following year, both plants had mycorrhizal fungi, while nearby plants outside the enclosures showed no traces of them.

“We concluded that the gophers themselves transported these critical fungi, likely in their feces as they are known to feed on these fungi in their meadows,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

The experiment went viral after a 2024 paper in Frontiers in Microbiomes reported microbial differences associated with the old gopher enclosures. That paper dates the Pumice Plain experiment to 1982, rather than the 1983 date repeated in some coverage. The researchers sampled the soil in 2014, when the gopher had been gone for about 32 years.

Allen, a soil ecologist and distinguished professor emeritus at the University of California, Riverside, thinks the gophers give us something else to consider. When we plant a damaged landscape, how do the microbes those plants need get there? Could gophers do the job? If so, people planting a former mining or industrial site would have a reason to let gophers stay, even when they eat some of the seedlings.

Some native gophers survived the May 18, 1980, eruption by hiding underground, beneath the snow cover. Allen says the snow and soil protected them in patches of meadow and land that had been logged. Where the ash wasn’t too deep, the gophers dug their way out, bringing the old soil up with them. They also brought microbes with them, including mycorrhizal fungi, which help plant roots obtain nutrients and water in exchange for carbon.

But the Pumice Plain was buried under more than 20 meters of sterile volcanic ash and debris, far beyond any gopher’s reach. Allen wanted to know whether a gopher could carry fungi onto ground like that from somewhere else. That’s why his research team took a gopher from a nearby clearcut and put it in the enclosure on the Pumice Plain. The results of the experiment were clear. The plants inside the enclosures had mycorrhizal fungi, but nearby plants outside did not. Allen suspects the fungi arrived in the gopher's droppings, although the experiment didn’t show how.

Decades later, the landscape around the experimental site had changed considerably. Allen says plants, gophers, and fungi have spread across the Pumice Plain, beyond the original plot. The later study, led by mycologist Mia Maltz, found differences in the microbial communities associated with historic gopher enclosures and comparison plots. It also examined the lasting influence of forest conditions before the eruption.

That finding leaves plenty to investigate. A different assortment of microbes doesn’t automatically mean healthier soil or faster recovery. Allen says that analysis of the communities is continuing. He wants to know whether gophers could bring those helpful microbes to other places where people are trying to get plants growing again.

When the nearest healthy soil is too far away

Allen thinks the question could matter most where damaged ground lies far from surviving vegetation. If healthy soil and vegetation are close by, he told Pop Mech, microbes may find their way back on their own. But microbes struggle to return to places like industrial sites, where healthy soil is scarce, and Allen thinks those sites could be worth testing to see whether gophers can help.

Allen’s work extends beyond volcanoes: at a Wyoming strip mine, his team moved gophers and soil from a healthy ecosystem onto disturbed ground. He suspects gophers deliver a broader mix of microbes than commercial treatments do, though he calls that a question for further research. Success would depend on conditions, though. As David Lindenmayer, a conservation biologist at the Australian National University, notes, an introduced animal first needs a habitat, and Allen adds that gophers need enough food to get started. Timing matters too, because the soil microbes that survived the eruption, which Lindenmayer calls “biological legacies,” die off without host plants, so the longer a site waits, the fewer remain to help new roots take hold.

That requirement brings an awkward complication. A gopher could make a meal of the seedlings it was brought in to help. The animals “could well destroy the restoration effort if they ate the plants desired for restoration and did not eat undesirable plants,” Allen says.

Lindenmayer also cautions that returning an animal to a changed landscape can produce surprises, because it’s hard to know how a gopher will affect the plants and animals that have moved in since it disappeared. Researchers would need to track whether gophers deliver useful microbes, whether those benefits outweigh the damage the animals do, and how the approach compares with other ways of helping a site recover. Allen’s experiment gives them a place to start: in a single day on volcanic ground, a gopher carried fungi to plants. The question now is whether more plants would survive with a hungry gopher around than without one.

#6347. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta

#6345. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

#6343. The Missing Engine Behind Quantum Computing Is Literally All Around Us

Scientists say they can corral up to 40 quantum-ready photons from everyday light, even at room temperature.

The answer to one of the biggest questions in quantum computing might have been all around us this whole time: light. In newly published research, a team of scientists from Louisiana and Mexico say they’ve found a way to corral up to 40 viable photons of light “at room temperature under high levels of noise and decoherence,” for use in quantum information crunching. If this finding is validated by further research and implementation, it could help move quantum computing closer to real life.

The paper was recently published in the peer-reviewed journal Advanced Science. The research starts from an understanding that quantum computing, or quantum information processing, is something fundamentally different from the paradigms we have today. The team explains in the paper how their field, reservoir computing, differs from the von Neumann setup that the vast majority of computers have now. Instead, it’s closer to a neural network, with “highly-interconnected quantum networks as reservoirs.”

In a von Neumann system, information marches through a central processing unit (CPU) almost on a ticker tape. One minuscule math problem at a time is crunched onto that ticker tape, then returned to its host area of the computer—like memory, hard drive, software, or your mouse—to be applied. Everything the computer does gets crunched, one math operation at a time, through the CPU. In a neural net, including a reservoir computer, multiple things can happen at the same time. The computing style is nonlinear, involving clouds of quantum particles.

If that setup sounds thrilling, you’ve now joined a large group of people who feel excited about it, even if they aren’t sure yet how it can be implemented. The industry is bottlenecked by logistics. There’s no general purpose quantum computer. “Scalability and fragility have long represented two major challenges to the practical realization of quantum technologies,” the team writes. But in their simulation, the scientists were able to extract little quantum pockets from everyday “classical” light sources, corralling reservoirs that they say show a marked improvement over classical computing.

“We demonstrate the potential of our platform to perform complex tasks by using random multiphoton reservoirs to map input signals into higher-dimensional spaces, which are then optimized by low-level neural networks,” the team writes. In other words, the simulation shows that the reservoir system can set up and explore functions, taking an input and turning out the function performed on that input, like an algebraic expression and then the integral of that expression.

The secret in this experimental setup is the Fock space, which lets scientists gather particles under one umbrella in order to study how they behave, mathematically. Once a number of particles within the classical light source are corralled in a special circuit, they can be used to do quantum computing, despite their “losses and noise.” Light is bent and manipulated at “room temperature,” which in quantum mechanics means above freezing.

This work is the next step down a path that has, so far, worked only in much smaller setups. “While these effects have been explored in the context of nanophotonic systems and quantum sensors, their implications for multiphoton quantum information processing have yet to be investigated,” the team explains. “These results highlight the robustness and scalability of hybrid quantum technologies against decoherence.”

Caroline Delbert is a writer, avid reader, and contributing editor at Pop Mech. She's also an enthusiast of just about everything. Her favorite topics include nuclear energy, cosmology, math of everyday things, and the philosophy of it all.

#6342. Archeologists Found a 1,000-Year-Old Viking Treasure That May Have Touched a Saint’s Hand

It was first sorted with English pennies, until its inscription revealed had a run-in with Norway’s future saint.

Experts cataloguing the largest Viking Age coin hoard ever discovered in Norway were stunned when one 1,000-year-old coin stood out from the more than 5,000 in the find. As archaeologist Anne Skogsfjord sorted and catalogued the coins, she found herself face-to-face with King Olaf Haraldsson, known as Saint Olaf. The coin’s inscription confirmed it: ONLAF R+ NORMANORV, which translates to “Olaf, King of the Norwegians.”

“Could this really be a coin of Olaf Haraldsson that I was holding? And it was,” Skogsfjord said in a statement from the University of Oslo’s Museum of Cultural History. “It was a very special moment. I realized that we had found a national treasure.”

The discovery came from what is already a remarkable find. Since its discovery in April 2026, the Mørstad Hoard has grown to about 5,500 coins, so cataloguing it is no simple task. Skogsfjord came across the Olaf coin while working through a group of Anglo-Saxon coins issued by Æthelred II, where it had first been sorted. However, its inscription soon revealed who had really issued it.

The find is extraordinarily rare. Fewer than 20 of Saint Olaf’s coins survive today, and most have turned up outside Norway. Only four examples of the type found in the Mørstad Hoard were previously known, and just one of those was found in Norway, in a hoard uncovered during the restoration of the church ruins at Stein in 1924.

“For those of us interested in Norway’s earliest monetary history, it hardly gets any better than this,” said Svein H. Gullbekk, professor of numismatics at the University of Oslo. “Here we have a coin bearing the king’s portrait and a cross, with another cross on the reverse. It is a Christianization coin on a grand scale. We can see how King Olaf used coinage to legitimize the new faith and to establish himself as a Christian king of European standing.”

The coin was struck around 1024–1028, near the end of the Viking Age, and minting it was itself a political act. “This is branding,” Gullbekk said. Olaf himself appears on the coin, facing left and wearing a conical battle helmet, which gave this coin type the nickname “Pointed Helmet.”

“Olaf Haraldsson himself decided what these coins should look like, and perhaps he was present when they were struck,” Gullbekk said. “It is entirely possible that this very coin from Mørstad was once held in the king’s own hand.”

Yet the coin was more than a political statement, as it was, unsurprisingly, used as money. Both sides bear numerous small knife cuts, likely made to test the silver content during transactions. “On that basis, we may assume that the coin changed hands several times during the approximately 20 to 25 years between its production and its deposition in the Mørstad Hoard,” said Associate Professor Florent Audy, who leads the museum’s cataloguing of the hoard. “That is yet another fascinating chapter in the coin’s history.”

The hoard itself was first found on April 10, 2026, by metal detectorists Rune Sætre and Vegard Sørlie in Rena, in eastern Norway’s Innlandet County. This autumn, the two detectorists searched the field again and, with landowner Ole Erik Hørstad, unearthed coin number 5,000. County archaeologists also carried out a follow-up investigation of the site in late September. And the count may keep climbing. “I am beginning to think that the hoard may soon exceed 6,000 coins,” Audy said.

In the meantime, the public will get its first look at the find. The Olaf coin will be shown when an exhibition on the Mørstad Hoard opens at the Historical Museum in Oslo on November 20, while cataloguing continues behind the scenes.

“When you think this Viking treasure cannot become any more exciting, new surprises emerge,” said Hanna Geiran, Norway’s director general of cultural heritage. “This St. Olaf coin is yet another reminder of how extraordinary this find is. The coin is not only a rare object, but also tangible testimony from a time when the foundations of the Norwegian kingdom and the Christianization of the country were laid.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6339. Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

They started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

Currently, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in new destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

And the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

First, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!)

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

However, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

At Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you plan on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like New York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

Can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy issues).

Living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing new cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!
