#6325. Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

Looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

We’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but big on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend plans in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the big roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

Canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

This is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines quickly.

Best for: hiking, conservation areas, mountain biking, skiing, and quick nature escapesDrive from Toronto: about 40–60 minutesSuggested day: Start with a hike at Rattlesnake Point or Kelso, have lunch in town, then add Mount Nemo or Crawford Lake if you want a second outdoor stop.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

The waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

Caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

After the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Things to do in Niagara Falls Where to Stay in Niagara FallsNiagara on the Lake Day Tours Niagara Day Tours from TorontoNiagara on the Lake

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

This is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

Best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

St. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

This is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole plan.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

The Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Best for: skiing, hiking, biking, spa days, village atmosphere, and four-season adventureDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Spend the morning hiking, skiing, or visiting Scenic Caves, then explore Blue Mountain Village and finish with Scandinave Spa if you want a slower end to the day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Best for: beach days, families, swimming, paddleboarding, summer energy, and easy sand-and-sun escapesDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Arrive early, set up on the beach, swim or paddleboard, grab lunch nearby, and stay for sunset if traffic is manageable.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

This is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Best for: lakes, paddling, fall colours, cottage-country scenery, breweries, and small townsDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Pick one town as your base, such as Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, or Huntsville, then add a lake stop, short hike, brewery, or boat cruise.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and big nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the plan simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

You won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

No car? Book this Toronto to Algonquin Provincial Park private Tour.

Best for: The Grotto, Georgian Bay, hiking, turquoise water, cliffs, shipwrecks, and big adventure daysDrive from Toronto: about 3.5 to 4 hoursSuggested day: Leave very early, visit the Grotto or hike a section of the Bruce Trail, stop in Tobermory if time allows, and expect a long drive home.

Bruce Peninsula National Park is one of the most spectacular places in Ontario, but it is a very long day trip from Toronto. The Grotto, Georgian Bay cliffs, turquoise water, and Bruce Trail scenery make it unforgettable.

This is best for travellers who do not mind a long drive and a full day outdoors. For most people, it works better as an overnight getaway, but it can be done in a single ambitious day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Reservations and parking rules matter here. Plan ahead, start early, and don’t wing it on a summer weekend.

Hamilton, Elora, and Niagara Falls are the best day trips from Toronto for waterfalls. Niagara Falls is the most famous, Hamilton has the greatest variety, and Elora gives you dramatic gorge scenery along the Grand River.

Wasaga Beach, Port Dover, Sandbanks in Prince Edward County, and the Toronto Islands are the best beach day trips from Toronto. Wasaga is best for a classic summer beach day, while Sandbanks is better if you want dunes and a longer road trip.

Niagara-on-the-Lake and Prince Edward County are the best wine-focused day trips from Toronto. Niagara-on-the-Lake is easier for a one-day trip, while Prince Edward County feels more relaxed if you can stay overnight.

Canada’s Wonderland, Toronto Islands, Niagara Falls, the Toronto Zoo, and Wasaga Beach are some of the best family-friendly day trips from Toronto. They offer easy activities, food options, and enough to fill a full day without complicated planning.

Milton, Hamilton, Elora, Algonquin Provincial Park, and Bruce Peninsula National Park are the best hiking day trips from Toronto. For an easy hike close to the city, choose Milton or Hamilton. For a bigger adventure, choose Algonquin or Bruce Peninsula.

Stratford, Elora, Paris, and Niagara-on-the-Lake are the best small-town day trips from Toronto. Each has a walkable centre, good food, independent shops, and enough charm to fill a relaxed day.

The best day trips from Toronto under 2 hours include Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Elora, Stratford, Paris, Caledon, Milton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Wasaga Beach. These are the easiest options if you want to leave in the morning and be back home by dinner.

Yes, Niagara Falls is one of the easiest and most popular day trips from Toronto. It takes about 90 minutes by car, and you can visit the falls, Journey Behind the Falls, Clifton Hill, the Niagara SkyWheel, and the Hornblower boat cruise in a single day if you start early.

For nature close to the city, Hamilton’s waterfalls, Milton’s conservation areas, Elora Gorge, and Caledon are some of the best choices. For bigger wilderness, Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are spectacular, but they work better as long day trips or overnight escapes.

Yes, but your options are more limited. Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Toronto Islands, and some towns along GO Transit or VIA Rail routes are possible without a car. For waterfalls, conservation areas, beaches, and rural towns, driving is usually much easier.

#6324. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6322. American Airlines Heavily Penalizes Solo Travelers: Two Tickets Cost Less Than One

American Airlines quoted $496 for one passenger to fly from Miami to Charlotte, but just $155 per person when booking two passengers on the same flight. That means two tickets cost $310 total—$186 less than buying just one. Traveling alone more than tripled the per-person fare. That is one example from a new investigation into higher fares for solo travelers, and it raises an obvious question: why should traveling alone carry such a steep penalty?

Thrifty Traveler has published a revealing follow-up on airlines charging solo travelers more. His team examined 5,000 nonstop domestic one-way flights, sampling 1,000 each on American Airlines, United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Alaska Airlines, and Southwest Airlines.

American charged solo passengers more on 33.5% of the flights sampled, compared with 10.6% on United. The researchers found no such pricing on the flights sampled from Delta, Alaska, or Southwest.

The Miami–Charlotte example is particularly striking: $496 for one passenger versus $155 per person when searching for two, both for main cabin economy. Two tickets cost $186 less than one!

American did not respond to the publication’s requests for comment. United declined to comment.

Thrifty Traveler traced the pricing to fare rules requiring a traveling companion to qualify for certain cheaper tickets. Search for one passenger and those fares disappear. Airlines have been distinguishing between customers willing to pay more for decades through advance-purchase requirements, minimum stays, and restrictions on changes. But requiring another passenger is a particularly suspect way to accomplish that.

Presumably, the calculation is that someone traveling alone is more likely to be a business traveler with an expense account (all we can do is infer that since AA and UA declined to comment). Even if that assumption works across a large pool of bookings, it does not necessarily say anything about the person actually buying a ticket. I frequently travel alone and still care very much about what I pay!

A passenger visiting an elderly parent, taking a solo vacation, or flying to meet a spouse already at the destination needs one seat. Why should that person have to produce a companion to unlock a substantially lower fare?

The airline can describe this as a discount for traveling together. From the perspective of someone who needs only one ticket, the result is the same: a higher price for the same transportation. Even when the example is not as egregious as the AA example above, it still seems particularly punitive.

How counterintuitive that a customer entering the correct number of passengers must now wonder whether asking for an additional seat would lower the total bill. We already spend enough time comparing basic economy restrictions, baggage charges, and seat fees. Now checking whether you are being penalized for traveling alone becomes another part of the booking process.

When shopping for a solo trip, try repeating the search for two passengers. Compare the per-person price for the same flight and fare product.

If an airline wants substantially more money because I am traveling alone, booking Mr. EXTRA/SEAT may make sense…or more likely, give me another reason to book elsewhere.

Airlines are entitled to pursue revenue, and I do not expect every seat on a flight to sell for the same amount. But a pricing system that quotes $496 for one ticket and $310 for two deserves scrutiny…maybe not regularity scrutiny, but at least consumer scrutiny. The frustrating lesson is that searching for exactly what you need may conceal the much lower price available to someone bringing a companion…

Join our mailing list for a daily summary of posts! We never sell your info.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Yes, you will get full credit as long as it is booked 7 days or more prior to travel.

As a primarily solo traveler, I’ll check this going forward for every AA ticket I purchase. I’ll fly a different airline on principle, or use only miles until they’re gone.

It would be very useful for the rear rows of the 777, where the economy seats are in a 2-4-2 configuration. Being able to have a little row to yourself would mean more comfort and easy aisle and window access.

#6321. ALPA Elects National Leadership

ALPA’s board of directors on Wednesday reelected Jason Ambrosi to a second four-year term as president and filled other executive roles as it gears up for new fights on behalf of its members.

The pilots union said Ambrosi – a Delta captain first elected in 2022 – has led through “one of the most consequential periods” in ALPA’s 95-year history. During his first term, the organization negotiated 24 new contracts, resisted efforts to reduce the number of pilots required on the flight deck, and returned more than $150 million in dues to members.

“Over the past four years, through tragedy and triumph, bankruptcies and contract negotiations, and in the halls of Parliament and the Capitol, we have made our industry and profession stronger and safer,” Ambrosi said in a statement. “We negotiated numerous new contracts and helped pass an FAA reauthorization bill that protected our top priorities. That’s because our safety work and our pilot representation go hand in hand. Strong contracts protect our ability to speak up when we see something wrong. I’m honored that my fellow pilots have trusted me to continue that work.”

ALPA’s board also elected Captain Doug Grant of Hawaiian Airlines as the union’s first vice president; First Officer Tyler Hawkins of United as vice president of administration and secretary; and Captain Wes Clapper of JetBlue as vice president of finance and treasurer.

The term for new national officers will begin Jan. 1, 2027.

ALPA said its priorities over the coming years include keeping two pilots on the flight deck at all times and requiring ADS-B In on every commercial aircraft.

#6320. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6319. Review: Emirates First Class Lounge Dubai (DXB – B Concourse)

I returned to the Emirates First Class Lounge in Dubai’s Concourse B during my latest trip through Dubai. Below are my updated photos and impressions, followed by my original 2019 review for your comparison.

With 30 minutes until boarding, I stopped by this lounge after a longer visit at the Emirates First Class Lounge in Concourse A. This Concourse B lounge is virtually unchanged since my last visit and by now, feels dated…not that I would touch it because it still serves its purpose well. I did notice one important change, though.

The Emirates First Class Lounge in Concourse B is located airside in Terminal 3 at Dubai International Airport, beyond security and passport control. Take the elevator or escalator to Level 4. The lounge is open 24/7.

Paid access is subject to availability and covers one visit for up to four hours before scheduled departure. Business Class Special fares do not automatically include lounge access. Check Emirates’ current eligibility and pricing before your trip.

As you enter the lounge, you’ll note the high ceilings and the sooting sound of water fountains.

It’s massive, though does not feel as large as the Concourse A Lounge.

I had just had breakfast and wasn’t hungry, but one advantage to this lounge over the Concourse A lounge is that it has better barista coffee at the bar (unless I missed it in the other lounge). I enjoyed an excellent flat white.

There’s also a Costa Coffee in the lounge.

Had I been here longer, I’m sure I would have enjoyed a nice a la carte meal in the dining room.

In addition, there was a separate stand-alone bar in the smoking area with a limited section and drinks and Arabic coffee.

There was also another coffee nook with a small selection of breakfast items (it was 6:30 am). Let me commend Emirates here because you’ll notice if you scroll down to my prior review that the coffee machines were automatic prior to the pandemic and those simply cannot compare to a proper manual coffee machine. The coffee has been upgraded!

This lounge has a large smoking section that is not separately ventilated from the rest of the lounge, though thankfully the cigarette smell was not too bad.

Restrooms and showers are available – I did not go inside the restroom, but there are pictures of both the restrooms and shower suites below in my prior review.

The spa is located one level above the lounge, with treatments available for purchase plus 15-minute complimentary treatments for first class passengers, though there’s a desk in this lounge from which you can reserve your treatment.

A quite area with recliner chairs is available for longer layovers (there’s also an airport-operated transit hotel located one level up as well as a full gym, but that’s not included for first class passengers).

A large children’s play room offered space for kids and even had a Pacman-style arcade video game.

While this does not feel as massive as the Concourse A lounge, I actually prefer this lounge for the superior coffee. Yes, it does look a bit dated by now, but it is quite functional and is a great place to wine and dine before your flight. I look forward to returning.

The review below was originally published on June 4, 2019. Photos, menus, and observations in this section reflect that visit, including references to renovations and temporarily closed facilities.

I say it is huge–and it was–but not nearly as big as the Concourse A lounge, which I’ve reviewed before here. The lounge is undergoing a remodel of sorts, which is desperately needed. On the one hand, the lounge is just fine the way it in that is still functional and clean. But it is bereft of character and simply dated in appearance.

We walked down the long hall from check-in, though security and passport control, upstairs, down another concourse, and finally up another escalator to the lounge..it was quite a hike from curbside to lounge and Emirates offers no escort (or gulf cart).

The lounge is open 24/7, but was virtually empty when we arrived at 4:30 AM. I used the “calm before the storm” to capture some photos of the lounge.

Seating is spread out around the lounge and includes chairs, couches, and desks.

The spa is currently under renovation (or perhaps just closed). There was still an attended “Timeless Spa” desk in which spa treatments could be scheduled. First Class passengers were then directed to the business class lounge for treatment. I took advantage of a complimentary 15-minute back massage shortly after arrival and had no wait for a treatment. It’s a small gesture, but an appreciated one.

Actually, the plan was to eat first…both John and I were hungry. But the restaurant does not open until 5:15 AM so we ended up having to wait. A buffet is available 24/7 and included mostly breakfast selections.

Shortly after the restaurant opened, we sat down for breakfast…dinner actually. I wrote about it here. Here’s the a la carte menu:

As you can see, if you’re not in the mood in the for breakfast there are lunch/dinner items available. The nice leather-bound, multi-page menus have been replaced by oversized menu cards.

I enjoyed some berries and juice from the buffet followed by a filet mignon with French Fries and a salad. The food was excellent, although the coffee was quite disappointing. Best to stick to Arabic coffee and avoid the machine-dispensed.

Around the lounge there are a couple of additional food stations, one offering Mediterranean food and the other offering Japanese food. There’s also a full bar is self-serve and was open during Ramadan.

Complimentary shoe-shine is available. There’s a station in the middle of the lounge, though the shoe shiner approached us in the restaurant and asked if he could take our shoes. In their place, he offered us slippers.

The children’s room, with video games, was roped off.

The restrooms reminded me a bit of the Concorde Room in London Heathrow…that’s not a good thing. I’d call the showers and restrooms still functional, but past their prime.

Rather than a separate room for smokers, an area directly adjacent to the dining room has been designated for smoking. While there are no walls, barriers, or other partitions, I did not smell any smoke (and there were plenty of smokers there). Perhaps the super-high ceilings were helpful in that regard. It’s fairly rare to see smoking so integrated into a lounge.

The staff in the lounge was all Filipino and provided friendly and attentive service. Some of the passengers did not treat them well, especially in the restaurant. They barked orders and were simply rude. As I remind myself, I remind you: let’s treat everyone with respect.

You cannot really compare an Emirates First Class Lounge to ones like Air France or Lufthansa. Emirates offers first class on such a wider scale that it has a larger and less-personal first class ground experience by necessity. I did appreciate the tasty lunch and spa treatment during my three hours in the lounges. That said, now that I have reviewed both lounges next time I will just stay a bit longer in my hotel.

#6318. One of the Most Unusual Jobs at Sea? Looking After 24 Cats and Dogs

This is the latest installment of our bimonthly column Crews on Cruise, spotlighting the people who work behind the scenes of the world’s most memorable voyages—from bartenders and entertainers to ship captains and expedition leaders.

Oliver Cruz has one of the more unusual jobs at sea: He is the kennel master aboard Cunard’s Queen Mary 2, a 2,759-guest ocean liner that has been making transatlantic crossings between Southampton and New York since 2004. It is also the only cruise ship in the world to offer dedicated kennels at sea during its transatlantic voyages, with 24 spaces for dogs and cats traveling with their owners.

Cruz joined the ship in 2011, initially as a spa attendant. But when the housekeeping department learned that he had spent eight years back home in the Philippines working as a zoo guide and animal handler, with everything from snakes to crocodiles, he was moved to the kennels. He has been there ever since. “Dogs are angels,” Cruz says. “Not all angels have wings. Some of them have fur.” No surprise then that Cruz has 15 dogs of his own at home and is a member of the Philippine Animal Welfare Society.

His charges aboard Queen Mary 2 have ranged from teacup Yorkies to a Bernese mountain dog whose three daily meals each included roughly three pounds of minced meat and more than 10 ingredients. Some are regulars: Cruz has cared for one dog on 32 crossings. By now, he can rattle off their names, personalities, dietary quirks, and preferred sleeping arrangements, and even remembers which “house,” as he calls the kennels, his repeat guests slept in on previous voyages.

One occupational hazard: Cruz estimates he has more than 50 dog bites on his body, nearly all sustained while diving in to break up fights. “Nobody bites me intentionally,” he says. Experience has taught him that “the way you treat a husky is not the same way you treat a Shih Tzu.”

We caught up with Cruz earlier this year to talk about life in the kennels, his unusually demanding clientele, and why managing their human parents can sometimes be the hardest part of the job. As Cruz puts it, “You need the knowledge, but you also need the heart."

What does a typical day on the job look like?“On embarkation day, we go down to the terminal and first cross-check all the paperwork. There are very complicated requirements, especially coming into the UK, so we check things like the stamps and the timing of vaccinations.

From there, we bring the dogs up to the kennels and explain the visiting hours and the dos and don’ts to their owners. The dogs have an outdoor area we literally call the poop deck, with an American fire hydrant for the American dogs and a British lamppost for the British dogs. For the sake of their holiday, I let them experience both.

Owners can leave toys, blankets, even used pajamas or socks inside the houses so the dogs can smell them and feel more comfortable. If two dogs live together and get along, we take out the partition so they can cuddle overnight.

Then there's the feeding. Every dog has its own portion sizes and diet, and it all has to be right. The food ranges from boiled chicken breast to grilled steak, steamed salmon, Cumberland sausage, scrambled egg, fruits, vegetables—basically whatever they need. The food comes from the same kitchen that cooks for the guests, but I am very strict: no salt and pepper.

Sometimes people who don’t have pets in the kennels try to come in because the dogs are cute—maybe 20 or 25 people in a day. I have to explain that the dogs are already trying to adjust to an unfamiliar environment as well as the other dogs. They don’t need more strangers coming in to see them.”

What is your favorite part about this job?“Meeting all the new dogs on the first day and making my family bigger. After seven days of bonding, playing, and running around together, saying goodbye is the saddest part.”

What is the most challenging part about working at sea?“The parents. Sometimes I tell the owners, ‘No treats,’ but I can see them secretly feeding their dog oily food like bacon from the kitchen. I have to say, ‘Mama, I’m not so happy seeing you do this.’

And once I had somebody take their own dog back to their cabin without telling me. That evening, I was about to close the kennel when I did my usual count and realized one was missing. It was a very stormy evening, and I was running around like a headless chicken. I was soaking wet and crying. I asked housekeeping to send people around the ship to help me find this dog, but nobody could.

Finally, I phoned the owner and she said, ‘Oh yes, Oliver, she’s here.’ I was dying that night!”

What is the coolest or weirdest thing about living on a ship?“The weirdest thing: When I’m home, I feel strange. When I’m here, I feel at home.

I play drums and guitar in the Filipino crew band, and we perform in the crew bar. We play a lot of Red Hot Chili Peppers. I even got to play with Travis Barker here on Queen Mary 2. They were filming something on the ship and shot us playing together. I remember singing ‘All the Small Things’ and ‘What’s My Age Again?’ That was one of the coolest things.”

What is your favorite place you’ve traveled so far?“Liverpool. I’m a big Beatles fan. I have John Lennon tattoos all over my body. When I’m there, I visit Mendips, John Lennon’s childhood home, Strawberry Field, and Quarry Bank School. And I always spend the night at the Cavern Club, sometimes until two in the morning. That’s my place.”

What is your favorite place to hang out on board the ship?“The kennels, honestly. It’s a different experience staying here for seven days, getting to know each other’s dogs.”

Tell us about a memorable guest interaction that sticks out to you.“One of the most memorable was a dog named Paisley. She had come from a shelter and, according to her owner, had been mistreated before. She was aggressive and would bite, and she was having a difficult time in the kennel.

When the other dogs were put away, I would let Paisley out and spend time with her alone. I told her, ‘Paisley, you are not the boss. I am the boss.’

One day, her owner came in and saw Paisley sitting on my lap and licking my face. She started crying and said, ‘What did you do to my dog?’ That was the start of a very good relationship. I will never forget her.”

What’s your top tip for first-time cruisers?“Always remember that you and your dog are reflections of each other. So you need to be calm and happy. If you are really nervous, the dog will feel that nervousness too.

And for cats, give them time. Cats are the boss. They don’t trust places and people easily, so do not force them. One day, the cat will come to you. Once they become talkative and start asking me for attention, I know: That’s it. We are friends.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6317. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

#6316. United Airlines CEO Accuses Boeing And Airbus Of Colluding To Avoid Building New Planes

Scott Kirby says Boeing and Airbus have quietly agreed not to develop new aircraft because neither faces enough competition to force its hand. I understand his frustration with the slow pace of aircraft development, but that is a substantial allegation, and the United Airlines CEO’s argument overlooks both an airplane his own airline ordered and the competition concerns he dismisses when discussing airline mergers.

I have already discussed Scott Kirby’s appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast with John Collison and Ben Thompson. The full conversation is worth a listen, even if I disagree with some of his conclusions. As always, Kirby offers a remarkably candid look at how he thinks about the airline business.

One exchange that deserves a closer look concerns Boeing and Airbus, the lack of an all-new Boeing 757 replacement, and whether the aircraft manufacturers have become too comfortable with their position in the market.

In the interview, Kirby argues that the Boeing–Airbus duopoly has weakened the incentive to invest in new aircraft. He says:

“I think the fundamental problem is Boeing and Airbus have a global duopoly, and they have quietly, not officially agreed, but they have quietly agreed: ‘Neither one of us will invest in new airframes.’”

He attributes that reluctance partly to investors and says he has spent more than two decades asking for a 757 replacement. His proposed remedy is another aircraft manufacturer to challenge the incumbents.

First, that is quite a serious accusation. Kirby does not present evidence of an agreement during this exchange. Two companies independently deciding that an expensive development program does not offer an attractive return is different from agreeing to avoid competing. I can accept that limited competition may reduce the urgency to invest. But that does not establish collusion.

There is also a rather large omission from this argument: Airbus has developed a functional replacement for the Boeing 757.

The A321neo family fills much of that commercial role, with the A321LR and especially the A321XLR extending it to longer routes. These are not identical aircraft with interchangeable capabilities in every operating condition and I concede that an A321XLR does not solve every requirement an airline might have for replacing both 757s and larger 767s.

But it is difficult to argue that Airbus simply refused to answer the 757 replacement question.

In fact, United announced its order for 50 A321XLRs in December 2019 specifically to begin replacing its Boeing 757-200 fleet. Its own announcement described the aircraft as an “ideal one-for-one replacement” for older aircraft on certain intercontinental routes.

Airbus advertises a range of up to 4,700 nautical miles for the XLR, opening longer routes with single-aisle economics (though it seems the actual range is much shorter…)

An aircraft does not have to be designed from scratch to represent innovation. Improving an existing platform’s efficiency and extending the routes it can economically operate can achieve the same goal. Kirby may want something substantially better–he mentioned the superior efficiency of delta wing design (a triangular wing shape) like the SR-71–I would welcome that too. But wanting a more ambitious airplane does not mean show collusion or that Airbus has not already offered a 757 replacement.

This debate also brought me back to two stories I wrote seven years ago.

In July 2019, I covered United’s push for clarity on Boeing’s proposed new midmarket airplane, commonly called the 797. I wrote:

“Boeing is still studying the business case for the NMA, but has shifted the bulk of its attention to the troubled 737 MAX program.”

That same story identified the A321XLR as Airbus’ answer to United’s replacement needs.

Two months later, I covered Delta’s interest in the proposed 797, including its substantial need to replace aging 757s and 767s. Boeing’s MAX crisis was already consuming attention and engineering resources. Meanwhile, Airbus was securing XLR orders.

“But Boeing’s pain has been Airbus’ gain.”

That sounds like competition to me, even if Boeing failed to offer the product its airline customers wanted.

There is ample room to criticize Boeing’s priorities. But a company struggling with its existing aircraft programs may lack the resources or appetite to launch another enormously expensive one. It may also conclude that the potential market does not justify the investment.

Neither explanation requires a quiet agreement with Airbus.

Finally, one more thought on competition.

Kirby recognizes that when United has fewer suppliers to choose from, those suppliers may feel less pressure to deliver the products United wants. Another competitor could force them to work harder for his business.

But when I apply similar reasoning to his proposed merger with American Airlines, Kirby wants us to focus on the benefits of a larger network and a better airline.

Aircraft manufacturing and airline operations have different economics. Adding a manufacturer is an immense undertaking, and combining airlines can create useful connections. I do not suggest that the two markets are identical.

Nevertheless, the underlying concern is common: customers lose bargaining power when credible alternatives disappear.

If United benefits from having another manufacturer compete for its aircraft orders, passengers can benefit from having American compete with United for their tickets. A larger route map does not eliminate that competitive pressure’s value.

Kirby is persuasive when explaining why he wants more choices as a customer. He is much less persuasive when explaining why we should accept fewer!

That said, I’d love to see Lockheed get back into the commercial airline business…coming soon, an L1011-800! 😉

I would welcome a compelling new aircraft that advances what airlines can offer passengers. Kirby is right to push manufacturers to do better. But the A321XLR demonstrates that development has not stopped, and Boeing’s failure to launch the 797 does not establish an agreement to suppress innovation.

More fundamentally, Kirby understands why a customer should worry about too few competitors. I wish he would give that concern equal weight when the customer is buying a United Airlines ticket!

But in this case, I think Kirby is projecting the Big Four’s tacit agreement on airfares. The Big Four have agreed, not officially, quietly agreed, not to compete on airfares.

#6315. The First Miss Marple Mystery in 50 Years Is An Alpine Thriller

When we think of Agatha Christie and travel, our minds naturally drift to the nimble Hercule Poirot, especially following Kenneth Branagh’s cinematic revival of the franchise which took the globe-trotting detective from the plush interiors of the Orient Express to a glamorous river steamer on the Nile to a decaying Venetian palazzo. The world of June Marple, the elderly amateur detective Christie featured in a dozen novels and 20 short stories, is considerably quainter. An unassuming spinster settled in the English countryside, the majority of Miss Marple's mysteries have taken place right in her own backyard. But a new novel by Lucy Foley is setting Poirot aside and blowing the dust off the mild-mannered Marple by whisking her away to an extravagant Swiss Alps adventure.

The first Miss Marple mystery in 50 years, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel places the incorrigible Victorian gossip in the same shoes as the likes of 007 and Sherlock Holmes as she finds herself at the center of another whodunnit deep in the bowels of The Grand Alpine Hotel, a cozy Swiss ski chalet. With hidden speakeasies, ice-skating waiters, and unforgiving mountainsides, it’s clear Marple is far away from the fictional English hamlet of St. Mary Mead where many of her stories have played out. Condé Nast Traveler spoke with The Guest List author Lucy Foley, who answered the Christie estate's call to pen the latest installment of the Marple franchise, on why she wanted to set this historic new installment abroad, the layered history of the Alps, and what makes Miss Marple such a great traveler.

Why transport Miss Marple from the quaint world of St. Mary Mead to the Swiss Alps?

The location is where this whole project came to life for me. I felt that as an Agatha Christie fan, I needed to write something that felt like it added something to the Miss Marple canon and was in conversation with the original books but also did something new.

The estate said they wanted my take on a Miss Marple book rather than a paint-by-numbers Agatha Christie, and so I went back and forth on whether I should set it in St. Mary's Mead. But then I had this idea of taking Miss Marple on another holiday since she only gets to go on one in the original books. I felt for her because of that, and the project sparked to life.

I also wanted it to be in conversation with a very specific [type of] 1950s masculine action thriller. They were books often set in very rugged places like the mountains written by authors like Ian Fleming and Eric Ambler. I love their work because you get to travel on the page, and that's something I always look for in my reading. But I thought, it's so funny, they're so clearly written by men and for men.

What fun to take that landscape, and then put these two little old ladies, say Miss Marple and Mrs. Bantry at the center of it. That really is the nexus of power in the book to see how that changes things.

Describe your research itinerary for this novel.

I went to several different spots in the Alps. My big trip was to Chamonix in the French Alps, but from there, you're very close to Italy and Switzerland, so I drove to Zermatt, went to Saint Moritz, went through the Mont Blanc tunnel to Le Corbier and various Italian resorts.

It was so important to get the texture right. I've been going to the mountains since I was a child. My parents, who are keen skiers, have been taking us since we were small, but it's interesting when you're looking at them from the point-of-view of research to try and get all of those details right, especially all the historic details. The way people thought about the Alps fundamentally changed at one point in history. It was really the Romantics that came along and reframed the idea of the mountains as a place of beauty and wonder. Before that, people had always thought of them as this terrifying and quite ugly place with dragons and bad spirits, as only death and danger awaited you there. That is still built into the way we see the mountains and experience them, this strange dichotomy.

What were your expectations of studying this region and its hospitality traditions? How did your travels meet or subvert those expectations?

Every time you go out into the mountains as a skier, or as a climber, you're exposing yourself to more danger than we don’t ever otherwise really experience. I've done things like the Vallée Blanche, which is a ski itinerary above Chamonix. You're skiing down parts of the Mer de Glace Glacier. You're told from the beginning there are steep drops, and you have to put your crampons on, and you're roped up, and you're walking along this ridge, which is terrifying. Then when you're actually on the glacier itself, you’re warned about not hanging around too long in any particular place because of the danger of crevasses.

I made so many new discoveries on this trip , like the location of the hotel, which sits above Chamonix. I found it almost by happenstance. It's called Refuge du Montenvers, it's wonderful, and I really recommend people visit. You take a little red train up there, and once the last train has gone for the day, it’s just you and the mountains. That was wonderfully atmospheric and directly informed the setting of the hotel in the book.

I also discovered things like, when traveling to St. Moritz and visiting Badrutt's Palace Hotel and Kulm Hotel, these wonderful photos of ice-skating waiters from back in the day. I didn't realize that they had been a thing. These guys that would wear full black tie and go out on the ice with a tray laden with a Champagne bucket, Champagne coupes, the whole lot, and do tricks out on the ice. Things like that are such fun to put directly into the book.

You transport readers to a 1950s chalet in Switzerland, which was a famously neutral European country. What was the importance of these hotels in their postwar hey-day? What role did they play in the changing social landscapes on the continent at the time?

In almost the first scene in the book, you see all these different groups of people on the train on the way up the mountain, who are suddenly thrown together once again. You've got the Italians, the French, the British, the Americans, and you've even got some Germans, and people are bristling at that. It's only been five years post the end of the Second World War, so they can't believe that they're cheek by jowl with their former enemy. In Britain, we still had rationing in the 1950s. People were still underweight and, certainly in other parts of Europe, really feeling the pinch. I found it interesting to differentiate that on that train ride the hotel. Diana Glass, Dolly Bantry's [Marple's devoted friend and right hand] assistant, says she can tell the Italians because they have the best luggage, the French have the best furs, and the Brits all look a bit hungry and gray.

I was also really interested in the geography of the region—in this part of the Swiss Alps, which is close to the border with France and Italy, you had these mountain passes that were slightly more porous than other borders because they're more difficult to man and defend. What would that have looked like during the Second World War, and how would that have informed the immediate history of this hotel? And who might have been milling around in the area during the Second World War? Of course that feeds into the backstories of some of the characters. Without going into too much spoiler territory, some of them have returned to the region, have been here more recently than perhaps they've let on, and have rewritten their own wartime histories to further their own ends.

Agatha Christie herself once gave away her formula for what makes a good mystery: “The whole point of a good detective story was that it must be somebody obvious but at the same time, for some reason, you would then find that it was not obvious, that he could not possibly have done it. Though really, of course, he had done it.” For you, what makes a hotel such a great keeper of that suspense?

There is a specific geography with a hotel—and you sometimes have these hidden spaces as well that you might only know about if you're a seasoned or a more favored guest. In this one, I had great fun with putting in things like a secret bar, which you have at the Kulm Hotel.

You also have anonymity in a hotel. People can come and check-in and become someone that perhaps they're not at home. I think Christie does that so well in At Bertram's Hotel, this idea that it's a weirdly democratizing space in some ways and also quite an anonymous space where people might not be who they seem.

What makes Miss Marple such a great traveler?

That ability to observe; she is such a great reader of character, of people, and that's something that she can apply wherever she is. It's funny, she's always referring things back to her experience in St. Mary's Mead because it's this wonderful microcosm of everything that humanity can be. But you see that even in A Caribbean Mystery, which is the furthest she travels in the original books.

There is always something that can be applied back to her lived experience. She really takes people as they are, wherever they're from, wherever she finds herself, and she sees the truth of them. I think that actually is something that differentiates her from Poirot. We often see him having his head turned by some pretty young thing who he can't possibly imagine doing anything unpleasant, and actually they turn out to be pure evil or malice, and Marple, she would know from the outset.

She's very enigmatic in a way. Do we ever really see the true Marple? At times we see flashes of real rage, in A Pocket Full of Rye, she's motivated by anger to solve that murder. In Nemesis, there's this scene where she becomes the figure of nemesis, in this very powerful, shape-shifting way. She can be what another character needs her to be at any given time, a little bit like the Gray Man from spy fiction, but she is also very much herself and very unique at the same time.

If you had the opportunity to do so, where would you want to send Ms. Marple next?

I don't know if I'm going to show my hand too much here, at the moment it’s very much a one-time thing, but I'll give a little Christie Easter egg, so I won't actually say the place, but I'll let people go and do their own research. Miss Marple hasn't always lived in St. Mary's Mead. We find out that in her youth she lived in a different country for a time, so I think I would take her back there.
