#6314. Learning to Hunt Pheasant at an All-Women Retreat in South Dakota

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

The sorghum hissed when the wind came through it—two years of drought had left the South Dakota ground hard and the dry grass loud. I walked forwards with my 20-gauge Beretta half-raised and my eyes narrowed; the sound of every grasshopper that clattered up out of the stubble made me twitch like a woman with a bad nerve.

Pheasant shooting with Hunt Like a Girl in South Dakota

Then the pheasant rooster came up, multicolored and shining in the sun, trailing a tail of feathers like a kite. I aimed, let loose the shot, and it stopped dead in the air in an iridescent burst.

The pride went through me before anything else did. The tears came second, running unexpectedly down my face while a dozen women I had only known for two days hollered happily for me. Laying the rooster across my arm, I petted him and told him I was sorry.

After decades hearing about other people's forays into the woods to catch their own meal, without ever pulling a trigger myself, I had come to South Dakota and signed up for Hunt Like a Girl, a three-day long, women-only retreat for first time hunters. Founder Karen Butler started a broader program in 2008 under the moniker Shoot Like a Girl after developing a passion for the sport; Hunt Like a Girl eventually grew out of it, taking women out of the shooting range and into the wilderness with the goal of teaching them how to hunt small game like pheasant, turkey, and duck, safely and responsibly.

Guests being briefed at A1 Al's Pheasant Ranch near Emery, South Dakota

For my trip, Hunt Like a Girl took over pheasant hunting lodge A1 Al's Pheasant Ranch outside Emery, a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it farm town around 45 minutes from Sioux Falls. The ranch offers an all-inclusive hunting experience across more than 6,000 acres of private wildlife habitat, with guided pheasant hunts featuring trained bird dogs, as well as classes on firearms safety and ethical hunting. There are also opportunities to learn more about how hunting can provide food and help foster regional wildlife conservation courtesy of guest speakers. Bird processing services—in other words, the breaking down of the meat—are also provided, so guests can take their catch home at the end of it.

Programs like Butler’s are meeting growing demand: Women make up roughly 22% of American hunters, of which there are roughly 3.7 million total, according to a 2022 federal survey of hunting and wildlife-associated recreation—making women the sport's fastest-growing demographic. The National Shooting Sports Foundation has estimated that close to half of the 11 million Americans who bought a first-time firearm for shooting sports, self-defense, and hunting during 2020 and 2021 were women.

The various reasons why a woman may want to learn how to shoot a gun and harvest her own meat vary person-to-person, of course, with self-sufficiency and empowerment among them. Girl & A Gun, a US-based organization that introduces women to firearms and helps them develop shooting skills in a supportive, women-focused environment, surveyed new women shooters for the last five years running and found that 35% now name the social side of learning marksmanship as their main reason for joining.

At the all-women-retreat, guests participate in guided pheasant hunts, and take classes on firearms safety and ethical hunting.

Butler, who was in her late 20s and in the middle of a divorce when she first picked up the activity, wants other women to find community through the practice like she did. Amid dealing with a custody battle that cut time with her two small boys down to alternating weeks, says Butler, her friends hauled her camping on the backside of Pikes Peak in central Colorado and introduced her to target shooting during the trip. Butler, who had never fired a gun before, recalls hitting a Gatorade bottle and then asking whether she could try to hit the cap itself. Butler walked away with not just a sense of accomplishment, but one of camaraderie she hoped to find again.

"At a time when I felt the very worst about myself, shooting sports made me feel the best about myself,” she says. “I want other women to feel that same feeling I have. I found this whole new family of people. It’s a very supportive community.”

Butler never looked back, eventually learning to hunt and even feeding her two sons meat she carried home herself. “I really look at hunting as nutrition and food, and not necessarily a sport,” she says, noting that many women who sign up for her retreat are looking to feel more connected with their food sources, and to experience firsthand how it is grown, raised, and brought to the table.

In light of this, most meals during my stay were centered around what we were hunting: cold pheasant salad on soft rolls, for example, and pheasant pasta, slow-braised in white wine and butter. Butler also walked us through how to break down the bird ourselves—find the breastbone with your thumb, run the knife along the keel, and the breast comes away in one clean piece the color of a dark plum. Throughout the lesson, she emphasized if something had died for you, then the least you owed the creature was to use it.

We also learned the important role that hunters play in habitat conservation across South Dakota. Second Century Habitat Fund pays South Dakota landowners to maintain sorghum—the preferred environment and food source for ring-necked pheasants—through 10-year contracts, keeping the land productive for both agriculture and wildlife. Roughly 80% of South Dakota belongs to private owners, so every acre of sorghum cover becomes habitat for pheasant and other birds and mammals instead of endless rows of corn. Sorghum also acts as an effective carbon sink and doesn't require a lot of water, making it an all around sustainable crop. Like in many other states across the US, South Dakota hunters and anglers also help finance wildlife conservation through hunting and fishing license fees, as well as federal excise taxes on firearms, ammunition, archery equipment, and fishing tackle.

Participants to walk in formation through the South Dakota sorghum.

On my first morning, the pheasants were already awake by the time I stepped onto the lodge’s porch at first light. I learned that they do not call so much as announce themselves, a high dry crow of a sound, one bird and then another, and then a third from somewhere far out of sight among the sorghum where they live. Our lessons began across a gravel road from the lodge, where Christa Forrester, the chief of staff at Shoot Like a Girl, ran the safety briefing, covering where to orient the muzzle points, and place an index finger when it is away from the trigger. She didn’t hold back in describing what happens when either lesson is forgotten.

For our inaugural hunt, we started with a meditation as we faced the rows of sorghum, gathered in a circle with our shotguns held muzzle high—a ritual we would participate in each morning during our stay. Butler told us to close our eyes and asked us to notice every sound and smell, the feel of the wind, and whatever was moving around inside us. She directed us to feel gratitude for what we were about to do, for the birds we searched for, for the nature that surrounded us. I stood in the grass with my eyes shut, and felt the breeze against my cheek.

During each hunt that followed, the guides kept us in a line, telling us to slow down or speed up so we stayed in formation, each woman at a safe distance from the next with the dogs working out in front. The field underfoot was uneven and seamed with gopher holes, and we were told, more than once, to watch our feet, because the last thing you wanted was to trip and fall with a shotgun in your hand.

Most of the walking took place in silence. We held our collective breath between steps, waiting for the flash of black and copper that meant a rooster was coming up out of the cover. I learned to enjoy listening to the dogs as they weaved in and out of the rows of sorghum as they tried to flush the roosters out, and found myself instinctively beginning to track sound the way an animal does. I felt more “in the moment” than I had in years.

And then, every now and then, the silence would be broken by the sound of fire. One woman turned out to be a sharp shot and brought down more roosters than the rest of us. Another had to be fitted with a smaller shotgun to match her petite frame and struggled through the first two days without making a shot. On the final morning, she took two birds out of the sky back to back so cleanly that the stunned guide beside her just said, “Well, there you go.”

For me, I had trouble remembering the order of things when a bird came up. The whole motion is supposed to happen in a second and a half: Gun to shoulder, safety off, then aim and shoot. So I started singing it to myself like a mantra as we walked to keep my hands and my head on the same page.

Still, when I shot that first pheasant, the uncontrollable tears surprised me a bit, though I’d expected to feel emotional. When I admitted to the tears, Butler told me what I had felt was “reverence” toward something beautiful and alive. I took his feathers, sparkling violet and jewel green and rusty brown, and promised him I would make something beautiful out of them. And later, I took the breast filets Butler had taught us to cut away from the bone, now vacuum-packed and frozen, and promised I would make something healthy and delicious.

For writer Heide Brandes, successfully catching a pheasant came with mixed emotions.

Back home in Oklahoma, I made a stew out of the breast meat with wild rice and mushrooms, and as I stood at my own stove I thought about the field where my pheasant had been hiding. But it wasn’t about the kill.

“I can hunt all day, never pull the trigger, and drive home satisfied,” Butler had told me. “That feeling of being out there in nature and hunting is reverence too.” It was a feeling I’d had to go out and earn myself.

#6313. Minute Review: American Airlines 737 MAX 8 First Class

American Airlines’ 737 MAX 8 First Class is not going to win awards for innovation, but on a recent flight from Dallas to Burbank, a comfortable seat and a fantastic Texas barbecue dinner made for a very pleasant journey and the subject of this week’s Minute Review.

I’m continuing my series of 60-second flight reviews, and today we’re taking a quick look at American Airlines First Class on the Boeing 737 MAX 8.

There’s nothing particularly revolutionary about the Oasis and seat and many hate it, but at least it’s a standard domestic recliner with more legroom than economy class, power, storage, and individual air vents. For a flight of a few hours, though, it gets the job done just fine. I know some of you think this should not be called “first class” or even “business class” (since it is similar to an international premium economy seat), but AA markets this flight as first class so that’s what I’m calling it.

But the real reason I booked this particular flight was dinner.

I previously wrote about American Airlines’ new Pecan Lodge barbecue platter, which I deliberately routed through Dallas to try. It included smoked beef brisket, sausage, macaroni and cheese, coleslaw, pickles, onions, peppers, and barbecue sauce.

And it was excellent…I’m still salivating over it again today.

The brisket remained tender and juicy despite being reheated onboard, the sausage was flavorful, and even the macaroni and cheese came out wonderfully. This was a genuinely delicious barbecue dinner, not just decent airlines food.

Would I deliberately connect in Dallas again just to eat it?

#6312. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6311. United Adds New Route to Bermuda

United Airlines is adding a second nonstop service to Bermuda.

Starting April 3, 2027, the carrier will connect Chicago O’Hare with L.F. Wade International Airport in Hamilton. Flights will operate on Saturdays only, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

Currently, United serves Bermuda from Newark, New Jersey.

“We’re excited to add nonstop service between Chicago and Bermuda, giving customers across the Midwest a convenient new way to experience the island,” Tom Kozlowski, United’s senior manager of Latin America, Caribbean, and Hawaii planning, said in a news release. “This new service builds on our existing connection through Newark/New York and makes it easier for travelers from Chicago and beyond to plan a visit to Bermuda.”

#6310. Why You Might Find Yourself Fishing, Foraging—Or Even Hunting—On Your Next Vacation

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America, from harvesting sea urchins along California's Sonoma Coast to salmon fishing in Southeast Alaska.

There are two types of luxury hotels these days: Those where you don’t have to lift a finger. And those where you might find yourself elbow-deep in the cavity of an elk that you, of all people, just harvested. As in: stalked, shot, and gutted, and butchered.

Camouflage not your style? Maybe you’re digging chanterelles in windswept western Scotland. Or prying mussels off rocks along South Africa’s Cape Peninsula. Or: totani-fishing off the Amalfi Coast in a wooden boat built by a local fisherman whose family has been squid fishing in the Tyrrhennian Sea for generations. (And then, yes, cleaning it, cooking it, and eating the totani e patate of your dreams.)

Whatever you’re doing, if you’re a food-obsessed traveler in 2027, you may find yourself foraging, fishing, or even hunting on your next trip. Call it the next iteration of farm-to-table—but one thing is clear: The hospitality industry has officially gone wild.

At some of the world’s most exclusive hotels, old-world service is giving way to old-world skills. The kind most urban-dwelling, laptop-pecking, Door Dash-ordering professionals have lost. And are looking to gain... on vacation.

Guests at Casa Angelina go totani (squid) fishing off the Amalfi Coast

Travelers learn to clean their catch before making it into an ultra-fresh totani e patate

“Travelers are increasingly curious about the culture behind what they eat,” says Leopoldo Elefante, executive chef at Casa Angelina, on the cliffs of Praiaono, Italy, which launched its “totani ritual” last year, and other local culinary experiences like it. (Nighttime ancient lantern fishing or Pomodoro picking, anyone?) Whether it's couples, kids, or grandparents, it appears that everyone wants to get their hands dirty. “They don’t simply want to taste a local dish, they want to understand where the ingredients come from.”

In other words: people don’t just want to enjoy an exceptional supper anymore, they want to help source it.

It begs the question (and a butchered metaphor): Why are people paying to milk a cow when they can get, say, a bowl of fresh yogurt with housemade granola, local berries, and drizzled with maple syrup for $26?

For Clare Sammells, an associate professor of anthropology who focuses on food and tourism at Bucknell University, the answer lies in the liberating nature of travel. “Travel allows you to try things you’d never do in your daily life,” she explains. “You’re in a new, sacred space. You don’t have to set an alarm and put on a suit and go to an office. You can eat and drink whatever you like! Suddenly doing something outside your normal life starts to seem more possible. Maybe you can envision yourself as someone who does butcher a hog.”

It’s not that big of a leap from the farmers’ market, really. Sampling persimmons from a guy growing six varieties in California’s Central Valley. Picking huckleberries around Montana. Diving for sea snails in South Africa. It all stems from the same, ever-deepening desire: to know where our food comes from.

This is not a new craving, of course. We lazy food-lovers have been trying to find our way back-to-the-land ever since factory farming and the industrial meat complex destroyed it. And, we keep getting closer! We’ve strolled all the local organic markets, and thanked the farmers on all the menus. We’ve attended all the fancy dinners in all the fields and toured all the chef’s gardens.

In Asheville, North Carolina, travelers can sign up for foraging hikes through the Blue Ridge Mountains to learn how to safely harvest wild edibles like porcini mushrooms.

Uni foraging has become a popular activity for visitors to California, with Sea Ranch Lodge offering a “Uni Two Ways” workshop, including a natural dye making class and tasting menu.

Now we want to don gumboots and tromp through the woods and pull up our own porcinis! Wrangle into wetsuits and snorkel off the craggy coast of Sonoma and collect a dozen different seaweeds! Trod gently over tide pools and pluck purple sea urchin and slurp super fresh uni!

We want to get … closer. Personal. Not just to our food but, well, to the earth itself. We want to, you know, touch grass. And then eat it. (Wheat, bristle, bent, all fair game.) And inns, influencers, outfitters, and chefs from Santa Barbara to Sussex are making it possible, perfecting the art of what could be called five-star self-sufficiency.

Take Vermejo, Ted Turner Reserve’s 558,000-acre wildlife reserve in New Mexico, once a traditional hardcore hunting lodge. Today, it offers bison safaris, snowtubing, and spa treatments– as well as hunting and fishing trips catering to those who want a cushy bed with their cow elk or cutthroat trout—and a talented chef to either teach them how to filet it, prepare it, and pair it. Plus a conservationist who can explain the role hunting plays in biodiversity and conservation.

Vermejo, Ted Turner Reserve’s 558,000-acre wildlife reserve in New Mexico, offers hunting and fishing trips with a conservation focus.

This idea may be a novel trend for some travelers, but for Indigenous communities across North America, sustainable hunting, fishing, and foraging has always been a fundamental part of daily life. Today, adventurous travelers can respectfully connect with that ancient knowledge by staying at Indigenous-owned lodges like Wahous Wilderness Lodge, the Ahousaht First Nation’s flagship hospitality venture in British Columbia’s remote Clayoquot Sound (which offers fishing experiences and a “tide-to-table” culinary philosophy), or by dining at Indigenous- focused restaurants helping revitalize Native American foodways from Oaxaca to Minneapolis.

Hotels and restaurants aren’t the only ones getting the claytonia perfoliata-curious out there. Independent foraging guides are multiplying like mushrooms after a rain. From niche Instagrammers like @feminist_fisherwoman to YouTube stalwarts like @catchncookcalifornia and Taku Kondo (@outdoorcheflife), they are making the outdoors our oyster—leading such hands-on adventures as crab snaring in Half Moon Bay, spearfishing in Santa Barbara, and quail hunting in Tucson.

That’s what happens when people get a taste of eons-old traditions—and berries beyond the grocery store—says Nick Weston, founder of Hunt Gather Cook: They hunger for more. He has been bringing “newbies” from London to Los Angeles to Shepherd’s Barn on his Firle Estate, in Sussex, since 2011. His butchering courses and live-fire feasts sell out. “The only thing I’ve found people are uncomfortable with is cutting off a rabbit’s head with a machete.”

Whether you’re going nuts in your own backyard or spearfishing lionfish off the coast of Florida, connecting with your environment in this way “sparks a true sense of place that can develop into a deeper sense of environmental stewardship,” says Sam Shepherd, a biology professor and director of agriculture and catholic environmental stewardship at Ava Maria University in the Scottish Highlands.

Today, such slow immersion in a local food system is increasingly accessible to travelers, Shepherd explains, adding that it "contrasts starkly with tourism based on brief curated visits in which the local food and culture can become a side-show.”

On the North Fork of Long Island, Lin Beach House takes a more laidback approach. Run by the married duo behind Matchbook Distillery, Brian Kwasnieski, a commercial fisherman, and his wife, Leslie Merinoff Kwasnieski, the contemporary six-room Victorian invites people to, per the website: “Pull the fish. Cut the herbs. Blend the gin. Come back for dinner.” And people do. Pickling, clamming, and preserving, too.

“We’ve had a lot of financial analysts lately,” says Leslie with a laugh. “People love scooping the fish!” Brian practices the sustainable method of pound trap fishing, which avoids bycatch, she explains. He usually heads out on his boat at 4 a.m. to bring in pufferfish, porgy, and mackerel.

“Oh, no,” Leslie corrects. “We let them sleep in until 10.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6309. Royal Caribbean Out-Earned Hilton’s Whole 2025 In A Quarter

Royal Caribbean earned $1.7 billion in Q3 2026, or $6.45 per share, up from $5.74 a year ago. Revenue climbed 9% to $5.6 billion, and the company raised its full-year adjusted earnings guidance to between $17.85 and $17.95 per share. RCCL Management said bookings are up in the mid-teens since the last call, and 2027 sailings are up in the high teens, booked at record rates.

Net yields (revenue per passenger cruise day) rose only 0.9%, so most of the growth came from more capacity rather than higher spend per guest. That capacity is spread across three brands many travelers don’t realize share a parent. Royal Caribbean International is the big-ship family product, Celebrity Cruises is the premium line, and Silversea is the luxury line. A traveler who would never book Royal might happily book Celebrity, and plenty of Silversea guests have no idea Royal Caribbean owns it. Each serves a distinct market, and all three feed RCCL’s results.

Comparisons are fun, but until I looked at the numbers, I wasn’t aware of just how impressively cruise stacks up against even asset-light industries like modern hotel chains. The four big cruise companies with public data available earned about $8.6 billion in net income on roughly $60.8 billion in revenue. That includes Carnival at $2.8 billion, Royal Caribbean at $4.3 billion, Viking at $1.1 billion and Norwegian at $423 million (a GAAP figure; its adjusted net income was Norwegian at $423 million.05 billion). These four operate on a net margin of about 14%. MSC Cruises, the other giant, belongs to the privately held MSC Group and does not publish comparable results.

Hotels, comparatively, are less profitable for the most part. Marriott earned $2.6 billion, Hilton earned $1.5 billion, and Hyatt lost $52 million. IHG earned $759 million on $5.2 billion of revenue. The four combined for about $4.8 billion, or a little over half of what the four cruise companies made.

Car rental is worse. Avis Budget lost $995 million, including a $518 million impairment on its electric vehicle fleet, and Hertz lost about $747 million, according to the wider-than-expected losses. Together that is a $1.7 billion loss on about $20 billion of revenue. Enterprise Holdings (Enterprise, National, and Alamo) is a private company and does not report results publicly.

Airlines are the only group that earns more than cruising in nominal dollars, and only because of their sheer scale. IATA put 2025 global airline net profit at $45 billion on $1.065 trillion of revenue, a 4.2% margin, and cut its 2026 forecast to $23 billion at 2.0%. Simply, four cruise companies earned about 19% of what every airline in the world made combined, on less than 6% of the revenue.

Hotel companies like Marriott and Hilton are asset-light, so their revenue includes massive amounts of reimbursed costs and franchise fees, and most of the physical buildings are owned by other entities. A fair comparison would use margin on fees, and I would not suggest these numbers are apples-to-apples. Cruise lines own the ships, the fuel bill and the debt, with Royal Caribbean carrying about $22.4 billion of it, so their profit has to cover a much heavier balance sheet even after accelerated (and substantial) depreciation.

Passenger captivity on a ship is unrivaled throughout the travel industry. Travelers pay for the room, the meals, the drinks, the excursions and the Wi-Fi in one transaction, all on a property the cruise line controls. Royal Caribbean says close to half of this year’s guests are repeat customers and about 40% belong to its loyalty program. A hotel chain would love to know exactly how much each guest spends in its properties but they don’t; cruise lines know it down to the cent.

Royal Caribbean’s $1.7 billion, Carnival’s $1.9 billion and Norwegian’s $491 million add up to about $4.1 billion in net income in a single quarter. That roughly matches what Marriott, Hilton and Hyatt earned together in all of 2025. Hilton’s own third quarter net income was $536 million, about a third of Royal Caribbean’s. That’s absolutely incredible, especially when

Two caveats belong here. My sample includes only the hotel companies and cruise lines that publish numbers I could confirm, so MSC and plenty of private hotel owners are missing. The fiscal years also do not line up perfectly, because Carnival’s year ends in November. But it’s also worth noting that Hilton has about 18x the keys that Royal does, owns less of the product itself (and carries fewer costs), and still falls woefully behind Royal.

When I wrote about Royal Caribbean’s $3 billion Sandals deal in September, part of the claim was that Royal knows the customer base well (it does) and that it knows the market well (it does) but understanding the power of capturing the total spend for a client trip is the magic. With this much cash coming off the ships, buying 50% of Sandals, expected to close in early 2027, gives Royal Caribbean a stake in the land-based all-inclusive business. The same logic is why I argued that every big hotel brand wants your all-inclusive money. The cruise industry is not trying to beat hotels at hotels; rather it’s buying the segment of the hotel business that already works like a cruise.

My agency sells both cruises and hotel rooms, and the difference in how the two operators treat the traveler’s wallet is all the difference. Cruise companies have figured out how to capture the whole vacation budget on a floating property they control, and the earnings show it. I expect the gap with hotels to widen next year as 2027 bookings convert at record rates, and I expect more hotel companies to copy the model through all-inclusive resorts and bundled pricing. But I was still shocked that Hilton, which owns very few hotels, and is mostly a marketing arm for a far larger footprint, is dwarfed by a cruise line in a single quarter.

#6308. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6307. 6 Places in the US Where Travelers Can Hunt, Fish, or Forage for Their Own Food

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

My boyhood summers tasted like wild fruit and fish. When I gathered blueberries from the pine and oak woods around my father’s New Hampshire home, he would stir their purple sweetness into pancake batter. When I pulled brook trout from the waters of a long-abandoned granite quarry, I would sauté them in a cast iron skillet until delicate flesh flaked from translucent bone.

Mount Monadnock in New Hampshire, where the author learned how to forage and fish.

At twenty, I went vegan and quit fishing. For food, I looked to the grocery store and, seasonally, the garden. Though I still gathered the occasional handful of berries or chanterelles, I took little sustenance directly from wild nature.

Ten years later—my black-and-white dietary ethics shaken by the realities of agriculture and my body demanding a wider array of nutrients—I began a journey back to omnivory and the wild. I took up a fishing rod again. I paid more attention to mushrooms emerging from the forest floor. And I began learning to hunt.

Indigo milk caps, an edible wild mushroom

Picking portobello-like indigo milk caps, casting for trout or striped bass, or sitting at the base of a maple with rifle in hand as dawn brightened the frosty deer woods, I began to remember that the land is a source not only of beauty but also of food, that the earth feeds our bodies as well as our souls. Over the past two decades, I have gradually awakened to this continent’s vast diversity of wild edibles and to the deep meanings wild foodways still carry across cultures. Many of us, of course, have lost these practices. We have forgotten how to eat wild.

If you want to reconnect with the entire nature-to-plate experience, you need to get out there and harvest with your own hands. Even if you aren’t ready to dive into relearning ancient skills, across the country you can find opportunities to experience wild foods, each a gift flavored by local land and culture, each a chance to savor what a place tastes like, straight from the source.

Sochan gathering in Great Smoky Mountains National Park is a Cherokee tradition.

People have walked the Blue Ridge Mountains in search of edibles since the end of the last Ice Age. Of the tens of thousands of species that inhabit the region’s lush and astonishingly biodiverse forests today, a handful dominate Asheville’s vibrant foraging and culinary scene.

Ramps, or wild leeks, bring the earthy, garlicky promise of spring. Pawpaws, the continent’s largest edible native fruit, ripen in late summer and early fall, delivering a near-tropical blend of mango and banana to the tongue. And a bounty of edible fungi—from morels and black trumpets to lion’s mane, chanterelles, and chicken of the woods—fill mushroom hunters’ baskets in every season but winter.

Overharvesting, both legal and illegal, has triggered some restrictions. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, for example, the collection of ramps has been forbidden since 2004 and daily mushroom harvest is limited to a pound per person. The prohibition on gathering ramps extends to the Eastern Band of Cherokee, though a recent agreement with the National Park Service permits several dozen members to gather sochan within park boundaries.

Outside the park, opportunities still abound for all. In the nearby Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests, for instance, you can gather up to three pounds (or one gallon) of ramps or mushrooms for personal use, though truffles and chaga are off limits. Even if you don’t see yourself setting off into the woods in search of dinner, or exploring foraging possibilities within Asheville itself, the area offers a cornucopia of ways to enjoy and learn about wild edibles.

A non-resident fishing license from D.C., Virginia, or Maryland lets you head out on your own.

Blue catfish are invasive to Chesapeake Bay and a predator of the ever-popular blue crab

Covering nearly 4,500 square miles, the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal tributaries are famous for blue crabs, beloved by locals and visitors alike. Though the bay still supplies a significant portion of the nation’s catch, blue crab numbers have been impacted by habitat loss, overharvest, and predation.

Among the crab’s predators are locally invasive blue catfish. Introduced to Virginia rivers decades ago, the fish have proved able to tolerate the saltier waters of the bay and are now outcompeting native species. To mitigate the negative impacts, diverse stakeholders—including scientists, government agencies, seafood producers, restaurants, and grocery stores—are working to build a thriving “River to Table” market.

In recent years, Virginia and Maryland have each recorded millions of pounds in annual commercial blue catfish harvest. Though consumers are advised to eat smaller fish or to trim away belly fat and dark meat to remove contaminants, blue catfish is increasingly popular table fare. Delicious fried, grilled, smoked, or blackened, it is available in a growing number of restaurants and grocery stores around the region.

You can also catch your own, with or without a fishing guide. In most tidal waters, neither state limits how many blue catfish recreational anglers can keep. If you go, be prepared for some big, hard-fighting fish. Blue cats regularly run 30-plus pounds and can get much larger.

Farmers Jeffry Bellcourt (standing) and Bob Libby harvest wild rice using traditional methods on Rice Lake in northern Minnesota.

Centuries ago, the Anishinaabe migrated from the Atlantic coast to the western Great Lakes region. At the heart of their migration stories is a prophecy telling them to travel west until they found the place where food grows on water. That food was manoomin, or wild rice, an annual grass that grows in shallow water. An important traditional food for multiple Indigenous nations, wild rice (psiŋ in Dakota) continues to carry deep cultural meaning and is central to food sovereignty efforts in the western Great Lakes region.

To harvest wild rice in late summer, two people work from a canoe, one navigating with a long forked pole, the other using a pair of smooth cedar sticks to gently bend tall stalks over the gunwales and tap the ripe grain loose. (Mechanized harvest has been banned in Minnesota since 1939.) Knowledge of when and how to harvest is passed down by other harvesters and comes with experience. Once dried and parched, grain must be separated from chaff. Though some people still use traditional methods, most finishing is now done mechanically.

Nutty and smoky, manoomin works any time of day, from rice and berries with maple syrup for breakfast to a hearty stew for dinner. Natural wild rice grains are a mix of earthy hues and cook in 20 minutes or less. In contrast, “paddy” or “cultivated” variants grown in Minnesota and California are glossy black and take much longer. Minnesota law requires clear labeling to distinguish the two.

Though Minnesota residents and nonresidents alike can purchase a wild rice license, harvesting and processing is a complex process. For Tribal communities, it is also an ancient and ongoing relationship. For those new to ricing, learning from experienced harvesters or attending a Tribal-led camp or educational event is a respectful place to begin. Visitors can also support Tribal communities by purchasing manoomin directly from them.

Restaurants across Pensacola, Florida offer fishermen the option to cook their catch.

Harbor Docks combines fishing trips with restaurant preparation.

Dubbed the “Gloucester of the Gulf,” the commercial fishing hub of Pensacola, Florida, anchored a late 19th- and early 20th-century fishery that hauled in millions of pounds of red snapper each year. After World War II, recreational fishing surged as well. The pressure, combined with bycatch from shrimp trawlers, proved too much: between 1950 and 1990, red snapper numbers plunged. Since the 1990s, federal managers have capped the annual catch, split it between commercial and recreational fishermen, and limited anglers to two fish per day.

Sweet, mild, and firm, red snapper can be roasted as Snapper Veracruzana, fried as snapper bites, baked whole with Thai seasonings, or grilled with lemon sauce. You’ll find it at seafood markets along the Florida panhandle and Alabama coast. You’ll also find it at restaurants, many of which will cook your catch. Snapper season peaks in summer but often runs into fall.

Many snapper are released because they’re undersized, out of season, or over the two-fish limit. When anglers reel up a snapper from deep water, the fish’s swim bladder often expands, leaving it unable to swim back down. To keep released fish alive, Florida Sea Grant’s Return ’Em Right program urges anglers to use descending devices, which return fish quickly to depth, and offers free devices to those who complete an online course. In recent years, federal rules have also required anglers to carry them.

State and federal laws ban nearly all sale of wild game in the US, but federal rules allow USDA inspection and then sale of some non-native species, including axis deer.

In the 1860s, the British colony of Hong Kong gave the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi eight axis deer. The beautiful spotted animals, native to India, were released on the island of Molokaʻi. In the absence of predators, they multiplied swiftly. In 1959 and 1960, nine deer were relocated to Maui. There, too, numbers soared.

Alongside other large herbivores, none of which are native to Hawaiʻi, axis deer have devastated crops and stripped hillsides of drought-stressed vegetation, allowing rain to erode soil and sweep it into wetlands and onto coral reefs, harming critical habitats. To accelerate deer control measures, Hawaiʻi has issued more than two dozen emergency proclamations in recent years.

Many families hunt deer and prize the meat, especially on Molokaʻi, but hunting alone hasn’t kept numbers in check. So islanders have turned to an unconventional solution: commercial harvest. State and federal laws ban nearly all sale of wild game in the US, but federal rules allow USDA inspection and then sale of some non-native species, including axis deer. In 2007, Molokaʻi hunter Desmund Manaba became the first in Hawaiʻi to win approval to harvest axis deer and sell the meat. In 2012, Maui County backed a harvesting cooperative of its own.

Today, shooters working for Maui Nui Venison take deer from private ranches each night. Fresh or processed into snack sticks, most of the meat is sold. A portion is distributed for free to local families through the company’s Holo ʻAi program, which the company links to Hawaiʻi’s long tradition of food-sharing and which helped ensure food security during the COVID-19 pandemic and after the devastating 2023 wildfires.

Prickly pear fruit can be eaten raw or squeezed into juice.

Visitors to Arizona's Sonoran Desert can purchase wild foods gathered by O’odham harvesters.

The word “desert” may conjure ideas of emptiness, barrenness, a lack of life. Sitting on the eastern edge of the Sonoran Desert, Tucson, Arizona, dispels all such notions. Designated as a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015, Tucson boasts both the longest continuous agricultural history of any city in the United States and a rich set of wild foods traditions.

Among other plants, cacti are on the menu. For millennia, Tohono O’odham people have gathered food from—and maintained vital relationships with—multiple species, following a calendar set by the desert’s two rainy seasons. From late summer into fall, during and after the summer rains, people harvest prickly pear fruit, which can be eaten raw or squeezed into juice. In spring, after the winter rains, harvesters pluck cholla buds. Reminiscent of lemony asparagus tips, they can be cooked and eaten fresh or dried for later use.

In June, before the summer rains return, people gather saguaro fruit, knocking it from towering cacti with a kuipad, a long pole made of saguaro ribs, then dry the protein-rich seeds and make jam from the fruit. They also make syrup, fermenting some into wine for the rain ceremony that marks the O’odham New Year.

Foraging is prohibited in Saguaro National Park, with exceptions for O’odham harvesting traditions. Though gathering is legal on private land with permission, participating in guided harvests and walks is an ideal place to begin. You can also purchase foods gathered by O’odham harvesters.

#6306. In Southeast Alaska, Connecting With My Indigenous Roots Through Salmon Fishing

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

As the fish on the end of my line ferociously attempts to swim away from our boat, I can tell from the forcible tug that it's a prized Chinook salmon. I stay steady and let the fish (known as a king in Alaska for its large size) tire itself out before calmly reeling it in, following the advice of the expert guide standing alongside me. He hoists my catch into our North River cabin cruiser, and I meet my worthy opponent: a plump, silver-blue salmon with black speckles, weighing in around 15 pounds. As I take a moment to catch my breath and admire the scenery around me—pristine waters reflecting the blue sky above, dense forests, coastal cliffs—I realize my Indigenous ancestors likely fished this exact spot centuries before me.

A decade ago, I returned to my birthplace of Ketchikan in Southeast Alaska to reconnect with my Tlingit heritage, having only recently learned of my Alaska Native ancestry and found my Indigenous family members. I felt inspired by our tribe’s rich culture, especially after hearing stories about it from my brother, but at the same time I felt unmoored and unsure of my place within it, as someone who had grown up in Minnesota, far from my tribe’s ancestral homelands. I have since returned several times, but on this recent trip to Alaska’s Inside Passage, salmon fishing was making me feel like I belonged.

Steamboat Bay Fishing Club on Noyes Island in Southeast Alaska

The adventure began long before I arrived at Steamboat Bay Fishing Club on remote Noyes Island, where unadulterated, old-growth forest stretches right up to the edges of its serene shoreline. To get there from Ketchikan, I hopped a floatplane for a 45-minute flight over Tongass National Forest—the planet’s largest intact temperate rainforest—before being dropped off at the lodge’s private dock.

Certified by Alaska Green Adventure for its sustainability efforts, the luxury resort has operated on the island since 2013 and hosts a max of 24 guests. Typical three-night stays include guided fishing, curated chef’s dinners, rejuvenating massages, nature walks, and late-night storytelling and stargazing around the fire pit. Throughout my visit, I spied bald eagles, orcas, humpback whales, sea otters, and sea lions. The stay was unlike anything I’ve ever encountered before.

It’s still an awe-inspiring experience for Haida-Tsimshian fisherman and artist Everett Athorp, who has served as a fishing guide at Steamboat Bay since it opened. “I’m amazed by the beauty of the place,” he says. “There’s nothing like getting out on the water on a beautiful day and seeing the sunrise and all the wildlife. I can’t picture myself doing anything else—I just love the freedom of being out on the water.”

Athorp’s easygoing, unassuming demeanor belies his decades-long experience and expertise, which are rooted in the knowledge passed down by his Indigenous ancestors. Regulars who return to the resort every summer request to hit the water with him, eager to hear his stories of growing up in Alaska and to learn about the significance of fishing for the state’s 229 federally recognized tribal nations.

“Salmon are so important to Alaska Native culture,” says Athorp, who lives in nearby Klawook on Prince of Wales Island. “Fishing is a livelihood and a way of life here. I’ll tell my guests about the old ways people fished, using traps and wooden halibut hooks. I hope they come away with a respect for the salmon, the fishery, and the land—and an appreciation for the opportunity to be here, even if it’s a slow fishing day.”

In Alaska, fishing isn’t just a hobby—it’s a means of survival, especially for the state’s vast rural population, who depend on subsistence hunting and fishing to feed their families. Dating back millennia, Alaska Native communities have stewarded and sustainably harvested wild salmon runs, building smokehouses and summer fish camps (many of which are still in use). Oral histories, formline artwork, and traditional dances all honor the role of salmon as not only a vital food source but also an important cultural symbol; my Tlingit tribe considers salmon to be sacred beings representing abundance, renewal, and life itself.

Steamboat Bay’s main lodge is dotted with artistic homages to salmon and other important animals, including carved paddles, bentwood boxes, and a massive carved Western cedar panel perched above the fireplace. It’s all made by Athorp, who is also an accomplished carver. The craft is another important cultural component of his Haida-Tsimshian heritage, and his creations are an act of resistance and cultural preservation—carrying on the work of his grandfather, Jones Yeltatzie.

Haida-Tsimshian fisherman and artist Everett Athorp holds one of his works

“My grandfather went to Mt. Edgecumbe boarding school in Sitka, so he had to [teach himself the artistic method] when he was a kid,” says Athorp. The institution was established by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in the 1940s to offer a high school education for rural Alaska Native students, who historically were restricted from learning about their cultures. “Because he was self-taught, [his technique] was a little rough. Looking back at it now, he was trying to keep the tradition alive.” Today, Athorp is the one passing those skills on to both Native and non-Native aspiring artists.

Out on the water, I find myself settling into a rhythm as the hours pass. In some ways, it feels familiar, given that I grew up fishing Minnesota’s lakes for walleye, sunfish, and other freshwater species. But those Midwestern summers couldn’t have prepared me for quintessential Alaska fishing experiences like fighting a king salmon, hooking a barn-door halibut (so named for its size), or watching in disbelief as a sea lion snatches my hard-won catch right off the line.

But as any seasoned angler knows, fishing is never just about fishing. Much of the day is devoted to seemingly ancillary activities like shooting the breeze with my boatmates. We become fast friends, and I learn that although this trip holds particular significance for me, they too seem to have found what they were seeking amid Alaska’s unadulterated beauty. All of us have been offered a taste of a time-honored Tlingit tradition, and it's here, floating out in uncharted waters as my ancestors once did, that I finally feel like I've found my place.

#6305. Can Emirates Make Denver Work Without A Smaller Jet?

At Routes World in Frankfurt, Emirates President Tim Clark named Denver International Airport, Detroit and Philadelphia as the next candidates for nonstop Dubai flights in the United States. It would be the first new US station since Miami returned in June 2021; Emirates currently serves 12 US airports. Clark would not say which aircraft would fly the route though that largely depends on the size of the market and distance. Of the three possible destinations, the distances are 7,758 miles to Denver, 7,083 to Detroit and 6,928 to Philadelphia.

Emirates Denver service has been rumored for a while. Former DEN CEO, Phil Washington, said in spring 2025 that the airport’s next new route would “likely be Dubai with Emirates,” while Emirates said it had no official plans. Emirates and United have been codeshare partners since 2023, a tie-up Live And Let’s Fly detailed when the partnership was first announced.

Emirates’ unique fleet gives it an incredible advantage in large markets, but makes smaller market expansion a challenge. According to Emirates’ own fleet figures from late 2025, 235 of its 269 aircraft, or 87%, were A380s and 777-300ERs. Those big birds carry roughly 350 to 500 seats depending on the configuration. Emirates had just 13 A350-900s at that point, and it has no 787 in service even though 35 are on order (though many have speculated they will be converted to 777-X orders assuming it eventually passes certification.)

That informs the decision on every new expansion city. Most airlines test a new market with a smaller jet, run it at three or four weekly flights and grow it if demand holds. A perfect example of that was British Airways growth at Pittsburgh. It started with subsidized service 4x weekly on a Boeing 787-8, but based on its success moved to 5x, then 6x, and now daily service and fluctuates between the 787-8 and 787-9 with some frequencies operating a 787-10 or very occasionally a 777-200. Emirates cannot do that. Its smallest widebody, the A350-900, is only now reaching the US network, entering service to Orlando on November 1 with 298 seats. A 777-300ER to Denver means filling roughly 350 or more seats, on a route 7,758 miles long, departing an airport at about 5,400 feet of elevation. High elevation (hot and high) hurts takeoff performance, and it makes a full-length route even harder especially at a frequency of more than 5x weekly.

The ideal test would be a 787-8 if it had the legs, a smaller airplane at the right size to prove the market and to link Denver to Dubai without staking a big fleet commitment on it. But Emirates has no 787s flying (it may never operate the type depending on the order book swaps I mentioned before), and the reality is that with a 20% reserve range variance, the altitude, an especially in the summer, it can’t make the trip even if they had it.

That means a Denver bet has to be a larger aircraft than ideal if it makes the cut. The other mentioned possible destinations come with their own challenges. Philadelphia has more international service but also a much larger market. It faces flights on Qatar for connecting global service along with a heavy American Airlines slate, British Airways, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus for Europe/Middle East, and connections to Asia or Africa. Detroit has an even smaller market with more competition from Air France, Royal Jordanian, Turkish, and a heavy Delta tilt.

Denver does not have nonstops to the Middle East or Africa, and Narita is its only Asian destination, flown by United on a 787. DEN served 34 international destinations in 19 countries in 2025. The question is how many people in Denver need to get to Dubai or beyond, and cannot do it more easily another way.

Travelers who can already connect through Frankfurt or Munich on Lufthansa, through Istanbul on Turkish, or through Toronto on Air Canada, and favor Star Alliance, have little reason to switch. Many of the rest are captive to United, either because of status or because of corporate contracts, and United already flies its own long-haul routes to Europe and Tokyo. Emirates is left with a smaller pool of travelers who are not tied to a hub carrier and want to go to India, the Gulf, Africa or the Indian Ocean, along with the premium leisure market that wants Emirates’ product.

What Emirates brings from the other end is a global network. Denver would feed Dubai’s connections to South Asia and Africa, and Emirates has the reach to sell Denver as a gateway to places United cannot. But that seems like a tough challenge. I’m a fan of Denver and have visited several times personally, I grew up in nearby Omaha, my brother lived there for some time – Denver has plenty to offer to the world. But I am trying to imagine the pitch to a family in Singapore, or a upwardly mobile couple in Mumbai. Can Emirates convince locals in the UAE to choose Denver over Switzerland for those who want to hit the slopes? I’m not so sure.

My prediction is that Denver stays a candidate, but not yet a route, until Emirates has a smaller widebody aircraft in meaningful numbers. Then again, some markets where Emirates has been successful would shock readers of this site. Manchester, England had three and sometimes four daily A380s and is not a particularly premium market with even more competition. If Emirates does move forward with Denver, I expect the airline to start with a seasonal schedule, probably timed to the winter ski market, and to treat the first year as a test. Emirates built its network on massive airframes and highly premium configurations, which is great for flooding a market where you can be successful and challenging to experiment. Then again, financial performance for Emirates is less public and pressured than publicly traded companies so maybe it doesn’t matter anyway.

#6304. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.
