#6303. A Day at Sea With the Octopus Fisherman of the Yucatán

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

The turquoise, bathtub-warm water of the Yucatán is extra sudsy today. Our little skiff, known around here as an alijo, is bobbing like a toy as our captain gently tugs on a few lines descending into the water. “Paciencia,” he repeats, reaching for the next line, before a knowing draw confirms, still, no octopus.

We’re just a 20-minute boat ride from the sleepy town of Rio Lagartos, aboard the Yahilin, captained by 55-year-old Limberth Orlando Alcocer Diaz, who has been fishing since the age of eight. His parents were fishermen too; these waters provide supple mero, a white fish loved for ceviche, and juicy shrimp that Alcocer Diaz promises is some of the tastiest you’ll find in the region. But there is another catch unique to this coastline, and the reason I'm here today: the octopus maya.

The writer and local chefs join fisherman Limberth Orlando Alcocer Diaz aboard the Yahilin

A grilled octopus maya is prepared at Maroma, a Belmond Hotel, in Riviera Maya

“The octopus maya is a bit smaller than the kind you get from the Mediterranean—it looks beautiful on the plate,” says chef Cesar A. Landeo, who has joined me and Alcocer Diaz on board Yahilin. A bucket of bait crabs wiggle between us. Landeo is currently the executive chef at the luxury Maroma, a Belmond Hotel, located about three hours from Rio Lagartos by car and where I'm staying—the night prior, I'd enjoyed a wood-grilled octopus, sourced from these very waters. Another chef, Karla Encisco, who has worked for various Cancún hotels over the years and now acts as a hospitality consultant, is on the other side of me, sharing tips for cooking octopus in a dry-pot method that uses only the seawater released by the animal for steaming. We're all here with the same shared interest: to trace the seafood I was enjoying at Maroma to its source, and gain a better understanding of the divisive choice to eat them at all.

This part of Mexico has earned a reputation for its sustainable approach to octopus fishing—and to understand why, you need to set sail with someone like Alcocer Diaz. He is one of several hundred fishermen who use a unique artisanal method built off of just two long pieces of bamboo (known as “jimbas”), a few cords, and a live crab and maybe some lobster as bait. Some records show this style of fishing has existed for hundreds of years among the Maya, but it has been employed commercially for the last five or six decades. And it is built entirely around an understanding of the animal we’re searching for.

Live bait crabs are used to catch octopus using an artisanal fishing method unique to the Yucatán.

Known colloquially as both the four-eyed octopus, the petite octopus maya is recognizable by divers and fishermen for its “false eyes” that sit below the real ones. A coral red in color—at least, when it isn’t camouflaging—it also lives a pointed existence of roughly one year. As Alcocer Diaz explains, once females have laid their eggs in a cave, they will guard them diligently from predators, abandoning their need for food until, finally, once the eggs hatch, the mothers literally drop dead, famished and withered.

Alcocer Diaz mimics a thin, spindly tentacle with a finger to describe the ones he’s seen. “Not even scavengers will eat what’s left of them,” he says while threading his bait. It’s not much better for the males, who may mate several times during a season before their own demise, expiring after they’ve completed a summer of procreation. Octopus fishing here is only allowed from August 1 to December 15, and not a day later, to catch the cephalopods at the sweet spot of their lifespan, with enough time to repopulate.

It's also why the jimba method is key to the process: By tying a crab or a lobster’s torso to a line and launching it overboard, letting it dangle from the bamboo, only males will take the bait they encounter on the sea floor while the females remain on their starvation-inducing egg-watch. The males willingly wrap themselves around the shellfish, just as they would to feed normally, and when fishermen check a line and notice a pound or two of extra weight attached—“it just feels different,” Alcocer Diaz tells me in Spanish—they reel them in.

Two long bamboo poles, a few fishing lines, and live bait are the backbone of this method

An octopus maya, smaller than its Mediterranean or Pacific counterpart

“They are really intelligent,” says Alcocer Diaz with a sense of awe, mimicking how the octopuses he catch will simply walk off his fiberglass boat and back into the water if he doesn’t act quickly. His method is swift: a spike between the eyes for a sudden brain death, a method more recently popularized under the ethical Japanese process of ikejime.

The animal’s intellect is, of course, why some diners will turn down the chance to eat a perfectly grilled pulpo. It’s also the reason that Encisco, who is often tasked with preparing these eight-armed creatures, still can’t watch the documentary My Octopus Friend. Lando admits his wife raised the same concern when he left early this morning for our excursion. (“‘Fishing octopus?’ she said to me, ‘But aren’t they so smart?’”). Alcocer Diaz considers it as a fact in the cycle of life. Everything he does, from gassing up his boat to choosing which seafood to fish based on the weather or season, comes from an understanding of his place on the food chain: “I just want to feed my family,” he says. I'm hoping that, by the end of our expedition, I'll have an answer of my own.

Pelicans and seagulls watch passing fishing boats outside the town of Rio Lagartos, Mexico.

As pelicans circle our boat, used to seeing scraps of fish tossed off the side of the ajilos, I prod Alcocer Diaz for a greater mission, or calling, driving his choice to use this artisanal method, and his commitment to respecting the rules of the “veda,” the months when octopus fishing is banned in the region so that the population can regenerate for the next season. He talks about sustainability as crucial to maintaining his livelihood. Later, over a lunch of octopus ceviche at a portside restaurant in town, Alcocer Diaz's friend Wabi Martin Tabasco Marfil—another fisherman in the same co-op—breaks down the logic further for me: “If we fish everything today, what will be left tomorrow? If we take all the little fish, how will the big fish survive—and then, how will we get the big fish?” It's a needs-based understanding of sustainability.

Reinforcing this commitment among local fishermen is an ongoing effort—both on the part of the fishing cooperatives organized by workers in every single port, all the way up to the chefs who purchase their seafood to put on a menu, and, finally, the consumers who order it. This is how Pesca Con Futuro (Fishing for the Future), an organization connecting chefs with sustainable fishing collectives throughout Mexico, came to fruition. “In almost all cases, consumption shapes how food is produced,” says Citlali Gomez Lepe, the biologist who founded Pesca Con Futuro eight years ago. Today, the group helps chefs restaurants and hotels source shrimp from the Gulf of Mexico, red lobster from Baja California, and rainbow trout from Michoacan, to name just a few products, with over 60 fisheries involved.

“If consumers of fish and seafood in Mexico show a preference for [artisanal and sustainably sourced] products—and if the market transmits that signal all the way along the value chain to the fishers themselves—then those fishers who operate according to best sustainability practices will find allies at the end of the chain,” says Gomez Lepe. Both Encisco and Landeo source seafood via Pesca Con Futuro for the hotels they work with, as do familiar culinary names like Gabriela Camara and Javier Plasencia, among many dozens of other Mexican chefs who act as ambassadors.

Chef Cesar A. Landeo plates grilled octopus at Maroma, a Belmond Hotel

Fisherman Wabi Martin Tabasco Marfil fishes for octopus maya

“We realized chefs have a huge voice in what lands on the table,” Enciso says, when I ask why she got involved with Pesca Con Futuro. “For those of us who work in hotels, we can educate the people who come into their restaurants.”

On the Riviera Maya, where the scenic coastline is home to a smattering of hotels from 1,800-key all-inclusives to luxury brands like Belmond and local boutiques, the sheer number of diners here presents a challenge—or an opportunity for sustainability, depending on how you look at it. Enciso is an optimist about the power we each hold when we sit down for our lobster dinner on vacation—whether that's choosing to eat only in-season seafood, or asking where your crustacean was sourced. “There’s a phrase I love,” Enciso says. “Little people in little small places doing little things can change the world.”

A day on the water requires more patience than I’d expected. After two hours of lurching on the waves, and hopelessly tugging lines that lead Alcocer Diaz to shake his head in the negative, we decide to return back to shore. “On a good day, you can get 50 kilos of octopus,” says Alcocer Diaz—that's about 25 octopuses. But last season was fantastic, he says. “Some days we got 70-80 kilos.” Today, the weather was against us, with an approaching storm muddying the waters and making it difficult for our eight-armed friends to see the bait. Despite our best efforts, the only octopus we will see today is on our plates.

Back on land, we sit for lunch at El Perico Marinero and order the famous pulpo rojo, all of which has been purchased from the local fishing co-op. I have no complaints when it lands on the table. A special ceviche distinct to this part of the Yucatán, it features octopus that has been sliced, battered, and fried into crispy pieces before being tossed in lime juice with chopped onions and sliced jalapeños. Every tentacle is a crunchy delight. Circling us like the morning's pelicans are plates weighed down with more octopus prepared in other ways: sautéed in garlic and butter, or cooked in a tomato-rich sofrito “a la Mexicana.”

Hotels that work with programs like Pesca Con Futuro can offer local, sustainably sourced seafood to guests—an answer to diners who are increasingly interested in knowing where their seafood comes from.

Belmond Maroma is one of several hotels in the Yucatan that uses seafood from Pesca Con Futuro. Follow founder Citlaly Gomez Lepe's advice and always ask your hotel where their seafood comes from. “Your questions will detonate through the restaurant, chefs, and businesses, making them all ask themselves the same questions,” she says. “It triggers a chain reaction and signals that consumers care about this information.” You'll either learn something interesting about the food you are going to eat—and who caught it—or you may inspire a hotel to find better sources, knowing this matters to guests.

While joining fishermen for octopus excursions isn’t a common tourist experience, there are fishing collectives that are open to it. Ask your hotel about sustainable seafood experiences ahead of time, and see what can be arranged.

That said, dining on sustainable seafood here still isn't a given. As we pass plates of battered shrimp and sliced habanero swimming in lime, the fishermen commiserate over a growing number of hurdles. The demand for local sea cucumbers, which get exported to China, is too high to sustain; there is also an ongoing battle between artisanal fishermen and those who use shortsighted methods to turn a quick buck. Limberth speaks of divers from a neighboring state who hit the water late at night to fish during the seasonal bans Limberth vouches that, while diving just offshore, he has seen an increasing number of bleached rock caves underwater—usually the result of freediving fishermen, who squirt the chemical into an octopus hideout to send them fleeing for an easy catch. I can’t help but think of the octopus eggs left behind.

The impact of climate change also remains an ongoing issue. “When the water is warm enough to dive without a wetsuit, I know I won’t see octopuses the rest of the season. They go deeper. Way deeper,” Limberth says, pointing further out toward the continental shelf. Even then, studies have shown that the octopus maya is vulnerable to high water temperatures, dying once they hit 80 degrees.

As we watch the water lap against boats beside the boardwalk, I begin to understand why many of our conversations keep ending on the words “círculo de la vida”—the circle of life. The fishermen respect the vulnerabilities in an octopus's lifecycle; and yet, they must continue to fish, and protect their future ability to fish, so that they can sustain their families. After a day out at sea with Alcocer Diaz, I still can’t answer the existential quandary of whether or not to eat octopus, but I can appreciate how considered the creature is in their fishing method. On the flip side, I feel guilty for a months-prior omakase dinner in New York City that featured creamy octopus eggs, not understanding how precious they are.

Alcocer Diaz, meanwhile, is preoccupied that our fishing efforts were unsuccessful. So much so, that he motorbikes off at the end of lunch, returning with some achiote-rich rechado (a chili paste for cooking, and regional specialty) as a parting gift.

An ajilo (skiff) boat sets off on the water

A couple of days later, I sit with Landeo on the restaurant terrace of Maroma. The menu before me has a blue icon beside various dishes to indicate that the key ingredient has been sourced via Pesca Con Futuro—the chef hopes that, soon, all of his seafood will come through the collective.

“When I started working here on the Riviera Maya, I thought it was going to be like Disneyland in terms of ingredients,” Landeo says. “But there have been real challenges. The majority of hotels here are all-inclusive, so the product they use is different than what we offer.” He hopes that Pesca Con Futuro can continue to get the buy-in from chefs and hotels that it needs to expand even further—and that all begins with diners. “For me, Pesca Con Futuro just makes sense.”

We look out at the sloshing sea, struck by the stories the fisherman told us.“I also want my son to find a world better than the one I got,” he says. “And it's why I want to work responsibly.”

Maybe we aren’t so different from the octopuses, diligently guarding their offspring. It's all a bet on the future.

#6302. Foraging for Purple Sea Urchins Along California's Sonoma Coast

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America. Joseph Ogilvy is the author of Tin Can Coast, published in July 2026.

It’s low tide, not long after dawn, and we’re about to disturb the tide pools of a small Sonoma cove in a hunt for sea urchin. Our group of would-be foragers are in Sea Ranch, a couple hours north of San Francisco, on the tough end of the California coast, where fog-pressed hills tumble into the Pacific. The tide pools of Pebble Beach are covered in shaggy mats and bundles of kelp, and the spots that aren’t blanketed in seaweed are a carnival of alien creatures: sea stars, anemones, crabs, abalone, a muddled parade of luminous colors and implausible body shapes.

Nathan Maxwell Cann, a foraging guide with Flora & Fungi Adventures

Nathan Maxwell Cann, our guide, spectacled, moustachioed, and clad in a well-worn chore jacket and waterproof boots, talks the group through the principles and practice of sea urchin gathering. He tosses out the explanation of what we’re looking for with the easy, self-deprecating banter of a former bartender. For a long time he worked in restaurants in North California, but a few years ago he caught the tidal foraging bug and became a self-professed ‘kelp guy’ with a sideline in urchins.

He shows us our prey. Out of the water, urchins look like curled-up hedgehogs, which is the root of their name in Spanish, Italian, and even English (many years ago our word urchin was used for the hedgehog). Their purple spikes project outward from a roughly hemispherical shell, known as a test. Most are somewhere between the size of a golf ball and a fist, and their only real feature is a malevolent-looking mouth armed with five overlapping teeth for grinding and shearing kelp.

The purple sea urchins devastating California's kelp forests is one of the few seafoods that exist in abundance—or rather, overabundance.

In the water, their flare of spines look like dark starbursts against the rock. At first you only see the big ones, but the longer you stare into the pools, the more urchins you will make out; what seemed shadows resolve themselves into potential pickings, far more than could possibly be taken by hand.

There are huge number of purple sea urchins in this cove, and there are even larger numbers of purple sea urchins throughout California’s coast. Whole swathes of seafloor where kelp forests used to stand are now home to nothing but thousands of the prickly echinoderms, so-called urchin barrens. Similar barrens can be found in Alaska, Tasmania, New Zealand, South Africa, and beyond. Sea urchins have become one of the few seafoods that exist in abundance—or rather, overabundance.

The idea of urchins as a pest wasn’t intuitive for me. When I first encountered them, they were luxuries, delicacies for the gourmand who'd graduated beyond oysters, requiring a great deal of time and discomfort, most of it mine: I was a commis chef in a London restaurant, and one of my duties was cleaning urchins. The restaurant served the roe raw in the shell or tossed with spaghettini; I was busy pulling shards of their spines out from underneath my fingernails.

With California's sea otters hunted to the brink of extinction and sea stars struck down by an uncontrollable plague worsened by the state’s warming waters, the sea urchins have few natural predators left.

In the restaurant business, at least, urchins were still precious things. Only a few years later did I see the other side of their nature. After various twists and turns I found myself writing a book about the history of California and its ocean. The story followed the back-and-forth of human and marine life; how fishing and the sea shaped the state and how the state’s history shaped them in return. For most of the story, the urchin was a minor character compared to sea otters or sardines. In recent years, however, the unsuspecting urchin has moved to center stage: It’s not really coherent to call a brainless shellfish a villain, but within the drama of the intertidal zone, it’s not totally incorrect either.

To put it bluntly, the urchins are out of control. They’re blindly mowing down kelp forests, leaving barrens in their place. And those kelp forests are—or were—marvels of diversity, providing a shelter for a wild array of ocean creatures from jeweled top sea snails to barrel-bodied harbor seals. The problem is the urchins' insatiable appetite for seaweed; unchecked, they will graze through the kelp stipes, dooming them to float away into the deep ocean.

For most of California’s history, predators have kept urchin numbers down, but there aren’t many predators that can get past the wall of spikes and shell. The ones that really make a difference are sea stars and sea otters: Sea stars spew out their stomachs and envelop the urchins, dissolving the edible parts in their digestive juices then ejecting the empty shells. Otters just bash and bite their way through.

The problem in Sonoma and the shore north of it, is that it’s been 150 years or more since a wild otter smashed open an urchin. In the early 19th century, California’s sea otters were hunted to the brink of extinction, the unparalleled softness and value of their fur drawing fur trappers all the way from Russia into California. Two centuries after the hunt, the sea otters’ range is still restricted to a couple hundred miles of the Central California coast.

For a time the sea stars did double duty controlling the urchins, but in recent years they have been struck down by an uncontrollable plague, worsened by the state’s warming waters, called, quite literally, sea star wasting disease. The stars have grown lethargic and limp, with lesions spread across their bodies, their arms falling off or disintegrating. Their population has collapsed, allowing the urchins to chew kelp and multiply at their leisure.

The real skill in urchin foraging lies in not falling over—the kelp-slicked rocks are slippery under the feet, and the ocean pulls at our ankles.

So, ecologically speaking, the job of our small group of foragers is to be the otters. The principles of urchin harvesting internalized, we ditch our shoes and move on to the practice, clambering around the rocky intertidal zone. Our little group is still shaking off our early morning bleariness while scattering over the rocks, bending over to peer closely into the tide pools. Gathering urchins has much the same feeling as mushroom picking or birdwatching (or indeed easter egg hunting). You quickly enter into a kind of focused flow state, punctuated by little jolts of childish joy as you spot what you're looking for. But compared to other forms of foraging, urchin gathering is easy as pie. None of my companions, mostly ocean-curious thirty-something Californians from the Bay and beyond, have been urchin foraging before, but their coolers and bags are soon brimming. The primary motivation of my fellow foragers is split: half are most excited by the prospect of eating our catch, the other half by the experience of going out and catching it.

Once your eye settles on the color and shape of them, they’re everywhere. Picking the urchins up from their niches just takes a little clasp and a wiggle with a pair of tongs. The real skill in urchin foraging lies in not falling over—the kelp-slicked rocks are slippery under the feet, and the ocean pulls at our ankles, while the busy strangeness of the tide pool creatures makes it easy to get distracted.

As Cann puts it, urchin gathering is really just “a reason for being out in the tide pools.”

As my net bag begins bulging with spines, I find myself more and more absorbed with what John Steinbeck called the ‘hurrying, fighting, feeding, breeding animals of the tide pools’; the scuttling of a hermit crab fleeing from my shadow, the respiration holes of an algae-camouflaged abalone peeking from a crevice, the waft and flicker of an anemone’s tentacles. The coos and camera clicks of my fellow foragers suggest they are just as absorbed. Which is kind of the point. As Cann puts it, the urchin gathering is really just “a reason for being out in the tide pools.” The constraint of the task encourages a deeper looking, and gives us, part of a society suspicious of aimless activity, an excuse to mess around and explore a strange world.

And besides, they taste good. Back on dry ground, we each grab a stout pair of kitchen shears and crunch a rough circle out the top of an urchin, scooping and tossing its muddy, briny viscera, rinsing the creature in a bucket of seawater and using a mussel shell to spoon out the five golden tongues of roe, arranged in a star shape. The roe is rich and buttery, starting off savory and briny, then mellowing into a higher note of sweetness. It’s bracing stuff, especially at 8:15 in the morning. It tastes powerfully of place. Cann explains that the umami savor comes directly from the kelp it feeds on. No wonder that, at the Sea Ranch Lodge just down the coast from our expedition, the head chef Ryan Seal makes a sea urchin zabaglione as the base for a carbonara, introducing urchin-hesitant guests to the delicacy while showcasing an intrinsically Sonoman flavor.

Sea Ranch Lodge chef Ryan Seal uses the local sea urchins to make an “uni carbonara” with squid ink chimaera pasta, pancetta, and furikake.

Still on the shore, we stand around in a group chatting while we open more urchins and swallow the meat inside. Even with the appeals and distractions of the intertidal world and a few early morning tongues of uni, our bags are still overflowing. But our gathering has barely made a dent in the cove’s urchin numbers. As substitute otters we have come up short; the real thing can eat dozens of urchins in a day.

And still, uni foraging workshops are increasingly common all over Northern California, adding to the many beachcombers who pick urchin on their own. The urchins are still dominating the coast though. From an ecosystem perspective, our efforts are little more than “a drop in the bucket”, as Cann acknowledges. Restoring the kelp forests will require a more forceful campaign. The Giant Giant Kelp Restoration Project in Monterey has an enormous submarine vacuum to suck urchins from the barrens. In Northern California, scuba divers just crush them with hammers. Entrepreneurs all over California and the West Coast have begun ranching operations, gathering the often underweight urchins from the barrens and fattening them up on sustainably harvested kelp before selling them to restaurants. Another company in Mendocino, Marblis, is compacting the shells into what they call urchinite, pitched as a substitute for marble countertops.

Our morning workshop of tongs and kitchen shears, by contrast, is a symbolic gesture. By mid-morning, my fellow foragers and I will be heading back home with fond memories and a few meals worth of seafood delicacies. The urchins will continue to chomp their way through the kelp forests of Sea Ranch.

Kelp forests—which simultaneously serve as a carbon sink, wildlife habitat, and protection against erosion—are vital to Sonoma's coastal ecosystem.

Before we split to find the coffee we both need, Cann and I stand in the parking lot and talk through what the urchin gathering is really about, given that we’re not singlehandedly saving the kelp. It’s a form of education or consciousness-raising for sure. There’s nothing like feeling the kelp between your toes or swallowing urchin roe just minutes after it has left the water to make the stakes of ocean conservation feel close to home. You can make the case that activities like this develop virtues of generosity and curiosity in ourselves; my fellow foragers filter out of the car park smiling and carrying dripping containers; they tell Cann what they’ll do with their haul, who they’ll invite for dinner or share their newfound knowledge with.

Steinbeck advised his readers to look “from the tide pool to the stars and back to the tide pool again.” Maybe that’s what the foraging is really about. The focus on one small creature opens you up to its myriad connections to everything else. At the same time, it puts you in that web, gives you a visceral way to feel the relationship between yourself, the urchin, and the rest of the tide pool world; you can quite literally taste the kelp forest in the uni. I’ve seen the sea urchin as a pest and a delicacy, an ecosystem villain and a precious treat worth getting splinters for. But it was only when I planted my feet in its rock pool home and plucked one from the water and threw back its roe that I really saw it in its place.

#6301. 12 best things to do in Icy Strait Point and Hoonah, Alaska, on a cruise

Icy Strait Point will be your favorite cruise port in Alaska — or your least favorite.

You might love the densely forested setting of Chichagof Island, which has the world's highest bear population per square mile and is surrounded by waters teeming with wildlife — an ideal destination for touring. Within Icy Strait Point, you can fly down a 5,495-foot-long zip line, dine on fresh Alaskan seafood and immerse yourself in southeast Alaska's history and Native culture.

However, if you love cruise ports that drop you into the middle of real-world Alaska, Icy Strait is not that. It's a purpose-built cruise port (think: a cruise line's private island meets a ski resort), and everything there has been carefully designed to entice you to spend money. You will need to walk or take a shuttle to the city of Hoonah to see where real Alaskans live.

If you're inclined to pooh-pooh this kind of port, I urge you not to give up on Icy Strait Point. I was impressed with how well its creators made authentic Alaskan elements accessible to cruise visitors at the port. I didn't have to go far to try salmon dip and halibut pizza washed down with a locally brewed beer. I toured exhibits about the salmon cannery that once occupied the site. With a longer stay, I could have gone on a whale-watching cruise in waters so populous that I'd get a 100% refund if a whale wasn't spotted during the tour.

Plus, the port's owners, Huna Totem Corporation, are deeply rooted in the local community. Many of the staff you'll meet in port are Native Alaskans and live in nearby Hoonah; it's a popular spot for high school students to work summer jobs. Huna Totem only leases retail space to locally owned businesses (one gallery exclusively sells art by local Alaskans), and proceeds from the on-site bookshop help fund school activities in Hoonah. Don't miss the doughnut shop run by the local Salvation Army, which uses the profits to provide food for Alaskans in need.

Icy Strait Point packages authentic Alaska into a beautiful, easily accessible port. Whether your ship stops for an entire day or just an evening, here are the top 12 things to do in port.

(Note: Excursion and activity prices vary by cruise line and date, and they are subject to change.)

Icy Strait Point has two cruise piers: Wilderness Landing (closer to the zip line) and Ocean Landing (closer to the rest of the port's shopping, dining and activity centers). A half-mile walking trail connects them.

You might certainly enjoy a leisurely nature stroll through the woods (keep an eye out for deer), but I think it's more fun to ride the gondola between them. Icy Strait Point has two gondolas — you'll want the free Transporter Gondola. The four-minute ride takes you through the rainforest and over the port's adventure course area. Time your ride, if possible, to avoid the long lines of tour groups.

Icy Strait's ZipRider is a superlative ride. The port touts it as "the world's largest ZipRider." I'm not sure what that means, but I can tell you that six side-by-side zip lines run 5,495 feet in length and drop 1,330 feet in elevation. You are both harnessed and seated in a swing chair, so you're upright but not dangling. You'll soar 300 feet above the rainforest as you reach speeds of more than 60 mph on your flight down the mountain.

Related: The 6 best Alaska cruise shore excursions — from heli-hiking to whale watching

It's truly thrilling — not only because of the height and speed but also because you actually have time to enjoy the ride and take in the views on this long course.

As a bonus, you get to take a second gondola ride on the Skyglider Gondola, which lasts seven minutes and takes you to the top of Hoonah Mountain.

The area near Point Adolphus on Chichagof Island is known for its large summertime population of humpback whales. Boats depart Icy Strait Point on multiple whale-watching excursions each day to reach these wildlife-filled waters.

In fact, the area is home to so many whales that Huna Totem says every whale-watching tour has seen whales since Icy Strait Point opened in 2004. They are so certain you will see a whale that they will refund 100% of the tour cost if you don't.

More expensive tours combine whale watching with seafood feasts or bear-watching excursions.

If land mammals are more your thing, Chichagof Island is also known for its grizzly bear population. You can (safely) see one in the wild by signing up for a bear search. These tours take guests to the Spasski River Valley, where you'll walk along designated paths to viewing platforms in the hopes of spotting the large brown bears. You might also see deer, eagles and other wildlife.

Related: Alaska cruise guide: Best itineraries, planning tips and things to do

The waters around Icy Strait Point are full of halibut, so if you're eager to try your hand at ocean fishing in Alaska, you can sign up for a tour. Each fishing boat can take up to six guests, and while you must man your own pole, you'll need to release any fish you catch. (So, don't think you can take your catch back to the ship for dinner.) A fishing tour here is also a miniature wildlife cruise, so you might spot whales, porpoises, sea lions and other aquatic animals while you're out on the water.

For a hands-on tour that gives you a literal taste of Alaska, don't miss Icy Strait Point's "In Alaska's Wildest Kitchen" excursion. Guided by local cooks, you'll learn how to prepare local fish (most likely salmon and halibut) by filleting it and then cooking pieces over an open-air grill. Back inside, you'll get to taste the dishes and take home the recipe cards.

Some folks just want to enjoy Alaska's wealth of seafood without having to catch and prepare it. Luckily, there are plenty of ways to fill your bellies with fish in Icy Strait Point.

You could sign up for a tour that includes a seafood feast of shrimp and crab, Andouille sausage, veggies and s'mores for dessert, often combined with a tribal show. Or, you could grab a bite to eat at one of the port's three waterfront restaurants, food trucks and other food sellers.

Duck Point Smokehouse Restaurant by the Ocean Landing dock has cozy fireplace-side indoor seating and an outdoor patio, plus a bar serving Alaskan brews (including the delicious made-on-island Cannery Red Ale). This is where I enjoyed a smoked salmon dip with Parmesan toast points for dipping and my first-ever halibut pizza.

Over by the Cannery, The Cookhouse restaurant is the place to go for halibut fish-and-chips and salmon BLT sliders, while the Crab House specializes in locally harvested Dungeness and Alaska snow crab. The go-to drink is the Alaska Crabby bloody mary, garnished with crab meat, shrimp, pickled Alaska beach asparagus and an actual crab leg.

At the base of the SkyPeak Gondola, you can stop by the Wild Tacos food truck for shrimp and halibut tacos, among other non-seafood options.

Or, more specifically, learn about the salmon canning process and the history of the salmon industry in Hoonah. The Hoonah Cannery buildings, which now house restaurants and shops, were once the site of a salmon canning operation. Spend some time taking in the free museum displays featuring photographs, machinery and other memorabilia from when these buildings housed a factory.

While you're at the cannery, you won't want to miss the chance to purchase souvenirs at shops exclusively owned by Alaskan locals and Native Alaskans. The bigger shops in the main part of the building sell all the signature souvenirs you'll find in any Alaska port, but duck into the discreet shops off the hallway for more original gifts. At Dei L'e.ann, you'll find works by Huna Tlingit artists, as well as soaps, salves and lip balms from Tlingit Botanicals.

Related: 10 things you should never buy on a cruise ship (or in port)

The Alaska Native Heritage Center, near the cannery, offers Icy Strait Point visitors the opportunity to experience and learn about Tlingit culture. The theater offers performances of the 30-minute "Tribal Connections Show," which you can book individually or as part of a tour (often with the seafood feast). Tlingit folks from Hoonah will perform songs and dances and tell stories to share their traditions with cruise ship guests.

Stretch your legs and search for wildlife along Icy Strait Point's various nature trails. From Ocean Landing's Adventure Center, you can strike out on a nature trail (about a 12-minute walk) or walk the half-mile trail to the other pier. From the top of the Skyglider Gondola, you can enjoy the mile-long Hidden Lake Loop Trail (yes, there really is a lake up there).

Alternatively, you can meander along the beach path (a good spot for wildlife sightings) or walk the mile-and-a-half route to the city of Hoonah.

Speaking of Hoonah, it's the main city on Chichagof Island, and it's home to many of the Tlingit people and Alaska locals who work at Icy Strait Point. If you'd prefer to see a real town and not a developed port, you can visit Hoonah by cruise excursion, shuttle bus or a 30-minute walk.

In Hoonah, you can hit up some of the local shops for gifts and souvenirs, try a local beer at Icy Strait Brewing or enjoy comfort food all day at The Fisherman's Daughter. You can also watch local carvers create totem poles or work on canoes at their workshop in town.

Price: $10 (shuttle), $85 to $130 (tour with tribal show)

You might never have heard of Icy Strait Point before your cruise. However, combined with the neighboring city of Hoonah, it has a wealth of activities and attractions to offer cruise passengers. Having spent just an evening in port, I'd recommend looking for itineraries with a longer stay so you can go out on a wildlife tour and have time afterward to do a little shopping and eating within the port complex.

Planning a cruise? Start with these stories:

Select ships do make short four- or five-hour calls in Icy Strait Point, but that shouldn’t reduce your tour options by a lot. Most tours run 1 to 2.5 hours and can be easily accomplished on a short visit. The longest tours are halibut fishing (3.5 hours) and tours that combine a whale watch with another activity, such as the seafood feast (3.5 hours) or bear viewing (5.5 hours). Days are long during most of the cruise season, allowing for evening excursions; however, cruisers on an evening stop in September might find it getting dark halfway through their visit.

Average summer temperatures in Icy Strait Point range from low 50s to mid 60s Fahrenheit, and the later in summer you visit, the higher the chance of rain. Don’t let imperfect weather stop you from outdoor fun. Bring warm layers and rain gear and head out on the port’s many outdoor adventures, like whale watching or ziplining.

Yes, guests must weigh between 75 and 275 pounds. Children 16 and younger must meet the weight requirements and be accompanied by a parent or guardian. If the parent does not wish to ride, the child would need an adult escort at the top of the zipline and another waiting for them at its terminus.

No, you do not need to book your tour in advance to get a refund if no whales are sighted. However, you will want to book your tour in advance because whale watching from Icy Strait Point is popular and tours sell out. Note that the operator has never had to provide a refund because whales are always seen in this area.

Yes, it’s a roughly 30-minute walk into town (about 1.5 miles) on a flat route. Many cruise passengers walk one way and ride the shuttle the other way.

#6300. Air Transat Adds New European Destinations

Canada’s Air Transat will add two new European destinations and five new routes to the continent in summer 2027.

The carrier announced Thursday that it will serve Geneva from Montreal and Birmingham, England, from Toronto. It will also connect Quebec City with Lyon, France, and Barcelona, and Montreal with Faro, Portugal.

Air Transat has not served Geneva or Birmingham before. The airline currently serves Lyon and Barcelona from Montreal, and Faro from Toronto.

Operating dates and frequencies for the new routes are:

Montreal-Geneva: Tuesdays and Saturdays, June 19 to Oct. 23

Toronto-Birmingham: Tuesdays and Fridays, June 22 to Oct. 22

Quebec City-Lyon: Tuesdays, June 8 to Oct. 26

Quebec City-Barcelona: Mondays, June 14 to Oct. 25

Montreal-Faro: Mondays, June 14 to Oct. 25

Additionally, Air Transat’s seasonal services from Quebec City to Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, and from Montreal to St. Maarten are being extended to year-round.

#6299. Southwest Denies A 787 Order. Remember Its Bag Promise?

On its October 22nd, 2026 earnings call, CEO, Bob Jordan, shot down reports of a widebody order as having “no credibility.” The reports came from a Reuters exclusive two weeks earlier, citing three unnamed sources who said Southwest was looking at Boeing 787s for a long-haul push, possibly leased or second-hand, with a launch window of roughly three years. At the time, Southwest’s only comment was that it had no news forthcoming on its fleet plans. We have heard this before.

His reasoning was mostly that it would require significant changes in the business model. Operating aircraft with more than 175 seats would send the airline back to its pilots, and the pilot contract likely opens next year. Another 737 variant would be “significantly easier” than a widebody. Long-haul flying would be upside “if we decide to pursue that.” My eyerolls are likely audible at this point.

I know how this goes because I have watched the free bag story (and every other unique characteristic that Southwest would “never” change) play out. In July 2024, Jordan told investors that bags flying free was the number one reason customers choose Southwest, behind only fare and schedule. On September 17, 2024, a Southwest spokesperson told The Points Guy there was “no work currently underway” to change the policy, and Jordan, pressed on the question, would only say never say never, as CBS reported.

Six months later, on March 11, 2025, Southwest ended the policy. The airline set fees of $35 for the first checked bag and $45 for the second on flights booked on or after May 28, 2025. Jordan’s explanation was that bags flying free was not part of the airline’s DNA, and that open seating was not either. What he should have said was that it wasn’t part of Elliott Management’s DNA and they were running the show – at least while they were still heavy investors. Analysts warned at the time that dropping the policy could damage the brand and turn Southwest into just another airline. It most certainly did that, but as reported in recent weeks, it has, in fact, helped the stock price and financials significantly.

But there is no demonstrable difference between Southwest and any of the top 5 US carriers except one, no long haul international service.

The bags went first, and assigned seating arrived on January 27, 2026, with eight boarding groups, four fare tiers and extra-legroom rows on every flight. Basic fares board last. Open seating, which was the other half of the cattle-call charm, was gone. This has all been covered over the last 18 months but it’s important preamble when considering the next logical step for the airline, and the claims it is denying. What remains uniquely Southwest is one fleet type, and a partially point-to-point map and a reputation for friendliness, and the fleet may be next. Jordan said Southwest is not building toward any one thing, but the addition of 11 lounges, a premium credit card, and first class tell a different story.

It’s a sea of sameness (to steal another industry trope.) Delta and United sell the same choices at similar prices, and Southwest sells them with a smaller map and limited international reach. Every concession after the bag fee was an admission that the discount model was not enough on its own, even though I personally believe that it was.

The numbers explain why management keeps moving the goalposts. In the third quarter, revenue per available seat mile jumped a record 21.6%, but capacity fell 0.4% and unit costs excluding fuel rose 3.8%. Capacity for 2026 is up only about 1.2%. That mix tells me growth came from price and fees, not from flying more, but in order to keep up that frothy pace it will have to find new markets to enter.

Domestic markets are mature, and Southwest’s biggest rivals already own the best international partners. Southwest has partnerships with Icelandair, China Airlines, EVA Air and Turkish Airlines, and Jordan said international loyalty partnerships and partner redemption launch next spring (I can’t wait to see what the redemptions look like.) Partners only go so far, though. Will some EVA Air customers book connecting flights on Southwest for its customers, maybe, probably, but that’s not going to move the needle.

Alaska already saw this writing on the wall and made a move. The rest of the premium push doesn’t come close to working if Southwest customers still buy tickets to Rome on another carrier. Chicago Midway can technically accommodate a 787, as can Dallas Love, and at LAX and Baltimore that’s a very easy fit. But all of those markets have real competition from major carriers. Other Southwest hubs like Fort Lauderdale face serious challenges with nearby Miami, Houston Hobby against United at Intercontinental, Denver for both international carriers and United.

But Southwest wanted to assimilate the carrier to every other carrier so it has to compete with every other carrier too. And in that regard, I can’t see a lounge program as aggressive as 11 locations working without it. If the fleet was exclusively Airbus, the international case is easier with longer legs and a JetBlue-like model (though that’s not working out well for them at the moment and they already have premium cards, lounges, and international partners.)

Unless Southwest sees unprecedented growth from what it’s already doing – possible, but not probable – this is the last frontier. So why deny it? Doesn’t that indicate a lack of forward thinking?

I will take the other side of the denial. My prediction is that Southwest announces a widebody order or lease within eighteen months of the pilot contract opening, and that Jordan or his successor will explain it as a natural evolution of the brand. The pattern is set. Every sacred cow gets slain once the numbers demand it, and the statement of the day is always true until the day it is not. Travelers should treat Southwest’s promises the way they treat any airline’s, as information about the current quarter and not a commitment about the next one.

#6298. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

#6297. The Key to Stress-Free Travel Is the Right Gear—These Travel Accessories Pull Their Weight

The secret to a seamless travel journey is having the right travel accessories at your side. Whether you're boarding an early flight, hopping on a cruise ship, or catching a cross-country train, it pays to be prepared with smart gadgets and gear that make all the difference. From the packing cubes and laundry bags that help me fit the excessive amount of clothes I insist on bringing to the eye mask and neck pillow that make getting sleep at 30,000 feet possible, the best travel accessories pull their weight every time. After more than six years as a travel editor, I've figured out which essentials are worth bringing along. My lineup of foolproof travel accessories keeps me comfortable on long-haul flights, protects my suitcase from getting lost in transit, and ensures all my things are exactly where they should be.

To help every trip you take be a smoother one, I've put together a list of the very best travel accessories to pack on your next vacation. From in-flight necessities and organization hacks to tracking devices that deliver even the most anxious travelers peace of mind, these are the essentials I recommend most.

A tote bag is the ideal personal item—it's roomy enough to store all of your in-flight essentials and is usually pretty pliable, meaning you can squeeze it under the seat without taking up all of your foot room. Look for one with comfortable shoulder straps, a zipper or magnetic snap closure, and a few interior pockets to store your phone and passport. A trolley sleeve is a nice feature, too, so you can slide it over your suitcase while cruising through the airport. My personal favorite is MZ Wallace's Metro Tote—it's got more pockets than I know what to do with, and its super-soft straps never dig in to my shoulders. Cuyana's sleek System tote, L.L.Bean's iconic Boat and Tote, and Calpak's expandable Luka tote all come highly recommended by my fellow editors too.

A good toiletry bag keeps your products organized and your suitcase spill-free. These smaller options from Dagne Dover and Away offer enough space for your skincare essentials without taking up a ton of space in your suitcase. If you're going on a longer vacation or want to keep all of your products in one place (skincare, makeup, shower essentials, etc.), you might want to opt for Bagsmart's hanging toiletry bag that can be hooked onto the back of the bathroom door at the hotel. It keeps the counter clutter-free, and makes finding exactly what you need a breeze. Peak Design's best-selling wash pouch is another smart pick for longer journeys—commerce director Madison Flager has used hers for over five years and it's still in good shape.

Browse more toiletry bag recommendations.

A rule to live by: Never check your valuables, especially jewelry. Keep necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and rings safe and neatly organized inside a jewelry case that gets stowed in your carry-on luggage or personal item. These durable, compact cases have enough room to store a few different jewelry options. Mark and Graham's case is on the larger side, making it ideal for destination weddings, special events, or longer vacations.

Browse more jewelry case recommendations.

Rather than buy plastic minis every time you travel, get yourself a set of leakproof travel bottles to hold your at-home favorites on the go. My holy grail product, the Cadence capsules, are great for storing toiletries and beauty products, as well as small loose items like vitamins and bobby pins. I also regularly travel with a few of these silicone bottles from Amazon to hold shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. They're leakproof, easy to refill, and aren't super bulky in my toiletry bag.

Browse more toiletry bottle recommendations.

Instead of bringing entire bottles of medication or vitamins, pack a compact pill case that holds only as much as you'll need for the length of your trip. No matter where I'm headed, I always pack the Holii pill organizer—it's small enough to fit in my Dopp kit and has enough compartments to separate what I'll need for each day. Dosey's seven-day pill case is a nice pick for weeklong trips—and it looks so cute on any hotel bathroom counter.

I've recommended Afform's makeup bag to my mom, my sisters, my friends, and even strangers in the airport bathroom. It really is that good! The standout feature is its foldable shape: After you unzip the bag, each side can be pulled down to lie flat, allowing you to see all of your products at once. It's designed to keep each product secured in an upright position, reducing the risk of any spills. The bag's structured silhouette and flat base offer the stability and durability I want all of my breakable—and pricey—beauty products to have while in transit. For something less expensive, Eachy's best-selling makeup bag has a lot to offer—with plenty of room for full-size blushes and bronzers, as well separate compartments and multiple pockets to hold smaller products.

For years, I tossed my makeup brushes in a cosmetic pouch when I traveled—and I suffered the consequences. Not only did it make finding the right brush I need difficult, it also meant the rest of my makeup products ended up covered in leftover powder, blush, and bronzer. This all changed when I finally caved and tried out a dedicated brush holder a few years ago. With this $15 Amazon find, all of my makeup brushes stay in one place and can lay flat in the same direction, keeping them organized and away from other products. It’s large enough to hold several long, thin eyeshadow brushes and thick, dense foundation brushes (and a Beauty Blender too). The case's magnetic flap keeps my brushes secure and the soft silicone material means I can wash it off with ease.

All of those tech items you're bringing along mean you're going to have plenty of charging cubes and cables to keep track of. Save space in your backpack by keeping everything wrapped up in a travel organizer designed specifically for your electronic accessories, like the ones below from Peak Design and Bellroy. These are especially great for long flights where you're more likely to switch between devices.

Browse more travel tech organizer recommendations.

There's no sense in bringing your full-size day-to-day wallet on vacation—chances are, you only need a few cards and some cash. A slim travel wallet allows you to carry just those essentials, and makes it less of headache if it gets lost or stolen. Bellroy's RFID-blocking wallet is a smart choice for travelers, while Coach's sleek leather card holder fits in even your tiniest purses.

Browse more travel wallet recommendations.

A crossbody bag makes the most sense for travel—whether you're sightseeing around London or exploring the Disney parks, you want something to keep you hands-free and ready to go no matter what's on the agenda. These lightweight bags take up little suitcase space and have enough room for your daily essentials: wallet, keys, sunnies, lip balm, and hand sanitizer. Senior features editor Megan Spurrell swears by Baggu's nylon Crescent bag for its versatility and roominess, while commerce director Madison Flager's go-to crossbody is this sleek convertible style from Lo & Sons (you can remove the long strap and re-clip the sides to make it a shoulder bag whenever you need!).

Browse more crossbody bag recommendations.

Some instances call for a slim bag that holds your phone and little else. Whether you're headed to dinner on a cruise ship, down to the hotel pool, or to an outdoor concert, these tiny bags will keep your phone and a few cards secure, without the extra bulk that comes with carrying around a larger purse or tote. Senior commerce editor Hannah Chubb is a big fan of the Hailey crossbody phone case from Bandolier—she's had it for over four years and it's still going strong.

Browse more slim phone bag recommendations.

Also handy: a high-quality passport case (bonus points if it has space to hold your credit cards) to keep your most important document protected. Made of genuine Italian leather, Mark & Graham's sleek passport case is a thoughtful gift for any traveler in your life (especially since it can be monogrammed).

Browse more passport holder recommendations.

Is there anything more humbling that trying to fit a floppy sunhat into your suitcase? It takes up so much space and often leaves your favorite hat completely squished. Last summer, Chubb shared her top tip on how to pack the bulkiest thing in your vacation wardrobe: Use a hat clip. With one, your hat can hang securely from your personal item or suitcase without any fuss. Chubb's favorite one, the Toptote, fits in the palm of your hand. Its design is simple: Stick the brim of your hat between the two magnets, and it gets locked in place, letting your bag do all the heavy lifting.

For a comfortable journey at 30,000 feet—especially long trips where you’re hoping to get some shut-eye—an eye mask is crucial. The 100% silk option from Zimasilk and the soft, sculpted eye mask from MZoo are two highly rated Amazon finds. Both mold to fit to your face, provide total darkness, and stay in place.

Another comfort essential: a travel pillow. It can take some time to find the style you like best, and your pick might vary depending on whether you're in-flight or in a car or on a train. Cabeau's Evolution S3 and Ostrichpillow's Go memory foam pillow are among our editors' go-to's. They offer great head and neck support and are soft on the skin.

Alright, alright, a pair of foldable slippers isn't exactly a necessity for travel, but it is a simple in-flight luxury that makes your time in the clouds a little bit cozier. This one is for the travelers out there who insist on taking off their shoes on the plane (leave your socks on, please!), but still want to be kind to their neighbors. As you prepare for takeoff, slide on a pair of these lightweight slippers. They're not too structured, meaning you can fold them back up and tuck them into a small compartment of your personal item.

Frequent fliers who run cold would be wise to invest in a travel blanket—it'll keep you warm, and if you're on a red-eye, may help you actually get some sleep. Go for something lightweight that can be packed into a small pouch when you're not using it.

Browse more travel blanket recommendations.

We love a good pair of compression socks to fight that pins-and-needles feeling that comes from sitting still for too long, be it on a long-haul flight or a road trip. Our editors swear by socks from Bombas and Comrad—they're comfortable, stay in place, and help reduce swelling.

Browse more compression sock recommendations.

Even if you're not the type of person with a multistep in-flight skincare routine, a few basics can go a long way in keeping your skin happy and healthy after a long day of travel (just make sure all your products are in a TSA-approved size). For a quick dose of hydration, spray Summer Friday's Jet Lag mist before or after takeoff. I also love the brand's lip butter balm to keep my lips moisturized without feeling sticky. For some serious hydration, commerce producer ElleAnna Revell recommends Dieux's lipid-rich face moisturizer. And don't forget your hands—a shea butter cream will do the trick.

A few years ago, I slipped on a set of eye patches before takeoff—and I've never looked back. Now I always travel with a few under-eye patches stashed in my toiletry bag. I do it for the first-class feeling it gives me, but also for the much-needed dose of hydration and brightening it offers my dark circles. All of these options are great, but I recommend Peter Thomas Roth's if you have dry skin; if you hate the slipping and sliding eye patches tend to do, try Rhode's, these bad boys don't budge.

This $30 airplane tray table cover is one of my favorite in-flight travel accessories. It slides onto your tray table like a pillowcase, and completely covers the surface—so you can eat and work off of it without worrying about all those germs. Another bonus: It features four pockets to store essentials like your tablet, passport, water bottle, and phone. This means you won't accidentally leave your most important documents or electronics in the seat's safety manual compartment.

When you need some peace and quiet, swap your noise-canceling headphones in for earplugs. Traveler editor Jamie Spain is a big fan of Loop's earplugs for all kinds of situations—planes, crowded coffee shops, and nightclubs alike. They block out unwanted noise and are comfortable enough to wear for hours at a time.

Another must for general wellness: hand sanitizer. Buy a set and drop one in all your most-used totes and crossbody bags so you're never without. Wet Ones wipes are nice to have on hand too, especially if you're traveling with little ones.

If you’re prone to overpacking like I am, give yourself some added peace of mind with a digital luggage scale; it’ll let you know how much damage your souvenirs did before arriving at the check-in counter on the way home. I recently used this one from Etekcity on a trip to Charleston, South Carolina, and it gave me a nice warning that my bag was nearly overweight (no extra fees here!).

Browse more luggage scale recommendations.

Speaking of luggage, it's a good idea to attach a smart tag to your checked bag so you can easily track it. You'll have peace of mind knowing your personal belongings have made it safely to the right destination, and are right where you left them when you venture outside your accommodations.

Whether you're traveling solo or with kids, using a luggage connector to keep your suitcases looped together makes navigating through the airport a breeze. This three-piece set of luggage straps allow you to attach multiple suitcases together—and it's super simple to attach to any carry-on or checked bag.

Always travel with a luggage tag on your suitcase. It's helpful if your bag is lost and makes spotting your suitcase on a luggage carousel easier. If you want to make your luggage tag even easier to spot, I recommend personalizing it with your initials or snagging one in a bright color.

There's nothing like a dead battery to slow down a trip. Whenever my phone battery is running low, I pull out my tiny portable charger from iWalk. It charges my phone quickly and is only about the size of a lipstick. Both of the options below are compact enough to fit in a small fanny pack or crossbody bag.

A power adapter is a must for international travel to make sure you can get devices charged up in the airport and your hotel room. These both offer several different plugs, so you'll be good to go for travel to most anywhere in the world. Plus, you can charge multiple devices at once.

Go cordless with this itty bitty audio transmitter. It plugs into the same jack that corded headphones would, allowing travelers to use their own wireless headphones to watch in-flight entertainment. I always slip this into my carry-on so I can watch movies with my over-ear noise-canceling headphones.

Another gadget I love: This handy phone mount, which lets you position your phone at eye level rather than having to lean it on your tray table or hold it in your lap.

Whether the plan is to listen to music, watch a movie, or just drown out noisy neighbors, most of us won't board a plane without headphones—especially a pair that are noise-canceling. Make sure you have your go-to on hand, plus a pair of corded earbuds (if you forego the aforementioned Bluetooth adapter).

Even travelers with a library full of books at home have to admit it: E-readers are an essential travel accessory for bookworms. I love bringing my Kindle Paperwhite with me when I travel—it's lighter than even one paperback book, and lets me bring as many options as I want along for the ride.

This isn't a must for every trip, but a portable speaker is a nice addition to your packing list for beach vacations, bachelorette parties, or any time you're staying in a rental home. JBL's Go 4 portable speaker is small enough to slip into a fanny pack, while this Turtlebox option offers some serious sound.

If you're traveling to a wedding or heading out on a business trip, you may want to bring a portable steamer along to make sure your formalwear looks its best after you take it out of your suitcase. These editor-tested steamers are lightweight, packable, and actually get the job done.

Don't underestimate the power of a good packing cube. As a chronic overpacker, compression packing cubes save me every single time. They're designed to press clothing items down tightly so you can fit more inside my suitcase. Packing cubes also help keep me organized; you can sort them by outfit or by clothing type. I usually put bulky items like jeans and dresses in the larger cubes and socks, underwear, and tees in the small ones. These sets from Amazon Basics and Bagsmart are affordable and work just as well as more expensive options on the market.

Laundry bags are the newest addition to my lineup of travel accessories. I used to think it was a little unnecessary to pack a small laundry bag with me on a trip, but don't knock it til you try it. I love having a dedicated spot for my dirty clothes so they stay separate from the clean items in my suitcase. And this way, I don't end up leaving my already-worn outfits on the hotel floor (I hate clutter!). I recently bought this two-pack of laundry bags, and I'm planning to bring them on an upcoming trip to Newport, Rhode Island. They are so teeny tiny when empty, and when I'm back from my trip, I can easily dump the whole thing right into the washing machine—easy peasy!

I can't tell you how many times these on-the-go stain removers have saved me. From destination weddings to formal cruise dinners, it's always a good idea to have a little something to help with accidental spills. For small stains, I typically reach for a Tide To-Go stick. It's easy to discreetly pull out of my purse and is completely mess-free. For larger or tougher stains I really need to work on, I swear by Shout Wipe & Go wipes. I'm convinced they have magical powers.

This might seem like a no-brainer, but don't forget to pack a trusty reusable water bottle, so you can stop buying overpriced plastic bottles at the airport. Our editors love Owala—its bottles are durable, easy to hold, and keep water cold for hours. If you're tired of lugging around a 30-ounce water bottle, throw Hydro Flask's Micro Hydro in your tote or shoulder bag. In most situations, a few gulps on the go is really all you need! The smoothest travel days start with a healthy dose of caffeine—I don't make the rules! I usually bring Owala's SmoothSip Slider tumbler with me because it's so compact and most importantly, it's actually leakproof. If I need to, I can safely toss it in a backpack or tote without worrying that my coffee might spill all over my laptop or Kindle. Plus, it keeps my coffee hot all day long every single time. Stanley 1913's travel mug with a top handle is another slim, lightweight pick you can trust.

We've all been there: You're fast-walking through the airport, hands full, hurrying to get to your gate on time while juggling your suitcase, phone, and a precarious iced coffee. This $10 travel accessory is here to lend a helping hand when you need it most. Simply slide it onto the handle of your suitcase and you'll have two cup holders, one for a coffee and one for a water bottle, as well as a hidden pocket for your phone and wallet, giving you the hands-free moment you need while navigating through the airport.

Time changes, long-haul flights, and jam-packed days can leave us feeling more run-down than we might like on vacation. LMNT electrolytes and Nuun Sport tablets are great at keeping you hydrated on long, active days in warm climates. Plus, they're easy to slip into any bag you're traveling with.

Do yourself a favor and pack a portable fan. A lightweight, handheld option will give you the breeze you need, whether you're in the back of a crowded bus or van, standing in line at Disneyland, or kicking back in a beach chair. Flager praises her Jisulife mini fan for its impressive battery life—it truly lasts all day long. I, on the other hand, love my small Gaiatop portable fan; it's simple to use, works really well, and has three different speed settings.

Browse more portable fan recommendations.

Depending on your destination, a travel-size umbrella might be worth the space in your suitcase. And if you're driving, tossing one in the backseat is a no-brainer. Weatherman's travel umbrella is by far the best model I've ever tried and it's super lightweight. For something slightly more affordable, Repel's windproof travel umbrella is a great alternative.

#6296. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Good thing you did the Edit deal as the Thompson doesn’t honor Hyatt Globalist benefits. So, no upgrade and no breakfast for Globalists.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

Am I the only one finding Edit hotels are north of $1000 a night? Whatever the credit Chase is giving is for staying at an Edit property isn’t enough to offset the exceptionally high rate.

I’ve stayed at that Thompson many times and been upgraded to suites and the Upper Stories. The previous poster is empirically wrong.

doesn’t Edit usually require a two night minimum? How did you get the benefits for only a one night stay?

#6295. Am I eligible for the Chase Sapphire Preferred's 75,000-point bonus?

I highly recommend the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees) to a wide range of travelers. With solid earning rates, excellent travel protections and a strong welcome offer, there's plenty to like about this mid-tier card.

Speaking of that welcome offer: New Sapphire Preferred Card holders can earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Using TPG's October 2026 valuation of Chase Ultimate Rewards points at 2.05 cents apiece, this bonus is worth $1,538, which is strong value relative to the card's $95 annual fee.

With a considerable stash of valuable points on the line, you'll want to be sure that you're eligible to earn them.

Here's what you need to know about Chase's application rules and eligibility requirements for the Sapphire Preferred.

Being approved for and earning the bonus on the Sapphire Preferred requires keeping a few key details in mind:

Being an authorized user on someone else's Sapphire Preferred account does not prevent you from applying for your own card and earning the welcome bonus, provided you meet all other eligibility requirements.

As with any Chase credit card, a top consideration should be the issuer's 5/24 rule, which states that applicants who have opened five or more new credit cards in the past 24 months are likely to have their applications denied. An important note here is that Chase doesn't typically include business cards in its 5/24 calculation.

Holding another Sapphire card, such as the premium Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees), does not disqualify you from being approved for and earning the bonus on the Sapphire Preferred.

As long as you're under 5/24 and haven't previously earned the welcome bonus on the Sapphire Preferred, you're in a good position to qualify for the offer.

But remember, there are general eligibility requirements to consider. If you have a poor credit score or flaws in your credit profile, you may still be denied for the card.

Related: I thought I wasn't eligible for a second Chase Sapphire Preferred bonus — I got approved anyway

Yes. If you already have (or have had) the Sapphire Reserve, you're still eligible to add the Sapphire Preferred to your wallet — assuming you meet all the other application requirements.

Holding the Sapphire Reserve and having earned its welcome bonus does not prevent you from earning the Sapphire Preferred's welcome bonus, even though they're in the same card family.

Related: After more than 16 years, why the Chase Sapphire Preferred should still be your first rewards card

The Sapphire Preferred's 75,000-point offer can unlock a domestic getaway or an aspirational trip, whether you're seeking out a luxury all-inclusive vacation or multiple domestic flights across the U.S.

With the card offering a valuable bonus (in addition to many other perks), now is the time to make sure you're eligible. As long as you're under 5/24 and haven't previously earned the welcome bonus on the card before, you should be in a good position to qualify — even if you hold its sibling, the Sapphire Reserve.

And remember, if you're an authorized user on another person's Sapphire Preferred account, you're generally still eligible to apply, assuming you satisfy Chase's other approval and bonus requirements.

To learn more, read our full review of the Sapphire Preferred.

Apply here: Chase Sapphire Preferred Card
