#6280. Copenhagen is Opening a Stunning New Bathhouse Along Its Harbor This December—And It's Shockingly Affordable

Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since.

In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days. In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists.

The new bathing house was designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates and has been 8 years in the making.

The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor.

Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag.

Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 82-foot pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbor with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbor itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools—known as "water culture houses"—where entry is typically under 100kr (about $10). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK ($150 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden.

Kai will open on Paper Island on December 5, 2026.

Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.”

The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbor from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen.

Copenhagen's harbor is the heart of the city's year-round swimming culture.

If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbor is the place to start—but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbor for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition.

Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area.

#6279. Boeing 747 Cockpit: How Flying The Queen Of The Skies Differs From Modern Jets

TimeDepot.Twn | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

The Boeing 747 is instantly recognizable for its distinctive upper deck, enormous wingspan, and four-engine configuration. Yet some of its most significant changes have taken place behind the cockpit door. Across successive generations, the aircraft’s flight deck evolved from an instrument-heavy environment requiring three crew members to a more integrated digital cockpit designed for two pilots. For the crews who operate it, that evolution involves more than replacing older instruments with modern displays. It changes how information is presented, how tasks are distributed, and how pilots monitor the aircraft throughout a flight.

The original 747 entered airline service in 1970 with a captain, first officer, and flight engineer. The 747-400, which entered service in 1989, introduced a redesigned flight deck built around a two-pilot operating concept, while the 747-8 continued that approach with updated avionics and displays. Although all these aircraft belong to the same family, they represent different stages in the development of commercial flight decks. Understanding those differences helps explain why flying the Queen of the Skies is not simply a matter of managing a larger version of a modern twin-engine jet.

The early Boeing 747-100, 747-200 and 747-300 were designed around a cockpit philosophy that relied on dedicated crew members to manage different aspects of the flight. Their instrument panels contained numerous individual gauges, switches, and controls, while aircraft systems required regular monitoring and management. Pilots had to maintain the flight path, navigate, communicate with air traffic control, and coordinate the flight while also monitoring the aircraft’s technical condition. With so much information to manage, dividing responsibilities among three crew members provided a practical way to handle the workload.

The flight engineer occupied a dedicated station behind the pilots, where a separate panel provided access to aircraft-system controls and indications. Responsibilities included monitoring fuel, electrical, and hydraulic systems, checking system status, and assisting with procedures that required detailed technical attention. The flight engineer was not a substitute for either pilot. Instead, the role allowed one crew member to concentrate on aircraft systems while the captain and first officer focused on flying, navigation, communication and overall flight management. The exact division of duties depended on the aircraft’s procedures and the airline’s operating practices.

This arrangement was not unique to the 747. Other large airliners from the same period also used flight engineers because their systems and cockpit layouts benefited from a dedicated systems specialist. As avionics advanced, manufacturers found ways to integrate information, improve alerting, and automate selected tasks. Those developments created the opportunity to reconsider how cockpit responsibilities were divided. For Boeing, the next major step in the 747’s development would be a redesigned flight deck that allowed two pilots to manage the aircraft without a separate flight engineer.

When the 747-400 entered service in 1989, its redesigned flight deck marked a major departure from the cockpit arrangement of earlier 747 generations. The aircraft introduced a two-pilot operating concept supported by more integrated avionics and electronic flight displays. Instead of relying on a third crew member to manage a separate systems panel, the flight deck brought more information into the pilots’ working environment. This redesign was part of a broader industry shift toward automation and cockpit systems that could help crews manage complex aircraft with fewer flight deck personnel.

One of the most visible changes was the move to electronic flight displays, commonly described as a glass cockpit. These displays consolidated important flight information into a format that pilots could interpret without relying exclusively on numerous individual mechanical instruments. The 747-400 also used an Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System, or EICAS, to present engine information and aircraft alerts. By organizing information and helping identify conditions that required attention, these systems supported the redistribution of duties between the captain and first officer. They did not remove the need for system knowledge or careful monitoring.

The transition also changed how pilots worked together. Rather than having a flight engineer dedicated to system monitoring, the captain and first officer had to coordinate aircraft handling, communications, checklist duties and system awareness within a two-person crew. Automation could reduce some routine workload, but pilots still needed to understand the systems, verify the information presented and respond appropriately when an alert appeared. The 747-400 therefore represented more than a visual update. It introduced a different way to organize the flight deck, one that laid the foundation for the later 747-8.

The Boeing 747-8 continued the two-pilot approach established by the Boeing 747-400, but it introduced a more modern suite of avionics and flight deck displays. Its cockpit uses liquid-crystal displays and incorporates updated systems designed to improve how flight information is presented and managed. Boeing also drew on technological developments associated with its newer aircraft programs when developing the 747-8. The result was an updated cockpit that retained the familiar 747 operating concept while incorporating advances in display technology, navigation and information management.

The 747-8’s flight deck includes an updated flight management system, electronic checklists and a vertical situation display, among other features. These tools help pilots access information and monitor aspects of the flight more cohesively. An electronic checklist, for example, presents procedural steps through a display rather than relying solely on a traditional paper checklist. A vertical situation display gives crews another way to visualize the aircraft’s vertical flight profile. Such features can support awareness and workflow, but pilots must still verify the aircraft’s configuration and follow the applicable procedures.

Dedicated flight engineer station alongside pilot instruments

Integrated into the two-pilot flight deck

Conventional checklists and instrument-based procedures

Digital flight deck with integrated avionics

The differences between the original 747, the 747-400, and the 747-8 become clearer when you compare their cockpit features side by side. While the original models relied on a three-person flight deck, the 747-400 introduced a two-pilot glass cockpit, and the 747-8 built on that design with updated displays and avionics.

The 747’s four-engine layout is one of its clearest differences from modern long-haul twin jets such as the 777 and 787 Dreamliner. Its cockpit has four thrust levers, corresponding to the four engines, and pilots must understand the aircraft’s engine indications, thrust management and relevant procedures. A twin-engine aircraft has fewer engines to monitor, but that does not automatically make its operation simpler in every respect. Each aircraft has its own systems, limitations and procedures, and pilots must be trained to manage the specific design they are flying.

The difference extends beyond the engine controls. The 747 uses a conventional flight-control architecture with mechanically linked pilot controls and hydraulically powered control surfaces, rather than the fully fly-by-wire architecture used on the Boeing 777 and 787. In a fly-by-wire aircraft, electronic systems process pilot inputs and command the flight-control surfaces. On the 747, the control system operates differently, even though later versions also incorporate extensive electronics and automation. It would therefore be misleading to describe the 747 as an aircraft without advanced technology. Its systems reflect a different design approach, developed and refined across several generations.

The 747’s aerodynamic configuration also shapes how it is operated. Features such as split ailerons and triple-slotted trailing-edge flaps form part of its design, while its size and four-engine layout influence performance planning and aircraft handling. Pilots learn how these characteristics affect the aircraft through type-specific training, procedures and experience. Familiarity with another Boeing jet can provide useful background, but it does not replace learning the 747’s own systems and handling characteristics. The differences become particularly apparent when crews transition between aircraft, because familiar cockpit concepts can sit alongside very different technical implementations.

The 747’s distinctive upper-deck structure places the cockpit high above the main landing gear and forward fuselage, giving pilots a different visual perspective from that of many other airliners. This position contributes to the aircraft’s familiar profile, but it also matters when crews judge the aircraft’s position on the ground. The view from the cockpit does not directly show the location of every part of the aircraft, so pilots must learn how their visual references relate to the aircraft’s dimensions and geometry.

During taxiing, turns and runway alignment, crews need to account for the 747’s size, wingspan and landing gear arrangement. The aircraft’s cockpit position affects the sight picture, while its overall dimensions influence the space required to maneuver safely. Pilots use airport markings, visual references, ground guidance and standard procedures to maintain appropriate clearances. These considerations are not exclusive to the 747, but the aircraft’s size makes familiarity with its geometry particularly important. A pilot transitioning from a smaller jet must adapt to the way the aircraft’s position appears from the flight deck.

Landing requires the same combination of visual judgment, instrument information and procedural discipline. Pilots must manage the approach path, airspeed, aircraft configuration and touchdown while accounting for the aircraft’s handling characteristics. The elevated cockpit provides a distinctive view, but successful landings do not depend on visual perspective alone. Crews use established approach procedures and flight instruments alongside outside references, applying the techniques appropriate to the aircraft and conditions. The 747’s size and cockpit location make type-specific familiarity valuable, just as its systems and control architecture require knowledge tailored to the aircraft.

The 747’s development illustrates how changes in technology can reshape airline operations over time. Early versions relied on a three-person flight deck, with the flight engineer dedicated to monitoring and managing aircraft systems. The 747-400 introduced a redesigned cockpit intended for two-pilot operation, and the 747-8 continued that model with updated displays and avionics. This evolution depended on more than removing a crew position. It involved changing how information was presented, how tasks were distributed and how the remaining pilots monitored the aircraft.

The progression also demonstrates why automation should not be mistaken for the elimination of pilot workload. Integrated displays, alerting systems and electronic checklists can make information easier to access and help organize tasks, but crews must still understand what the aircraft is doing. They need to recognize relevant alerts, monitor automated functions and respond when conditions require action. Modern flight decks may present information differently from older ones, yet effective operation continues to depend on system knowledge, sound judgment, disciplined procedures and communication between pilots.

Ultimately, the 747’s cockpit reflects the wider evolution of commercial aviation. From the original flight engineer’s station to the 747-400’s glass cockpit and the 747-8’s updated avionics, each generation adapted the aircraft to changing technology and operational priorities. The Queen of the Skies remains distinctive not only because of its size and four engines, but also because its flight deck captures a pivotal transition in how airliners are operated. For pilots, flying the 747 means understanding both the legacy of its design and the systems that make each version different.

#6278. The Best Islands in the World: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best cities in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The six islands of the Bazaruto Archipelago—Bazaruto, Benguerra, Magaruque, Santa Carolina, Bangue, and Shell—are a protected conservation area and national park off the eastern coast of Africa. Nicknamed the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, the islands have only seen the arrival of big-name resorts within the past decade, like the impeccable andBeyond Benguerra Island in 2015.

Pro tip: This is one of the few habitats of the endangered manatee-like dugong, which sailors sometimes mistook for mermaids.

Getting there: Fly to Vilanculos on the coast of Mozambique; from there, take a seaplane to your final destination.

Instagram and Pinterest have created renewed interest in this island in the Indian Ocean, thanks to its so-called underwater waterfall—a visually stunning runoff of sand and silt best viewed from above. Roughly 550 miles east of Madagascar, Mauritius may also be home to a lost continent hiding beneath the waves.

Pro tip: Don’t trust the scales on Mauritius: The island has a stronger gravitational field, causing things (and people) to weigh more.

Getting there: The island’s Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam International Airport is your link for flights to other cities in Africa, as well as to major cities in Europe, Asia, and Australia.

With its white coral sand beaches, turquoise waters, and laid-back island vibe, few destinations offer a sense of escapism quite like Zanzibar. Add to that plenty of sunshine and consistently pleasant temperatures, and it’s easy to see its appeal. For the history buffs among us, don't skip historic trade center Stone Town, famous for its meandering lanes, minarets-crowned buildings, and the 19th-century House of Wonders where the Sultan used to live.

Pro tip: Visit the island during the dry season from June to October, when temperatures average out at 77 degrees. This time range also overlaps with the high season for safari, should a two-for-one trip be of interest.

Getting there: To get to Zanzibar, fly directly to Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ), or arrive by ferry from Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

Our readers aren’t the only ones who consider this African nation one of the best islands in the world: Prince William and Kate Middleton and Victoria and David Beckham spent their honeymoons on the North Island of the Seychelles. Yet some stretches of sand are so deserted that parts of the movie Castaway were filmed here. The ultimate draw, however, is the nature—the white beaches here are so beautiful that visiting them borders on a religious experience.

Pro tip: Seychelles is one of the best spots in the Indian Ocean for snorkeling. Head to the islands of La Digue and Félicité for the best variety of sealife.

Getting there: Air France, Air Seychelles, and Turkish Airlines have regular flights that connect to Seychelles International Airport (SEZ), just south of the capital of Victoria.

A chain of 26 atolls and more than 1,000 islands in the Indian Ocean, the Republic of Maldives is one of the most sought-after tropical destinations in the world. It’s dense with villas and overwater bungalows, and the diving is unreal (though, sadly, some of the coral has been threatened by bleaching). Still, there’s a dive for all skill levels at Ari Atoll, where you can swim with rays and, deeper down, reef sharks.

Pro tip: Cheval Blanc Randheli, the number one resort in the Indian Ocean (per this year’s reader survey), has 45 luxe villas—some tucked among the coconut groves, some jutting out directly over the water.

Getting there: Fly into Malé’s international airport and transfer there to the appropriate resort or atoll.

If your idea of the perfect vacation involves three-day beach parties, Koh Pha Ngan is the Thai island for you. Famous for its full-moon parties at the Haad Rin peninsula's Sunrise Beach, this island is for hardcore partygoers and the anything-goes crowd. During peak season, the island can see upwards of 20,000 visitors dancing and cavorting on the white sands under a full moon. If you can't make it at the right time of month, don't worry—there are half-moon and black-moon parties in intervening weeks, too, and there's action every night of the week at the island's beach and cocktail bars.

Pro tip: There are secluded beaches far from the crowds (like local favorite Bottle Beach, arguably one of the best beaches in Thailand), and plenty of spas where you can check yourself in for an afternoon of recovery, from the basic to the deluxe (such as the Ayurvana Spa at Santhiya Resort on Thong Nai Pan Noi Beach in the north of the island).

Getting there: From Koh Samui, take the ferry or a high-speed boat from a nearby pier like Maenam or Bangrak to Thong Sala Pier or Haad Rin Pier.

India's Andaman Islands are chock-full of beaches for thrill seekers looking to snorkel among sea life and peer through shipwrecks, as well as relaxing sandy stretches for more meditative types who prefer their quiet strolls backgrounded by sherbet-hued sunsets alike. Whether you're enjoying Havelock Island's serene Radhanagar Beach or Elephant Beach, whose shores are a veritable water sports arena, these islands provide 365 days of sun, sand, and fun.

Pro tip: Beyond the beaches, hike through the Baratang Limestone Caves' striking natural corridors through one of the most renowned natural wonders of these islands.

Getting there: Direct flights to Port Blair's Veer Savarkar airport fly from Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, and Vizag. Alternatively, travelers may also choose to arrive at Port Blair via ferry from Kolkata or Chennai.

The Phi Phi Islands lie in the cozy cradle between Phuket and the Straits of Malacca off Krabi Province. Each of the six islands—Ko Phi Phi Don, Ko Phi Phi Le, Bamboo Island, Mosquito Island, Bida Nai, and Bida Nok—have their own charms to offer. From silky soft white sand to dramatic limestone cliffs, the beaches found on these islands are among Southeast Asia's finest.

Pro tip: For a feel of local life, stop by Ko Phi Phi Don, the largest and most populated island of the group. If flopping in solace is more your speed, pop over to Ko Phi Phi Le, which lays claim to some of the island's most stunning vistas and coastal stretches.

Getting there: As there are no airports on any of the Phi Phi Islands, visitors will have to arrive via ferry from ports such as Phuket or Krabi.

Phuket is not exactly a hidden gem, but that's because it's such a magical place to vacation, whether you want a busy immersion in city life or a quieter experience. Since it’s the biggest island in Thailand, you’re sure to find something to fit your desired itinerary. In general, though, we recommend skipping the overcrowded west coast and heading to quiet corners like Cape Panwa, where you’ll find luxury accommodations and rum distilleries that feel a bit more removed from the oft-touristed track.

Pro tip: Phuket Town receives far fewer tourists than the western beach areas. Here you can sample colorful spices at markets, visit aging Taoist temples, and snap photos of the colorful street murals.

Getting there: There are more than a dozen daily flights from Bangkok to Phuket, with most trips clocking in at an hour and 20 minutes.

Nowhere on the planet offers the same combination of surfing, spirituality, and sun-kissed pleasure as Bali. The island has sadly become synonymous with the concept of overtourism, but there are still enclaves of hidden cultural treasures and undiscovered gems—if you know where to look. For a primer on everything Insta-famous and off-the-beaten-track, check out our list of the best things to do in Bali.

Pro tip: The shoulder months of April-May and September-October are the best times to visit Bali. Not only can you enjoy lower airfares and hotel rates during the low season, but you’ll also have the rare ability to see the island without its usual crowds.

Getting there: Many airlines fly directly from the United States to Bali, including Singapore Airlines, Delta, and American.

Thailand’s second-largest island is famous for its palm-lined beaches, buzzing nightlife scene, and luxurious hotels. AVANI+ Samui Resort was voted one of the best resorts in Thailand by our readers, though the hillside villas at Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui and floor-to-ceiling bookshelves at The Library are also worth checking out. In terms of beaches, be sure to visit the five-mile Chaweng Beach, lined with coconut trees and surrounded by a natural reef. Just note that the northern end of the beach is party central.

Pro tip: If you are looking for parties, check out Green Mango, one of Koh Samui’s oldest and most famous clubs.

Getting there: You can fly directly from Bangkok to Koh Samui. A more budget-friendly option may be to fly to Surat Thani and then catch a ferry to Koh Samui—it will add a couple of hours to your travel time, but the views are pretty spectacular.

Located off the northwestern coast of Malaysia, the Langkawi archipelago has pristine beaches, coral reefs, and lush mountains—plus that famous Sky Bridge you’ve definitely seen pictures of. This collection of 99 islands is also a foodie wonderland (eating is the unofficial national sport here), with spicy peanut satay skewers and macheted coconuts sold everywhere from high-end hotels to sidewalk stands.

Pro tip: The Ritz-Carlton, Langkawi was voted the best resort in Asia by our readers this year—chalk it up to a world-class spa, multiple beachfront restaurants, and a location in a 10 million-year-old rainforest.

Getting there: Take a one-hour flight from the Malay capital of Kuala Lumpur.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Earn 2 Delta Comfort Flight Certificates + 50K Miles

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

Atmos Rewards has Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines in its DNA, but its points can take you all over the world. Better yet, its two personal credit cards make it easier than ever to earn points and unlock travel perks.

Both the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card and Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card earn the same valuable Atmos Rewards points but with different earning rates, benefits and extras.

The $95 Ascent includes competitive airline perks for Alaska and Hawaiian flyers, while the $395 Summit adds lounge passes, faster progress toward elite status and a Global Companion Award. Both are genuine solutions for travelers, so the question boils down to whether the extra benefits justify an added upcharge in Summit's annual fee.

For frequent Alaska and Hawaiian flyers, the answer is yes.

New applicants for the Atmos Ascent can earn up to 80,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare: Earn 60,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. Earn an additional 20,000 bonus points after spending a total of $5,000 on purchases, also in the first 90 days from account opening.

Per TPG's October 2026 valuations, the points in the current Ascent offer are worth up to $1,240. That figure does not include any potential savings from the Companion Fare.

Meanwhile, the Atmos Summit is offering new cardholders the ability to earn 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

That makes the Summit offer worth up to $1,938 when you combine the value of the base points and the Global Companion Award, according to TPG's valuations.

Winner: Atmos Summit. Its bonus is worth more than the Atmos Ascent.

Atmos Summit cardholders receive an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award each account anniversary and can earn a 100,000-point Global Companion Award after spending at least $60,000 on the card in the prior anniversary year.

Atmos Ascent cardholders instead receive an annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) each account anniversary after spending at least $6,000 on the card in the prior anniversary year.

The Summit's Global Companion Award effectively serves as a discount on award tickets on Alaska, Hawaiian and participating partner airlines worldwide. It can be used in any cabin, subject to award availability.

By contrast, the Ascent benefit only applies to paid Main Cabin travel within North America on flights operated by Alaska or Hawaiian, but it can still deliver significant savings. TPG director Carly Helfand saved over $400 by using the Ascent’s Companion Fare for a last-minute round trip from Portland, Oregon, to Chicago with her husband.

The Atmos Summit grants two Alaska Lounge passes per quarter. If purchased separately at $65 each, this is a $520 value. To use the pass, you must be flying on a same-day ticketed flight on an Alaska, Hawaiian, or eligible partner airline.

Meanwhile, Atmos Ascent cardholders receive $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership, which costs $795 per year and includes access to all Alaska Lounges and nearly 90 partner lounges.

These benefits feel somewhat mismatched: The Atmos Ascent is aimed at less frequent travelers who likely have no need for an annual Lounge+ membership. Meanwhile, someone flying often enough to want (and pay for) a Lounge+ membership is probably a better fit for the full premium perks package on the Summit card.

Regardless of which card you're leaning toward, keep in mind that the Ascent cardholder discount is not stackable with discounts available to elite members. If you already receive the same discount through Atmos status or a milestone benefit, the Ascent perk is redundant.

The Atmos Summit comes with several additional benefits that may look like fine print but can make a meaningful difference. For example, Summit cardholders receive a $50 voucher for Alaska Airlines flights canceled or delayed by 2 or more hours.

While that won’t rescue your trip’s logistics, at least it takes some of the sting out of the disruption.

The partner award fee waiver can be especially valuable for frequent Atmos redemptions. TPG contributing editor Matt Moffitt saved $365 in partner award booking fees over the past year with the Summit, showing how quickly that benefit can add up.

Lastly, the points-sharing benefit is understated but potentially useful: Instead of paying to move points to another member account, Summit cardholders can designate up to 10 Atmos members to transfer points back and forth, with no transfer fees. That's a helpful way to reach the necessary points balance for an award faster.

Winner: Atmos Summit. Its companion award, lounge passes and faster path to status make it the clear winner, while smaller perks like fee-free points sharing add even more value.

The cards earn points at the following rates:

The Atmos Ascent and Atmos Summit both earn Atmos Rewards points. These cards share an earning rate of 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases.

Plus, both cards earn a 10% rewards bonus on all points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account.

The cards earn drastically differently in non-airline spending, though. The Summit favors dining and spending abroad, while the Ascent rewards several everyday categories, especially transportation and streaming.

The Atmos Summit's bonus earnings on foreign transactions are unique in the rewards card space, making the product a fantastic option if you make many purchases outside the U.S. Meanwhile, the Ascent may be more rewarding for commuters and households with significant gas, transit, cable or streaming expenses.

In addition to redeemable award points, both cards earn points toward Atmos status with no spending caps. Atmos Summit cardholders earn 1 status point for every $2 spent on the card, while Ascent cardholders earn 1 status point for every $3 spent.

The Summit card also provides a lump sum of 10,000 status points each year on their account anniversary, putting Summit cardholders halfway to Atmos Silver before accounting for any additional flying or card spending.

Winner: Atmos Ascent. It's easy to get sidetracked by the Summit's higher earning rates, but most cardholders won't spend enough to justify an extra $300 in fees to earn a few extra points.

You can redeem Atmos Rewards points earned on the Atmos Summit or Atmos Ascent in the same ways. Our favorite redemption options are for flights on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld or a nonalliance partner airline.

Atmos Rewards offers outsize value thanks to its popular award chart, which is filled with redemption sweet spots to maximize. For instance, TPG lead loyalty programs writer Katie Genter recently redeemed 55,000 points to fly Condor business class from Frankfurt to Punta Cana, a ticket that ordinarily costs more than $1,500 one-way.

That represents a value of about 2.36 cents per point, even after accounting for $208 in taxes — a big step up from TPG's estimated value of Atmos Rewards points.

However, you can find great values with economy redemptions, too. Katie also redeemed just 30,000 Atmos Rewards points to fly on Alaska Airlines' inaugural flight to Europe. This route, from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci Airport (FCO), often sells for well over $700 one-way in high season. Another popular redemption is using Atmos Rewards points to book short-haul American Airlines flights for as few as 4,500 points.

Winner: Summit. Both cards share the same redemption options, but the Summit gets a slight edge because it waives partner award booking fees.

If you have the Atmos Summit, you can transfer your Atmos Rewards points to several hotel partners shown below. The Atmos Ascent does not have this feature.

We generally don't recommend transferring your Atmos Rewards points to hotel partners, since award flights can be more valuable. However, if you have a specific redemption in mind and need just a few more points to reach it, the ability to transfer points can be an added benefit.

Winner: Atmos Summit, since it provides access to transfer partners while the Ascent does not.

There is no restriction on holding more than one Atmos Rewards card, so if you choose, you could hold both of these credit cards. Bank of America’s application and approval rules still apply.

Holding both could make sense if you value the Ascent's $99 Companion Fare and everyday bonus categories alongside the Summit's Global Companion Award, lounge passes and status boost. However, given the cost of the annual fees, most travelers will find one card or the other adequate for their needs.

Not everyone needs an Atmos credit card, though. Even though Atmos Rewards are fabulous for partner travel as well, a big reason to get one of these cards is for the perks when flying Alaska and Hawaiian. If they're not part of your regular travel, a general travel rewards card will offer more flexibility.

Get the Atmos Summit if you fly Alaska or Hawaiian regularly and will use its Global Companion Award, lounge passes and faster path to status. Its premium perks make it the clear choice for travelers who are deeply invested in Atmos Rewards.

Get the Atmos Ascent if you mainly want a free checked bag, preferred boarding and a lower annual fee. It delivers the basics most occasional Alaska and Hawaiian flyers need without the premium annual fee upfront.

Related: Are premium credit cards worth the annual fee?

If you're hoping to upgrade from the Atmos Ascent to the more premium Atmos Summit, you can reach out to Bank of America and request a product change.

However, if you opt for an upgrade instead of applying, you may miss out on the Atmos Summit's welcome bonus. So, consider your options before you make a decision.

If you hold the Atmos Summit and want to downgrade to the Atmos Ascent, you can also contact Bank of America to make that product change.

Related: 4 major considerations before upgrading your credit card

There's no question the Summit has a better all-around package, but there’s no reason to pay extra if you'll leave perks untouched.

Because both cards earn the same 3 points per dollar spent on Alaska and Hawaiian purchases, the Atmos Summit doesn’t improve your return when booking flights. The extra cost in annual fees buys access, flexibility and a head start on status.

For travelers who simply fly Alaska and Hawaiian from time to time, the Atmos Ascent is a smarter fit.

To learn more, read our full reviews of the Atmos Ascent and the Atmos Summit.

#6276. Where to Stay in Big Sky, Montana, When You’re Dreaming of the Wild West

I’ve visited Big Sky, Montana, a handful of times over the past six years, and I’m still completely smitten. This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. Winter ski days beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak give way to summer rafting trips and fly-fishing on the Gallatin River, while fall brings horseback rides that sprawl across open ranchlands, and spring offers hikes through wildflower-strewn meadows. The iconic Yellowstone National Park is about an hour south too, putting geysers, steaming hot springs, and roaming bison within day-tripping distance.

The city itself is a quaint yet buzzy collection of restaurants, shops, and watering holes, all adding a welcome dose of small-town charm to all that wilderness. And lately, the destination’s hospitality scene has been booming, with a new wave of stylish hotels and mountain retreats bringing some fresh takes to the city’s rugged Western roots. From luxe resorts with front-row views of the towering peaks to authentic dude ranches and design-forward Airbnbs with cozy fireplaces, there’s an accommodation for every style of Big Sky getaway on the list below. Read on for the best places to stay in Montana’s sweet mountain hub.

A peek at Big Sky's small but mighty town center, where the mountains and Main Street look great together.

Stay at Lone Mountain Ranch, just five minutes from the town center, for a dreamy dude ranch retreat.

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Mountain access, gorgeous standalone cabins, private hot tubs, spa and wellness facilities (with indoor-outdoor lap pool, heated onsen soaking tub, cold plunge, steam room, and sauna)

Famed for its sumptuous yet tasteful resorts in far-flung destinations like Mauritius, Rwanda, and Malaysia, One&Only’s 2025 Moonlight Basin opening was the brand's American debut, as well as its first foray into the outdoor adventure space. A luxury alpine retreat like this requires a specialized type of hospitality, and the team here—a crew who can do everything from book your activities to whisk you between buildings on a side-by-side ATV—knows exactly what they’re doing. Guests get a direct line to the slopes via the One&Only gondola, as well as access to plush locker rooms, tuning equipment, and gear rentals that will impress even members of Yellowstone Club (the famously tiny private ski community next door).

Moonlight Basin is worth visiting outside of ski season too. Situated on 240 secluded acres within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the resort links two sections of protected wilderness in southwestern Montana’s Rocky Mountains, providing critical migration routes for species like moose and bobcats, which means you're in for some exceptional wildlife sightings. Add fly-fishing, stargazing at the on-site observatory, and unwinding at the 17,000-square-foot spa, and even the most discerning ski bums will find themselves spoiled rotten. —Hannah Towey

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Lone Peak, Madison River Valley, Big Sky Mountain, Madison Base Area

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: White-glove service, buzzy après bar, full spa, on-site activity center, ski-in/ski-out location

Montage Big Sky has always been more rugged than refined, but the buzz around this slopeside resort has Aspen and Jackson Hole loyalists rethinking their next ski vacation. The first five-star resort in Big Sky ushered in a whole new era of luxury for this mountain destination, with an 11,000-square-foot spa (the first true spa in the region), a buzzy bar scene, and stellar restaurants.

Most of the 139 rooms, suites, and residences have terraces and balconies with mountain views, and gas fireplaces turn on with a flip of a switch. Head to Beartooth Pub & Rec for a menu of comfort foods, like Wagyu nachos and oversized hot pretzels served alongside cold-smoked beer-cheese dip. —Jen Murphy

Neighborhood: Spanish PeaksThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Ousel Falls Trail, Lone Peak, Beehive Basin Trail, Gallatin and Madison Rivers

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: True dude ranch experience, tasteful cabin design, horseback riding experiences for all levels, easy access to town

Lone Mountain Ranch, one of Montana’s longest-standing dude ranches, has plenty going for it: a wonderfully attentive staff, character-filled cabins, and a calendar of special events that draw in both longtime regulars and first-time horseback riders. The on-site wranglers are happy to work with riders of all levels one-on-one, even if that means helping you get past a few preexisting fears before climbing into the saddle. The ranch’s roots reach back to the early days of Yellowstone, with its owners involved in conversations around Big Sky’s formation and the region’s ranching, logging, and wilderness preservation. Yet unlike many of Montana’s more remote ranches, it’s conveniently less than a 10-minute drive from town.

You may still find little reason to leave: Set among towering aspens, the 150-acre guest ranch has 25 restored historic cabins, each with its own Wild West–inspired name and one to six bedrooms. And then there are the signature experiences, including Cowgirl Up, a weeklong retreat that brings women from around the world together to experience ranch life and release their inner cowgirl.

Neighborhood: Lone MountainThings to do nearby: Big Sky Town Center, Ousel Falls Trail, Moonlight Basin, Gallatin River, Big Sky Resort

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s (iconically named) Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s hiking and wildlife spotting in the warmer months. It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to look elsewhere. A big plus? The town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Neighborhood: Cowboy HeavenThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Lone Mountain, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, in-unit washer and dryer, indoor wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, patio with outdoor furniture, longer stays allowed

With three floors and two separate living areas, this Big Sky rental gives small groups room to spread out between outings. And there’s plenty to get out for: Big Sky Resort is about 1.2 miles away, Beehive Basin Trailhead is roughly 2.6 miles, and Ousel Falls Park is another nearby option for low-key but scenic walks.

Inside the light-filled abode, fun Western touches are everywhere. In true Big Sky fashion, you’ll find everything from hanging longhorns and antlers to framed photographs of bison and horses. Through a wall of windows, you can look past the cozy fireplace into the hilly woods—the towering trees are gorgeous year-round. Do note this base might be best for four, rather than six, despite what the listing says. There are two generously sized bedrooms, but two sofa beds in the living room.

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Beehive Basin Trailhead, Gallatin River, Lone Mountain, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, firepit, spacious design, game room, fully equipped kitchen, patio space with seating and grill, proximity to Yellowstone National Park

For a fun departure from the usual cabin-in-the-woods vibe, this modern mountain retreat sleeps up to eight and puts you in a handy spot for mountain treks, foodie-forward itineraries, and all the trips in between. It’s incredibly spacious, with a large patio for grilling local ingredients, warming up around the fire, and stargazing. In winter, take advantage of the trails practically right next to the property for snowmobiling; you're also in a prime position for skiing at Moonlight Basin, Big Ski Resort, or Bridger Bowl ski area (a bit further north). According to the listing, a sauna is set to open on the property—check in with the hosts to see if it will be set up by the time you visit.

It’s worth noting that this is the closest Airbnb to Yellowstone on this list. You can drive to the West Yellowstone entrance in around 45 minutes.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: Gallatin River, West Yellowstone, Lone Indian Peak, Buck Ridge Trailhead, Crown Butte, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, shared firepits and sauna, board games and books, kid-friendly amenities

This gem of a rental is high on my Big Sky bucket list for more reasons than one. To start, the tastefully designed home is all about panoramic views of misty, moody Ramshorn Ridge. With heaps of walking paths and a mountain-facing hot tub under string lights, guests will be almost poetically connected to Montana’s wide-open landscape. But you won’t be too far from the mountain town’s buzz: This home is part of Aspects, a 10-home village set in a ryegrass field in the Gallatin Valley, meaning you’ll have access to the community’s saunas and two firepits, which you can share with like-minded travelers.

Downtown Big Sky is just a five-minute drive away, while hiking trails branching from Yellowstone are within 15 minutes of the home. Along with its great location, I’m personally captivated by this home’s aesthetic design touches—from the light wood walls that warmly envelop the dining space to the vibrant art that brings fun, unexpected pops of color throughout the home.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: The Riverhouse BBQ, West Yellowstone, Downtown Big Sky, Cinnamon Mountain, Gallatin River

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unique design, minutes from Big Sky Resort, sauna, private walking/biking trail from the property

A little off-grid, a bit otherworldly, and just a couple of miles from Big Sky Resort, this Earthship Airbnb is a unique kind of Montana hideaway. Set on 20 private acres in Michener Meadows, the solar-powered house is designed to bring the outdoors in, with its own potable spring water and a private walking and biking trail winding around the property.

Neighborhood: Michener MeadowsThings to do nearby: Ousel Falls Park, Dudley Creek Trailhead, Table Mountain, Horn and Cantle, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to Big Sky Town Center; patio with grill; indoor fireplace; fully equipped kitchen; shared access to indoor pool, hot tub, and sauna

For those in search of an easy, breezy Big Sky stay, this convenient condo is a boon. Tucked just outside of the city’s small but mighty town center, you’ll be within walking distance of cozy cafés, outdoor gear and gift shops, and hyper-local pubs and restaurants. Back at “home,” your launchpad is as design-friendly as it is inviting. There’s a snug living room with an electric fireplace, a raised patio with a barbecue, string lights, and a table for enjoying meals made in your fully equipped kitchenette. It’s pretty spacious for a condo—each of the bedrooms boasts a king bed, and there’s a bathroom for each duo.

You’ll also be a short drive to the ski resort and practically right next to Big Sky Golf Course, where you can enjoy an award-winning 18-hole expanse and Nordic skiing, depending on the season. A plus for those chasing the snow? There’s an in-unit washer and dryer for all your ski gear, so it’ll be clean and dry for more mountain fun the next day.

Neighborhood: Meadow VillageThings to do nearby: Big Sky Golf Course, Big Sky Resort, Big Sky Town Center, Lone Mountain Trail, Blue Moon Bakery, Historic Crail Ranch, The Reflector Trail Loop

#6275. Planning Your First Trip to New Zealand? Here's Where to Go

Living in Sydney, I’m guilty of thinking of New Zealand as somewhere I can always go next month. It’s close enough for a skiing trip, which is usually my first excuse to book. I love Queenstown for that, but what I’ve particularly enjoyed discovering on my travels is how naturally New Zealand brings together its spectacular outdoors and a tradition of luxury hospitality, in every season.

Aotearoa is easy to admire from a car window, but I’ve found that the places I remember most are those where I’ve stopped and spent a little more time. Wellington is overdue for another visit, and Fiordland is somewhere I'd like to explore properly. Then there are the lodges, each with its own character and reasons to return: Huka Lodge for its history, Cabot Lodgefor its working-farm roots, and many others worth discovering.

Below are the five places I’d build a trip around, leaving enough room in the itinerary to linger a little longer wherever I find myself wanting to stay.

I’d start with Queenstown if you’re coming for the mountains, with time allotted for Arrowtown and a few days in Fiordland National Park. For the North Island, Auckland is a useful starting point before heading towards Rotorua for its geothermal landscapes and Māori culture, then Lake Taupō. If food is your priority, I’d make Wellington part of the trip. My main advice is to choose a few places you’re interested in and give each at least a few days.

It can be, although a luxury lodge and a helicopter aren’t compulsory parts of an itinerary. I’d spend on a stay I really wanted, then balance it with somewhere simpler, ideally with a kitchen so you can cook some of your own meals. Skiing and guided activities can take a sizable bite out of the budget, so decide which matter most before booking everything else. If you’re considering a camper van, compare the total hire cost, including fuel and campsite fees, with a car and accommodation. I’d also leave room on the budget for eating out and wine tasting.

Seven days is sufficient for a trip, but I wouldn’t try to cover both islands in that time. On the South Island, you could spend the week around Queenstown and Arrowtown, adding Te Anau if Milford Sound is a priority. Or drive from Christchurch to Lake Tekapo and spend time in the Mackenzie region. On the North Island, Rotorua and Taupō work well together.

I always prefer to spend an extra night somewhere than keep repacking. Leave some flexibility, too: if you’ve come for stargazing and the sky clouds over, you’ll appreciate having another evening available.

Arrowtown, 20 minutes from Queenstown, is an idyllic place to visit.

Queenstown is great for the skiing, but I’d make time for nearby Arrowtown even if it meant losing a day on the slopes. I love the old cottages and shopfronts, and how much of its gold-mining history is still visible. The partially restored Chinese miners’ settlement beside Bush Creek is worth walking through before lunch.

Food is another reason to stay. At Aosta, northern Italian cooking makes good use of Central Otago produce. Nearby Ayrburn occupies a former 150-acre farm, with restaurants spread across its restored buildings. Billy’s, in the original homestead, serves modern Chinese food. I’ve visited both Arrowtown and Ayrburn, and would happily organize another Queenstown trip around eating here, with some skiing fitted in.

Where to stay: Arrowtown House is a small boutique hotel in town, making walking to dinner easy. Millbrook Resort, nearby, has more of a resort feel, with apartments as well as rooms and a spa for sore ski legs.

I still think about the water outside Huka Lodge. The Waikato River is this extraordinary emerald color, and I could have spent much of my stay watching it. Huka also got me interested in New Zealand’s lodge history: it began as a fishermen’s camp in 1924. There’s something appealing about discovering that a place has been welcoming people for the same reason for more than a century.

You don’t have to stay there to spend time beside the river. Follow the riverside walks towards Huka Falls, where the water forces its way through a narrow rock channel. I’d also get out on Lake Taupō, with a boat or kayak trip to the Ngātoroirangi Mine Bay Māori rock carvings. Created by Matahi Whakataka-Brightwell and his team, they’re a striking example of contemporary Māori art.

Where to stay: Huka Lodge has a certain stateliness, with its manicured grounds beside the Waikato River and a history of royal guests. I have dreams of running away to Poronui Safari Camp, in the wider Taupō region. Its two canvas tents sit beside the Mohaka River, with hot showers and food supplied by the kitchen. It’s booked exclusively for up to four people.

The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges on crystalline Lake Tekapo

I visited Dark Sky Project while reporting on quiet destinations for Traveler and loved having someone explain what I was looking at. The indoor experience brings Māori astronomy and science together, and houses an enormous restored 19th-century telescope. It gives you a way into the subject even if your astronomical knowledge is limited. For nighttime stargazing, book the Summit Experience at Mount John Observatory, within the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve. I’d arrange it early in the stay, leaving another night available if the weather doesn’t cooperate.

There’s plenty to look at during the day, too. Lake Tekapo gets its milky turquoise color from fine glacial rock flour floating in the water. It’s a good place to spend a few days on a South Island drive from Christchurch, with time for the Southern Alps and a separate excursion into Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park.

Where to stay: The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges take their inspiration from musterers’ huts. Inside, there are two bedrooms and a kitchen, with timber-lined rooms and a wood-burning fireplace. After a late night stargazing on Mount John, you can have a lie-in and cook breakfast whenever you’re ready.

The city of Wellington, a great place to visit for good eating and galleries.

New Zealand received its first Michelin restaurant selection in 2026, although you hardly need the guide to eat well here. For me, Wellington would be a few days of galleries and restaurant bookings, with enough time between them to walk around and see what’s changed since my last visit some years ago City Gallery’s reopening has moved it up my list and is the sort of thing I’d build a weekend around. I’d leave plenty of time for eating, though.

Puffin is on my list for a glass of natural wine. I’m also keeping an eye on Rita, a small restaurant in an Aro Valley cottage known for its changing set dinners. The team is also opening a daytime deli called Super Rita, expected to open in early next year.

Where to stay: The Intrepid Hotel is the one I’d book: 18 rooms in Te Aro, near Cuba Street, with Puffin downstairs. I like the idea of a nightcap in a locals-filled wine bar and a short walk upstairs to bed.

The Cabot Lodge, a working farm, is an intriguing stay in Fiordland

Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound are still on my list, and I’d like to give Fiordland a trip of its own. I’d stay around Te Anau rather than make the long journey out and back from Queenstown. There are glowworm caves across Lake Te Anau, while nearby Manapouri is the starting point for the most direct land-and-water route to Doubtful Sound: a boat across Lake Manapouri, followed by a coach over Wilmot Pass to the fjord.

I also have a shopping recommendation for the journey. At The Key, on the approach to Te Anau, Davaar sells knitwear (that has a cult following) made from wool grown on the family’s working sheep station, Davaar Station. Founder Kate Macdonald is the fifth generation, and her sister Anna runs the food caravan next door. I bought a jumper a few years ago when she had a pop-up in Arrowtown that I still love. It’s exactly the sort of place I want to find when traveling: a homegrown product with a family story; make the best souvenirs.

Where to stay: Cabot Lodge interests me because it’s on a working farm overlooking Lake Manapouri, and near Doubtful Sound departures. For a night at Milford itself, Milford Sound Lodge has chalets overlooking the river and rainforest. I’d decide which sound I wanted to spend more time exploring before choosing where to stay.

#6273. Livery of the Week: Aer Lingus

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Aer Lingus’ standard livery is centered on the shamrock, a symbol that has represented the Irish carrier for more than 80 years. Although the airline has changed its aircraft appearance several times, the three-leaf emblem remains the most recognizable feature of its fleet.

The current design was unveiled on Jan. 17, 2019, during a ceremony at Dublin Airport. It marked Aer Lingus’ first major aircraft rebranding in more than two decades, replacing the predominantly green-and-white scheme introduced in the 1990s.

The redesign retained the shamrock but introduced a revised version with a slight tilt and more pronounced heart-shaped leaves. According to Aer Lingus, the changes were intended to represent movement and the airline’s Irish heritage while giving the logo a more contemporary appearance.

The most noticeable change was the shift away from the green upper fuselage used on the previous livery. The updated scheme features a predominantly white aircraft with a teal vertical stabilizer and engines. Large teal “Aer Lingus” titles appear along the forward fuselage.

The shamrock appears in several locations beyond the tail. Aer Lingus incorporated the emblem into the airline’s wordmark, near the aircraft’s boarding door and on the wingtips. The airline specifically positioned the wingtip design to make it visible to passengers looking out from the cabin.

The aircraft’s lower fuselage also received a teal treatment, making the color visible from below. The combination of white and teal replaced the darker green that had dominated much of the airline’s branding for decades.

Aer Lingus worked with global design consultancy Lippincott on the rebranding. The airline considered more than 50 shamrock designs before selecting the final version. The updated identity also included a new typeface, redesigned digital platforms and changes to other customer-facing materials.

Two aircraft were presented in the new colors during the January 2019 unveiling: an Airbus A330-300 named St Munchin and an A320 named St Schira. The A330 made its first scheduled flight in the updated livery the following day, operating from Dublin to New York.

Aer Lingus has also retained several connections to its earlier aircraft designs. Its 1960s-inspired retro livery, introduced in 2011 to celebrate the airline’s 75th anniversary, featured a darker green-and-white appearance that contrasted with the newer scheme.

More than seven years after its introduction, the 2019 design remains the standard appearance of Aer Lingus aircraft. The colors and placement of the branding have changed, but the shamrock continues to link the carrier’s modern fleet with its earlier history.

#6272. Boeing Cleared To Sell Parts & Jets To Belarus Despite Fears They’ll End Up In Russia

Boeing has officially been cleared to resume direct business with Belarusian flag carrier Belavia, which flies 12 aircraft from the US planemaker. The airline had been placed under sanctions by the US, but these were initially eased back in September of 2025. Now the US has gone a step further after its Commerce Department licensed Boeing to deal directly with Belavia in terms of both parts and planes.

Belarusian officials welcomed the decision, but some fear that it could be used as a way of getting Boeing components and aircraft to Russia through the back door, given Belarus's allyship with the latter nation. Russia remains under sanctions amid its military activities in Ukraine, almost five years after its initial invasion back in February of 2022. This has forced its airlines to rethink their fleet strategies.

BelTA and Reform News recently reported that US officials had cleared Boeing to undertake direct transactions with Belarusian flag carrier Belavia. The publications cited Belavia CEO Igor Tcherginets, who confirmed on October 31 that his carrier can now "directly obtain spare parts, components and software for the aircraft currently operated by the airline" from Boeing.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Tcherginets added that the US Department of the Treasury had also previously issued such an authorization. While American sanctions on Belavia were initially lifted more than a year ago, Politico reported at the time that the US did not want this to lead to Russia getting its hands on spare parts through the Belarusian back door. According to Tcherginets, Belavia is also now allowed to make larger purchases:

"In addition, this opens the way for negotiations on purchasing aircraft directly from Boeing."

Coverage of the matter by Reform News highlights the fact that this latest approval came about following productive talks between officials from Belarus and the US. These, the publication said, were held in Minsk in September, with Aleksandr Lukashenko, the President of Belarus, meeting US Special Envoy John Coale, who formed part of a wider American delegation that was visiting the Belarusian capital.

The aim of these talks from the Belarusian side was reportedly to outline areas that would require US resolution in order for constructive dialog between the two nations to continue. With aviation playing an increasingly important political role as a form of soft power, and the timing of this recent announcement, it seems fairly likely that enabling direct work between Boeing and Belavia was one such talking point.

The US and Belarus remain in talks, with Belaruskali CEO Andrei Rybakou having also had his personal sanctions lifted. He described the authorization for Boeing and Belavia to work directly together once again as "another positive decision." However, if this decision is later used as a loophole to allow spare parts to flow into Russia and aid its sanction-hit airlines, you might expect it to be swiftly reversed.

Sanctions don't just ground aircraft. They can dismantle entire airlines, one spare part at a time.

The news is a welcome relief for Belavia when it comes to keeping its Boeing fleet running, with the ability to directly obtain spare parts again easing its maintenance concerns. As it happens, ch-aviation shows that only just over half of its overall fleet is made up of jets from the US planemaker: eight normal Boeing 737-800s, one private 737-800, one 737 MAX 8, one 737-300, and one 767-300ER.

These 12 aircraft are joined by ten others from various non-Boeing manufacturers. For instance, on the Airbus side of things, three A330-200s are present, while Embraer is represented by one E175LR and four E195LRs. Belavia's other two aircraft that are currently listed by ch-aviation as being part of its present fleet are a pair of Bombardier private jets: one Challenge 850 and one Global Express XRS.

#6271. A New York City Weekend Guide for Design Lovers

The thing that makes visiting (or living in) New York worth every penny is that you don’t have to go out of your way looking for inspiration. You might be struck by a vintage sign advertising color TVs in the East Village; a grandpa on the Upper East Side pairing bright red socks with his loafers; or that never-gets-old view of the Brooklyn Bridge from an elevated subway track. Design is, indeed, everywhere in NYC, but sometimes you need a bit of a roadmap to plot your next moment of awe.

Like many New Yorkers, I derive a lot of joy from looking at pretty things and existing in cool spaces. When I feel like I’m staring at a blank page—or I just want to spend a weekend more intentionally—the places below are the ones I turn to for a creative spark. These spots span boroughs and cover art, architecture, and fashion—from former artist residences and Japanese-inspired stationery stores to restaurants and spas with covetable interiors.

For the aesthetes who have already seen the latest exhibition at MoMA, this weekend guide for design lovers is intended to point you in a few other directions (and no, this does not include that viral room full of dirt in SoHo).

The Cooper Hewitt is the only museum in the United States devoted exclusively to both historical and contemporary design.

For many New Yorkers, to go uptown is to go to the museum. And while the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds down the fort, there are a few other players along Museum Mile that always seem to take me by surprise whenever I visit. The Cooper Hewitt, for instance, showcases “design objects” in the broadest sense that span across centuries—you might find an Egyptian ceramic from 1100 BCE in one room, and a Swedish midcentury-modern lamp in another. It’s also a lovely hangout spot; earlier this year, the museum hosted a Hi-Fi listening room, and when the weather’s nice, visitors can take advantage of the garden (tickets are not required and Wi-Fi is free), admiring the gorgeous architecture of Andrew Carnegie’s former mansion.

The “Einspänner” at Sabarsky—double espresso with whipped cream.

A short walk away, the Neue Galerie, which specializes in early 20th-century German and Austrian art, is where I go to gush over furniture designed by the likes of Josef Hoffmann and Adolf Loos. The museum is set to reopen on November 12 for its 20th anniversary, but in the meantime, you can visit the stunning Café Sabarsky—the Viennese restaurant located within the museum—and pretend you’re at the helm of the next great intellectual movement with your friends over fancy whipped-cream-topped coffees.

Further downtown, in Midtown East, the Paul Rudolph Institute is a must for anyone who enjoyed The Brutalist. Join the monthly open house at the Rudolph-designed duplex within the iconic Modulightor building, once the headquarters of the lighting company the architect co-founded with his life partner, Ernst Wagner. Docents are on-site to answer any questions as you wind your way through the all-white apartment, with its disjointed staircases and built-in shelving units, though private tours are also available.

When it comes to shopping, I believe one can gain a lot from staring into the windows along Madison Avenue, or even heading inside to get a feel for the luxe fabrics, sans purchase. But for second-hand designer clothing, Upper East Vintage (by appointment only) and Designer Revival (Gentleman’s Resale is also right next door), both on the Upper East Side, are your best bet. I’m also always delighted by what I find at Spellman Gallery, a small showroom owned by an art appraiser with fantastic taste—you can discover all kinds of treasures, from a rare vinyl record to a painting worth a few thousand.

Browsing beautiful items will inevitably stir up an appetite, and for a restaurant that has tables equipped with landlines during live art auction sales, check out Marcel 945 Madison, housed inside the historic Breuer Building that is now the global headquarters of Sotheby’s. While the restaurant serves (very expensive) French bistro fare, it’s all about the rotating art on the walls—including works by Roy Lichtenstein and Willem de Kooning, to name a few past residents—which are also available for purchase.

With its glass blocks, chrome light fixtures, and black leather booths, Bridges in Chinatown is a design-lover's dream.

If you prefer to walk amongst grittier cast-iron buildings or people-watch from plastic stools, then it’s best you head downtown. Start with a trip to the Judd Foundation, where you can book a slot to explore 37 of minimalist Donald Judd’s artworks, each permanently installed in the late artist’s former residence and studio on Spring Street, and get a glimpse of how an artist lived and breathed in SoHo before the luxury flagships arrived. Over in Greenwich Village, the Renee and Chaim Gross Foundation boasts over 12,000 of American artist Chaim Gross’s sculptures, drawings, and prints, as well as his personal collection of global art. The late artist’s personal home, which he shared with his wife Renee, is light-filled and lived-in—an intimate experience that cannot be replicated at a traditional museum.

The Lower East Side, specifically Orchard Street, is where to go to shop independent designers. Browse Colbo—more of a multidisciplinary space than a retail store—for unisex neutrals as you sip an espresso. Adjacent to the shop, Colbo Next Door is a great spot to grab a glass of wine and listen to vinyl. Further along Orchard Street, you’ll find Lara Koleji for vintage Miu Miu, as well as Tumbao, a curation of the very best in Latin American fashion design. On East Broadway, also in the LES, Aeon Bookstore is one of my favorite bookstores in New York, a basement-level shop with a small-but-mighty selection of used titles, whether you’re looking for a coffee table book on the Bauhaus or a beautiful edition of Lolita.

Gem Home on Mott Street saves the day whenever I’m in need of a unique, last-minute gift—say, a stainless steel ice cream bowl or spiral toothbrush holder—and the shop, which is also a café, has recently started hosting dinners in collaboration with French pop-up Mon Petit Canard. Continuing on with the theme of downtown cool, Bridges is a swoon-worthy restaurant space that’s bound to get your interior design wheels turning, and there’s a famous Comté cheese tart that’s a work of art in and of itself.

If you've ever wondered what the subway looked like decades ago, the New York Transit Museum has your answer.

If you’re spending a day in Brooklyn, make sure to pop over to the New York Transit Museum in Downtown Brooklyn—talk about a celebration of design. In addition to touring over 20 different vintage train cars, you’ll view an otherwise quotidian part of New York City life in a new light. Graphic design nerds in particular will geek out over the exhibits dedicated to Massimo Vignelli, who designed the 1972 subway map we love and use today. For a different kind of museum experience, Pioneer Works in Red Hook was born out of a former 1866 red-brick warehouse, and today it’s dedicated to all kinds of arts and science programming. On view right now, for instance, is a multimedia exhibition by Helsinki-based artist Tuomas A. Laitinen, drawing on more than a decade of research on octopus intelligence, sleep, and consciousness.

There’s only one place I trust for buying jeans, and it’s Front General Store's Outpost, which boasts an entire wall of vintage Levi’s and then some—think worn-in Burberry trench coats, military deadstock, and new shoes from Japanese or British brands you might not have heard of. The vintage shopping in Brooklyn, of course, doesn’t stop there: 10 ft Single by Stella Dallas in Williamsburg is a reliable favorite for threadbare T-shirts and Ralph Lauren sweaters, and if you’re on the hunt for a conversation starter of a chair, Dream Fishing Tackle in Greenpoint is part fishing supply center, part midcentury-modern furniture store. If it wasn’t already clear, NYC loves a retail space that’s also something else: Chyelle in Bushwick and Apartment Ra’el in Bed-Stuy both serve up coffee and beautiful homeware. For those obsessed with paper and pens (guilty), Yoseka Stationery in Greenpoint stocks the very best in Japanese stationery design—from Hobonichi journals to Kaweco fountain pens.

In a sea of white-marbled wellness spaces, Spencer’s Spa in Williamsburg proves good design is integral to relaxation. I’ve had excellent facials at both the Brooklyn and SoHo locations, lingering for as long as possible afterwards in the lounge areas, which seem to take inspiration from traditional Japanese, Art Deco, and Scandinavian design (I like to take pictures of all the unique lamps and objects so I can reverse image search them for my apartment later on). But if you’d rather find your zen within New York City’s nightlife scene, James Murphy–owned club Nightmoves in Williamsburg, music venue Public Records in Gowanus, and listening bar Eavesdrop in Greenpoint all boast incredibly impressive custom sound design.

The Noguchi Museum is one of the most peaceful pockets of the city.

Akari Light Sculptures abound at the Noguchi Museum, and you can even bring one home.

A trip to Queens would not be complete without a visit to the Noguchi Museum in Astoria, where you can feel a sense of serenity walking around Isamu Noguchi’s biomorphic sculptures, then buy one of his Akari light sculptures in what is perhaps the best museum gift shop in New York City. While the museum is home to its own sculpture garden, there’s also one practically across the street—make sure you allot some time to strolling Socrates Sculpture Park, where you’ll encounter a whole host of experimental installations (they’re always rotating), with the Manhattan skyline as the backdrop.

In Long Island City, the industrial hub-turned-creative enclave in western Queens, MoMA PS1 is at once nostalgic and of-the-moment, showcasing contemporary art within former elementary school halls—it’s especially fun in the summer when it's running its Warm Up series, when everyone gathers outside for DJ sets and music performances. Also in the neighborhood, Somerset House is a staging and interior design gallery that sells collectible furniture and art—think Pierre Jeanneret armchairs and Poul Henningsen lamps—by appointment only. For something a bit more accessible, Lichen in Ridgewood sells a similar catalog of vintage furniture, plus its own in-house designs ranging from glass coffee tables to futuristic sconces.

This bank-turned-hotel features original vaulted ceilings that rival those of Grand Central Station. Sip a martini at the Swan Room, the property's see-and-be-seen lobby bar.

Situated in NoMad, The Fifth Avenue Hotel gives you access to both Museum Mile and downtown shopping. The 19th-century, Renaissance-style mansion is dressed in maximalism.

Once a barrel factory in the early 1900s, this hip Williamsburg hotel is your gateway to industrial-chic rooms, a cinema with red velvet seats, and the acclaimed Le Crocodile restaurant.

The Mercer is SoHo in a nutshell, with loft-like suites, a neutral color palette, and a buzzy restaurant. Minimalists, this one’s for you.
