#6270. Discover Airlines Adding 13 Airbus A350s, Starting With Four Ex-Lufthansa Jets

Discover Airlines is Lufthansa Group’s long haul leisure carrier based in Germany. The airline has been growing in recent years, as Lufthansa Group (unsurprisingly) sees a lot of potential with its low cost operations. As a matter of fact, Lufthansa Group seems committed to growing everything except its flagship brand, Lufthansa.

In 2024, we first learned that the Discover Airlines fleet will grow in the coming years, and that we’ll eventually see the introduction of a new business class product. Then in 2025, we learned that the airline would start to acquire Airbus A350s. We now have a lot more details about what that will look like, including the timeline, as well as the first routes to be operated by the plane.

Discover Airlines has plans to acquire a total of 13 Airbus A350-900s. This will be a two-step process:

For context, Discover Airlines’ long haul fleet currently consists of 13 Airbus A330s — that’s now limited to the A330-300 variant, as the A330-200 variant has just been retired.

The current expectation is that the first former Lufthansa A350 will join the fleet in June 2027. It will initially operate short haul routes for crew familiarization, before flying long haul from Frankfurt (FRA) to Calgary (YYC) and Orlando (MCO).

The second A350 will then join the fleet in December 2027, with service on the plane being added to San Jose (SJO) and Belize City (BZE). The third and fourth A350 will then join the fleet in the summer of 2028.

By mid-2028, Discover Airlines expects its long haul fleet to grow to 20 aircraft, which includes the four former Lufthansa A350s, as well as some additional former Lufthansa A330s that will be added to the fleet.

It’s worth remembering that Lufthansa is the least profitable airline of Lufthansa Group. Rather than addressing that directly, Lufthansa Group’s solution to this issue is to continue outsourcing flying. For example, Lufthansa is about to drop flights to Seattle (SEA), as those will instead be operated by Discover Airlines. So it really shows you what a core part of Lufthansa’s plan this subsidiary is.

Discover Airlines isn’t the only Lufthansa Group leisure subsidiary getting A350s. SWISS’ leisure subsidiary, Edelweiss Air, is fully refreshing its long haul fleet, replacing A340-300s with A350-900s. In Edelweiss’ case, those are former LATAM jets that were retired early. These planes will also soon get new interiors, and the first aircraft should be retrofitted with all-new cabins in the coming months.

In typical Lufthansa Group fashion, Discover Airlines has acquired most of its aircraft simply by being given Lufthansa planes as they’ve been retired. So most of Discover Airlines’ A330s have the typical “old” Lufthansa business class, in a 2-2-2 configuration.

So you might be thinking that these initial four A350s that Discover Airlines is getting also have those interiors, given that most Lufthansa A350s also have business class seats in a 2-2-2 configuration.

However, not surprisingly, there’s another angle here. In 2021, Lufthansa opportunistically picked up four ex-Philippine Airlines A350s, as the carrier was going through a reorganization. Lufthansa maintained the cabin interiors, which funny enough, actually elevated Lufthansa’s business class experience considerably, given that these planes have Thompson Aero Vantage XL seats.

There was always the question of what Lufthansa would eventually do with these planes, so it’s not surprising that they’re now going to a different subsidiary. Meanwhile Lufthansa’s A350s with the old business class are all eventually going to be reconfigured with Allegris cabins. So when these four special A350s are taken over by Discover Airlines, you can expect that interiors will be maintained.

Now, what about those nine factory fresh A350s that will join the fleet starting in 2029? We don’t yet know what we can expect from those interiors. From a standardization standpoint, I suppose it’s possible that the airline gets the same business class you’ll find with Lufthansa’s A350 Allegris business class and SWISS Senses’ A350 business class.

However, what’s interesting here is that Discover Airlines is also rolling out a new business class product on its existing A330s. This is an off the shelf product, which is probably smart from the company’s perspective, given all the certification issues we’ve seen over time. So I suppose it’s possible that this will also be introduced on the A350s… we’ll see!

Discover Airlines will be modernizing its long haul fleet, as the airline will eventually take delivery of 13 Airbus A350-900s. In 2027 and 2028, we’ll see the airline acquire four Lufthansa A350s, and specifically, the planes that are former Philippine Airlines aircraft. Then in 2029 and beyond, we’ll see the airline get nine factory fresh A350s, part of the larger Lufthansa Group order.

This represents a major fleet modernization for the airline, and it’ll be interesting to see how this all plays out, especially when it comes to the brand new planes. Between this and the existing A330s getting new cabins, the Discover Airlines passenger experience is getting a nice boost.

What do you make of Discover Airlines acquiring Airbus A350s?

It has been less than three years since Mexico’s newest airport in Tulum welcomed passengers for the very first time.

The carrier on Friday confirmed it will end all service to Tulum International Airport (TQO) just after the holidays.

The news was first spotted by Ishrion Aviation.

In a statement, United said it makes “regular adjustments” to its flight schedule “based on seasonality, demand and other market factors.”

It’s not the first carrier to have second thoughts on Tulum.

The brand-new airport first welcomed international guests in March 2024, and airlines quickly added flights from major U.S. hubs.

The airport was billed as a more convenient link to Tulum’s resorts versus Cancun International Airport (CUN), which sits more than two hours to the north by car.

But within months, carriers started slashing service, citing disappointing demand.

Delta this winter will offer flights to Tulum only from Atlanta. It previously had routes from Detroit and Minneapolis.

American still has flights from Dallas and Miami, though it once offered service from Charlotte, too.

All told, air service from the U.S. to Tulum will be down more than 50% versus just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

While United flyers will lose nonstop service to one beach destination in Mexico, the carrier continues to expand its largest West Coast hub.

The carrier on Friday confirmed it’s adding two new transcontinental flights from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) — both to Virginia.

Twice-weekly flights to Richmond International Airport (RIC) will begin on March 28. Service will run on Thursdays and Sundays.

That same day, the carrier will launch service to Norfolk International Airport (ORF). Flights will operate on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

It’s United’s second SFO expansion in as many weeks. Just days ago, the carrier announced a trio of new domestic routes from its Bay Area hub.

These latest new routes from San Francisco come as the airline prepares to open its newest United Club — which even features an outdoor terrace — later this year.

#6268. Sleep Under the Stars at These Incredible Igloo-Like Airbnbs Around the World

Few travel experiences are as otherworldly as watching the night sky from the cozy cocoon of a glass-topped igloo. In the far north, that might mean watching the aurora borealis shimmer overhead, surrounded by pine forests and frozen lakes. But you don't have to travel to the Arctic Circle to experience an igloo-like stay. From snow-covered mountain landscapes in Germany to peaceful corners of Spain, these unusual stays can be found in some unexpected places across Europe and beyond.

The impressive northern lights in Finnish Lapland

Many interiors lean into a Nordic theme—think Scandi-style decor, underfloor heating, faux-fur throws, and panoramic windows designed to maximise stargazing. In Nordic destinations, many of these igloos give you the chance to enjoy classic experiences nearby, such as husky and reindeer sledding, cold-water swimming, or a spell in a geothermal spa. Elsewhere, the appeal might be waking up to mountain views, exploring the surrounding countryside, or simply enjoying the novelty of sleeping inside a transparent dome.

Wrap up, pour a hot chocolate, and settle in—here are the best igloos to bed down in for a memorable night under the stars.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private deck, hot tub

Set within 45 acres of secluded private woodland, this spacious dome is a cozy base for exploring the surrounding walking trails by day and stargazing after dark, thanks to the area's limited light pollution. Inside, there's a king-size bed, two fold-out single beds, armchairs, and a dining area, as well as a private bathroom with a hot shower and a small kitchenette equipped with a microwave, kettle, toaster, and fridge. Outside, the deck has plenty of seating and a barbecue, while a covered Scandinavian wood-fired hot tub overlooking the surrounding countryside can be used for an extra charge. Dogs are welcome too, making this a good option if you don't want to leave four-legged family members behind.

Location: Shropshire, United KingdomThings to do nearby: Ludlow Castle, Tenbury Museum, Mortimer Forest

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Lake views, fireplace, air-conditioning, hot tub

Perched on a hillside above Lake Superior, this geodesic dome combines the feel of camping with all the comforts of home. Designed to be enjoyed year-round, it has a gas fireplace and heating for chilly Minnesota winters, as well as air-conditioning for warmer summer days. There's room for up to four guests, with a queen bed and a second lofted bed, plus a fully equipped kitchen and bathroom with a walk-in shower. The highlight, though, is the large private deck, where a hot tub overlooks the lake and can be used throughout the year. The town of Two Harbors is also just a short drive away, with cafés, restaurants, shops and a local brewery.

Location: Two Harbors, MinnesotaThings to do nearby: Two Harbors town, Pierre the Voyager, Two Harbors Pierhead Light, Rock Beach

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, shared bathWhy we love it: Fjord views, secluded location, terrace

Perched on rocky terrain above Trondheim Fjord, Dome Smiberget makes the most of its spectacular waterfront setting. The geodesic dome feels wonderfully secluded, surrounded by trees with little between you and the water below. Inside, a wall of honeycomb-shaped windows wraps around the bed and seating area, framing sweeping views across the fjord and letting you watch the sky change without stepping outside. Come evening, you can stargaze from bed, while a small private terrace overlooking the water makes an idyllic spot to sit out when the weather plays along.

Location: Indre Fosen, NorwayThings to do nearby: Ulvestøtta monument, Sukkertoppen mountain hikes

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Outdoor grill, swimming pond, boules court

Drive through the scenic Dresden Elbe meadows to reach this rüdehof, which serves as both the headquarters of a family distillery and a tranquil countryside retreat—best enjoyed under a layer of icing-sugar snow in winter. The igloo is more like a hobbit house, with all you need to shelter from the cold, including a double bed, compact kitchen, shower room, and a dining area with panoramic, bucolic views. You're secluded as can be, around 90 minutes from Hamburg within a two-hectare wild and rugged estate, now yours to explore at your leisure. Stoke the fire and grill outdoors at suppertime, then settle in for some stargazing. If you're feeling brave, there's a swimming pond; then warm up in the hot tub afterwards. A boules court is available for a few leisurely games before supper.

Location: Amt Neuhaus, Niedersachsen, GermanyThings to do nearby: Stixer Wanderdüne hiking paths, Alte Eiche Forsthaus grüner Jäger momumental oak tree, Hamburg

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fireplace, sledding, northern lights viewing

This is glamping, but not as most know it. On the cusp of Rovaniemi's thick pine forests, this igloo is furnished in true Nordic style with thick down blankets, plenty of wool rugs, cozy bedding, and a crackling log fireplace to huddle around in the evenings. Wrap up and head into the garden for wintry fun, including sledding—or simply huddle under the duvet to watch as frost forms and snow falls gently behind the windows.

Location: Rovaniemi, FinlandThings to do nearby: Ounasvaara Ski Oy ski resort, Ounasvaara Winter Trail, Forestry Museum of Lapland

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Panoramic views, breakfast included, kitchenette station

Spain isn't the first place you'd think of for igloo adventures, but this Airbnb might just change your mind. Deep in Spain's Selva de Irati forest, this immersive retreat pairs stylish design with wild beauty, perched on a hilltop overlooking the lush Aezkoa Valley. Interiors are simple and sparse, leaving space to focus on the comfortable silence and the nature that surrounds—there are dreamy panoramic views over the mountains from every angle. Previous guests have loved this experience, saying the sunsets from here are especially lovely. For something a little different, it's hard to beat.

Location: Orbaizeta, SpainThings to do nearby: Mirador de Zamariain viewpoint, Museo de Roncesvalles, Irati Forest

#6267. Philippine Airlines Business Class Airbus A350 Review: Great Seats, But Missing Heart

For the long haul segment of the return portion of my first class quest to Japan, I flew Philippine Airlines’ Airbus A350-1000 business class on the 11hr55min flight from Manila (MNL) to San Francisco (SFO). I was very much looking forward to this flight, given that this is the carrier’s new flagship aircraft, featuring all-new cabins.

Ultimately my Philippine Airlines business class flight was good, especially when you account for value, given that Philippine Airlines tends to undercut the competition on price. If you can get over the awful ground experience in Manila, then there’s definitely value to be had here.

On the plus side, the cabin was brand new, and the food was pretty good. However, there were also some shortcomings, like the inoperable Wi-Fi, and there was maybe an x-factor missing with the soft product. Furthermore, while the crew was friendly enough, they didn’t have the warmth or attentiveness of the crew on my previous flight, as it felt like they were just going through the motions and disinterested.

So my conclusion is that this flight was a great deal, and I’d absolutely recommend this product if the price is right. But I feel like if Philippine Airlines tried a little harder, it could truly have a top tier product.

I booked my return itinerary from Osaka to Manila to San Francisco as one ticket, with the first flight on the Airbus A330 (which I’ve already reviewed — that seat sucks!), and the second flight on the Airbus A350. I booked the following ticket, which cost $1,746.63:

9/19 PR411 Osaka to Manila departing 3:15PM arriving 6:40PM9/19 PR104 Manila to San Francisco departing 11:15PM arriving 9:10PM

However, I ended up offsetting the cost of this ticket with points, so I really booked it with 116,442 Chase Ultimate Rewards points, because I could redeem for 1.5 cents each toward the cost of the ticket. That’s a reasonable paid fare, and in this case, I preferred redeeming points rather than having to spend the cash out of pocket.

In a previous installment, I reviewed the Philippine Airlines Mabuhay Lounge Manila, which is just awful, in my opinion. It was so bad that I went and sat out in the terminal, which is saying something, because the airport’s Terminal 1 makes JFK Terminal 1 (not the new one!) look like Singapore Changi, by comparison!

My flight was departing from gate five, with boarding scheduled for 10:30PM, 45 minutes before departure. All the US-bound flights from Manila depart from one area, with a centralized security check. It was quick for me, though obviously if you get “SSSS” on your boarding pass, you’ll get a more thorough inspection.

The gate area in this part of the terminal is just so poorly set up, as it’s a sea of seats, without many ways to easily pass through there. And as you’d expect, there are typically multiple flights departing at peak times, so it gets quite busy. There is a dedicated seating area for business class passengers, but there’s nothing actually special about that.

Boarding ended up starting at 10:30PM, with dozens and dozens of wheelchairs passengers boarding first. Business class passengers were then invited to board around 15 minutes later.

I boarded through the forward left door, where I was greeted by the crew, and then turned right into the cabin. I’m usually really good at boarding first and getting pictures, but unfortunately by the time I boarded, around half of the business class passengers were seated (as wheelchair passengers get pre-boarding).

Philippine Airlines’ A350-1000s are equipped with the Collins Aerospace Elevation product, which is essentially the rebranding and slight evolution of the Super Diamond product, the world’s most popular reverse herringbone seat. Seats have 44″ of pitch, 21″ of width, and turn into 78″ flat beds.

The business class cabin consists of a total of 42 seats, spread across 11 rows, in a 1-2-1 configuration. This takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors.

Next to the seat you’ll find a console, where there’s a wireless charging pad, as well as two storage compartments that can be opened.

One storage compartment is shallow and has a vanity, so this is ideal for storing a cell phone, passport, etc. The other storage compartment is a bit deeper, and has the entertainment controller, along with USB-A and USB-C outlets, and a headphone jack.

Next to the storage compartment is the small panel that can control all the seat functions, including seat recline, lighting, etc.

In the back part of this area you’ll find the literature pocket, as well as a lamp that can be adjusted via a button at the top of it.

Underneath the seat and to the side you’ll find the AC power outlet, which is kind of hidden, unless you crouch over.

In this seat, the entertainment monitor is fixed to the shell of the seat in front, and it’s a 20″ 4K UHD screen.

The tray table in this seat folds out from underneath the entertainment monitor. When stored, it’s folded over in half, so to fully utilize it, you pull it out and then flip it over.

The seat has a good size ottoman, which becomes part of the bed when the seat is reclined.

Then on the aisle-side of the seat there’s an armrest, and if you open it, there’s a little bit of storage, big enough for a water bottle.

Beyond that you’ll find the door, which can be opened and closed manually. Of course it’s locked during takeoff and landing, since it can only be used inflight.

The two other things worth mentioning about the cabin is that there are no individual air nozzles (grrr!), and there are also no overhead bins in the middle of the cabin. That makes the cabin feel more spacious, though it also means that there’s not quite as much storage space.

All-in-all, Philippine Airlines has a really great hard product, so I have nothing but good things to say there. The seats are comfortable, the tech is great, and I appreciate that there are colors other than grey and black.

Philippine Airlines has audio and video on demand in its business class on the A350-1000. The airline has a solid selection of movies, TV shows, games, and audio. I couldn’t figure out exactly how many options there were of each, due to how they were organized. However, it was an extensive selection, though not to the level of what you’ll find on Emirates or Singapore Airlines.

I’m not usually much of a movie person on planes (or at all), but I ended up watching “The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel,” which was mildly entertaining.

The system also had a map feature, as you’d expect. One thing that disappointed me is that there was no tail camera, as that’s something you’ll find on many A350 operators, and it’s something I really enjoy.

Philippine Airlines also offers bluetooth audio on its A350s, which is a handy feature.

In theory, Philippine Airlines’ A350-1000s are supposed to have Viasat Wi-Fi, which offers relatively high speed connectivity. However, it simply didn’t work on this flight. It’s not that it was intermittent or slow, it just wasn’t possible to connect.

It seems like one or two of the carrier’s A350s have non-functioning Wi-Fi. I understand tech can be complicated, but it’s also super frustrating when you board a long haul flight expecting to have connectivity, only to find out that it doesn’t work.

Hopefully they get this resolved soon. On balance, the airline gets a thumbs down on entertainment based on my experience, since inflight Wi-Fi is something you expect as a standard nowadays on long haul flights.

Waiting at my Philippine Airlines business class seat upon boarding were a solid selection of amenities. There was a very plush pillow, a cozy blanket, and a mattress pad. While there was no luxury branding collaboration, the bedding was very good.

Many of the other amenities were presented in a unique storage pouch.

This included an amenity kit, with socks, a comb, a dental kit, eyeshades, and some products from L’Occitane.

There were also some flimsy slippers, which weren’t luxurious, but did their job.

Then there were headphones that weren’t particularly great quality, but thanks to bluetooth audio, I don’t consider that to be a big deal.

The menu and drink list were also at my seat upon boarding.

Toward the end of the boarding process, a variety of non-alcoholic pre-departure drinks were offered, and I opted for the cucumber iced tea. I was offered a warm towel to go along with that.

All-in-all, the amenities were decent. I thought the bedding was very good, while the other amenities were just okay. There were no pajamas in business class, not that you’d necessarily expect them.

The boarding process on this flight was really drawn out, as every seat onboard was occupied. The entire boarding also took place through the forward left door, which was less than ideal in terms of foot traffic, but presumably that’s all that was possible at this gate.

Boarding took longer than planned, and the main cabin door finally closed at 11:30PM. Around that time the first officer was on the PA to inform us of our flight time of 11hr55min, and cruising altitude of 39,000 feet. A few moments later, the safety video was screened, which was rather entertaining (and dramatic).

At 11:35PM we began our pushback, and at 11:45PM we began our taxi. We only had a very short taxi out to our departure runway, and at 11:55PM we were cleared for takeoff on runway 6. We had a long roll down the runway, and then a smooth and gradual climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff.

Philippine Airlines doesn’t offer dine on demand in business class. On this flight, dinner was served after takeoff, breakfast was served before landing, and then there was a snack menu available throughout the flight. You can find the dinner menu and drink list below.

Meal orders had already been taken on the ground, and the first round of drinks was served 30 minutes after takeoff. To drink, I had a glass of champagne, and on this flight Chanoine Freres Brut was on offer, which I wasn’t a huge fan of (even though it’s not cheap).

That was served with a chicken liver pate amuse bouche. I understand that’s supposed to feel high end, but it’s definitely not my favorite thing.

There were then two appetizer choices, and I opted for the smoked salmon with pickled carrot ribbons, compressed cucumber, and red radish. That was served with some bread rolls. The dish wasn’t memorable, and it was also quite small.

Of the three main course options, I chose the pan seared halibut, served with garden vegetables, honey lime reduction, and flavored rice. I appreciated that this was obviously plated onboard (rather than being heated in a casserole dish), but the taste was just okay.

Then for dessert, there was the choice of an orange yogurt mousse cake, cheese plate, or ice cream. I chose the mousse cake, served with pistachio crumble and candied orange peel.

Afterwards, I asked if I could also have a cheese plate (to see how it compared), which the flight attendant got me.

The meal was served really quickly, and within 75 minutes of takeoff, my tray was fully cleared. I was a bit conflicted on the entire meal experience.

For example, I was impressed by how everything was placed directly on the tray table, and the plating and presentation were quite nice. I also appreciated the pace of service, especially on a late night flight where many people are looking to sleep.

However, the food was just okay, and not great. There wasn’t a single dish I had where my expectations were exceeded, but instead, it all just tasted like relatively decent airplane food. I also feel like with the starter they could’ve added a salad, or something.

After the meal, I checked out the lavatory on the Philippine Airlines A350-1000. There were two located at the front of the cabin, which were reserved for business class. There were also two behind the cabin, but they were for premium economy. The lavatories were totally standard for an A350, and were modern without being overly spacious.

There were also some basic Philippine Airlines branded amenities.

The one catch is that two lavatories really isn’t enough for so many business class passengers. Beyond that, the lights on the bulkhead which are supposed to indicate whether a lavatory is occupied weren’t working. They always showed as green, even when all lavatories were occupied.

Once back at my seat, I decided to get some rest, so I reclined my seat and made my bed.

I thought the bed comfort was excellent, and while I wish there were individual air nozzles, I do have to give the crew credit for keeping the cabin really cool, so that didn’t turn out to be an issue.

I fell asleep with around 10hr20min remaining to San Francisco, while we were approaching the southern islands of Japan…

…and I woke up with around 5hr20min remaining to San Francisco, as we were just south of the Aleutian Islands.

As someone who is a poor airplane sleeper, that was a good night of sleep, as far as I was concerned!

Upon waking up, I tried to order a cappuccino, which was listed on the menu as being available on the A350. However, the crew informed me that wasn’t actually the case, and that they only had brewed coffee, so I ordered that instead.

I find it disappointing when airlines can’t get these kinds of basics right. It’s one thing if the machine were just broken, but the crew said it’s just not a thing. On the plus side, the brewed coffee was nicely presented.

I figured I should also check out the snack service, as you can find that menu below.

Of the options, I ordered the beef tapa, which had scrambled eggs, cherry tomato salsa, and steamed rice with garlic. This was delicious, and quite frankly, better than the main with my first meal. Obviously I made a mistake by not ordering the Filipino option the first time around, so I made sure to also choose a Filipino option for my pre-arrival main.

I watched a movie and then raw-dogged it for a couple of hours, and before I knew it, we were just two hours from San Francisco. At this point the cabin lights were turned on, in preparation for the pre-landing service.

You can find the Philippine Airlines business class breakfast menu below.

Service began with the choice of orange juice or a mango smoothie, along with warm towels being distributed.

After that, the table was properly set, with the fruit appetizer, along with a breadbasket. Once again, I feel like they could’ve put a bit more effort into this, and maybe added the option of yogurt or cereal. The small fruit plate just felt like an afterthought.

For the main course, I chose the chicken adobo, with a citrus-soy reduction, pickled cucumber, pickled mangoes and papaya, adobo flakes, and rice. This was relatively good.

Filipinos are known for being incredibly warm and hospitable, and Philippine Airlines always talks about how it’s “the heart of the Filipino.” On my previous (short) flight, I noted how the crew was incredibly friendly — they were genuinely warm, hospitable, and attentive. On this flight, I didn’t get the same impression.

Don’t get me wrong, the crew wasn’t rude, but they just lacked all the things I noted about the previous crew. There was definitely a lack of passion, they felt rushed, and they weren’t as attentive in interactions. I hate to nitpick, but let me give some general examples…

For one, the purser never came around to individually greet each passenger, or even check on them in any form, unlike on my previous flight. My only interaction with her was that apparently the million miler in the cabin could deplane before everyone else, so she’d yell at all other passengers “excuse me, million miler, million miler.”

The crew just also felt like they were going through the motions with no attentiveness. Not once did I see a flight attendant walking down the aisle between meals to see if anyone wanted anything (though when I pushed the call button, it was quickly answered). For example, when you’re served a midflight snack, you’d think they’d check on you after 10 minutes to see if it’s done, if they could clear the dish, etc. In this case, I had to push the call button for it to be removed.

I also just felt like they weren’t actually that nice, especially in terms of how they communicated. For example, when I asked for a cheese plate as well with the first meal, the answer was simply “I will check,” rather than “of course, if we have any left I will get it for you,” or something along those lines. Similarly, when I ordered the midflight snack, the response was simply “let me see if we have that.”

Of course these are all minor things, but I think the way I’d sum up my general interactions with this crew is that it felt like passengers were an inconvenience, rather than guests they were happy to have onboard.

For the last part of the flight I enjoyed the view out the window, as we initially had some daylight, which then turned into a beautiful sunset.

At 8:05PM local time the captain was on the PA to announce that we were 200 nautical miles from San Francisco, would be starting our descent shortly, and should be landing in 40 minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent a few minutes later, and then around 20 minutes after that the seatbelt sign was turned on.

We approached the Bay Area from the south, and made a couple of turns before lining up to land on runway 28L.

We had a smooth touchdown at 8:45PM, and from there had a 10 minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:55PM.

Once there, it took around 10 minutes for the cabin door to open, so I was off the plane by 9:05PM. I know I mentioned earlier how half the business class cabin was occupied by passengers in wheelchairs during boarding (hence my lack of good cabin pictures). Just to put that into perspective, below is the lineup of wheelchairs that met the plane, which went all the way to the door.

There’s nothing wrong with this, of course, I’m just pointing this out to a) justify why my cabin pictures aren’t as good on this flight (sorry!), and b) point out that obviously this route is very much about VFR (visiting friends & relatives), which isn’t surprising.

I’m happy I had the chance to fly Philippine Airlines’ new flagship Airbus A350-1000 business class. In terms of hard product, this is a huge upgrade over what the airline has offered in the past, with excellent business class suites with doors, and great tech.

The catch is that the soft product left a bit to be desired. The Viasat Wi-Fi was broken the entire flight, the cappuccinos promised on the menu don’t exist, and I thought the crew lacked warmth, especially compared to my previous flight. And all of that says nothing of the experience of connecting through Manila Airport, which is unpleasant, to put it politely.

The thing is, ultimately I’d fly with the airline again if the price is right, since you really can’t argue with Philippine Airlines’ business class pricing. If the price and schedule work, it’s definitely an attractive option. I just feel like if the airline invested a bit more in its product, it would truly be competitive with top carriers, and wouldn’t have to rely on discounting so heavily in order to fill cabins.

What’s your take on Philippine Airlines’ A350 business class?

Thanks for the input. I've been looking into PR once they announced they were going to join One World. OK, certainly not JL or CX in J however sans "soft product", it seems PR check basically all of the boxes I want when I travel in J. I will give them a try once they join One World.

"I made sure to also choose a Filipino option for my pre-arrival main"; both Arroz Caldo and Beef Tapa are Filipino dishes so you were in luck. I had the Arroz Caldo on my PR business class trip back in 2022 and it was the best thing I ate on the plane.

I'm a bit surprised by the lack of vegetarian options for the dinner entrées and midflight snacks. I haven't flown PR in decades, due to a combination of an aversion to MNL's airport and the fact that they don't offer a first class product, but one would think they'd still have *something* for the vegetarians in business class (and I'm guessing the back of the plane had the same problem). Lufthansa is flying ex-PR A350s with 1-2-1 config bet MUC and SEA for this winter schedule. Do they have the same seats as the ones reviewed here?

Probably the first time I've ever seen "missing heart" used to refer to anything in the Philippines. (On the other hand, very true!)

#6266. The 15 Most Haunted Places in the World and How to Visit Them

The most haunted places in the world may seem like something out of a fable that defies all logic. They're places where UFOs hover over Transylvanian forests, headless queens roam through castle corridors, and ghosts take shape of bears, children, and any other creature imaginable. No matter where you’re traveling, you’re sure to find some sort of haunted landmark, hotel, even landmark-turned-hotel—and usually a ghost tour to go along with it.

You might be guided more by scholarly than ghastly pursuits, though these locations are still worth your time. Spectral hauntings often come with spectacular history, architecture, and artwork, not to mention proximity to incredible cities and natural beauty. Whether you’re scheming up a Halloween trip or simply want to entertain the chills with a dash of the macabre, explore 15 of the most haunted places in the world below, if you dare.

Over the span of nearly one millennium, the Tower of London has served as an armory, prison, menagerie, and palace. Though best known today for its housing of the Crown Jewels, the UNESCO World Heritage Site also falls among the most haunted places in the United Kingdom. It's not uncommon to hear strange noises echo through the White Tower, while over a dozen ghosts—with backstories that range from ridiculous to outright tragic—are said to lurk in its limestone hallways.

The most infamous apparition is that of Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, who was executed in the tower in 1536 for being found guilty for treason and adultery. Today, some visitors may encounter her headless body roaming about, head in hand. Other specters include two young princes who were mysteriously murdered in the 1400s and even multiple accounts of a phantom bear, who made multiple appearances in the 1800s and was said to leave any witness dead.

There are two long-running explanations for the curses that plague this 16th-century fort in Rajasthan. The first is that a religious ascetic had destroyed the fort and nearby towns after its height surpassed that of his own home, casting Bhangarh in perpetual shadow. The second, equally melodramatic, is that a black magic priest fell in love with a princess and was crushed to death by a boulder after she rejected him; right before he passed, however, he condemned the premises to a fate of destruction.

Today, the scene at the fort is quite serene, and visitors can wander throughout royal palace ruins, Hindu temples such as Gopinath and Hanuman, as well as old marketplaces and townhouses like Nartakiyon Ki Haveli. The fort is open each day from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., as no visitors—those living, at least—can legally stay after sunset.

Built by lumber magnate Carl Beck for his family in the late 1800s, this house in Penetanguishene is one of Ontario's most troublesome. Legend goes that after Beck's wife passed away, his eldest daughter Mary was put in charge of raising her younger siblings. Years later, when Carl died, he inexplicably left Mary $1 in his will. Today, an angry female ghost—presumably Mary—is said to appear in the upstairs windows (you’d probably haunt the house too if your dad gave you a $1 inheritance). For any travelers curious about Victorian architecture with a side of paranormality, consider renting the Carl Beck House on Airbnb.

What's far scarier than a haunted graveyard? A haunted graveyard 50 feet underwater. Micronesia’s Chuuk Lagoon (formerly Truk Lagoon) served as a fortified base for the Japanese Navy during World War II and was attacked by American forces during a three-day air strike in 1944. Dozens of warships, planes, tanks, and railroad cars sank to the bottom of the lagoon, where they still remain in what is known as the “Ghost Fleet of Truk Lagoon.”

The ship graveyard is immensely popular amongst scuba divers, with PADI dubbing it “one of the best wreck diving destinations on the planet.” Underwater explorers can swim up close to the wartime vessels, which are littered with weapons, gas masks, and, according to some superstitious divers, a few waterlogged ghosts.

This Victorian-era prison in Belfast is often referred to as Europe’s Alcatraz and for good reason. During its 150 years of operation, the jail contained some 25,000 inmates (men, women, and children), publicly hung many prisoners, and buried their bodies within the prison walls. The institution officially shut its doors in 1996, but the ghosts of deceased inmates are said to still roam the iron walkways today.

If this sounds like the sort of place you want to spend time in, you’re in luck—Crumlin Road Gaol offers daily tours, live concerts, and reasonably priced meals at its in-house (in-prison?) restaurant. It even serves as a venue for conferences and, believe it or not, weddings.

Though travelers have been coming to Estes Park since 1909 to enjoy The Stanley Hotel’s stately Georgian architecture and world-renowned whiskey bar, its reputation took a dark turn on October 30, 1974, when Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha, checked in. The hotel was about to close for the season, and the couple were the only guests there. King was particularly struck by the endless empty corridors that he walked through after dinner, and the property as a whole ended up serving as inspiration for The Shining’s Overlook Hotel.

Of the eerie stay, King said, “[The hotel] seemed the perfect—maybe the archetypical—setting for a ghost story. That night I dreamed of my three-year-old son running through the corridors, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide, screaming. He was being chased by a fire-hose. I woke up with a tremendous jerk, sweating all over, within an inch of falling out of bed.” In the years since, the hotel has leaned into the reputation King bestowed upon it with ghost tours and a resident psychic.

Named after a shepherd who, along with his flock of 200 sheep, vanished without a trace in the forest, Hoia-Baciu hit it big in 1968 when a military technician photographed a supposed UFO hovering over the trees. Some believe it to be a portal capable of transporting visitors to places unknown. Those who pass through (and live to tell the tale) have reported rashes, nausea, and anxiety. The curved, spindly trees that make up the forest are particularly conducive to a twisted feeling, as is the location in Transylvania—a real nexus point of abnormal activity.

The St. Augustine Lighthouse is visited by over 200,000 people annually, though it's just as well-known for its otherworldly guests. Several tragic events that occurred at the now-historic site have contributed to the alleged paranormal activity. The ghost of a lighthouse keeper who fell to his death while painting the tower has been spotted watching over the grounds. Ever since the horrific death of three young girls, who drowned when the cart they were playing in broke and fell into the ocean, visitors have claimed to hear the sounds of children playing in and around the lighthouse.

Less than half a mile from the canals of Venice, Poveglia Island has served as a quarantine zone for bubonic plague victims, storage space for Napoleon’s weapons, and the site of an early 20th-century psychiatric hospital. The latter played host to horrific medical experiments and finally closed for good in 1968 after a doctor threw himself off the institution’s bell tower. Locals still claim to hear echoing chimes from the island—even though the bell was removed decades ago. Though it's illegal to visit Poveglia, you can see the island and decaying hospital at a safe distance from the beaches of nearby Lido or by hiring your own boat charter to pass a little closer (do not disembark onto the island).

Himeji Castle dates to 1333 and is regarded as one of the greatest remaining examples of Japanese castle architecture. It also has some rather eerie folklore associated with it—most notably the story of Okiku, a palace servant who was falsely accused of losing valuable dishes and thrown to her death in the castle’s well as punishment. Her ghost now sulks in the castle at night, counting dishes in a mournful tone; she reaches nine before shrieking and returning to the well’s depths. A visit to Himeji Castle is best done as a day trip from Osaka, about two hours away by train.

On the northern edge of Ireland's Wicklow Mountains, at the summit of Montpelier Hill, the ruins of a lone building remain. As many tales begin, the hill was originally site to an ancient grave, which wealthy Irishman William Conolly disregarded (even taking stones from) while building a hunting lodge in the 1720s. It's no surprise that terror ensued, and after Conolly's death, private club Hell Fire Club occupied the space, where they were said to engage in black masses, ritual murder, and other occultish happenings. At one such meeting, an unfamiliar guest with horse hooves as feet disappeared as mysteriously as they arrived. A curious farmer who had witnessed another night unfold was apparently left so terrified he no longer remembered his own name. Today, an enormous black cat with striking eyes is said to haunt Montpelier, which, beyond its murky past, offers forest trails and guided paths that make for an otherwise pleasant walk (before dusk).

Hidden among the canals of Xochimilco, Isla de las Muñecas (“Island of the Dolls”) is something of an internet legend and dark tourism mecca. The backstory centers on a man named Julian Santa Barrera, who reportedly encountered the body of a girl floating in the channels. Shortly thereafter, he found a discarded doll in the same canals, and he hung it from a tree on an artificial island in her honor—and to ward off evil spirits. So he continued, adding more and more dolls to appease the ghost of the young girl.

After Barrera passed away in 2001, his family opened the island to the public, and travelers have been seeking it out ever since. As if the mere idea of the island isn’t unnerving enough, there have also been reports of the dolls whispering to each other and moving their eyes.

Often considered the “king of Czech castles,” this early Gothic fortress in South Bohemia has undergone sieges and assaults from the 1400s onward, though, today, the source of its terrors is an impish creature called Rarášek, who is said to trip and poke at any unassuming visitor. A ghastly woman, known only as “the White Lady,” also resides here, while hellhounds allegedly guard a secret passage to the castle tombs.

Beyond the paranormal, visitors can enjoy self-guided tours through Zvíkov's cellars, courtyards, and rooms—be sure to stop and take a look at St. Wenceslas Chapel's frescoes.

The entire city of Savannah is essentially one giant ghost story, due in large part to the mysterious tunnels that run below the town’s streets. The underground structures play a major role in many of Savannah's most haunted locations, including Forsyth Park, the fountained green space you probably recognize from a postcard or two.

According to Savannah Magazine, doctors at the adjacent Candler Hospital (now the Savannah Law School) performed autopsies in the tunnels below. Maria Pinheiro, a historian and spokesperson with Ghost City Tours, says these below-the-surface rumblings make Forsyth Park particularly ripe for sightings of shadowy shapes that, even if unclear, it's certain they are not of this world.

#6265. Southwest Premier Card Review: Is The $149 Mid-Range Card Worth It?

Chase and Southwest have a great portfolio of personal credit cards at three different price points. This is my in-depth review of the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card, the Southwest personal card with a $149 annual fee (which is neither the highest nor lowest annual fee product).

Now is an especially good time to consider this card, both because it’s offering an elevated welcome bonus, and because it’s your last chance to use credit card welcome bonuses to qualify for Southwest’s Companion Pass benefit under the old system.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card

Before I get into my Southwest Premier Card review, here’s a broad look at the card and its key features:

In my opinion, here are the pros and cons of the Southwest Airlines Premier Card:

When applying for credit, cards, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that potential cardmembers consider. So let’s cover those details for the Southwest Premier Card, as the card has a great bonus, nuanced eligibility requirements, and a relatively manageable annual fee.

The Southwest Premier Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can earn 85,000 bonus points after you spend $2,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This is a limited time, elevated offer, as the most recent base offer was for 55,000 points.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome bonus are worth $1,020, making this a solid welcome offer.

When it comes to Southwest credit card eligibility rules, the Southwest Premier Card isn’t available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card.

Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, there are general application rules for Chase cards, including the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you usually won’t get approved for a Chase credit card if you’ve opened five or more credit card accounts in the past 24 months.

The Southwest Premier Card has a $149 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost. Southwest’s personal credit cards have annual fees of $99, $149, and $229, so this is the “middle child” of the Southwest and Chase personal card portfolio.

The Southwest Premier Card has no foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about extra charges.

In addition to the benefits, one of the main reasons you’ll want to consider picking up a card is because of its return on spending, so you’re sure it aligns with what you’re looking for. In the case of the Southwest Premier Card, it has a limited number of bonus categories, and spending can also help you toward earning elite status with Rapid Rewards. So let’s cover those details.

As far as the Southwest Premier Card’s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:

It’s good that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Based on my valuation of 1.2 cents per point, that’s like a 3.6% return on Southwest purchases, a 2.4% return on grocery stores and restaurants (up to the cap), and a 1.2% return on everything else.

The Southwest Premier Card also lets you earn unlimited Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward Southwest status. Through the end of 2026, you can earn 1,500 TQPs toward A-List status for every $5,000 spent on the card. Starting January 1, 2027, every Southwest credit card will earn 1 TQP per dollar spent, so $35,000 in spending on any of them would get you to Silver status.

A-List is Southwest Airlines’ version of elite status, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number. A-List status ordinarily requires earning 35,000 TQPs in a calendar year, so spending on a Southwest Premier Card could help you earn that. Whether or not that’s worth it depends on how much you’d otherwise fly with Southwest.

Currently, Southwest Rapid Rewards elite status has two levels: A-List and A-List Preferred. Beginning January 1, 2027, though, the program will grow to three tiers, with new names: Silver, Gold, and Platinum. Qualifying for Silver status will require the same 35,000 TQPs needed for A-List, while Gold and Platinum will require 65,000 TQPs and 140,000 TQPs, respectively. I covered these Southwest Rapid Rewards program changes in detail here.

This brings me to another big upcoming change to the Southwest program and how cards like the Southwest Premier Card fit into your strategy — and this is a pretty unwelcome one.

One of the best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With a Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket) and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting January 1, 2027, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

This eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only change: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending, won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Card, as it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that welcome bonuses earned before the end of 2026 do count toward Companion Pass qualification, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity ends.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares.

Basic award fares tend to offer the highest redemption value, and in my experience the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. For instance, I’ve seen Basic awards from Tampa (TPA) to Liberia, Costa Rica (LIR) for 12,000 points and $24.21. The same fare cost $200 in cash, giving you a very strong value of 1.46 cents per point.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. How do the perks compare to Southwest’s lower and higher annual fee cards?

The Southwest Premier Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card lets you pick a Preferred seat on Southwest, if any are available, starting 48 hours before departure. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight, so this perk is another potential money-saver.

Another Southwest Premier Card benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

On your cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 6,000 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 6,000 bonus points get you around $72 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers nearly half of the annual fee right there.

Each year on your Southwest Premier Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 15% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this excludes Basic fares.

The Southwest Premier Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

The Southwest Premier Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card is Southwest’s mid-range card, and the $149 annual fee is in line with many other co-branded airline credit cards. The card is offering a fantastic bonus, which is one good reason to consider this product.

On an ongoing basis, the 6,000-point anniversary bonus can get you around $72 worth of airfare. Whether the Southwest Premier Card is worth it in the long run depends on how much you value the other perks like a free checked bag, and whether you plan to use spending on the credit card to qualify for Southwest elite status.

As I mentioned above, the Southwest Premier Card is the mid-range option in Chase’s lineup of Southwest cards. Here’s a look at how it compares to the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more), which is the entry-level option:

If you don’t care about working toward Southwest status through credit card spending and you want to keep your annual fee to a minimum, the Southwest Plus Card is likely a better option for you.

On the other end of the spectrum, there’s the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card, which is the most expensive of the three personal Southwest credit cards. Here’s how it differs from the Southwest Premier Card:

If you fly Southwest all the time and want as many benefits with the airline as possible, the Southwest Priority Card could be the right choice. It’s also the best pick if you want to spend your way toward status before the end of 2026, since it earns TQPs at the fastest rate of the three cards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. This means that you could earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, and your points will be more flexible (since you can also transfer them to other airlines and hotel programs).

So, should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest Airlines credit card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards credit card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

The Southwest Premier Card is a solid mid-range airline credit card. It has a nice welcome bonus, plus ongoing perks that justify the annual fee. However, if you’re not particularly interested in extra perks when you fly Southwest, you’re much better off earning points with Chase Ultimate Rewards and then transferring them to Southwest Rapid Rewards, given that it gives you higher points earning rates and more flexibility.

#6264. 5 Things Passengers Don’t Know About Premium Economy

Premium economy has become one of the most important battlegrounds in the modern air travel industry, but many passengers still do not fully understand what product they are buying. Sitting between standard economy and business class, it is not just a few extra inches of legroom but rather a deliberately designed product aimed at travelers who want noticeably more comfort without paying for the comfort of a lie-flat bed.

On many long-haul aircraft, premium economy comes along with wider seats, deeper recline, more generous seat pitch, upgraded meals, priority services, and a quieter, more exclusive cabin environment. This ultimately helps explain why the cabin has spread so rapidly across international fleets and why airlines now treat it as a major revenue opportunity rather than a niche upgrade for a relatively small target market. The idea itself is also newer than many people might assume.

The concept as a whole is generally traced back to EVA Air in 1991, before it was adopted by carriers all around the world as the demand continued to grow for a middle-ground cabin that could balance affordability and overall comfort. As for passengers, that makes premium economy one of the least understood but most strategically important cabins in the sky today, and a class where the fine print often matters just as much as the name on the ticket itself.

The first thing that makes premium economy stand out is that it is usually built around a genuinely different seat, not just an economy seat that has been pushed a little further away from the seat in front of it. That distinction matters significantly more than most passengers may realize.

On long-haul aircraft, premium economy commonly offers much more seat pitch than standard economy, all while coming along with wider seats, greater recline, and often a leg rest or a footrest. In overall practical terms, that means the product changes how the body sits, shifts, sleeps, and endures a multi-hour flight.

A few inches may sound minor on paper, but over eight, ten, or twelve hours, they can transform the experience, especially for taller travelers or anyone who needs to work, eat, or rest in relative comfort. Premium economy also tends to avoid the cramped feeling that defines modern economy cabins, where every movement can feel negotiated with the person in front, behind, or next to you.

This extra personal space is just one reason why the cabin has become so commercially successful. It appeals to passengers who do not need a lie-flat seat but are interested in paying for a noticeable step-up from economy.

In that sense, premium economy's most important feature is also among its most basic, as the seat is designed to feel different from the moment one sits down. These are all key factors driving the industry's trend towards more premium seating. Ultimately, passengers are capable of enjoying these kinds of seats more than those in economy, and they are willing to pay up for the experience.

Premium economy stands out not only because of the seat itself, but because of the environment surrounding it. On many aircraft, the cabin is physically separated from the main economy section, creating a smaller and quieter space with fewer rows, less foot traffic, and a more controlled overall atmosphere.

That difference itself is relatively easy to underestimate when looking at booking screens, but it often shapes the passenger experience as much as legroom does. A smaller cabin generally means that fewer people are passing through the aisle, fewer disturbances take place during rest periods, and a stronger sense of order is maintained from boarding all the way through landing.

It can also make service feel significantly more attentive, since cabin crew is dealing with a more limited number of passengers than in the large economy cabin behind. From a psychological perspective, this matters because premium economy is not just selling comfort, but also relief from the density of mass-market flying.

The overall appeal lies partly in space, but also partly in separation. That is primarily why airlines often position premium economy as a distinct long-haul product rather than an add-on seat assignment. It gives travelers some of the emotional advantages associated with premium travel, including calm, exclusivity, and reduced chaos without the enormous price jump to business class, according to Forbes.

A third key characteristic that makes premium economy stand out is the bundle of onboard extras that often come with it. Passengers will sometimes assume that they are paying only for a larger seat, but airlines usually package premium economy as a broader service tier. Depending on the carrier, that can mean upgraded meals, complimentary alcoholic beverages, amenity kits, larger entertainment screens, power outlets, better tray tables, and more thoughtful presentation overall.

None of this turns the cabin into a business class product, but that is exactly the point. Premium economy is designed to succeed because it offers a curated middle ground. The passenger receives enough added comfort and service to feel materially better off than in economy, all while the airline avoids the cost structure of a true premium cabin with lounge access and lie-flat seats.

The extras also change the emotional tone of the flight. Everything from a welcome drink, improved meal, or small amenity kit can create the sense that an airline has recognized the passenger as someone buying an upgraded experience rather than merely transporting them at the lowest price.

In a competitive long-haul market, that kind of perception matters. Premium economy is increasingly attractive because it feels intentional. It is not just economy with an upsell attached, but rather a product designed to provide a more polished journey from takeoff to landing while staying within reach of travelers who would otherwise never pay business-class fares.

Premium economy also stands out primarily because its value often begins on the ground rather than in the air. Many passengers tend to focus entirely on the seat, but one of the most overlooked advantages of the cabin is that it may include elements of priority treatment at the airport.

Separate or priority check-in, earlier boarding, additional baggage allowance, and sometimes faster security access are all features that can come with a true premium economy fare. These benefits may sound secondary compared with seat dimensions, but for many travelers, they have a cumulative effect that shapes the nature of the entire trip.

Long-haul flying is tiring before the aircraft even leaves the ground, and reducing friction in the airport can make the journey feel smoother from the outset. It is also one of the clearest ways that airlines differentiate premium economy, which is often designed as a mini-premium travel experience, not just a better chair to sit in.

This helps fundamentally explain why the product has grown so quickly among leisure travelers who are willing to spend more for comfort and among corporate travelers whose employers will not approve business class tickets. It delivers practical comfort gains at many points in the journey, helping create a sense of elevated travel that begins at check-in and continues through boarding, baggage, and arrival processes.

How to decide whether to splash out on Premium Economy or stick with Economy on Cathay A350 long haul routes.

Perhaps the most important reason that premium economy stands out is structural rather than physical in nature. It fills a gap in the airline marketplace. Airlines introduced the product because they identified a large group of passengers who wanted something better than economy, but could not justify the price of a business-class ticket. That logic remains at the heart of the cabin's operations today.

Premium economy is successful because it captures travelers in the middle, people who value comfort but still think in terms of trade-offs. In effect, it is one of the clearest examples of modern airline segmentation strategies. The cabin offers a noticeable improvement in space, service, and exclusivity while remaining far below the cost of a lie-flat premium seat.

Historically, this middle-market appeal helps explain why the concept spread after EVA introduced it in 1992 and why so many long-haul carriers later invested in it. Airlines realized that they could earn more revenue from passengers willing to pay a supplement for a more comfortable journey. Passengers, on the other hand, saw it as an opportunity to make long-haul flying tolerable without crossing into luxury pricing.

That balance is what makes premium economy quite distinctive. It is not an accidental compromise, but rather a deliberate commercial product built around the needs of travelers who want premium touches without premium-cabin expenses. In that sense, premium economy stands out because it may be the most carefully targeted cabin in the modern aviation industry.

These welcome bonuses are the best way to earn a large number of United miles at once. That's why it's very important to make sure you apply at the right time.

#6262. Which Credit Card Should You Use For Marriott Hotel Stays? Here’s The Math

When you’re staying at a Marriott property, what’s the best credit card to use to maximize your return on Marriott hotel spending? Should you use a co-branded Marriott credit card, or are you better off using another credit card offering bonus points on travel? This is a question that comes up every so often, so I’d like to address it in this post…

I’ve written in the past about the best credit cards to use for hotel stays. However, more specifically to Marriott, which credit card should you put all of your Marriott spending on? Let’s take a look at the various approaches that you can take.

Let me start by acknowledging that we all value points currencies differently, so you should apply your own valuation to the math. My below analysis is based on my own valuation of various points currencies.

I also want to emphasize that the credit card you use won’t impact your ability to earn elite qualifying nights, take advantage of elite perks, and accrue the standard points that you can earn with the Marriott Bonvoy program. The credit card rewards offered when paying for your Marriott hotel stay are incremental.

Marriott has co-branded credit cards in the United States that are issued by both American Express and Chase. All of these credit cards with annual fees have the same rewards structure for Marriott spending, as they offer 6x Marriott Bonvoy® Points on all eligible Marriott spending.

This includes cards like the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more), just to name a few. Personally, I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, so to me these cards offer an incremental 4.2% return on that spending.

I think the one thing worth pointing out is that the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers 1,000 Bonvoy bonus points per Marriott stay when paying with the card, in addition to the rewards that you usually earn.

Technically that would be the best co-branded card for Marriott spending, since you earn 6x points, plus 1,000 bonus points per stay. That being said, I’d otherwise consider this to be one of the less compelling Marriott cards in terms of the overall value proposition.

I generally recommend putting most of your spending on cards earning transferable points currencies, given that they offer the most flexible rewards, and also have excellent bonus categories.

I’d argue that the two best cards for hotel spending are the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) and Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more), as they offer 4x transferable points for direct hotel purchases. Since I value Ultimate Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like a 6.8% return on that spending, which is excellent.

It’s worth noting that there are other cards earning 3x points on hotels, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), and I’d value that at a return of 5.1%. Lastly, the Wells Fargo Autograph Journey Card (learn more) actually offers 5x points on hotel purchases, which is excellent, though I don’t value those points as much as other transferable points currencies.

Personally, the Chase Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve Business are my go-to cards for hotel spending. Simply put, I can’t turn down 4x Ultimate Rewards points, in comparison to earning 6x Bonvoy points with the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Amex for my Marriott spending.

The difference in math is just too great, since I value 4x Ultimate Rewards points at way more than 6x Bonvoy points. But this also brings me to a related topic of how points valuations sometimes don’t dictate my consumer behavior. For example, back in the day, the Chase Sapphire Reserve offered 3x Ultimate Rewards points on hotel spending.

So I valued that at offering a 5.1% return, rather than a 4.2% return on a Marriott credit card. Despite that, I’d use a co-branded Marriott card for my Marriott spending. Why? Well, this gets at a consideration that’s hard to factor into my valuation of points. I’m talking about the ease of earning various points currencies.

I can earn transferable points currencies in all kinds of ways, including with my everyday spending. However, there aren’t many ways to efficiently earn Bonvoy points, short of staying at Marriott properties. As I often talk about when sharing my points strategy, there’s merit to collecting points that are harder to earn, even if they’re not the points currency that you necessarily value the most. This was one of those cases, at least for me. However, with the Chase Sapphire Reserve nowadays earning 4x points per dollar spent on hotels, my logic on that has evolved.

Everyone has their own credit card strategy, and at times it can be tough to decide which card is the best for a particular spending category.

In the case of spending at Marriott properties, I’d argue that the Chase Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve Business are nowadays the most lucrative, given that they offer 4x Ultimate Rewards points on that spending, which I value at a 6.8% return. I’d say that beats the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Amex, offering 6x Bonvoy points, which I value at a 4.2% return.

Which credit card do you use for Marriott hotel spending?

#6261. Air Fares Still ‘Quite Low,’ A4A CEO Says

Air fares have risen about 22% year-over-year, largely due to the surge in jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

But considering the very low-cost environment that prevailed prior to 2026, tickets are still relatively inexpensive, Airlines For America CEO Chris Sununu said this week.

“Airline costs are actually quite low,” Sununu told CBS’ The Takeout. “They’ve risen 22 percent in the last year because of the Iran war, but from all-time lows. So no, overall, flying in the United States is still incredibly affordable.”

“If you want that premium seat, that first class seat, obviously you pay a little more for that,” he continued. “That economy seat is still very affordable.”

Airline ticket prices have risen since February, when the conflict began. The collapse of ultra-low-cost Spirit Airlines in May and major carriers’ shift toward premiumization could also be playing a role.

When pressed by host Major Garrett on reports that U.S. airlines are letting seats go empty instead of lowering prices to effectively discipline the market, Sununu said that was “100 percent” false.

“If a flight is not making money, believe me, it’s been pulled off because jet fuel is so high,” he said. “Instead of three flights a day from Wichita to Green Bay, there’s two flights. So, no, when you get on a flight now, it’s going to be more often than not very very crowded.”

Asked about the FAA’s sweeping air traffic control modernization effort, Sununu was positive and credited Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford with launching the first serious system-wide upgrade in decades.

“For forty years they’ve done nothing,” he said. “And they’ve done more in the last twelve months than they have in the previous forty years. And that is coming as a cynic of Washington, who has seen the political landscape littered with failed infrastructure projects.”

The main benefit for customers, Sununu added, will be efficiency.

“It’s always going to be safe,” he said. “But over the past few years they’ve had to slow the system down, because it is so antiquated, to ensure the safety. But now we get that efficiency back.”
