#6238. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London

I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay.

I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights.

Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after.

Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy.

Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn.

Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame.

The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months.

Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio.

#6237. Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards: Save 25% On Select Awards

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has its monthly Promo Rewards promotion, whereby members can save 25% on select award tickets over a limited travel period. The program has just published its new Promo Rewards list for November 2026, offering discounted short haul and long haul awards for travel over the coming months.

There are quite a few destinations bookable with this promotion, including several in the Americas, with options in business class, premium economy, and economy. This has the potential to be a great deal.

I’m a big fan of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program, especially for long haul premium cabin redemptions. Not only does Flying Blue largely have attractive award pricing for business class travel, but the program also has access to more Air France and KLM award space than other programs.

The Promo Rewards offer is published every month by the Flying Blue program, and offers 25% discounts off select awards for travel on Air France and KLM. The Flying Blue program has dynamic award pricing, and this promotion specifically applies for the lowest, saver level award costs.

Flying Blue has published its November 2026 Promo Rewards, valid for bookings between November 1 and November 30, 2026. Most of these Promo Rewards have long travel windows, and can be used for flights all the way through April 30, 2027.

As a reminder, Flying Blue has standardized saver award pricing, so ordinarily you’ll pay the following amounts for one-way transatlantic awards between Europe and most of North America, when booking a “Light” fare:

Let me emphasize that with the recent Flying Blue devaluation, the entry level pricing is now for a “Light” fare rather than a Standard fare, so it comes with fewer inclusions. For example, a long haul business class “Light” fare doesn’t offer any flexibility, and also doesn’t offer lounge access.

However, if you have Flying Blue Platinum status, then you still receive most of the perks of a “Standard” fare automatically. So as an example, a Promo Rewards ticket that costs 45,000 miles in business class for a “Light” fare would now cost 56,250 miles for a “Standard” fare.

Here are the awards that are available with the Promo Rewards list this month for travel between Europe and North America, along with the pricing:

On top of that, the Flying Blue Extra program was recently launched (the cost starts at €379 per year), which is essentially a paid membership program that offers extra perks. One of the perks of Flying Blue Extra is access to additional Promo Rewards, so eligible members receive access to the following extra Promo Rewards availability to North America this time around:

There are of course also Promo Rewards opportunities outside of North America, including some business class options to South America, so check out the full list.

All of the lowest priced awards in the above markets through April 30, 2027, should be bookable with the Promo Rewards pricing (though not necessarily the extra award availability that Flying Blue Platinum members receive). You can use all of these awards for travel to and from destinations across Europe, so you can travel beyond Amsterdam and Paris.

If you’re having trouble finding availability, remember to use Flying Blue’s secret award calendar. Also keep in mind that children ages two to 12 receive 25% off Flying Blue award tickets, including Promo Rewards.

One of the things that’s awesome about the Flying Blue program is how easy it is to rack up miles:

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program offers a Promo Rewards promotion, whereby members can book discounted award tickets in select markets. This can be a great deal, especially when you consider how easy Flying Blue miles are to come by, and also how much award space is sometimes available through Flying Blue.

With the latest Promo Rewards, you can save 25% to several destinations in the Americas, with options in economy, premium economy, and business class. This has the potential to be quite a good deal, so if you have any travel you’re interested in booking, this would be a great time to do so.

A free flight is rewarding, but so is knocking $100 off your credit card bill. Cash back is less flashy, but far more straightforward: you can use it wherever your budget needs it most. The question is whether your purchases earn a forgettable 1% back or enough to make a noticeable dent in your next statement.

By matching cards to your spending and layering in welcome offers, bonus categories and card-linked deals, you can earn more cash back on purchases you were already planning to make.

Knowing how you spend your money is an important step before applying for a new cash-back credit card. Do you spend heavily on specific types of purchases, such as dining and travel? Or does your spending shift from month to month?

This is also a great time to consider what you want from your rewards credit card and how you would maximize cash-back rewards.

To understand your spending habits, take some time to review charges on any existing credit cards. Issuers like Chase assign categories to card charges, making it easy to identify what types of transactions dominate your budget.

Whether you're spending on ride-hailing services or on groceries, mapping out your spending habits will help you pick the best card.

Once you've identified how you spend, you can select a cash-back credit card that complements your typical spending habits. No single cash-back card will earn the highest rate on every purchase, but knowing this can help you compare options that coincide with your particular needs.

For those who enjoy cooking at home, a bonus-earning rate on groceries might be the best way to maximize cash-back rewards. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is an excellent choice as it offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $6,000 per year; 1% cash back thereafter), all for a low $95 annual fee once the $0 introductory annual fee for the first year is up (see ).

Additionally, Blue Cash Preferred cardmembers also earn 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming services and 3% cash back on transit and at U.S. gas stations. Members receive cash back in the form of Reward Dollars that they can redeem as a statement credit and at Amazon.com checkout.

If your spending habits change from month to month, consider the Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards credit card. Cardholders earn 6% back in the category of your choice for the first year (3% thereafter) and 2% back on grocery stores and wholesale clubs for the first $2,500 of combined bonus category and grocery spending per quarter; after hitting that threshold, you’ll earn 1% back on these purchases.

You can change your preferred choice category once per month for extra earning flexibility.

Related: Cash back vs. travel rewards: How to choose a credit card

A welcome offer can deliver a substantial chunk of cash back soon after you open a card. Before applying for any card, compare current offers and make sure the spending requirement fits the purchases you already plan to make.

The following cash-back credit cards are currently offering solid welcome bonus offers:

Customers with flexible spending habits may also want to look into cards with rotating rewards categories. These cards feature a new group of eligible merchants or spending categories each quarter. One quarter might include gas stations and electric vehicle charging, while another could feature restaurants.

The Chase Freedom Flex has no annual fee and earns a strong 5% cash back on purchases in activated bonus categories each quarter on up to $1,500 in purchases, then 1% after that. Similarly, the Discover it® Cash Back card earns 5% cash back on up to $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter in rotating bonus categories (activation required), and 1% cash back on all other purchases.

Both Chase’s rotating bonus categories and Discover’s quarterly bonus categories change throughout the year, with past lineups featuring popular merchants and spending categories such as Amazon, Target, grocery stores, drugstores and more.

Pairing a bonus-category card with a flat-rate cash-back credit card allows you to maximize your earnings where it matters most and still earn strongly on spending that falls outside of its categories.

Use a card that earns 2% cash back whenever your bonus-category card would earn less, like the Citi Double Cash. It offers 2% cash back on all purchases — 1% cash back when you make a purchase and 1% cash back as you pay for your purchases.

Many issuers offer shopping portals and card-linked deals that can stack with a card’s standard rewards.

Chase Freedom Unlimited® (see ) and Freedom Flex cardholders, for example, can access Chase's shopping portal, earning additional cash back on their purchases on top of standard rewards.

The stores on Chase's shopping portal vary and occasionally change, so it's worth checking which shop is offering a bonus and maximizing cash-back rewards.

Additionally, credit cards may provide targeted merchant offers. American Express, Chase, Capital One and Citi all have offers that can be activated via an issuer's mobile app or website to earn even more rewards. Generally, these offers have a limited redemption window, varying cash-back percentages and limits on how much cash back you can earn from each offer.

Cash back excels in its simplicity, and these strategies should provide big wins without any mental gymnastics.

Just don't skip the math entirely. Interest charges can erase months of cash back surprisingly fast, so the top strategy remains the most basic: pay your balance in full to ensure your earnings are truly a bonus.

#6235. Aman At Sea: Amangati “Superyacht” Sets Sail Spring 2027, From $6K+ Per Night

In 2027, we’re going to see the launch of a new ultra-luxury cruise line, as hotel group Aman is getting into the cruising industry, with the Aman at Sea concept, and its Amangati “superyacht,” as it’s called.

I’d like to provide an update about this concept, as sailings are now bookable well into 2028, so we have a sense of both the summer sailings in Europe and winter sailings in the Caribbean. If you think the recent entrants into the market are expensive, wait until you learn the details of this one.

It’s interesting to see the increasing trend of luxury hotel groups launching cruise lines, or perhaps more accurately, licensing out their names to partner on new cruising concepts. For example, in 2022 we saw the launch of Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and in 2026, we’ve seen the launch of Four Seasons Yachts and Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

Amangati (“peaceful motion” in Sanskrit) is expected to set sail in the spring of 2027, as Aman’s first superyacht. Yes, this marks the Aman brand getting into the luxury cruising industry, on a ship that’s being described as a “floating sanctuary.”

The 600-foot ship will be around 23,000 gross tons, and will have a hybrid propulsion system, using battery power to reduce emissions and improve efficiency. It’s currently being built in Italy’s T. Mariotti shipyard, and it will be delivered to Neptune Co., which is a joint venture between hotel group Aman and Cruise Saudi.

The ship is expected to feature a total of 47 suites, each with a balcony and floor-to-ceiling windows. The suites will be among the largest at sea.

When it comes to amenities, the ship will have four restaurants, a jazz club, a 52-foot pool, a beach club and marina, a spa with a Japanese garden, two helipads, and much more. Sinot Yacht Architecture & Design is behind the design, and the intent is to take cues from traditional ryokan architecture.

For those not familiar, Cruise Saudi is owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, and is intended to promote the cruise and tourism industry in Saudi Arabia. However, it doesn’t appear that the plan is actually for the ship to cruise in Saudi Arabia, at least for the foreseeable future. So it seems to primarily be part of the country’s larger investment in the cruising industry.

Here’s how Aman CEO Vlad Doronin describes the idea behind the ship:

Aman has published the inaugural voyages for Amangati, for sailings between May 7, 2027, and March 31, 2028. Unsurprisingly, the ship will spend summers in Europe and winters in the Caribbean, with transatlantic sailings in November and March.

In both summer in Europe and winter in the Caribbean, sailings will be five to eight nights each, and they’re roughly what you’d expect in terms of itineraries. You can either book directly through Aman at Sea, or through a travel advisor.

An eligible travel advisor will be able to add a minimum of a $500 shipboard credit, while paying the standard rate. You can generally expect pricing parity between all booking sources, so you won’t find discounted sailing prices anywhere.

Before we talk about the pricing for Aman at Sea, what’s included with journeys? It’s an interesting topic, because historically ultra luxury cruises have been all-inclusive. However, Four Seasons Yachts is countering that trend, by not including lunch, dinner, or alcoholic drinks.

With that in mind, Aman at Sea will include the following with the cost of sailings:

As you can see, Aman is sort of taking a middle ground approach here. Alcohol aside from beer isn’t included, and neither is dining at the specialty restaurants.

How much are Aman at Sea rates? Pricing is per suite rather than per guest. As it currently stands, I see five-night journeys starting at $32,500, while I see seven-night journeys priced as high as $54,600. So we’re looking at somewhere around $6,000-8,000 per night for an entry level suite. You’ll generally find that Caribbean sailings are a little cheaper than European sailings.

Admittedly these suites are massive by ship standards, but that’s definitely on the very high end of the market, and easily 50%+ more than Four Seasons Yachts is charging (though with some more inclusions).

Prior to 2026, I hadn’t taken a cruise since I was a kid. However, this year I’ve given all three of the luxury cruise lines associated with hotels a try, and I’ve shared my thoughts on Four Seasons Yachts, Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection. I’ve even done a direct comparison of the three concepts, based on my firsthand experience.

Let me of course acknowledge that these cruise lines are all at the very top end of the market, so I’m not claiming or suggesting that they’re the best value options out there. Instead, I’ve taken such an interest in them because I find the crossover between hotels and cruise lines to be so interesting, and also find it noteworthy how these are all cruise lines targeted at people who historically haven’t considered cruising.

With that in mind, here’s how I’d broadly sum up the experiences offered by the three existing players:

In general, I’d expect Aman at Sea will probably be closest to Orient-Express Sailing Yachts in terms of exclusivity, while probably being more like Four Seasons Yachts in terms of design (since it’s not a sailboat). I will say, given the price point, I do find the lack of inclusions to be a bit frustrating. Then again, the standard suites will be absolutely massive.

The concept of luxury cruising is nothing new. However, there’s no denying that the industry is evolving a bit:

Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection is the only one of the concepts that has now been in service for some time, and based on what we know, the financial performance has left a bit to be desired. And that was before the cruise line expanded to three ships, and it’s before three competitors entered the industry.

Ultimately the success of these ventures comes down to whether they can convince people that cruising is “cool.” I don’t think these cruise lines will be cannibalizing brands like Silversea, but instead, I think they’re going after those who would otherwise vacation on land.

The other thing worth keeping in mind is that at some point, these cruise lines are competing with the concept of just chartering a yacht, which is a concept that will have more appeal for many people.

Obviously $6K+ per night is a massive amount to spend on a cruise. But the reality is that people easily pay that kind of money for peak season rooms in place like Saint-Tropez. Can these hotel-branded cruise lines convince people who want to “see and be seen” that it’s as cool to be on a ship as it is to be in the South of France? It seems like a tall order, but I guess time will tell.

Ironically, I think the volume of new entrants into the market is actually quite helpful in building demand, since cruises are finally being talked about more among non-cruisers. While they’re all competing for the same types of guests, I know a fair number of people have tried one of these cruise lines, then rebooked on another cruise line, etc.

Aman will be getting into the luxury cruising space in the spring of 2027, with the launch of its 600-foot Amangati superyacht. The ship looks incredible, and it seems like we’re seeing the luxury hotel groups all one-up each other.

The pricing is at the very top end of the market, which doesn’t come as much of a surprise. Will there be enough people willing to pay $6K+ per night for Aman’s cruising concept to keep these ships full, especially without most alcohol included? Only time will tell.

What do you make of Aman getting into the luxury cruise industry?

#6234. Air India Cancels All Flights To 8 Destinations: See Full List Now

Air India is India's second-largest airline in terms of scheduled flights and seat capacity (after IndiGo), and its largest international carrier. Like other airlines, it has been making changes to its domestic and international networks. Simple Flying took a look at the airline’s latest scheduled data and found that it has transferred some domestic services to its low-cost subsidiary, Air India Express.

Internationally, for the current winter season, the Star Alliance member has discontinued four European routes, including its services from Delhi Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) to the Danish capital, Copenhagen, and the Austrian capital, Vienna. Elsewhere, in the United States, Simple Flying previously reported that the airline had suspended flights to one of the country's major Midwestern aviation hubs until August 31.

Back in May, Air India announced that it would suspend its four weekly flights between DEL and Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), which operated via Vienna International Airport (VIE). The airline cited continued airspace restrictions over certain regions and record-high jet fuel prices for international operations as the main reasons for the decision.

It stated that “these changes are aimed at improving network stability and reducing last-minute inconvenience to passengers.” At the time, the suspension was scheduled to last from June 1 to August 31. However, Air India has since extended the suspension, and the latest schedule data from aviation analytics company Cirium shows that no flights are currently scheduled on the route.

Notably, along with Chicago, the airline also suspended its services between Delhi and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). Although flights did not resume as originally planned, the route is now scheduled to return in January 2027.

Indeed, the escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East since late February have caused considerable volatility in global energy markets. By late October, jet fuel prices had reportedly exceeded $206 per barrel. This is adding pressure on airlines' operating costs. As noted above, the rising fuel prices are one of the main factors behind its international network changes.

In fact, this winter, it has cut several of its European routes. On October 31, it ended its four weekly flights between DEL and VIE, leaving the Austrian capital without a nonstop connection to India. Around 173,500 passengers traveled between Vienna and Indian cities in 2025, including approximately 68,400 on routes to and from Delhi.

In fact, the Indian capital was Vienna’s biggest Indian market. Elsewhere, the Indian carrier has suspended its four weekly flights between DEL and Copenhagen Airport (CPH), and three-weekly flights between Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport, Amritsar (ATQ) and London Gatwick Airport (LGW). It is also scheduled to discontinue its three-weekly Delhi- Birmingham International Airport (BHX) service from November 4.

Overall, according to Cirium schedule data, the Star Alliance member’s European seat capacity between November 2026 and March 2027 is down by approximately 12% compared with the same period a year earlier. Notably, its Delhi- Paris Charles De Gaulle Airport (CDG) route has seen the sharpest reduction, around 50%. The airline has halved the frequency from 14 to seven weekly flights.

The very long one-stop services remain, but things are slowly changing. See more here!

As for its domestic network, most of the changes are not necessarily route cancelations. Instead, Air India has transferred several services to its low-cost subsidiary, Air India Express. This is part of the broader restructuring of the airline under the ownership of the Tata Group, which took control of the former state-owned carrier in 2022.

Since the takeover, the group has consolidated its four airlines into two. Vistara was merged into Air India, while AirAsia India, subsequently renamed AIX Connect, was integrated into Air India Express. The restructuring has allowed the group to separate its full-service and low-cost operations, and several domestic routes previously served by the mainline carrier are now operated exclusively by its budget subsidiary.

#6233. Southwest Performance Business Card Review: Is The $299 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card is the most premium card in the Chase and Southwest co-brand card portfolio. This card currently has a $299 annual fee and comes with many helpful perks when you fly Southwest, including a free checked bag, complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating when available, and an anniversary bonus of 9,000 points every year.

If you frequently travel with Southwest and qualify for a small business credit card, this card is worth a closer look. That’s especially true now, because not only is it offering a welcome bonus of 80,000 bonus points, but now is also your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the Companion Pass. I’ll get into all of that and more below, as this is my in-depth Southwest Performance Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card

Before I cover the Southwest Performance Business Card perks in detail, here’s a high-level view of this business credit card’s key details:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Performance Business Card:

When applying for a credit card, major considerations include the welcome bonus, the eligibility rules, and the fees, so let’s start by taking a look at those details for the Southwest Performance Business Card.

The Southwest Performance Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider the points to be worth 1.2 cents each. That means I consider the 80,000 points to be worth $960, which is a solid bonus for a card like this (though admittedly we’ve seen slightly better limited time offers in the past).

When it comes to Southwest credit card eligibility rules, you’re potentially eligible for the Southwest Performance Business Card (including the welcome bonus) if you don’t currently have this card, and if you haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. You can have any of the Southwest personal cards, and/or the Southwest Premier Business Card, and they won’t impact eligibility for this card.

Beyond that, be aware of the general restrictions on applying for Chase cards. This includes the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more cards in the last 24 months. That said, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Performance Business Card has a $299 annual fee, making it the highest annual fee Southwest Airlines credit card. However, it also comes with plenty of perks that can justify it, as I’ll explain below.

There is no cost to add authorized users on the card, so you can add authorized users to your card, and be rewarded for their spending.

The Southwest Performance Business Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a good card to use for purchases abroad.

One of the main reasons you’ll want to consider picking up a card is because of its return on spending, so you’re sure it aligns with what you’re looking for. In the case of the Southwest Performance Business Card, it has a limited number of bonus categories, and spending can also help you toward earning elite status with Rapid Rewards. So let’s cover those details.

The Southwest Performance Business Card offers some potentially useful bonus categories, as follows:

These are some pretty solid bonus categories, though in general, I would only use this card for everyday spending if trying to earn Southwest Airlines status. Based on my valuation of 1.2 cents per point, this is like earning a 4.8% return on the 4x points categories, 2.4% return on the 2x points categories, and a 1.2% return on the 1x points categories.

The Southwest Performance Business Card lets you earn unlimited Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward elite status. Specifically, you can earn 2,500 TQPs toward A-List status for every $5,000 spent on the card.

Southwest A-List status offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

A-List status ordinarily requires earning 35,000 TQPs in a calendar year, so spending on a Southwest Performance Business Card could help you earn that. Whether or not that’s worth it depends on how much you’d otherwise fly with Southwest.

Do note that Southwest recently announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status, and earning it will require 35,000 TQPs or 25 qualifying flights.

According to the Southwest Performance Business Card’s terms & conditions, cardholders can earn TQPs on card spending at the current rate of 2,500 TQPs per $5,000 spent through December 31, 2026. After that date, A-List status will become Silver status, and every co-branded Southwest credit card will earn 1 TQP per dollar spent, so $35,000 in spending would get you to Silver.

One of the best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. For those of you not familiar with Southwest’s Companion Pass, it allows someone else to travel with you for the entire year anywhere Southwest flies.

You still have to pay the taxes on their ticket, but the Companion Pass is valid on both award and revenue tickets. You can change your designated companion three times in a year, so you can potentially even use this for different people.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Performance Business Card, as it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that welcome bonuses earned before the end of 2026 do count toward Companion Pass qualification, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

While the Southwest Performance Business Card has a great bonus, the main reason you want to get this card is because of the perks that it offers. For those who fly Southwest with any frequency, the perks should more than cover the annual fee. In fact, for those who are frequent Southwest flyers, this card is almost too good to be true.

Just for having the Southwest Performance Business Card, you’ll receive 9,000 Rapid Rewards points on your account anniversary every year. As I said above, Southwest points can be redeemed for ~1.2 cents each toward airfare, so that’s the equivalent of ~$108 toward airfare annually.

The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation. If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can quickly help you recoup the annual fee.

For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way. If you maxed this benefit out with eight other travelers on a round-trip itinerary with checked bags, you’d be looking at over $800 in value.

When you book a Southwest flight as a Performance Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat at the time of booking, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation.

The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight, so this benefit can also save you some real money.

The Southwest Performance Business Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats for cardholders and up to eight travelers on the same reservation. These upgrades are space available and will start within 48 hours of departure. This is another nice elite-style benefit that can noticeably improve your travel experience on Southwest.

Southwest Performance Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. Once again, this perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Performance Business offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. To take advantage of this, simply pay with your card. You’ll automatically receive a statement credit on eligible inflight purchases.

For having the Southwest Performance Card you receive a credit towards TSA PreCheck, Global Entry, or NEXUS. You can take advantage of this benefit once every four years. (up to $120 as of 10/1/24)

If you are going to use this perk, I’d highly recommend registering for Global Entry over TSA PreCheck. For those of you not familiar, TSA PreCheck gets you expedited US security screening, while Global Entry gets you expedited US immigration clearance.

Why register for Global Entry and not PreCheck? Because Global Entry also comes with TSA PreCheck, while the inverse isn’t true (signing up for TSA PreCheck doesn’t get you Global Entry).

If you have a small business and fly Southwest with any frequency, then the Southwest Performance Business Card is a no brainer. To start, the card has an excellent welcome bonus that could get you a lot of travel, and could even help you earn Companion Pass — at least until the end of 2026, which is coming up very fast.

On an ongoing basis, the card is worth it as well. It has a $299 annual fee but offers 9,000 points per year (which I value at ~$108) and more. This card should pay for itself for anyone who flies Southwest often.

In addition to the Southwest Performance Business Card, Southwest also has the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card (learn more). How does that card compare? Here’s a quick look:

If you fly Southwest only a handful of times a year, you might prefer this card and its lower annual fee to the more premium Southwest Performance Business.

In addition to comparing the Southwest Performance Business with other Southwest business credit cards, I want to take a minute to recommend another points strategy if you occasionally book award flights on Southwest.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. This means that you could earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, and your points will be more flexible (since you can also transfer them to other airlines and hotel programs).

So, should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest Airlines credit card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards credit card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

The Ink Business Preferred Card could be an especially strong pick, considering you’re reading a review of a business credit card — and it has a significantly lower annual fee than the Southwest Performance Business Card.

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

The Southwest Performance Business Card is an exceptional option for those who frequently fly Southwest and want the best-possible experience with the airline.

In addition to the solid bonus, the card also offers 9,000 anniversary bonus points, space available Preferred and extra legroom seats, and more. The value of that should add up quickly if you fly Southwest frequently. This is especially true now that Southwest charges fees for checked bags and charges for assigned seats.

If you want to learn more about the Southwest Performance Business Card, follow this link.

#6232. Are Marriott Bonvoy Airline Mileage Transfers Worth It? They Could Be, But…

Among hotel loyalty programs, one thing that makes Marriott Bonvoy unique is the ability to (fairly) efficiently convert hotel points into airline miles. While most major hotel loyalty programs allow some sort of opportunity to convert hotel points into airline miles, it typically represents a very bad value.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at the opportunity to convert Marriott points into airline miles. Which airline programs can you move your Marriott points to, what’s the transfer ratio, and is it worth it?

It’s possible to convert Bonvoy points into airline miles, with your choice of nearly 40 different frequent flyer programs. Let’s take a look at which partners Marriott Bonvoy has, what the transfer ratios are, etc.

Marriott points generally convert into airline miles at a 3:1 ratio, and with most partners you get 5,000 bonus miles for every 60,000 Marriott points you transfer.

In other words, 60,000 Bonvoy points will convert into 25,000 airline miles (including the 5,000 bonus miles). You can take advantage of that bonus of 5,000 miles multiple times, meaning that you can convert Bonvoy points into airline miles at a ratio of up to 2.4:1.

Note that you can transfer a minimum of 3,000 Bonvoy points and a maximum of 240,000 Bonvoy points per day. So if you want to transfer more than 240,000 Bonvoy points, you’ll want to do so over multiple days.

Below is a chart with the airline frequent flyer programs you can transfer your Marriott points to, along with the standard transfer ratio, plus the ability to earn a bonus when transferring a minimum of 60,000 points.

While I covered these details above, let me specifically note the exceptions that apply here:

With the major transferable points currencies, converting points into airline miles is typically an instant process. So it’s worth being aware that Marriott points don’t convert into airline miles instantly. Rather, transfers generally take anywhere from a day to a couple of weeks, with transfers for most partners taking anywhere from two to five days.

I’d consider this to be a major weak point of this opportunity. I generally recommend converting points into airline miles in situations where you have a specific use in mind, and that could be a situation where you find award space on a particular flight.

Obviously that’s not exactly useful here, since it could take a couple of weeks for the transfer to happen, and odds are that whatever award availability you were looking at will be gone at that point.

The process of converting Marriott points into airline miles is really straightforward. Just go to the partner transfer page, click the “Transfer Points” button, and then you’ll be asked to enter the information for the account you want to move your points to. There you’ll be able to select how many points you want to transfer, and note that the amounts shown won’t reflect a bonus, if eligible.

It’s important to be sure that the names of the accounts match, as you can only transfer your Marriott points to an airline frequent flyer account that’s also in your name. Also keep in mind that once the miles are in your frequent flyer account, they’ll be subject to the standard airline mileage expiration policies of the program.

While I think converting Marriott points into airline miles could represent a good value, it’s not how I choose to redeem my Bonvoy points.

To briefly crunch some numbers, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. At a 2.4:1 transfer ratio (60,000 points per 25,000 miles), that’s like “paying” 1.68 cents per airline mile, which is a pretty decent cost.

Why do I choose not to convert Marriott points into airline miles?

I absolutely don’t think anyone is off base for choosing to convert Marriott points into airline miles. For that matter, this could be a good option if you’re in a crunch, and just need to top off an account for a high value redemption. However, it’s not how I choose to redeem my points, and I don’t think the value is there for most.

It’s more of a last resort redemption option, if you’re truly unable to get value elsewhere. In fairness, that might just be the direction the program is headed. While Bonvoy points have been significantly devalued over the years for hotel redemptions, the mileage conversion options have remained mostly consistent.

While the ability to convert Marriott points into airline miles has been around for a long time, we’re increasingly seeing two-way transfers, where you can convert airline miles into Marriott points.

The idea behind this is great — maybe someone has a lot of airline miles, but really wants to redeem for a hotel stay. Is this a good deal, though? Unfortunately the answer is almost always “no.”

Currently the below programs let you convert airline miles to Marriott Bonvoy, with both the transfer ratios and any exceptions listed.

While I suppose more flexibility is always a good thing, these transfers are almost never worth it. As a reminder, I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, and you’re getting at most one Bonvoy point per airline mile.

If you have the same valuation I do, at a 1:1 transfer ratio you’re getting up to 0.7 cents per mile, while at a 2:1 transfer ratio, you’re getting up to 0.35 cents per mile. That’s not a rate at which I’d be happy cashing in miles.

It’s possible to convert Marriott points into airline miles with over three dozen programs. While this is the best hotel points to airline miles transfer ratio that you’ll find with any program, it’s still not how I’d choose to redeem my Bonvoy points.

Yes, I appreciate the “insurance” that this redemption option provides, since it essentially creates a floor value for Bonvoy points. However, Bonvoy points are hard to efficiently earn through anything other than hotel stays, so I prefer to save them for hotel stays. I’d rather convert credit card points currencies into airline miles.

Where do you stand on the value of Marriott Bonvoy airline mileage transfers? Have you ever redeemed Bonvoy points this way?

ND’s point is the key one IMO. With Bonvoy award pricing all over the place, a lot of redemptions now come in well under 0.7 cents, so the miles route isn’t the last resort it used to be. United at 60K for 30K with that extra bonus is the standout. Randy’s instant datapoint is a nice surprise vs the usual 2 to 5 days. FWIW the flip side of keeping points for hotels is checking what cash would cost first. Google Hotels gives a quick baseline. The same Marriott can price diff depending on which country you search from as inventory and rates vary by market. A free tool like Arbitrica checks it from roughly 195 countries and finds the lowest price in the world. If that cash rate is low, moving the points to miles starts to look smart

Generally I agree with this article. The points can be used with Marriott for better value but if you need to just top off for an airline redemption it may be worth doing. Buying Marriott points could be of good value when there is a 50% or 75% bonus offer.

If one looks at Bonvoy point redemption for award stays these days, unfortunately the average appears well below $.007 USD, maybe somewhere between $.004-$.006. Bonvoy-> Airline Transfers are increasingly becoming a more competitive redemption option. Not all FFPs are created equal, just like not all previously referenced Bonvoy transfer partners are equal. There are some good opportunities. Actually, Bonvoy points transferring to the airline FFP of my choice(s) are now my preferred way to use my Bonvoy points.

In terms of converting Marriott points to United miles, neither Marriott nor United should be seen as a “savings bank” for loyalty credits. I move some Marriott points to United miles (enough to get the special bonus) when (1) my supply of United miles is running “low” and I need same for flight(s) in the not too distant future and (2) one of the special bonuses is currently in effect. In general, over the last 30 years I've been accumulating airline miles (remember TWA?) and hotel points (remember SPG?), I've never seen the value of these miles and points increase over time! Devaluations and additional charges (such as so-called “destination fees” or “resort fees”) as well as no real redemption chart for Marriott points hardly make those Marriott points any type of stable currency. For that matter, airline miles are not really any better. 😀 As an aside, the best airline loyalty redemption value I ever got was in 1985 when I redeemed 90,000 miles on TWA for a open-jaw, round trip for two, first class, from SFO to CAI, returning TLV to SFO.

Converting Bonvoy points to airline miles is a good deal when you have a lot of them and no longer stay at Marriotts because other hotel programs provide more value.

Here in New York City, it's one of the absolute best weekends of the year: Halloween and the New York City Marathon. Last year, a team of TPG staff came out to the race to cheer me on while I ran, which was a very caring way for my work family to spend their free time.

And speaking of free time, Club Med recently commissioned a study of 2,000 Americans and Canadians to find how people actually feel about their free time — and what they do with it. One statistic in the report really resonated with me: 81% of North Americans miss the sense of wonder they had as kids more than the free time they had then.

So this week I'm sharing some hotel news that speaks to that sense of wonder we all apparently long for, like a chic new hotel at the very tip of Africa to a revamped, sky-high cocktail bar with views of the iconic Las Vegas strip.

Here's the hotel news you need to know about.

One of the most anticipated hotel openings of the year, The Cape Town Edition, is now open. Set on the V&A Waterfront, the stylish hotel is the brand's first outpost in Africa. At the property, guests can stay in one of 142 rooms and suites, enjoy art and design selected as "a reflection of Africa's creative landscape," and eat at numerous dining and bar outlets. And for people like me who love to relax, the hotel has a spa.

In November, New York's celebrity-loved hotel The Mark is getting its first spa: The Mark Wellness & Longevity Spa by Augustinus Bader. The Mark is already The Met Gala's fashion hot spot, plus home to caviar-loaded baked potatoes at Caviar Kaspia, so it only makes sense to have a luxe spa. The spa, the first Augustinus Bader-branded location in the U.S., will feature three treatment rooms, state-of-the-art and science-backed treatments, plus in-room massage services. The opening comes hot on the heels of The Mark's recent room updates, making the hotel as fresh — and relaxing — as ever.

In 2024, Marriott took over the former Delano hotel at Mandalay Bay and converted it into the W Las Vegas. Now, two years later, the W brand is really making the hotel its own with the relaunch of Skyfall Rooftop Bar & Lounge. Situated on the 64th floor and offering panoramic views of Sin City, Rockwell Group recreated the space with bold interiors accenting the floor-to-ceiling windows. In the hotel's lobby, the Living Room bar has also been reimagined.

"Together, these spaces sophisticatedly blend glamour, futuristic energy, and immersive nightlife to capture the true spirit of Las Vegas while embodying the bold, playful quality signature to a W hotel," W Las Vegas said in a statement shared with TPG.

Going back to how we spend our free time, Club Med's report also shared that 88% of people experienced at least one positive impact the last time they challenged themselves to try something new. If you want to feel that positive impact, it might be time to go ... to Delaware.

Hotel Du Pont in Wilmington has launched the Equestrian Escape Package, which comes with equestrian-centric loaner pieces, like riding boots and jackets, from The Frye Company; a private riding lesson at the 200-acre Carousel Park Equestrian Center; and a gourmet picnic from the hotel's Le Cavalier French brasserie.

We've all been patiently waiting for the 69-room Thompson Rome, the first property from the brand in Italy, to open its doors. Well, that day has finally come. The hotel, right near Piazza Venezia and other major attractions, features restored elements from the hotel's original building, a contemporary Mediterranean restaurant, a rooftop cocktail bar and a lobby bar.

#6230. American Resumes Service to Haiti After Two-Year Pause

American Airlines on Sunday restarted service to Haiti after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince.

The carrier is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haitien, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

The inaugural flight on Sunday was staffed by an all-Haitian, Creole-speaking crew, the airline said.

“The connection between the United States and Haiti is incredibly meaningful, which is especially true in South Florida,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “We know the critical role air service plays in linking countries and communities, so we’re beyond proud to reinstate such a consequential connection for so many.”

U.S. airlines suspended service to and from Haiti in 2024 amid a rise in gang violence. Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince was temporarily closed after bullets struck aircraft taxiing on the tarmac.

So far, American is the only U.S.-based carrier to have resumed service to the country.

#6229. How To Redeem Alaska Atmos Rewards Points: Rules, Fees, & Sweet Spots

Alaska Atmos Rewards (formerly Alaska Mileage Plan) has long been a favorite points currency among miles & points geeks, given the carrier’s unique array of airline partners, generous stopover policy, and attractive redemption rates.

In this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at how to redeem Atmos Rewards points. How do you earn Atmos Rewards points, what are the rules around redeeming them, and what are the best uses?

There are several different ways to go about earning Alaska Atmos Rewards points, from credit cards, to outright buying points, to transferring them from other cards.

The Atmos Rewards program has three co-branded credit cards, issued by Bank of America, and they all have excellent welcome bonuses with limited eligibility restrictions:

What’s so great is that you can potentially qualify for all of these cards, so that’s an opportunity to earn lots of points. For example, I picked up both the Atmos Rewards Summit Card and Atmos Rewards Business Card on the same day.

The Atmos Rewards program is transfer partners with Bilt Rewards, so you can transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This could be a great reason to pick up one of Bilt’s credit cards, with options including the Bilt Blue Card (learn more), Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

You can even pay rent with an Atmos Rewards card and earn 3x points while paying a 3% fee, which could be a useful deal, especially if you’re pursuing elite status.

The program also partners with Marriott Bonvoy®, so you can transfer over Marriott points. The ratio is that 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy® Points convert into 25,000 Atmos Rewards points (if you convert in different increments, it’s a 3:1 ratio).

This can be a solid value, and there are lots of credit cards that can earn you Bonvoy points, including the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more).

The Atmos Rewards program is pretty aggressive about selling points, and the program seems to offer promotions on purchased points every couple of months. When we see these offers, you can expect bonuses in the range of 90-110%. This is often an opportunity to acquire Atmos Rewards points for under two cents each.

It doesn’t cost anything to join the Atmos Rewards program, so I generally recommend signing up ahead of time — you have to be a member for at least 10 days in order to take advantage of one of these promotions.

Not only are there great ways to earn Atmos Rewards points either through credit cards or by buying them outright, but Atmos Rewards is also a good program to credit flights to.

For one, Atmos Rewards is the last major US frequent flyer program to give members the option to earn points based on distance flown rather than dollars spent. Atmos Rewards allows mileage earning on a variety of airline partners, ranging from Condor to Cathay Pacific. Atmos Rewards lets you earn points for travel on the following airline partners:

The one thing worth mentioning is that you can only earn Atmos Rewards points on Korean Air, Philippine Airlines, and Starlux Airlines, if you book through Alaska, rather than through one of the partners.

Alaska Atmos Rewards has some great redemption opportunities, though there are also quite a few rules to be aware of. Let’s cover some of those basics.

Alaska Airlines belongs to the oneworld alliance, though the airline has an array of partners beyond oneworld. It’s possible to redeem Atmos Rewards points for travel on the following airlines:

All Atmos Rewards award redemption partners can be booked online at alaskaair.com. If you have a complicated itinerary or are having issues with the website, you’ll want to call the Atmos Rewards partner award desk, which can be reached at 800-252-7522.

When it comes to redeeming points, Atmos Rewards has three simple award charts that are a combination of zone and distance based.

There’s the Americas award chart, which covers any travel from the United States to anywhere in the Americas, including North America and South America.

Then there’s the Europe, Middle East, and Africa award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and travel within Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

Lastly, there’s the Asia-Pacific award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Asia-Pacific, within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

The most significant thing to understand here is that the “starting at” prices are actually what you’re going to pay if there’s saver level award availability. All partners have the same award pricing assuming there’s saver award availability.

There are a few other important things to mention:

The Atmos Rewards program awards status points for award travel booked through the program. This applies for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, and all other partner airlines.

Just book using Atmos Rewards points and have your Atmos Rewards number on the reservation, and you’ll earn one status point per mile flown, regardless of the class of service (this assumes you select to earn Atmos Rewards points based on distance flown).

This is a massive point of differentiation for the program, and if you ask me, it’s a contributing reason that many American loyalists might want to consider Atmos Rewards.

One of my favorite things about the Atmos Rewards program is that you are allowed a stopover on a one-way award ticket when traveling between regions. This is possible regardless of which partner you redeem with.

So if you book a roundtrip as two one-ways, this means you can potentially get two stopovers on a roundtrip ticket. To book a ticket online with a stopover, just use the multi-city function, and you can search each portion of the ticket individually.

Now, admittedly with the program being distance based, you are in some cases potentially paying more for itineraries with stopovers, but it’s still a useful feature.

On the surface, Atmos Rewards should have access to the same award availability as other partner airlines do, though in some cases Atmos Rewards inexplicably doesn’t have access to the same space. Most commonly:

This won’t be consistent, but it is something to be aware of, and it sure can be frustrating. There’s generally not any way to get around this.

When searching award availability on some partner airlines, you may see award pricing that’s way above what the chart suggests. This includes for some flights on Aer Lingus, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, and Starlux Airlines. In those situations, what’s happening is that there’s no saver level award availability, but Atmos Rewards has negotiated to have more award availability at a higher cost.

I know this kind of pricing frustrates some people and makes them think the program doesn’t offer good value. However, in these situations, other partner airlines simply wouldn’t have access to the award space. So I wouldn’t view it as a negative, but rather just as an opportunity you probably don’t want to take advantage of.

Atmos Rewards blocks many many partner awards within 72 hours of departure. I’ve been told that this policy won’t stick around, though I don’t have a timeline for when it will change, and it continues to be live. It’s certainly something to be aware of when it comes to last minute redemption opportunities.

Furthermore, Atmos Rewards doesn’t have access to any nonstop domestic American awards at the saver level within six days of departure. Don’t expect this to change, as it’s presumably a commercial decision on American’s part.

There are a couple of fees associated with redeeming Atmos Rewards points:

Atmos Rewards no longer has any change or cancelation fees for award tickets, which gives you lots of flexibility to speculatively lock in awards, or even change them if a better routing opens up. The only exception is that the $20 partner award booking fee can’t be refunded.

Atmos Rewards passes on carrier imposed surcharges (often referred to as fuel surcharges) for travel on some partner airlines. Specifically, these apply for travel on British Airways, Hainan Airlines, and Icelandair. Fortunately they don’t apply for travel on other partner airlines.

Atmos Rewards doesn’t allow award tickets to be placed on hold. To book an Atmos Rewards award ticket you need to have sufficient points in your account, though you can always cancel it for free.

Atmos Rewards points don’t expire. However, if you don’t have any account activity for over two years, your account may be locked for security reasons, and your points may be accessed by contacting Atmos Rewards and verifying personal details.

We all have different travel goals, so there’s never going to be a one size fits all answer as to what the best use of points is. Broadly speaking, my favorite way to redeem points is for aspirational redemptions in first and business class, since that’s where you’ll get the most outsized value.

However, nowadays I’d argue that the redemption sweet spot with Atmos Rewards is largely for shorter awards, given the distance based pricing. In some way, the Atmos Rewards award charts are almost a competitor to British Airways Club, in terms of the great value of short haul redemptions. Since you can redeem Atmos Rewards points for flights globally, I figured the best way to share some sweet spots would just be to take a look at each award chart individually.

Before I do, let me acknowledge a new reality of the miles & points hobby. The reality is that airlines are getting savvier when it comes to how they release award space, and in many cases, they open fewer award seats to members of partner frequent flyer programs. This is beyond any carrier’s control, but it does limit the arbitrage opportunities by using great frequent flyer programs.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for the Americas, which applies exclusively if traveling within the Americas (including North and South America).

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Honestly, I think this is the chart with the most consistently good pricing, whether traveling short haul or long haul. So if you can find award availability within the Americas, you should be pretty happy with the pricing. I redeem Atmos Rewards points constantly for travel on American, as it’s a way to get a good deal on domestic flights, especially in a premium cabin. It might not be the most aspirational thing on earth, but it sure is practical.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Europe, Middle East, and Africa, which applies if traveling within or between any of those regions, and also applies if traveling between the Americas and any of those regions.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Asia-Pacific, which applies if traveling within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and any other regions. Note that Asia includes the Indian subcontinent, since some other award charts put that in the same region as the Middle East.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Alaska Atmos Rewards is one of the most useful programs for redeeming points. Given the zone and distance based award chart, you’ll generally find the best value with the program for shorter distance itineraries, where pricing can be very attractive.

I’d say Atmos Rewards is a program that has become practical more than aspirational, and that’s something that I don’t mind, at least at this point in history. It’s not like there are many Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, or Qantas, ultra long haul first class awards to snag, so we’re not missing out on that much.

Atmos Rewards is my go-to program for most awards covering a distance of up to 1,500 miles, give or take.

What’s your favorite use of Alaska Atmos Rewards points?

#6227. United Airlines CEO Says American Airlines Promised Him Their Top Job—Then Fired Him

Scott Kirby says former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker took him to dinner, gave him a date when he’d retire, and promised him the CEO job. Three months later, Parker changed his mind and fired him. American wound up paying about $13 million to send its president to United Airlines, where he became CEO before Parker finally left American’s top job. And this year Kirby tried to buy the airline that had fired him. In a new interview he explains why he’s described his 2016 dismissal as a betrayal: “Three months before I got fired, Doug took me to dinner, down in the Design District, to say he was going to retire on a certain date, and I would be CEO on that date,” he said. “One day he walks in, stands in the doorway, and says ‘I’ve changed my mind, and you and I can’t work together anymore.’” That’s a much more specific account of what I’ve written about for years, including earlier this month. My read has always been that Parker wanted more time at the top. Kirby was ready to be CEO and wasn’t going to wait indefinitely. Robert Isom would stick around. American’s explanation was that it couldn’t retain all three executives. But Parker controlled which two would remain, and he kept himself. Isom took Kirby’s president title and waited until 2022 to become CEO. Kirby took the president job at United and became its CEO in May 2020. (The United transition was likely delayed by the April 2017 David Dao passenger dragging incident, because that delayed Oscar Munoz from taking on the Chairman’s role.) According to Kirby, Parker had already agreed to make way for him. This wasn’t just a subordinate getting impatient. I’ve also written about an episode from 2020, when Parker was embracing Black Lives Matter following George Floyd’s killing and thinking about his legacy. The staffer working on Parker’s legacy suggested he relinquish the chairman title while remaining CEO, with a Black board member becoming chair. They were subsequently fired. American compounded the decision by paying Kirby severance. There was no non-compete. Parker and the board never felt that a good investment, so instead they financed an executive’s departure to a competitor that could use his knowledge of their business. Kirby says he was “extremely motivated to prove something.” Kirby does attribute being fired to much of his sucess today. “I’m a better CEO of United than I would have been CEO of American. There were things, particularly about how to bring people along. … I don’t know if I would have learned them. I might not have if I’d have just stayed at American and never had to go through that.” Kirby helped run American during its early post-merger years. He owns much of that record, cutting first class meals in 2014, selecting seats with tighter pitch and no entertainment screens for the domestic fleet. No major U.S. airline has improved more over the past decade than United. Parker’s decision gave United someone who knew American’s weaknesses, wanted to beat them, and says he learned from the experience of being pushed out. Kirby says he’s reconciled with Parker, and considers Isom a friend. But Parker’s American descended but Kirby’s United improved, and that’s evident in the financial results of the two airlines. Topics on this pageAmerican AirlinesDoug ParkerScott KirbyUnited Airlines2017 United Express passenger removalBlack Lives MatterGeorge FloydOscar MunozRobert Isom+5 more More From View from the Wing

American wound up paying about $13 million to send its president to United Airlines, where he became CEO before Parker finally left American’s top job. And this year Kirby tried to buy the airline that had fired him.

In a new interview he explains why he’s described his 2016 dismissal as a betrayal:

“Three months before I got fired, Doug took me to dinner, down in the Design District, to say he was going to retire on a certain date, and I would be CEO on that date,” he said. “One day he walks in, stands in the doorway, and says ‘I’ve changed my mind, and you and I can’t work together anymore.’”

That’s a much more specific account of what I’ve written about for years, including earlier this month. My read has always been that Parker wanted more time at the top. Kirby was ready to be CEO and wasn’t going to wait indefinitely. Robert Isom would stick around.

American’s explanation was that it couldn’t retain all three executives. But Parker controlled which two would remain, and he kept himself. Isom took Kirby’s president title and waited until 2022 to become CEO. Kirby took the president job at United and became its CEO in May 2020. (The United transition was likely delayed by the April 2017 David Dao passenger dragging incident, because that delayed Oscar Munoz from taking on the Chairman’s role.)

According to Kirby, Parker had already agreed to make way for him. This wasn’t just a subordinate getting impatient.

I’ve also written about an episode from 2020, when Parker was embracing Black Lives Matter following George Floyd’s killing and thinking about his legacy. The staffer working on Parker’s legacy suggested he relinquish the chairman title while remaining CEO, with a Black board member becoming chair. They were subsequently fired.

American compounded the decision by paying Kirby severance. There was no non-compete. Parker and the board never felt that a good investment, so instead they financed an executive’s departure to a competitor that could use his knowledge of their business. Kirby says he was “extremely motivated to prove something.” Kirby does attribute being fired to much of his sucess today.

“I’m a better CEO of United than I would have been CEO of American. There were things, particularly about how to bring people along. … I don’t know if I would have learned them. I might not have if I’d have just stayed at American and never had to go through that.”

Kirby helped run American during its early post-merger years. He owns much of that record, cutting first class meals in 2014, selecting seats with tighter pitch and no entertainment screens for the domestic fleet.

No major U.S. airline has improved more over the past decade than United. Parker’s decision gave United someone who knew American’s weaknesses, wanted to beat them, and says he learned from the experience of being pushed out.

Kirby says he’s reconciled with Parker, and considers Isom a friend. But Parker’s American descended but Kirby’s United improved, and that’s evident in the financial results of the two airlines.

#6226. Singapore Airlines’ New First & Business Class Cabins Will Be Unveiled This Week

In November 2024, Singapore Airlines announced a huge investment into its premium passenger experience, which will see the introduction of all-new cabin products, plus the expansion of first class. These cabins will be retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s, and will also be available on newly delivered Boeing 777-9s in the future.

The product was initially supposed to roll out as of the spring of 2026, though as is all too common nowadays, the project was delayed due to supply chain constraints, etc. The good news is that the wait is almost over — the new product will be unveiled on Friday, November 6, 2026, with an entry into service planned for the first quarter of 2027. Let’s recap all the details we know as of now.

Singapore Airlines will be investing 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

With this project, we can expect changes across cabins. We’ll see first class added to the carrier’s ultra long range A350s, an all-new business class product, refreshes to premium economy and economy, plus an updated inflight entertainment system and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

How will the layouts of these jets change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines will be introducing new first and business class products. This isn’t just some new interim product, but rather this is intended to be the carrier’s new premium product in the long run. The same seats that are being installed on the Airbus A350-900s will also be installed on the carrier’s Boeing 777-9s, so these are very much “flagship” cabins.

Singapore Airlines initially intended to debut new premium cabins on its 777-9s, which were first supposed to be delivered in 2020. However, those have now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest. So clearly Singapore Airlines decided that it’s finally time to introduce new cabins, even if the 777-9 keeps getting delayed.

Singapore Airlines will introduce a new first class product on its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, which operate the world’s longest flights. This same product will be available on 777-9s in the future, but won’t be available on standard A350-900s. Furthermore, there are no plans to retrofit existing 777s with this product. A350s will have four of these seats, while 777s will have six of these seats.

Below is the first teaser picture of Singapore Airlines’ new first class.

Currently Singapore Airlines only has first class on its A380s and 777-300ERs, so it’s cool to see this product expand.

Official details about the new first class are limited, other than that it’s “designed with increasingly discerning travellers in mind,” and that the first class seats “promise to deliver an unparalleled in-flight experience.”

We have reason to believe that the new cabin will be in a 1-2-1 layout. Why? Well, Singapore Airlines filed a patent some time back, clearly for the carrier’s new first class product. The patent is for the 777-9, where the airline will have a first class cabin with six seats.

The plan seems to be to have individual suites along the windows, plus a double suite in the center. However, the center suite can be used by either one or two people, so if people are traveling separately, there’s a partition that can go up.

As you can see, there’s a bit of staggering with the cabin, to maximize the width of the suite, as the aisle curves a bit.

This looks like a very nice product, though to be perfectly honest, it doesn’t look like anything revolutionary. Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates. Admittedly the flexibility of the double suite in the middle is great for those traveling with someone, since that’s not something that was really considered with the new Japan Airlines and Emirates products.

For that matter, we have reason to believe that Cathay Pacific may offer the world’s best first class on its 777-9s, as it could very well be in a 1-1 configuration.

This is super exciting. Singapore Airlines is one of the best airlines in the world, with incredible service, food, drinks, and more. However, at this point the carrier’s business class hard product isn’t really cutting edge anymore.

With details being so limited, all we can do is speculate as of now. So I have a few thoughts:

In late 2024, when this project was first announced, Singapore Airlines shared the following timeline for debuting the new first and business class seats:

Unfortunately that timeline didn’t stick. Several months ago we learned how the first retrofitted aircraft wouldn’t enter service until the first quarter of 2027, best case scenario, with the expectation being that some long range A350s would be reconfigured before the first ultra long range A350 gets a makeover.

The revised timeline reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of one of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

So, is that still the timeline we’re looking at? It would appear so. Singapore Airlines has confirmed on social media that it will unveiling its all new products on Friday, November 6, 2026.

From the first sketch to the final detail, discover how the new Singapore Airlines travel experience comes together across every cabin class and every part of the journey.Unveiling on 6 November 2026. pic.twitter.com/dTML7QmOXe

This announcement is actually being marketed as being about more than just seats, as it’s described as “the new Singapore Airlines travel experience,” and we’ll learn how it “comes together across every class and every part of the journey.” We’ve already seen the airline tease details of a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins, so presumably this will all come together to form the new experience.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines plans to introduce all-new cabins on its Airbus A350-900s, which will also eventually be installed on Boeing 777-9s. Most exciting is an improved new business class product, which is long overdue. Singapore Airlines will also be adding first class to its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, with a boutique cabin having just four seats.

While this product was supposed to enter service as of the second quarter of 2026, the timeline has been pushed back to the first quarter of 2027, due to supply chain constraints and certification issues… a familiar story! The expectation is that the new cabins will be unveiled this week, on November 6, 2026. I’m mighty curious to learn the details, so I’m happy that the wait is finally (almost) over.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ plans to introduce new long haul cabins?
