“Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates.” Aren’t those the only 2 that have that? Ignoring the eff-up that is LH and LX’s new first class products…

This has the potential to be a massive improvement. I shifted all my SIN-US flying to United Polaris Studio as it is so much more comfortable, but having SQ soft product would be welcome for that long of a flight.

Tbh hard product is plateauing across the board. Beyond getting your own private bedroom like The Residence or something, there's only so much space someone can utilize on a flight. If it's already spacious enough to sleep, eat, and relax in, every incremental sqft of space is less and less useful. While they get a lot of positive PR for their A380 Suites, the soft product has always been what makes SQ standout because SQ otherwise has a very average hard product in business class.

"The expectation is that the new cabins will be unveiled in November 2026. I’m mighty curious to learn the details, so I guess we just have to be patient for a couple more months!" You mean a few more months or about 12 weeks ;) Once again, you have to appreciate the investment & effort for Singapore to come up with a bespoke product with the likes of Cathay, ANA, Qatar, Emirates and not just an off the shelf seat and apply your own CMF; they seem to have put in effort on the exterior shell of the seat as well as the carpeting. As they've worked with Jamco before, is it possible this could be based on the Quest platform? I recall someone basing this product off off the Jamco Quest.

This is long-overdue. If SQ goes with Safran Unity, even if they customize it, that would be a major upgrade from the current all-or-nothing lie-flat that they have now on the world's longest flight (a359-ULR). If we need to wait a little longer (November 2026, etc.) for more updates, that's fine.

I've kept the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card for several years now because it's been my favorite premium travel credit card for many reasons.

In all that time, I never once bothered to activate one of its perks: the complimentary Hertz President's Circle status.

Related: The best rental car loyalty programs in 2026

President's Circle is the top published tier of the Hertz Gold+ loyalty program, and earning it the traditional way means completing 15 rentals or spending $3,000 with Hertz in a calendar year.

The reason I overlooked it is that I rent a car maybe a couple of times a year and usually shop around for the best deal, with little brand loyalty.

But with a full day ahead of me recently to explore the spectacular Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, I wanted to put this elite status to the test to see whether it was a valuable credit card benefit.

President's Circle is the highest published elite tier in Hertz Gold+ Rewards, the rental company's loyalty program, which costs nothing to join. It sits above the entry-level Gold tier and the mid-tier Five Star elite status.

It's worth remembering that Ultimate Choice is available only at select Hertz airport locations, and you'll need to reserve a midsize or larger vehicle. The guaranteed upgrade requires a reservation made at least 48 hours in advance at a participating location, is capped at a full-size vehicle and does not apply to Manager's Special rentals or certain premium vehicle collections.

Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: Hitting the road on your vacation? Everything you need to know about rental car elite status

The following premium credit cards offer complimentary President's Circle status:

Related: The best credit cards for rental car elite status

To receive the President's Circle status benefits, it's important to follow the correct booking process, which is not onerous:

As a solo driver, there was no need for me to add a complimentary second driver, and I didn't need to call Hertz in advance, so I couldn't test the dedicated President's Circle line.

I received 1.5 Hertz Gold+ Rewards points per dollar spent on the rental, as advertised, but the real perks I was interested in were the pickup experience and the type of car I received.

When I arrived at the pickup location, my name was on the President's Circle board with a note to "see desk." This was my first Hertz Gold+ rental, and first-time members may need to verify their driver's license and payment card at the Gold desk before they can bypass the counter on subsequent rentals.

Make sure you go to the Five Star/President's Circle desk, rather than the main building desk. At larger locations like Denver International Airport (DEN), where I was, these are two separate buildings.

Being unsure, I went to the main building desk and had an utterly bizarre interaction with the staff there, who found my reservation, insisted my President's Circle status had expired, despite me only activating it a month earlier, refused to activate it and insisted that if I reactivated myself, I would have to cancel the booking and rebook if I wanted any status benefits, which would likely be much more expensive to do last minute. This is despite my showing them my live Hertz account, including the booking confirmation, and my President's Circle status level was clearly visible.

Fortunately, I sought a second opinion at the Five Star and President's Circle desk, where the staff could not have been more helpful, found my reservation, could immediately see my President's Circle status and had me on my way to the President's Circle lot within minutes.

This was the highlight of the day. More than 50 cars were waiting in the President's Circle section. I don't pretend to be an expert on cars (I don't currently own one), so I just chose the one that looked the most luxurious.

Walking up and down the rows and picking out exactly what I wanted to drive was great fun, and I settled on a shiny new 2026 Wrangler Sahara 4WD with just a few thousand miles on the clock, which I thought would be awesome for tackling the winding roads of the Rocky Mountain National Park.

Having originally booked a midsize-category Kia K4, driving off the lot in a Jeep Wrangler Sahara sure felt like a superior car, but I subsequently checked the sticker price for each car, new. At more than twice the Kia's retail price, the Jeep was definitely an upgrade.

With the keys already inside, I drove my chosen car to the exit, showed the attendant my receipt with the large "PC" status written on it and headed out the exit to the mountains.

Related: Delta adds Hertz status for all Medallion elites, revamps earning structure for rentals

After years of ignoring the Hertz President’s Circle status that comes with my Venture X card, I’m a little sheepish about not using it sooner.

Despite the initial confusion at the main counter, Hertz ultimately delivered on the status benefits I valued most, and for someone who doesn't know much about cars, I felt like a television game show winner, wandering the lot and choosing any car I wished.

The rental wasn't the cheapest from any agency in the area, so if an upgrade doesn't interest you, you still may wish to shop around. Ultimate Choice is available only at certain locations, so a downtown Hertz branch may not have a President's Circle section at all.

It’s probably not a perk I’d open a new credit card for on its own, but if you already hold one of the cards above, submitting the enrollment only takes a few minutes, and it turned what would have been a forgettable rental into one of the highlights of my trip. For special occasions like exploring one of the country's best national parks, I would definitely give my President's Circle status a spin again.

#6224. Leaked Southwest 737 MAX 7 Plan Targets March 2027 Flights—150 Seats, Starlink And Bigger Overhead Bins

Southwest Airlines plans to start flying passengers on its Boeing 737 MAX 7s in March 2027, according to an internal rollout document shared with me. The aircraft are slated to have 150 Recaro seats, Starlink internet, seat power and bigger overhead bins, much better than the airline’s aging small planes. The document lays out how Southwest expects to get there, starting with deliveries in mid-to-late December. December Deliveries, March Passenger Flights The Boeing 737 MAX 7 received FAA certification on August 3. That followed years of delays, with the approved design incorporating a revised engine anti-ice system and updates to flight controls and pilot alerts. Southwest still has to complete its own operating approvals. Its most recent quarterly filing lays out the training, inspections, documentation and validation flights with FAA personnel that are needed. Mid-to-late December 2026: Southwest expects to begin accepting aircraft from the batch of 27 already built. February 2027: Newly built aircraft begin arriving. Preparation: Configuration, maintenance and other work takes place at Paine Field, Phoenix and Kansas City. Before passenger service: Each prebuilt aircraft gets at least five flights after its preparation work, including a simulated extended-overwater operation lasting more than 3.5 hours. By the end of 2026: The airline intends to put the MAX 7 into published schedules, with passenger flying starting in March 2027. The date is marked subject to change. The plan also calls for regular flying to keep delivered aircraft ready before service begins. It lists “+90 flights” across the fleet for this work, without explaining how those flights overlap with the validation program. Southwest had disclosed the 27 prebuilt aircraft and late-year deliveries. Chief Operating Officer Andrew Watterson had also pointed to a spring break launch. But we now have more specific timing and the work planned between delivery and passenger service. 150 Seats, Starlink And Three Bathrooms Here’s how the planes will be equipped: 150 Recaro seats, with indicators identifying extra legroom seats. Starlink wifi and in-seat power. Larger overhead bins and a refreshed interior. Two exit rows and three lavatories, with two bathrooms at the back. A secondary physical barrier for the flight deck, cockpit power, locks for crew overhead bins, and a prerecorded announcement and music system. Southwest’s cabin design and Recaro seats were announced but this shows more than just a MAX 7 seat map. The 150-seat count is slightly more than in Southwest’s 2024 investor presentation which had 148 seats, 48 extra legroom seats and 100 standard seats with most rows at 34 and 31 inches of pitch. There’s a strong reason to stop at 150 seats. They need one flight attendant per 50 passenger seats. 151 seats would require an additional flight attendant. Three lavatories is actually an improvement over the two on Southwest’s 737-700s. Starlink is amazing and Southwest plans to install it quickly. I’ve written about avoiding Southwest because unreliable internet meant losing productive hours. They’ve committed to fleet-wide Starlink by fall 2027. The MAX 7 Has Two Jobs Southwest’s October 22 order position works out to 240 undelivered MAX 7s and 201 undelivered MAX 8s, plus 130 options, under contracts extending through 2031. That subtracts 46 MAX 8s already received from the totals in the filing. Those orders support both replacement and growth. But the immediate fleet plan is overwhelmingly replacement: Southwest expects 67 deliveries and roughly 60 retirements this year. They still had 271 Boeing 737-700s at September 30, averaging 20 years old. Replacing a current 137-seat 737-700 with a 150-seat MAX 7 adds 13 seats, about 9.5%. The larger MAX 8 can spread costs across more passengers when demand supports it; the MAX 7 leaves fewer seats to fill on thinner routes. In his August interview on The Air Show, Watterson said the first 27 MAX 7s would take over the extended overwater role of 28 older 737-800s. Those older aircraft would keep flying with a less demanding maintenance program. Watterson identified Burbank–Honolulu, hot-weather departures from Phoenix and Las Vegas to Hawaii, and interisland flying as uses. A Better Cabin Still Leaves A Premium Seat Gap I’ve argued that Southwest’s changes follow from one another. Once they gave up much of what made the airline different, they needed more of the products that make customers willing to pay competitors a premium. Better wifi, power and a modern cabin help. Larger bins also help accommodate the carry-ons that bag fees encourage passengers to bring onboard. The MAX 7 preserves something from the old Southwest, too: an aircraft in the same 737 family that can serve routes without needing the demand for a larger plane. It improves their options below 175 seats. A 150-seat jet still doesn’t solve the small-community feeder problem I’ve raised several times, including in discussing a potential long haul network. But they’re rolling out new planes, with new seats, and still not putting in first class. They’ll soon be the only major U.S. airline without it – even Frontier and Allegiant will have it! If there was a time to do it you’d think it would be now. Frontier is actually launching its first class on March 5, 2027 – right when Southwest plans to start flying these planes. If there was a time to do it you’d think it would be now. Frontier is actually launching its first class on March 5, 2027 – right when Southwest plans to start flying these planes. Southwest’s October 22 order position works out to 240 undelivered MAX 7s and 201 undelivered MAX 8s, plus 130 options, under contracts extending through 2031. That subtracts 46 MAX 8s already received from the totals in the filing.

Those orders support both replacement and growth. But the immediate fleet plan is overwhelmingly replacement: Southwest expects 67 deliveries and roughly 60 retirements this year. They still had 271 Boeing 737-700s at September 30, averaging 20 years old.

Replacing a current 137-seat 737-700 with a 150-seat MAX 7 adds 13 seats, about 9.5%. The larger MAX 8 can spread costs across more passengers when demand supports it; the MAX 7 leaves fewer seats to fill on thinner routes.

In his August interview on The Air Show, Watterson said the first 27 MAX 7s would take over the extended overwater role of 28 older 737-800s. Those older aircraft would keep flying with a less demanding maintenance program. Watterson identified Burbank–Honolulu, hot-weather departures from Phoenix and Las Vegas to Hawaii, and interisland flying as uses.

I’ve argued that Southwest’s changes follow from one another. Once they gave up much of what made the airline different, they needed more of the products that make customers willing to pay competitors a premium. Better wifi, power and a modern cabin help. Larger bins also help accommodate the carry-ons that bag fees encourage passengers to bring onboard. The MAX 7 preserves something from the old Southwest, too: an aircraft in the same 737 family that can serve routes without needing the demand for a larger plane. It improves their options below 175 seats. A 150-seat jet still doesn’t solve the small-community feeder problem I’ve raised several times, including in discussing a potential long haul network. But they’re rolling out new planes, with new seats, and still not putting in first class. They’ll soon be the only major U.S. airline without it – even Frontier and Allegiant will have it! If there was a time to do it you’d think it would be now. Frontier is actually launching its first class on March 5, 2027 – right when Southwest plans to start flying these planes.
